The default element masses come from the [CIAAW-based element data](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/element_data.hpp). A standard atomic weight represents a reference isotopic composition; it is not necessarily the mass of one particular isotope. An isotope has the same number of protons but a different neutron count.

The string interface recognizes isotope forms such as `"N15"` and `"C13"`, as well as `"D"` and `"T"` for hydrogen isotopes. For example, `Structure.get_default_atomic_mass("N15")` uses the stored nitrogen-15 mass, while its element identity remains nitrogen. One may also explicitly supply the `masses` array in atomic mass units. The [stored isotope records](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/element_data.cpp) and tests distinguish these values from standard atomic weights.

At the fixed-nucleus, nonrelativistic electronic level we are using, changing isotope mass while holding nuclear charges and positions fixed does not change the electronic Coulomb Hamiltonian. Mass matters when we later discuss nuclear vibration, mass-weighted Hessians, and dynamics. It should still be preserved as input provenance.

The data class permits custom floating-point nuclear charges, and [data tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_structure_comprehensive.cpp) demonstrate that storage capability. The native molecular adapter is narrower: its charge conversion requires finite, nonnegative, integral values within a tolerance of \(10^{-12}\). A data container accepting fractional charges does not imply the SCF backend implements a fractional-nucleus model. The PySCF structural conversion is based on element labels, so it should not be assumed to preserve arbitrary custom nuclear-charge fields either.

XYZ is a deliberately lossy interchange representation here. `to_xyz()` emits ordinary element symbols and six decimal places in Ångstrom. It does not export a separate custom-mass or custom-nuclear-charge array; an isotope stored as nitrogen plus a special mass will be printed as `N`. Consequently, an XYZ round trip should not be used as proof that all metadata or full coordinate precision survived. Structured serialization is the later provenance solution.

## A basis set is a vocabulary for orbital shapes

Knowing where the nuclei are still leaves infinitely many possible functions of electron position. A **basis set** chooses a finite vocabulary of functions centered on those nuclei. The molecular orbital labeled \(p\) is expanded as

\[
\phi_p(\mathbf r)=\sum_{\mu=1}^{K} C_{\mu p}\chi_\mu(\mathbf r).
\]

\(\mathbf r\) is an electron position, \(\chi_\mu\) is basis function number \(\mu\), \(K\) is the basis-function count, and \(C_{\mu p}\) is a molecular-orbital coefficient. These coefficients are optimized by SCF. They are not the determinant amplitudes from Lesson 2, nor the contraction coefficients used to define a basis function itself.

Most of this repository’s molecular machinery uses **Gaussian-type orbitals**. A Cartesian primitive centered at \(\mathbf R_A=(X_A,Y_A,Z_A)\) has the schematic form

\[
g(\mathbf r)=\mathcal N
 (x-X_A)^a(y-Y_A)^b(z-Z_A)^c
 e^{-\alpha |\mathbf r-\mathbf R_A|^2}.
\]

\(a,b,c\) are nonnegative integers specifying the angular polynomial, \(\alpha>0\) is an exponent, and \(\mathcal N\) is a normalization factor. A large exponent makes a tight function near the nucleus; a small exponent makes a diffuse function reaching farther out. The total angular momentum label is \(\ell=a+b+c\): s, p, d, f correspond to \(\ell=0,1,2,3\).

Gaussians are computationally useful because products and integrals involving them have efficient algebraic recurrences. One Gaussian is usually a poor imitation of the radial shape of an atomic orbital, especially near the nuclear cusp and far from the nucleus. A **contraction** combines several primitives with fixed weights:

\[
\chi_\mu(\mathbf r)=\sum_k d_{k\mu}g_k(\mathbf r).
\]

The \(d_{k\mu}\) values define the basis, while the separate \(C_{\mu p}\) values define the molecular orbitals in that basis. More primitives inside one contraction do not automatically mean more independently adjustable molecular-orbital coefficients.

The actual hydrogen STO-3G record in the [distributed archive](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/resources/compressed/sto-3g.tar.gz) has exponents approximately 3.425250914, 0.6239137298, and 0.1688554040, with raw contraction coefficients 0.1543289673, 0.5353281423, and 0.4446345422. These are source data, not a fitted result from this session. The three primitives form **one s basis function on hydrogen**, not three independent orbitals. “STO-3G” refers to a three-Gaussian approximation to a Slater-type orbital shape.

## Shells make the representation concrete

A `Shell` groups functions sharing an atom, angular momentum, and primitive/contraction data. A p shell has three angular orientations. A basis can contain several separate p shells with different radial flexibility; these are not three electrons placed in a shell.

The [actual `Shell` definition](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/basis_set.hpp) stores `atom_index`, `orbital_type`, `exponents`, `coefficients`, and optional ECP radial powers. It checks matching exponent/coefficient lengths; ECP radial-power arrays must have compatible length too. The public `OrbitalType` labels extend through i, or \(\ell=6\), with `UL` reserved for an ECP local-potential label. Such an enumeration does not promise that every compiled integral engine supports every calculation for every listed element and angular momentum.

The stored contraction coefficients are **raw, unnormalized** coefficients. Integral/backend conversion handles the required normalization conventions. Normalizing the list of coefficients as if it were a probability vector would be wrong: overlapping primitive functions must be normalized through their overlap integrals, not by dividing by the Euclidean length of the coefficient list. Individual contraction coefficients may legitimately be negative.

For example, an instructional explicit construction using those hydrogen parameters is:

```python
import numpy as np
from qdk_chemistry.data import AOType, BasisSet, OrbitalType, Shell, Structure

hydrogen = Structure(np.array([[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]]), ["H"])
h_shell = Shell(
    0, OrbitalType.S,
    np.array([3.425250914, 0.6239137298, 0.1688554040]),
    np.array([0.1543289673, 0.5353281423, 0.4446345422]),
)
explicit_basis = BasisSet(
    BasisSet.custom_name, [h_shell], hydrogen, AOType.Spherical,
)
```

This demonstrates the representation, not a nitrogen model and not an executed hydrogen calculation. `Shell` is a construction record with writable fields in its binding; assembling it is different from modifying a completed scientific `BasisSet`. An actual custom basis requires physically appropriate positive exponents, supported angular momenta, matching geometry, and tested normalization/order conventions. The container’s structural validation is not an automatic basis-design service.

There are two angular-function choices. **Spherical** shells use \(2\ell+1\) functions; **Cartesian** shells use \((\ell+1)(\ell+2)/2\). Both give one s and three p functions. A d shell has five spherical versus six Cartesian functions, and an f shell has seven versus ten. This changes the represented function space and counts, not merely a label printed on the result.

`AOType.Spherical` is the named-basis default. Although the data class can represent `AOType.Cartesian`, the current high-level molecular adapters should not be presented as supporting a complete Cartesian workflow. The [native conversion](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/utils.cpp) serializes its internal basis as `pure=true`, and its reverse conversion explicitly rejects a non-pure basis. The [PySCF conversion](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/conversion.py) also retains Cartesian TODOs and constructs spherical output. We use spherical functions consistently instead of relying on unsupported conversion behavior.

## What the familiar basis names buy us

A **minimal basis** supplies roughly the occupied atomic-orbital vocabulary. A **split-valence** basis gives valence orbitals additional radial flexibility. **Double-zeta** and **triple-zeta** indicate increasing radial flexibility in the family’s construction, not an exact universal multiplier of every function count. **Polarization functions** add angular flexibility, allowing the electron distribution to bend away from isolated-atom shapes. **Diffuse functions** add long-range flexibility, particularly relevant to anions, extended density tails, and some excited states. None of these additions changes the number of physical electrons.

Representative resources actually present include `sto-3g`, `6-31g`, `6-31g*`, `cc-pvdz`, `cc-pvtz`, `aug-cc-pvdz`, `def2-svp`, `def2-tzvp`, `ano-rcc`, and `lanl2dz`. The star in the Pople example denotes added polarization; `aug-` denotes diffuse augmentation in the correlation-consistent family. The `cc-pVXZ` family is designed for systematic valence-correlation convergence; selecting it does not itself turn on a correlated solver or freeze core electrons. The def2 family offers a different optimized hierarchy and includes ECP treatment for some heavier elements, not every element.

The [basis/functionals catalog](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/user/comprehensive/basis_functionals.rst) is helpful, but actual availability is determined by resources and supported element combinations. `BasisSet.get_supported_basis_set_names()` inspects the resource archives. `BasisSet.get_supported_elements_for_basis_set("cc-pvdz")` consults `basis_summary.json`. Listing an archive is not a proof that every element is covered, every high-angular-momentum integral is compiled, or an auxiliary fitting basis is suitable as the orbital basis. Archives with names such as `-jkfit` or `-rifit` serve auxiliary representations for integral approximations; they are not interchangeable substitutes for an orbital basis.

There is concrete external provenance here. The repository [credits Basis Set Exchange](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/user/features.rst) as the source of the distributed basis and ECP definitions. BSE and the original basis authors provide exponents, contraction weights, angular-momentum records, and references. QDK Chemistry packages and parses those definitions; it does not invent them by fitting the molecule during SCF. The archived nitrogen cc-pVDZ and cc-pVTZ records retain the original `dunning1989a` reference key.

Ordinary named loading reads installed resources and extracts packaged archives; it is not a live scientific search of the web. For this read-only lesson preparation, the relevant archive members were inspected directly in memory, without calling the package loader or extracting files.

## Count the nitrogen representation from its shells

The stored nitrogen cc-pVDZ record contains three s shells, two p shells, and one d shell. With spherical functions, one atom contributes

\[
3(1)+2(3)+1(5)=14
\]

basis functions. Two atoms contribute 28. This explains the tutorial’s recorded 28-spatial-orbital result; it is not an unexplained magic number.

The archived nitrogen cc-pVTZ record contains four s, three p, two d, and one f shell, giving

\[
4(1)+3(3)+2(5)+1(7)=30
\]

functions per atom, or 60 for N₂. The 60 count is derived from the resource definition, not from a newly run calculation. The two archives are [cc-pVDZ](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/resources/compressed/cc-pvdz.tar.gz) and [cc-pVTZ](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/resources/compressed/cc-pvtz.tar.gz).

Both models still have fourteen electrons and seven occupied spatial orbitals in a closed-shell RHF reference. The other orbitals are unoccupied, or **virtual**, in that reference. Virtual does not mean irrelevant: they permit orbital relaxation and provide destinations for excitations in correlated models. Before any active-space reduction, 28 spatial orbitals correspond to 56 electron spin modes, and 60 correspond to 120. That is a representation count, not a complete logical or physical resource estimate.

## Overlap explains why more functions can become numerically difficult

Basis functions centered on different atoms generally overlap. Their overlap matrix is

\[
S_{\mu\nu}=\int \chi_\mu^*(\mathbf r)\chi_\nu(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r.
\]

The star denotes complex conjugation; for the real functions used in this native SCF path it has no effect. A diagonal entry measures a function’s norm, and an off-diagonal entry measures overlap between two different functions. An orthonormal set would have ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. An atomic Gaussian basis usually does not.

If two functions are nearly duplicates, one combination almost cancels to zero. This is **near linear dependence**. Numerically, the overlap matrix then has a tiny eigenvalue, and dividing by its square root magnifies roundoff. Diffuse augmentation and geometries with closely overlapping functions can make this worse.

The native [orthogonalization routine](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf/scf_impl.cpp) diagonalizes the overlap, retains sufficiently large eigenvalues, and builds an orthogonalizing transformation. The low-level default threshold is \(10^{-6}\). If that low-level setting is negative, the routine instead uses the largest overlap eigenvalue divided by \(10^9\). That low-level configuration is not a `lindep_threshold` option exposed by the high-level `qdk` SCF settings at this revision; do not invent such a factory keyword. The number of retained molecular orbitals can therefore be less than the original basis-function count.

This is why we inspect both `basis.get_num_atomic_orbitals()` and `wavefunction.get_orbitals().get_num_molecular_orbitals()`. Their common equality in small well-conditioned examples is not a universal invariant.

## Choose a name, a constructed basis, or an orbital guess deliberately

The normal named-basis route is:

```python
basis = BasisSet.from_basis_name("cc-pvdz", structure)
number_of_functions = basis.get_num_atomic_orbitals()
first_atom_shells = basis.get_shells_for_atom(0)
energy, reference = create("scf_solver", "qdk").run(
    structure, 0, 1, basis,
)
```

The same native calculation can instead receive `"cc-pvdz"` directly and let the solver load it. Using an explicit object makes the actual shell/ECP representation inspectable before solving. `BasisSet.from_element_map` assigns a basis for each element present; `from_index_map` assigns one for each atom index. Missing element or atom assignments are errors, not an invitation to guess a default. Mixed choices produce a basis named `custom_basis_set`; that label alone cannot reconstruct its contents.

For N₂, giving the two nitrogen atoms different basis quality would break the symmetric representation even when their physical identities are equivalent. Per-atom customization is a capability to use intentionally, not a shortcut to making one side of a bond cheaper without consequence. The [basis tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_basis_set.py) demonstrate named, element-map, and index-map construction and their native SCF handoff.

An `Orbitals` input instead requests reuse of an initial orbital guess. The [native adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf.cpp) takes the basis from those orbitals, builds a starting density from occupied coefficient columns, and then optimizes again. It does not mean “return the old energy,” and it is not an automatic projection from cc-pVDZ to cc-pVTZ. Use a consistent structure, basis, orbital dimension, and spin convention. A geometry scan needs a correctly rebuilt or explicitly transferred guess, not a stale basis object whose centers still describe a different geometry.

Backend boundaries matter. At this revision `PyscfScfSolver._build_scf` accepts a name or orbital guess but explicitly raises `NotImplementedError` for any directly supplied `BasisSet` object, including one loaded from a standard basis name. Separate `basis_to_pyscf_mol` utilities can translate explicit shells; their existence does not remove that solver-level limitation. The PySCF solver also rebuilds its mean-field molecule using the basis name obtained from an orbital guess, so a custom guess basis must not be assumed to work as a named database basis. Spherical conventions, shell ordering, normalization, and the exact represented basis must be checked when transferring data.

## Effective core potentials change the Hamiltonian, not the element

For heavier atoms, explicitly representing tightly bound core electrons can be expensive and may require relativistic modeling. An **effective core potential**, or ECP, replaces selected core electrons and their interaction with the remaining electrons by an effective operator. It is more than subtracting electrons: its angular channels and radial functions alter the one-electron Hamiltonian.

Let \(n_A^{\mathrm{core}}\) be the number of electrons represented by an ECP on atom \(A\). The implemented effective nuclear charge and explicit-electron count are

\[
Z_A^{\mathrm{eff}}=Z_A-n_A^{\mathrm{core}},\qquad
N_{\mathrm{explicit}}=\sum_A Z_A^{\mathrm{eff}}-Q.
\]

`Structure.get_nuclear_charges()` retains the physical stored charges. `BasisSet.get_ecp_electrons()` supplies per-atom replaced-core counts, and `BasisSet.get_effective_nuclear_charges()` performs the subtraction. Do not overwrite the structure with already-reduced charges and then ask the basis to subtract the ECP again.

A useful source-grounded example, separate from nitrogen, is neutral AgH with def2-SVP. Silver has 47 physical electrons when neutral and hydrogen one, so the physical count is 48. The packaged silver ECP replaces 28 core electrons; hydrogen has none. The model therefore explicitly represents \(47-28+1=20\) electrons. Calling all nineteen retained silver electrons “the chemically active valence” would be misleading: an ECP partition and a later chemically chosen active space are different decisions.

The core–core repulsion convention changes with that effective Hamiltonian. For a separation \(R\) in Bohr, the structure’s physical nuclear expression is \(47/R\) Hartree for AgH, while `basis.calculate_effective_nuclear_repulsion_energy()` uses \(19/R\). The [native AgH test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_scf.cpp) checks physical charges, effective charges, the Hamiltonian constant, and agreement between the mean-field energy and its Hamiltonian expectation. These are repository test assertions, not newly generated AgH results. Comparing all-electron and ECP absolute energies without reconciling their Hamiltonians and energy references is not meaningful.

The [basis parser](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/basis_set.cpp) loads included ECP data automatically and currently accepts `scalar_ecp` records with one angular momentum per potential entry. It does not provide a general spin–orbit ECP treatment. ECP electron-count arrays must match the atom count and cannot exceed the corresponding nuclear charge. Native internal conversion preserves **per-atom** treatment: a test assigns an ECP to one Ag atom and an all-electron basis to another and verifies they remain different. One universal core count per element would lose that information.

In the native engine, **Libint** receives Gaussian basis/geometry data and evaluates ordinary overlap, kinetic, attraction, and electron-repulsion integrals. **Libecpint** receives ECP radial/angular data plus Gaussian shells and evaluates the extra ECP matrix elements. The [one-electron engine](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/util/int1e.cpp) uses both. Neither library decides which core electrons are safe to replace for the scientific question; that choice comes from the selected model and its validated ECP definition.

An ECP is also not the same as freezing occupied orbitals after an all-electron SCF calculation. Frozen-core correlation retains an all-electron reference and removes selected excitations from a later many-electron treatment. ECP selection changes the starting Hamiltonian and explicit-electron model itself.

## Make a controlled comparison, then hand off the right model

Our nitrogen tutorial intentionally changes only the basis from cc-pVDZ to cc-pVTZ. Geometry, charge, spin target, HF approximation, and native solver remain fixed. Its guarded reference energies are approximately −108.418633697214 and −108.445215657498 Hartree. These are values recorded in the example source, not calculations performed here. The difference is a **basis sensitivity within that HF comparison**, not a measured error against exact chemistry.

More basis flexibility can lower the variational minimum when one space contains another and the same variational problem is solved to the corresponding minimum. Arbitrary named bases need not be nested, SCF can converge to different stationary solutions, and DFT has different functional error. Therefore “a larger basis must always give a lower and more correct energy” is not a sound general rule. Stretched N₂ can still need multiple determinants even after the one-electron representation is improved.

We now have a complete input handoff: the geometry and units, element/isotope information, physical and explicit electron counts, requested spin, actual basis shells and angular convention, any ECP definition, and the chosen algorithm implementation/settings. We have not yet solved the electronic problem. Lesson 5 takes exactly these inputs and explains how integrals, density matrices, and the self-consistent field loop produce the first electronic solution.
lessons.caveats: Source and archive records inspected read-only at 97a3ff4f. Archive JSON was read in memory via standard-library tarfile, without extraction or package import; arithmetic only, no chemistry executed. Public data-model Cartesian capability is not advertised as supported through current native/PySCF adapters. Structure dimension checks are not comprehensive scientific validation. PySCF direct custom BasisSet input remains explicitly unimplemented. ECP accounting and constants are distinguished from physical nuclei; scalar ECP only. Recorded nitrogen energies are source guards, not session outputs.

lessons.title: Building the first electronic solution
lessons.body:
# Lesson 5 — Building the first electronic solution

## Turn the molecular model into something we can solve

We now have a specific problem: neutral singlet N₂, nuclei fixed 1.85 Å apart, initially represented in spherical cc-pVDZ functions. There are fourteen electrons and 28 one-electron basis functions. Our first calculation will optimize one determinant, not search all possible many-electron states.

That approximation is **Hartree–Fock**, or HF. Its orbitals adapt to the average field created by all occupied orbitals, including the exchange effect required by antisymmetry. Because that field depends on the orbitals we are trying to find, the numerical problem is circular. **Self-consistent field**, or SCF, is the process of resolving that circular dependence.

A future normal-environment call for the already-defined nitrogen `structure` is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create

solver = create(
    "scf_solver", "qdk",
    method="hf",
    scf_type="auto",
    eri_method="direct",
    convergence_threshold=1e-7,
    max_iterations=50,
)
energy, reference = solver.run(structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz")
orbitals = reference.get_orbitals()
```

This is an annotated use of the actual API, not an executed calculation. The `qdk` implementation is a classical native electronic-structure solver. No quantum processor is involved in producing this reference. The same SCF interface also offers Kohn–Sham density functional theory, or KSDFT, which we will derive after understanding HF.

## The physical operator becomes integrals

In atomic units, the fixed-nucleus all-electron Hamiltonian contains electron kinetic energy, attraction to nuclei, electron–electron repulsion, and a constant nuclear repulsion:

\[
\hat H = \sum_i\left[-\frac12\nabla_i^2
 -\sum_A\frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R_A|}\right]
 +\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j|}+E_{\mathrm{nuc}}.
\]

\(i,j\) label electrons; \(A\) labels a nucleus. \(\mathbf r_i\) is an electron position and \(\mathbf R_A\) a fixed nuclear position. \(Z_A\) is nuclear charge. The operator \(\nabla_i^2\), called the Laplacian, adds second spatial derivatives; the minus one-half factor gives electronic kinetic energy in atomic units. The nuclear term is attractive, so it has a minus sign. Electron repulsion is positive. The restriction \(i<j\) counts each electron pair once.

An **integral** turns one of these continuous-space expressions into a number for a particular pair or quartet of basis functions. We use real Gaussian basis functions here, matching the native SCF matrices. With \(\chi_\mu\) denoting AO basis function \(\mu\), the one-electron matrices are

\[
T_{\mu\nu}=\int\chi_\mu(\mathbf r)
 \left(-\frac12\nabla^2\right)\chi_\nu(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r,
\]

\[
V_{\mu\nu}=\int\chi_\mu(\mathbf r)
 \left[-\sum_A\frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf R_A|}\right]
 \chi_\nu(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r,
\qquad h=T+V.
\]

\(h\) is the **one-electron core Hamiltonian matrix**. “Core” in this phrase means the kinetic-plus-external-potential operator, not “only the chemically inert core electrons.” All explicitly modeled electrons interact with it. The many-electron \(\hat H\) is not this small matrix.

The overlap matrix from Lesson 4 is \(S_{\mu\nu}=\int\chi_\mu\chi_\nu\). It is dimensionless; the energy integrals are in Hartree. The four-index electron-repulsion integral, using the **chemist ordering** defined by this equation, is

\[
(\mu\nu|\lambda\kappa)=
\iint \chi_\mu(\mathbf r_1)\chi_\nu(\mathbf r_1)
 \frac{1}{|\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2|}
 \chi_\lambda(\mathbf r_2)\chi_\kappa(\mathbf r_2)
 \,d\mathbf r_1\,d\mathbf r_2.
\]

The first two functions share one electron coordinate; the last two share the other. “Two-electron integral” describes this operator structure, not a simulation containing only two electrons. An entire molecule’s electron interaction is assembled from these entries.

**Libint** evaluates these Gaussian integrals through efficient recurrences. We do not put a dense three-dimensional mesh around nitrogen to evaluate ordinary Coulomb integrals by brute force. QDK Chemistry supplies normalized shell data, centers, operator choices, and screening policies; Libint supplies numerical integral blocks. The repository wraps it in [`OneBodyIntegral` engines](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/util/int1e.cpp) and electron-repulsion engines.

With an ECP, this same stage uses effective nuclear attraction plus an extra ECP operator: \(h=T+V_{\mathrm{eff}}+V_{\mathrm{ECP}}\). **Libecpint** evaluates the extra ECP matrix elements from the Gaussian shells and radial/angular potential data. The actual [native setup](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf/scf_impl.cpp) constructs `H_ = T + V + ECP`, replicated across spin-density blocks as needed. N₂ in the tutorial has no ECP; this extra term is zero there.

## Occupied orbitals produce a density matrix

For a closed-shell restricted HF reference, alpha and beta electrons occupy the same spatial orbitals in pairs. If \(C_{\mu i}\) is the coefficient of basis function \(\mu\) in occupied spatial orbital \(i\), the spin-summed density matrix is

\[
P_{\mu\nu}=2\sum_{i\in\mathrm{occupied}} C_{\mu i}C_{\nu i}.
\]

The factor two is essential: both spin projections occupy each spatial orbital. For our initial N₂ model, the coefficient matrix has 28 AO rows and, if no dependent directions are removed, 28 MO columns. Seven columns are occupied. Multiplying the 28-by-7 occupied block by its transpose gives the 28-by-28 density matrix.

The density matrix is not the many-electron wavefunction written as a 28-by-28 table. It compactly describes one-electron information. It generates the spatial electron density,

\[
\rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_{\mu\nu}P_{\mu\nu}
\chi_\mu(\mathbf r)\chi_\nu(\mathbf r).
\]

This density integrates to the electron count. In a nonorthogonal AO basis the corresponding matrix check is \(N=\operatorname{Tr}(PS)\), not generally \(\operatorname{Tr}(P)\). A **trace** adds the diagonal entries of a matrix. The overlap matrix is needed because our basis functions are not independent orthonormal bins.

For unrestricted calculations we keep separate \(P^\alpha\) and \(P^\beta\), each built without the factor two; their sum gives the total density. The [native density-update code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/scf_algorithm.cpp) implements precisely these occupancy factors. This is one of the conventions an adapter must get right: a factor-of-two error is physical, not just a formatting discrepancy.

## Coulomb and exchange build the mean field

The current density and electron-repulsion integrals define two important matrices. The **Coulomb matrix** is

\[
J[P]_{\mu\nu}=\sum_{\lambda\kappa}P_{\lambda\kappa}
(\mu\nu|\lambda\kappa).
\]

It describes the electrostatic field generated by the electron distribution. The **exchange matrix** uses a different pairing of basis indices:

\[
K[P]_{\mu\nu}=\sum_{\lambda\kappa}P_{\lambda\kappa}
(\mu\lambda|\nu\kappa).
\]

Exchange comes from the antisymmetric determinant, not a new classical force or literal swapping of electrons along trajectories. It contributes only between equal-spin electrons. Together with Coulomb it cancels the unphysical interaction of a spin orbital with itself in HF, but does not account for all correlated avoidance between different electrons.

For a restricted closed-shell calculation using the spin-summed \(P\), the **Fock matrix** is

\[
F[P]=h+J[P]-\frac12K[P].
\]

The one-half exchange factor reflects our spin-summed density convention. It is not present in the same form when spin densities are stored separately:

\[
F^\alpha=h+J[P^\alpha+P^\beta]-K[P^\alpha],
\qquad
F^\beta=h+J[P^\alpha+P^\beta]-K[P^\beta].
\]

Thus each spin sees Coulomb repulsion from both spins, but exchange from its own spin sector. The native [Fock update](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf/scf_impl.cpp) follows these two cases: `J - 0.5*K` for restricted closed-shell density and the sum of spin Coulomb blocks minus the corresponding exchange block for spin-split density.

A Fock matrix is a density-dependent **effective one-electron operator**. Diagonalizing a 28-by-28 Fock matrix is not diagonalizing the enormously larger fourteen-electron Hamiltonian. That difference is the source of HF’s tractability and of its limitation.

## Orbital optimization is a constrained problem

We want a low-energy determinant, but cannot obtain it by multiplying every orbital by zero or allowing occupied orbitals to collapse onto one identical function. Orbitals must remain orthonormal. In AO coefficients, the constraint is

\[
C^{\mathsf T}SC=I,
\]

where the superscript \(\mathsf T\) means transpose and \(I\) is the identity matrix. For complex orbitals one would use a conjugate transpose; the traced native SCF path uses real coefficients.

Stationarity of the HF energy under this constraint leads to the generalized eigenvalue problem

\[
FC=SC\varepsilon.
\]

\(\varepsilon\) is a diagonal matrix of orbital energies. The equation is generalized because \(S\) is not the identity. It finds orbitals that are eigenvectors of the current mean field in the correct overlap metric. Since \(F\) itself depends on occupied columns of \(C\), solving it once is generally insufficient.

The actual numerical method transforms to an orthonormal representation. Write the overlap eigendecomposition as \(S=V s V^{\mathsf T}\), where \(s\) contains overlap eigenvalues. After removing directions below the linear-dependence threshold, construct \(X=V_{\mathrm{kept}}s_{\mathrm{kept}}^{-1/2}\). Then

\[
X^{\mathsf T}SX=I,\qquad F^{\prime}=X^{\mathsf T}FX,
\qquad F^{\prime}Y=Y\varepsilon,\qquad C=XY.
\]

Each column of \(Y\) is an ordinary eigenvector in the transformed basis. The native [eigenproblem implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/scf_algorithm.cpp) uses this transformation and LAPACK’s symmetric eigensolver on the CPU path. **Eigen** supplies matrix representations and operations; **BLAS/LAPACK** supply optimized linear algebra. They do not choose the electronic approximation.

## The SCF loop as it actually happens

First the native adapter resolves the basis and spin case, constructs the internal solver, and builds overlap and one-electron integrals. Named or explicit-basis input selects its `Atom` initial-density path. This [initial-guess implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf/guess.cpp) assembles atomic density blocks, using available atomic-guess files or generating them when absent. Generated guesses use [spherically averaged atomic HF](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/asahf.cpp): atomic angular degeneracies are treated without prematurely choosing a preferred bonding direction. This is an initial guess, not a statement that the molecule is a collection of noninteracting atoms.

An `Orbitals` input instead selects `UserProvided` density. The adapter takes occupied coefficient columns according to the requested electron populations. A restricted reference gives \(2C_{\mathrm{occ}}C_{\mathrm{occ}}^{\mathsf T}\); unrestricted input gives separate spin densities. This makes the restart mechanics concrete: we reuse orbital information to construct the starting field, then solve again.

At each outer iteration, the engine builds Coulomb and exchange contributions for the current density, updates the Fock matrix, evaluates total energy, and checks density and stationarity residuals. The numerical SCF algorithm then chooses improved orbitals and occupations. In the DIIS path it extrapolates a Fock matrix, solves the generalized eigenproblem, fills the prescribed lowest orbital columns, and constructs a new density. **Aufbau occupation** means this prescribed filling of the lowest orbitals in each spin channel; it is not a guarantee that we have discovered the globally correct electronic state.

The native default has `enable_gdm=True`, so later iterations may update orbitals through direct minimization instead of a fresh diagonalization at every step. It is therefore more accurate to say “update the occupied orbital subspace” than to insist all SCF implementations are only repeated diagonalization. After GDM, the native code rebuilds the field and updates canonical orbital eigenvalues.

The high-level native adapter exposes the choice between this atom-based start and an orbital-provided start through `basis_or_guess`; lower-level density-start options such as `Core` and `SOAD` exist, but are not additional arbitrary keys accepted by the high-level `qdk` settings. A source file containing an internal capability does not automatically make it a public workflow option.

The default iteration limit of fifty is the molecular outer-loop limit. Atomic-guess work and optimization substeps have their own mechanics; it is not fifty matrix multiplications or a wall-clock budget. When native SCF cannot satisfy its stopping criteria within that limit, it throws rather than returning an unconverged energy as a successful result.

## RHF, UHF, ROHF, RKS, and UKS are different restrictions

For a closed-shell molecule, **restricted HF (RHF)** uses one common set of spatial orbitals with paired occupations. **Unrestricted HF (UHF)** allows different alpha and beta orbital shapes. **Restricted open-shell HF (ROHF)** keeps one common spatial-orbital set but permits doubly occupied and singly occupied orbitals. These are different spaces over which the determinant is optimized.

The implementation name remains `"qdk"` or `"pyscf"`; RHF is not a required separate registry name. The method string and `scf_type` select the case:

| Request | Native HF / KSDFT | PySCF adapter HF / KSDFT |
|---|---|---|
| `auto`, singlet | RHF / RKS | RHF / RKS |
| `auto`, open shell | UHF / UKS | UHF / UKS |
| `restricted`, singlet | RHF / RKS | RHF / RKS |
| `restricted`, open shell | ROHF / rejected for DFT | ROHF / ROKS |
| `unrestricted` | UHF / UKS | UHF / UKS |

Here RKS and UKS are restricted and unrestricted Kohn–Sham orbital treatments. ROKS denotes the restricted open-shell Kohn–Sham route selected by this PySCF adapter; it is not a promise that all low-spin open-shell chemistry can be represented by one determinant.

The native [dispatch](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf.cpp) supports ROHF even though some overview documentation lists only RHF and UHF. The [native tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_scf.py) cover ROHF with DIIS, incore integrals, and GDM, and explicitly expect rejection of restricted open-shell DFT. The [PySCF tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_pyscf_plugin.py) include a lithium ROKS example. These capabilities were verified by reading implementation and tests, not by executing them here.

ROHF is not simply “average alpha and beta Fock matrices everywhere.” The native code partitions common orbitals into doubly occupied, singly occupied, and virtual blocks. It constructs an effective Fock matrix from block-specific combinations of the spin Focks: for example, doubly-to-singly occupied coupling uses the beta Fock, and singly-occupied-to-virtual coupling uses the alpha Fock. It then solves in the shared orbital space. At this revision that [ROHF construction](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/scf_algorithm.cpp) requires equal AO and retained MO dimensions, so removal of linearly dependent AO directions can make this route fail.

UHF can lower the energy by letting opposite spins localize differently, which can help a stretched bond. But the determinant may no longer be an eigenstate of total spin. **Spin contamination** means its \(\langle\hat S^2\rangle\) differs from the intended \(S(S+1)\), in units where \(\hbar=1\). Equal alpha/beta counts fix a spin projection, not necessarily a pure singlet. Nor does requesting unrestricted orbitals automatically break symmetry: both adapters warn when a closed-shell unrestricted calculation is requested without a spin-broken orbital guess. Our default singlet nitrogen calculation is RHF, not secretly a broken-symmetry UHF calculation.

## Total energy is not a sum of orbital energies

Each occupied orbital energy includes interaction with the mean field of the other occupied electrons. Adding all orbital energies therefore counts pair interactions incorrectly. For the restricted HF density convention above, the correct expression is

\[
E_{\mathrm{HF}}=E_{\mathrm{nuc}}+
\frac12\sum_{\mu\nu}P_{\mu\nu}(h_{\mu\nu}+F_{\mu\nu}).
\]

Equivalently, the one-electron contribution is \(\sum P_{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu}\), and the interaction contribution is \(\tfrac12\sum P_{\mu\nu}(F_{\mu\nu}-h_{\mu\nu})\). The native engine records these separately before adding the nuclear constant. UHF and ROHF use the corresponding sum over spin blocks with their spin-specific densities and Focks.

A deliberately **toy algebra example**, not a molecule calculation, makes double counting visible. Take one normalized spatial basis function occupied by two opposite-spin electrons. Assign \(h=-1.0\) Hartree, \((11|11)=0.4\) Hartree, and a fixed nuclear constant of 0.1 Hartree. Then \(P=2\), \(J=K=0.8\), and \(F=-1+0.8-0.4=-0.6\) Hartree. The electronic energy is \(\tfrac12(2)(-1-0.6)=-1.6\) Hartree and the total is −1.5 Hartree. The occupied orbital-energy sum is only \(2(-0.6)=-1.2\) Hartree; adding the nuclear constant to that incorrect sum does not fix it.

The real API already returns total SCF energy. For the all-electron N₂ example, this includes the nuclear repulsion computed with physical charges. With an ECP it uses the effective-charge core–core expression and ECP one-electron terms described in Lesson 4. Do not add nuclear repulsion again, and do not add an imagined energy for removed core electrons. An ECP total energy belongs to its effective Hamiltonian’s reference convention.

## Kohn–Sham DFT changes the energy model

HF restricts the interacting wavefunction to one determinant. Kohn–Sham DFT takes another route: use auxiliary noninteracting orbitals to represent the electron density, and express the missing physics through an **exchange-correlation functional**. A functional takes a function, such as a spatial density, as input and returns a number.

For a simple spin-unpolarized, non-hybrid discussion, the energy decomposition is

\[
E_{\mathrm{KS}}[\rho]=T_s[\rho]
+\int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r)\rho(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r
+E_H[\rho]+E_{\mathrm{xc}}[\rho]+E_{\mathrm{nuc}},
\]

\[
E_H[\rho]=\frac12\iint
\frac{\rho(\mathbf r)\rho(\mathbf r^{\prime})}
{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r^{\prime}|}\,d\mathbf r\,d\mathbf r^{\prime}.
\]

\(T_s\) is the kinetic energy of the auxiliary orbital system, \(v_{\mathrm{ext}}\) is nuclear attraction, and \(E_H\) is the classical Coulomb energy. \(E_{\mathrm{xc}}\) includes exchange, electron correlation, and the remaining kinetic-energy difference not already described by this decomposition. Exact theory motivates the separation, but useful calculations require an approximation for \(E_{\mathrm{xc}}\).

For a local or semilocal non-hybrid functional, the effective matrix has the form \(F_{\mathrm{KS}}=h+J+V_{\mathrm{xc}}\). The XC potential comes from differentiating the chosen energy functional with respect to the density. Spin-polarized variants depend separately on alpha and beta densities. The SCF loop still updates density and field until consistent; changing from HF to DFT changes what is being made self-consistent, not the need for iteration.

A **local-density approximation** uses the density at each point. A **GGA**, or generalized-gradient approximation, also uses spatial density gradients; PBE is an example. A **meta-GGA** can use quantities such as kinetic-energy density built from orbital gradients. A **hybrid** mixes some HF-style nonlocal exchange with density-functional contributions; B3LYP and PBE0 are examples of that category. A **range-separated hybrid** changes the exchange mixing with electron separation; CAM-B3LYP is an implemented and tested example here. These labels distinguish approximations, not automatically increasing levels of guaranteed accuracy.

In both adapters, `method="hf"` selects HF. Any other method string is treated as an XC functional name. Use `method="pbe"` or `method="b3lyp"`, not a generic `method="dft"` plus an invented `functional` key. Native processing normalizes names and consults the supported functional map; unsupported names fail.

The native [KS energy code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf/ks_impl.cpp) deliberately subtracts the XC potential contribution from its half-weighted Fock contraction and adds the separately integrated XC energy. A potential matrix is an energy derivative, not the XC energy itself. For hybrids, the exchange engine incorporates the functional’s exchange fractions; range-separated exchange can require both ordinary Coulomb and error-function-screened integrals. The [native range-separated tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_scf.cpp) compare direct and incore CAM-B3LYP calculations.

A KS determinant is an auxiliary/reference object, not the exact correlated interacting wavefunction. In particular, evaluating the ordinary electronic Hamiltonian in that determinant does not generally reproduce the reported DFT energy. The native [Hamiltonian constructor](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/hamiltonian.cpp) constructs physical one- and two-electron integrals in the supplied orbitals; it does not automatically insert the chosen XC functional as a new many-electron interaction. This distinction matters when KS orbitals become a starting representation for later quantum calculations.

## Numerical quadrature and the actual XC library boundary

DFT introduces numerical integration over space. On an atom-centered grid, a continuous integral is approximated by a weighted sum,

\[
E_{\mathrm{xc}}\approx\sum_g w_g\,
 f_{\mathrm{xc}}\bigl(\rho(\mathbf r_g),\nabla\rho(\mathbf r_g),\ldots\bigr).
\]

\(g\) labels a grid point, \(\mathbf r_g\) its position, and \(w_g\) its integration weight. Here \(f_{\mathrm{xc}}\) denotes an energy density, so the formula does not require an extra density factor hidden in the notation. The additional arguments depend on the functional family. More accurate grids generally cost more basis evaluations and functional evaluations; grid convergence is a numerical issue distinct from choosing the physical XC approximation.

**GauXC** manages molecular grids, basis evaluation, integration work, and XC matrix/energy assembly in the native path. The current [input defaults](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/include/qdk/chemistry/scf/util/gauxc_util.h) are `UltraFineGrid`, Mura–Knowles radial quadrature, and `Unpruned` grids, with a basis-screening tolerance of `1e-10`. These are low-level defaults. The high-level native SCF settings do not expose PySCF’s `xc_grid` option or arbitrary GauXC configuration keywords.

A crucial repository-specific correction concerns **Libxc**. Libxc is a community library for evaluating XC functional energy densities and derivatives; it is not a complete SCF solver or a grid generator. Documentation credits it in the DFT ecosystem. However, this revision’s concrete [GauXC adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/exc/GauXC/gauxc_impl.cpp) constructs `GauXC::functional_type` using **`ExchCXX::Backend::builtin`**, and the [dependency configuration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/cmake/third_party.cmake) explicitly sets `EXCHCXX_ENABLE_LIBXC OFF`. We must not teach that every native DFT call directly runs Libxc. For this path, ExchCXX’s built-in functional implementation sits inside the GauXC integration machinery. A Libxc-style functional catalog in a resource JSON file is not proof that every entry is active in this compiled backend.

Density conventions are adapted at this boundary. Native RKS stores the total density, but the GauXC call used here expects the alpha half-density, so the adapter passes half of it. For UKS, the adapter forms total density and alpha-minus-beta density for GauXC, then converts the resulting potentials back to alpha/beta form. Those conversions illustrate why “both libraries accept a matrix” is an inadequate interoperability specification.

## Direct versus incore: choose where the cost lives

With \(K\) AO basis functions, a full four-index integral tensor has \(K^4\) entries before symmetry/storage reductions. The native setting `eri_method` selects `"direct"` or `"incore"`. Both describe integral evaluation/storage strategies, not different electron-correlation models.

**Direct**, the default, evaluates needed shell quartets while forming J and K and avoids retaining the entire four-index tensor. It repeats integral work as the density changes but saves large tensor storage. It still needs matrices, shell-pair data, engines, and sometimes per-thread accumulation buffers; “direct” does not mean memory-free.

**Incore** generates and stores integrals for later contractions. In this implementation the [stored arrays](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/eri/INCORE/incore_impl.cpp) have four-index size, partitionable by the first index in the MPI design. They are not universally compressed to the smallest symmetry-packed form. Range-separated exchange may require an additional tensor. CPU builds retain them on the host; GPU-enabled branches can transfer storage to the device.

Illustrative single-tensor float64 storage, calculated only by multiplying counts by eight bytes, is about 4.69 MiB for 28 AOs and 98.88 MiB for 60 AOs. At 300 AOs it is 64.8 decimal GB. These figures are not total peak process memory, timings, or measured nitrogen resource use. They omit other arrays, scratch buffers, possible extra range-separated tensors, and parallel replication.

The direct [Libint2 implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/eri/LIBINT2_DIRECT/libint2_direct.cpp) avoids negligible work through multiple screening layers. It first rejects insignificant shell pairs by overlap. It uses Schwarz bounds and density-block magnitudes to reject quartets whose field contribution is too small. At an individual-integral level the relevant bound has the form

\[
|(\mu\nu|\lambda\kappa)|\le
\sqrt{(\mu\nu|\mu\nu)(\lambda\kappa|\lambda\kappa)}.
\]

The native high-level `eri_threshold` default is `-1.0`. Its actual dispatch rule uses a positive supplied value, otherwise chooses `convergence_threshold * 1e-5`, giving `1e-12` at the default SCF tolerance. `shell_pair_threshold` defaults to `1e-12`. These are screening controls, not certified final energy-error bounds. Making screening too loose can change the field or prevent agreement with a tighter reference.

The incore factory does not receive these direct-screening settings in the same way; it constructs its ERI object with a zero base threshold and generates its integral arrays through its own Libint route. Do not assume tweaking `eri_threshold` has identical semantics under both choices.

`eri_use_atomics=False` selects thread-local accumulation buffers in the direct engine; `True` uses shared-memory atomic updates. “Atomic” here is a parallel-programming term for an indivisible update, not an atomic-orbital approximation. Thread-local buffers trade memory for reduced contention and controlled accumulation. Floating-point reduction order can still affect last digits across thread counts or implementations.

The ordinary Fock build has quartic worst-case integral work, while dense eigensolution has cubic cost in matrix dimension. Screening changes practical cost substantially. The high-level route does not turn on density fitting merely because internal auxiliary-basis and `do_dfj` facilities exist; its default is `do_dfj=false`. Later factorization lessons will explain other representations rather than conflate them with this setting.

## Which stopping criterion did we actually request?

The scalar `convergence_threshold` is not a promised absolute energy error in Hartree. Native dispatch sets the orbital-gradient threshold to that value and the density threshold to one hundred times it. At the default `1e-7`, the latter is `1e-5`.

For ordinary RHF/UHF, the [convergence code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/scf_algorithm.cpp) checks a density-change norm and the antisymmetric residual corresponding to

\[
R=FPS-SPF.
\]

A zero residual expresses that the occupied density and its field are mutually stationary in the nonorthogonal basis. The implementation normalizes the density norm and maximum-entry residual measure by the AO dimension and requires both to pass. ROHF uses its effective Fock/total-density construction. Energy changes are logged, but the native boolean stopping test is not simply “energy changed by less than the tolerance.”

The first few native Fock updates use the full density; subsequently the code can accumulate contributions from density differences. `fock_reset_steps`, default `1073741824`, controls periodic full rebuilds, not the SCF iteration budget. A default of \(2^{30}\) makes periodic resets effectively absent over an ordinary short run, although initial full builds still occur.

The default DIIS/GDM combination is selected by `enable_gdm=True`; setting it false selects DIIS alone. **DIIS** uses recent residuals and Fock matrices to extrapolate a better field. **GDM**, geometric direct minimization, searches over orbital rotations while preserving orthonormality. Its detailed geometry, line search, and stability analysis belong to Lesson 6.

One preview requires exact semantics: the [actual hybrid switch](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/diis_gdm.cpp) occurs when the DIIS step limit is exceeded, or after more than one step when the absolute energy change is **below** `energy_thresh_diis_switch`, default `1e-3`. Some prose/comments say “exceeds”; the conditional uses `<`. `gdm_max_diis_iteration` and `gdm_bfgs_history_size_limit` default to fifty and control the DIIS-to-GDM transition limit and retained optimization history respectively. `level_shift` is applied by DIIS only for a positive value; the default `-1.0` does not activate it. A documented-looking key such as `max_scf_steps` is not in the actual high-level native settings schema here.

Convergence remains distinct from stability. A stationary determinant can be a local minimum, a saddle point, or the wrong spin-constrained solution for the question. Numerical convergence also says nothing by itself about finite-basis or electron-correlation error.

## The PySCF adapter implements the same handoff, not identical numerics

The optional implementation is created as `create("scf_solver", "pyscf")`. The [adapter code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/scf_solver.py) constructs a PySCF `Mole`, passes the run’s charge, converts multiplicity to PySCF’s spin difference using `multiplicity - 1`, and sets `unit="Bohr"`. The atom-label helper prints coordinates read from `Structure`; a stale helper docstring saying Ångstrom does not describe this path.

The adapter chooses PySCF RHF, UHF, ROHF, RKS, UKS, or ROKS as shown earlier. For DFT it assigns the functional string to `mf.xc` and the integer `xc_grid` setting to `mf.grids.level`. This setting defaults to three, accepts zero through nine, and is a PySCF grid-density control; it is not numerically equivalent to GauXC’s `UltraFineGrid` label.

It maps `max_iterations` to `mf.max_cycle`. More subtly, it maps `convergence_threshold` to **`mf.conv_tol = 0.1 * convergence_threshold`**, an energy-change tolerance. It does not explicitly set `mf.conv_tol_grad` to the same number. Therefore identical QDK setting names across the two adapters do not establish identical stopping tests.

Without an orbital guess, `_run_scf` calls `mf.kernel()` and uses PySCF’s initial-guess behavior. With compatible QDK orbitals it reconstructs an initial density through the conversion utilities and calls `mf.kernel(dm0=dm0)`. The resulting orbital coefficients, energies, overlap, basis and ECP records are converted back into QDK objects.

The energy returned by `kernel` is passed through unchanged as the **SCF total energy**. The adapter neither subtracts nuclear repulsion nor replaces the passed charge/spin with settings values. Several docstrings claim otherwise; tracing `_build_scf`, `_run_scf`, and `_to_wavefunction` resolves the discrepancy. Do not copy those descriptions into a scientific analysis.

There is another important contract limit: this regular adapter does not explicitly inspect `mf.converged` before returning the tuple. PySCF can provide a final iterate without the same fail-on-nonconvergence behavior as the native wrapper. A returned object is therefore not uniformly a convergence certificate across backends. Logs, diagnostic behavior, and independent checks belong in the trustworthiness step, rather than assuming every adapter enforces identical success conditions.

Basis interoperability also remains bounded. Direct custom `BasisSet` input is explicitly unimplemented in `PyscfScfSolver`, even though separate conversion utilities support explicit shell data. The initial-guess route must match the basis, geometry and spin treatment. PySCF loads named bases and ECP mappings through its own ecosystem; equal basis-name strings alone are weaker evidence than matching the actual converted definitions and conventions.

PySCF is an external electronic-structure engine. Its internal integral, XC, and linear-algebra dependencies should be recorded from the installed PySCF environment rather than attributed to QDK’s native Libint/GauXC path. In particular, Libxc’s role in a PySCF installation is determined by that installation; this adapter does not select or verify a universal XC-library backend. The [package metadata](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/pyproject.toml) also makes PySCF optional and excludes the PySCF dependency from the Windows `plugins` extra. No such optional package was imported or installed for this lesson.

## Parallel software is another boundary, not another physical theory

Native Gaussian integrals, dense matrix algebra, and XC quadrature can all use classical parallel libraries. OpenMP distributes work across CPU threads where enabled; MPI supports distributed processes in compiled paths; BLAS may have its own threads. These are performance choices, not quantum gates.

The high-level native `nthreads` setting affects OpenMP only when compiled with OpenMP, and only a positive value requests a change. The default `-1` leaves the runtime’s current setting in place; it is not proof that every physical CPU core will be used. The [current build defaults](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/CMakeLists.txt) disable GPU and MPI by default and do not enable OpenMP in the Windows default configuration. Nothing in a source walkthrough determines which options an already-installed binary has.

Nested parallelism can oversubscribe a machine: many grid threads can each invoke a threaded matrix library. The [GauXC boundary](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/exc/GauXC/gauxc_impl.cpp) uses a [scoped BLAS-thread guard](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/util/blas_threads.cpp) to request one BLAS thread during that work when the linked library’s control API is supported, then restore it. Performance and reproducibility checks must therefore include build and library context, not just the molecular input.

## What we have obtained, and what still needs to be trusted

The native adapter maps internal shells back into the public AO order, creates restricted or unrestricted `Orbitals`, and attaches a single canonical occupied `Configuration` through `StateVectorContainer` to a `Wavefunction`. In the HF case, the determinant has one configuration coefficient, while many MO coefficients were optimized. Those are entirely different quantities. The public `run` result is the energy/wavefunction pair, not the whole internal `SCFResult` containing every diagnostic field.

The output supplies a classical reference energy, orbitals for later transformation or integral construction, an initial many-electron reference, and a basis for classical diagnostics. It has not supplied correlation energies, a reliable dissociation curve, an active-space choice, a quantum circuit, or a hardware resource estimate. HF cannot represent all of the multiconfigurational structure that becomes important in stretched nitrogen. DFT incorporates approximated correlation through its functional but does not thereby provide a universally accurate ground-state wavefunction or a variational upper-bound guarantee.

The functional handoff is now clear: chemical input and BSE definitions become integrals through Libint/Libecpint; classical SCF and linear algebra optimize orbitals; KSDFT additionally uses functional kernels and GauXC or PySCF integration machinery; the resulting QDK objects feed later chemistry and quantum algorithms. Resource-estimation and error-correction specialists will eventually need the logical workload and error targets derived from that model. Better error correction cannot repair an inappropriate basis, a wrong spin state, or an unconverged classical reference.

Our next lesson therefore examines **trustworthiness of the first electronic solution**: how DIIS and GDM navigate the orbital problem, how failures are diagnosed, and why an SCF stability check asks a different question from an SCF convergence check.
lessons.caveats: Implementation and tests read at 97a3ff4f; none executed. All new numerical examples are toy arithmetic or analytic storage counts, not scientific output. Native XC uses ExchCXX built-ins through GauXC with Libxc disabled in dependency setup, despite broader documentation language. Native DIIS/GDM switch uses absolute delta-E below the threshold, contrary to some prose/comments. Regular PySCF adapter forwards total kernel energy and run charge/spin, maps tolerance to conv_tol only, and does not explicitly check mf.converged. Native ROHF supports a narrower retained-AO/MO shape and native ROKS is rejected; PySCF ROKS is source/test supported. Installed optional dependencies, compiled hardware features and exact external kernel internals were not inspected or assumed. Detailed DIIS/GDM/stability theory remains Lesson 6.

lessons.title: Making the classical solution trustworthy
lessons.body:
# Lesson 6 — Making the classical solution trustworthy

## A successful-looking energy is the beginning of an argument

Our nitrogen model has not changed: neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å, initially in spherical cc-pVDZ. Lesson 5 explained how SCF produces a determinant and energy. Now we ask whether that result is a sufficiently accurate solution of the intended mean-field problem, and whether another nearby determinant would lower its energy.

These are different questions. **Nonconvergence** means the numerical iteration has not satisfied its stopping conditions. **Instability** means an apparently stationary solution has a nearby downhill direction in an allowed orbital space. A **metastable solution** is a local minimum that may not be the lowest minimum accessible elsewhere. **Model error** remains even for a perfectly converged, stable HF determinant because HF and a finite basis do not describe all electronic correlation. Printing more decimal places addresses none of those distinctions.

Everything below is source-grounded preparation. No SCF calculation, stability check, or test was executed. Small mathematical examples are explicitly illustrative. We will not assign the stability results of the repository’s other nitrogen geometries to our 1.85-Å cc-pVDZ case.

## Why the same model can produce difficult iterations

SCF alternates between an electron density and the field that density generates. Near a well-behaved solution, a small density error may shrink each time around the loop. Near a small occupied–virtual energy gap, a small field change can strongly rotate orbitals or reorder occupations. The next density may then undo the previous change. This gives oscillation, slow convergence, or large jumps between electronic solutions.

An illustrative one-variable iteration makes the numerical issue visible. Let \(x_k\) represent one component of the error at step \(k\), not a nuclear coordinate. If locally \(x_{k+1}=-1.2x_k\), the sign flips and the magnitude grows. Mixing half of the old and half of the proposed new value instead gives \(x_{k+1}=0.5x_k+0.5(-1.2x_k)=-0.1x_k\), which shrinks. This example explains why damping can help. It does not assert that the native solver exposes a high-level damping keyword or that every molecular SCF problem reduces to this scalar map.

A poor initial guess can land in a different basin of attraction. A symmetry-preserving initial guess can stay on a symmetry-preserving stationary branch even when a symmetry-breaking solution is lower. An optimizer cannot always discover a downhill direction whose first derivative is exactly zero at the symmetric starting point. That is why “use more iterations” and “check stability” are not interchangeable remedies.

## Start with a meaningful guess and a consistent problem

The [native SCF adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf.cpp) selects its atom-based initial-density path for a basis name or explicit `BasisSet`, and its user-provided-density path for `Orbitals`. The [atom-guess code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf/guess.cpp) reads available atomic-guess data or generates atomic densities and assembles them on the molecule. Generated guesses use [spherically averaged atomic HF](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/asahf.cpp). This gives a sensible starting electron distribution before molecular bonding has been optimized.

For `Orbitals`, the adapter builds a density from occupied coefficient columns using the requested alpha/beta populations. Reusing a previous solution can therefore be much better than starting afresh. It must still describe the same compatible basis and centers. Passing cc-pVDZ coefficients does not automatically project them into cc-pVTZ, and a stale basis object does not move its centers merely because a different `Structure` is passed beside it.

The low-level engine contains other initial-density strategies, including core-Hamiltonian and SOAD paths. These are not all exposed as settings on `create("scf_solver", "qdk")`. The supported high-level control here is the input choice. The PySCF adapter similarly uses a compatible orbital input to make an initial density, otherwise calls PySCF’s default `kernel()` behavior. It does not expose every PySCF initial-guess option through its small QDK settings schema.

For closed-shell unrestricted requests, both adapters warn that automatic spin-symmetry breaking is not supplied. A restricted guess copied into two equal spin channels can simply return the restricted solution inside the larger unrestricted space. A deliberately perturbed unrestricted guess has a different purpose from an arbitrary random starting density: it probes an identified electronic direction while retaining the molecule and electron count.

## Read the stopping conditions, not just the last energy change

For ordinary native RHF/UHF, the orbital stationarity residual is associated with

\[
R=FPS-SPF.
\]

\(F\) is the Fock matrix, \(P\) the density matrix, and \(S\) the AO overlap matrix. A residual measures how far the occupied density is from being stationary in its own field. The [native convergence implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/scf_algorithm.cpp) checks both a density-change norm and a maximum-entry orbital residual, each normalized by the AO dimension. ROHF uses its effective Fock and total-density construction.

`convergence_threshold` defaults to `1e-7`. Native dispatch uses that for the orbital-gradient condition and one hundred times it, `1e-5`, for the density condition. An energy-change quantity is logged and used by optimization logic, but a small change in energy alone is not the native convergence test. Energy can appear nearly stationary while the density oscillates, particularly near shallow directions.

`max_iterations=50` is the default molecular outer-iteration limit, not a scientific accuracy target. Increasing it is reasonable when residuals decrease steadily. It is not a convincing remedy for a repeating occupation cycle, an invalid guess, NaNs, or a wrong charge. Native failure is explicit; keep the error message rather than substituting a plausible energy.

The PySCF adapter’s same-named tolerance is not numerically equivalent: it sets `mf.conv_tol = 0.1 * convergence_threshold`, without explicitly setting `mf.conv_tol_grad`. Its regular `run` path does not itself check `mf.converged` before returning the energy/wavefunction pair. Consequently, a returned tuple is not a uniform convergence certificate across implementations. The [adapter source](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/scf_solver.py), not the name of the setting, determines the contract.

Numerical consistency also depends on integral screening. In the native direct engine, a nonpositive `eri_threshold` triggers the rule `convergence_threshold * 1e-5`; a positive value is used explicitly. `shell_pair_threshold` defaults to `1e-12`. These omit small integral contributions; neither is a guaranteed final energy-error bound. Tightening an SCF residual while retaining excessively loose integrals may request an accuracy the underlying field cannot supply.

Near-linear dependence is another issue, not an optimizer personality. The native overlap orthogonalization can remove near-redundant basis directions. Its low-level default threshold is `1e-6`, and it is not a high-level `qdk` SCF settings key. Check the number of retained MOs and overlap warnings. Native ROHF currently requires the retained MO count to equal the AO count in its effective-Fock construction; removal of directions can make that route fail. Adding iterations cannot restore a missing linear-algebra capability.

## DIIS: use the history of errors rather than guess a mixing fraction

**DIIS**, direct inversion in the iterative subspace, collects recent Fock matrices and their residuals. Flatten each residual matrix into a vector \(e_i\); flattening simply assigns its entries a consistent order. DIIS seeks weights \(c_i\) that minimize the residual of a linear combination while preserving an affine combination:

\[
\min_{\{c_i\}}\left\|\sum_i c_i e_i\right\|^2,
\qquad \sum_i c_i=1,
\qquad F_{\mathrm{DIIS}}=\sum_i c_i F_i.
\]

These weights are optimization coefficients, not probabilities; negative values can be valid. In a toy scalar example with residuals 2 and −1, weights one-third and two-thirds cancel the residual while summing to one. Real molecular residuals have many components, so exact cancellation is usually unavailable.

Define the residual-overlap matrix \(B_{ij}=e_i^{\mathsf T}e_j\). Constrained minimization gives a small linear system for the weights and a Lagrange multiplier, a variable enforcing their sum:

\[
\begin{pmatrix}B&-\mathbf 1\\-\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}c\\\lambda\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The native [DIIS implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/diis.cpp) builds these inner products, rescales the overlap block by its largest entry, and solves the augmented system by column-pivoted QR. Its internal default history size is eight. When the history fills, it drops the oldest pair. If the residual-overlap block is zero it returns the current field; if the augmented system is judged too nearly dependent using its `1e-12` determinant test, it prunes old history rather than trust enormous unstable weights.

That last point matters physically. Several almost identical past errors provide little independent information. Keeping more of them does not necessarily improve the direction; it can make the extrapolation ill-conditioned. DIIS then diagonalizes its proposed field and reconstructs occupations. It is fast near many ordinary solutions but is not a line-search method requiring every proposed energy to decrease.

The low-level DIIS history and damping configuration should not be confused with available high-level settings. At this revision, do not pass invented `diis_subspace_size` or `enable_damping` keywords to the public `qdk` factory. Inspect the concrete schema before configuring a backend.

## Level shifts stabilize the iteration without adding a new molecular force

A positive `level_shift` selects a modified trial field in the native DIIS implementation instead of its ordinary Pulay extrapolation. The default `-1.0` leaves this disabled. The implemented expression is

\[
F_{\mathrm{trial}}=F+\mu(S-SPS),\qquad \mu>0.
\]

This is an iteration device that separates occupied and unoccupied directions. With an orthonormal basis and a spin-resolved idempotent density, it leaves occupied levels unchanged and raises virtual levels. With the native RHF spin-summed density, \(P=2\Pi_{\mathrm{occ}}\), it shifts occupied levels by \(-\mu\) and virtual levels by \(+\mu\); the gap is enlarged by \(2\mu\). Using the actual density convention explains why the factor matters.

The physical field used for the SCF energy and residual is kept separate from the trial field. Nevertheless, a large shift can slow relaxation or steer the iteration to a different stationary solution. For final interpretation, especially orbital energies and a stability check that uses them, refine with unshifted settings on a fresh solver rather than assume any shifted trial eigenvalues are physical canonical energies.

The engine also uses incremental Fock updates after initial full builds. `fock_reset_steps`, default `1073741824`, governs periodic rebuilding from the full density; it is not another iteration cap. More frequent rebuilding is a numerical consistency tool, not a correction for missing electron correlation.

## GDM: optimize orbital rotations directly

DIIS proposes fields. **Geometric direct minimization (GDM)** instead asks which orbital change lowers the energy while automatically preserving orthonormality. Let \(\kappa\) be a real antisymmetric matrix, meaning \(\kappa^{\mathsf T}=-\kappa\). Define

\[
U=e^{\kappa},\qquad C_{\mathrm{new}}=CU.
\]

The matrix exponential makes \(U\) orthogonal, so if \(C^{\mathsf T}SC=I\), the new coefficients satisfy the same condition. We optimize rotation parameters rather than repair broken orbital normalization after each step. For RHF the physically changing directions mix occupied and virtual orbitals; rotations wholly inside the occupied space leave the determinant unchanged up to phase. UHF has separate alpha and beta directions. ROHF needs blocks connecting doubly occupied, singly occupied, and unoccupied spaces.

Let \(g\) be the derivative of the energy with respect to the independent rotation parameters. A Newton step would solve \(H p=-g\), where \(H\) is the orbital Hessian, or second-derivative matrix, and \(p\) is a direction. Computing and storing the exact Hessian repeatedly is expensive. **Quasi-Newton** methods approximate its action from observed changes.

The [native GDM code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/gdm.cpp) uses a limited-history BFGS two-loop recursion. BFGS is named for Broyden, Fletcher, Goldfarb, and Shanno. Each accepted step supplies an orbital displacement \(s\) and a gradient change \(y\). The approximation is updated to be consistent with the observed relation \(H s\approx y\). Limited history retains these vector pairs instead of materializing a huge dense inverse Hessian.

Its starting diagonal approximation uses pseudo-canonical orbital gaps: it diagonalizes appropriate occupied and virtual blocks without changing the represented occupied subspaces, and transforms the history into that same coordinate system. For ordinary RHF/UHF, the positive denominator is built from

\[
h_{ia}^{(0)}=\max\left\{\gamma\bigl(|\Delta E|+
|\widetilde\varepsilon_a-\widetilde\varepsilon_i|\bigr),
\epsilon_{\mathrm{machine}}\right\},
\]

where \(i\) and \(a\) label occupied and virtual orbitals, the tildes denote the block-canonical energies, \(\Delta E\) is the latest accepted energy change, and \(\gamma\) is four for restricted closed-shell or two for unrestricted spin blocks. This is a **preconditioner**: it scales different directions so an energetically stiff rotation is not stepped as aggressively as a soft one. It is not an exact curvature measurement proving stability.

If the latest curvature product \(s^{\mathsf T}y\) is too small or invalid, GDM clears its history. If its proposed direction has \(p^{\mathsf T}g>0\), it points uphill and the history is discarded. Without usable history it falls back to the diagonal-preconditioned negative gradient. `gdm_bfgs_history_size_limit` defaults to fifty and must be at least one. More history costs memory proportional to the rotation-vector dimension and may not be more robust.

## A line search makes each expensive trial count

Having a direction does not determine how far to move. A **line search** tests positive step lengths \(\alpha\) along it, evaluating trial orbitals, densities, energies, and gradients. These trial evaluations rebuild real Coulomb/exchange and, for DFT, XC contributions; one GDM iteration can therefore cost several field evaluations.

The native [Nocedal–Wright line search](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/line_search.h) brackets a step then narrows the bracket. It uses the sufficient-decrease and strong-Wolfe tests. If \(f(\alpha)=E(Ce^{\alpha\kappa(p)})\), they have the form

\[
f(\alpha)\le f(0)+10^{-4}\alpha f^{\prime}(0),
\qquad |f^{\prime}(\alpha)|\le0.9|f^{\prime}(0)|.
\]

The first asks for enough decrease relative to the initial downhill slope; the second asks that the slope flatten sufficiently. A step that is tiny merely because it avoids all difficulty is not necessarily useful. These are local numerical conditions, not a guarantee of the global electronic minimum.

If a BFGS line search fails, native GDM retries using steepest descent. If that also fails, it accepts a zero rotation only when its gradient-norm condition is already sufficiently small; otherwise it aborts with an error.
