This is a useful distinction between “nothing needs to move” and “the algorithm cannot find a valid move.” The current GDM iteration also explicitly rejects MPI world sizes greater than one because of its trial-field participation limitation. Compiled MPI capability elsewhere does not make this particular optimization path distributed.

## The native hybrid switch is precise

Public `enable_gdm=False` selects DIIS. Its default `True` selects DIIS followed, when appropriate, by GDM, not pure GDM from the first iteration. The [actual switching condition](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf_algorithm/diis_gdm.cpp) is: exceed `gdm_max_diis_iteration`, or after more than one step have an absolute energy change **below** `energy_thresh_diis_switch`.

The defaults are fifty and `1e-3` Hartree respectively. The threshold must be positive; the internal DIIS limit is clamped to at least two. Once the switch occurs, the algorithm stays in GDM. Some documentation/comments describe the opposite inequality; the current condition uses `<`. We can understand the intended division of labor without that misleading wording: DIIS approaches a candidate solution, then direct orbital minimization refines it. Neither step proves that symmetry-forbidden downhill directions have been explored.

## Stability is curvature, not another convergence tolerance

Near stationary orbitals, express the energy in independent rotation coordinates \(x\):

\[
E(x)\approx E(0)+g^{\mathsf T}x+\frac12x^{\mathsf T}H_{\mathrm{orb}}x.
\]

\(H_{\mathrm{orb}}\) is the **electronic orbital Hessian**. It is not the nuclear Hessian of Lesson 7. SCF stationarity makes \(g\) small. If \(H_{\mathrm{orb}}v=\lambda v\) with a negative \(\lambda\), then a small motion in direction \(v\) lowers the energy to second order even though the first derivative was zero.

For an illustrative toy surface, \(E(u,v)=E_0+0.2u^2-0.05v^2\), the point \(u=v=0\) has zero gradient but Hessian eigenvalues 0.4 and −0.1. It is a saddle. Here \(u,v\) are orbital-rotation coordinates, not changes in the N–N bond. No numerical conclusion about our nitrogen calculation follows from these invented coefficients.

An **internal instability** lowers energy inside the same orbital restriction, such as RHF to a different RHF determinant. An **external instability** relaxes a restriction, here typically common alpha/beta orbitals becoming different: RHF to UHF or the corresponding KS channel. Native external checking is not an exhaustive search over all complex, noncollinear, or spinor states. The PySCF external helper explicitly excludes real-to-complex instability.

Even an internally and externally stable result is only locally stable in the checked channels and within the selected numerical thresholds. It can still be above another minimum far away. A lower unrestricted solution may be spin-contaminated; it must not simply be relabeled a spin-pure singlet because it has seven electrons of each spin.

## What the stability checkers actually compute

The interface is `create("stability_checker", implementation).run(wavefunction)`, returning `(is_stable, StabilityResult)`. The native implementation is `"qdk"`; the optional plugin is `"pyscf"`.

The native [checker](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/stability.cpp) uses orbital energies, coefficients, a basis, and electron counts to build an occupied–virtual response problem. It reconstructs Aufbau densities, so use this for an appropriate SCF reference, not as a stability theory for arbitrary correlated coefficients that happen to fit in `Wavefunction`. It does not replace the converged reference requirement with an independent stationarity certification.

It applies the Hessian to trial vectors without building the entire Hessian matrix. A trial orbital variation induces a trial density; Coulomb/exchange and, for DFT, the XC response kernel give its field response. Adding orbital-energy-gap terms completes the action. **Davidson diagonalization** iteratively finds low eigenvalues in a small expanding subspace, preconditioned by diagonal information. This native eigensolver is supplied by **MACIS**; the integral and XC-response libraries provide the expensive operator actions. These are concrete library boundaries, not separate chemical approximations.

Native defaults are `internal=True`, `external=False`, `max_subspace=80`, `davidson_tolerance=1e-8`, `stability_tolerance=-1e-4`, and `method="hf"`. It finds one lowest eigenpair per requested channel; `max_subspace` limits search-space size and is clamped to the rotation-problem dimension. It is not a setting for how many physical unstable states to report. Davidson failure is an eigensolver failure, not evidence of stability; a larger useful subspace or better-conditioned reference may be needed.

For our unreduced RHF model, seven occupied and 21 virtual orbitals give \(7\times21=147\) independent occupied–virtual rotation coordinates. That source-derived dimension is not a computed eigenvalue. UHF concatenates alpha and beta rotation blocks. Returned vectors use the public occupied-index-fast convention; use the provided rotation utility instead of guessing how to reshape a raw vector.

The classification is `lowest_eigenvalue > stability_tolerance`. With the default negative threshold, a weakly negative value such as −0.00005 passes this numerical criterion, while −0.0002 does not. These are illustrative values. The Davidson solve tolerance and the physical decision threshold serve different purposes and should be assessed together near zero curvature.

Native checking rejects ROHF/ROKS references even though native SCF can produce ROHF. It also rejects external checking on unrestricted references. Requesting neither channel is an error. Its explicit zero-electron case returns stable status with empty eigenpair arrays. For other results, inspect `has_internal_result()` and `has_external_result()` before requesting eigenvalues; an unchecked channel has a default status, not a completed calculation. [`StabilityResult`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/stability_result.hpp) provides the two statuses, eigenvalue arrays, eigenvector columns, and smallest-eigenpair getters. It is a result report, not proof that every possible direction was checked.

The [PySCF checker](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/stability.py) explicitly requires a single-determinant state-vector container. It supports internal RHF, ROHF and UHF analysis and RHF external analysis, including corresponding supported KS response paths. External ROHF/UHF requests raise errors. Its defaults include `external=True`, `nroots=3`, `with_symmetry=False`, `davidson_tolerance=1e-8`, `stability_tolerance=-1e-4`, `method="hf"`, `xc_grid=3`, and `pyscf_verbose=4`. `with_symmetry` controls point-group restrictions where supplied by PySCF, not whether alpha and beta are identical.

This adapter rescales internal RHF eigenvalues by one-quarter and UHF eigenvalues by one-half to align reporting conventions; external values are left unscaled. Comparing raw eigenvalues from different implementations without matching conventions is therefore unsafe. In contrast to native checking, disabling both PySCF channels returns empty data with stable defaults. That documented-by-test behavior means “nothing requested,” not “minimum established.” Always match the checker’s `method` and relevant grid settings to the SCF model; it does not infer the functional reliably from a generic wavefunction object.

## Perturb the orbitals, then solve again

A negative eigenvector is a direction, not a new converged state. The [rotation utility](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/utils/orbital_rotation.cpp) unpacks the vector into an antisymmetric matrix, exponentiates it, and returns new `Orbitals`. It invalidates orbital energies because rotated orbitals are no longer guaranteed canonical.

For an RHF external perturbation, `restricted_external=True` constructs unrestricted orbitals by rotating alpha while retaining the original beta coefficients. Internal restricted perturbations rotate their common orbital set. For unrestricted input the vector contains separate alpha and beta blocks. The input assumes Aufbau occupations.

Here is a complete single-retry illustration using `reference`, `orbitals`, and `structure` from Lesson 5. The factor 0.1 is an explicitly illustrative perturbation amplitude, not a native setting or a universally good step:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.utils import rotate_orbitals

checker = create("stability_checker", "qdk", method="hf", external=True)
stable, report = checker.run(reference)
if not stable:
    external = report.has_external_result() and not report.is_external_stable()
    if external:
        eigenvalue, direction = report.get_smallest_external_eigenvalue_and_vector()
    else:
        eigenvalue, direction = report.get_smallest_internal_eigenvalue_and_vector()
    n_alpha, n_beta = reference.get_total_num_electrons()
    guess = rotate_orbitals(orbitals, 0.1 * direction, n_alpha, n_beta, external)
    retry = create(
        "scf_solver", "qdk", method="hf",
        scf_type="unrestricted" if external else "restricted",
    )
    retry_energy, retry_reference = retry.run(structure, 0, 1, guess)
    recheck = create("stability_checker", "qdk", method="hf", external=not external)
    retry_stable, retry_report = recheck.run(retry_reference)
```

The recheck matters: neither the perturbation nor a lower returned energy proves final stability. Changing the perturbation scale affects which basin the reoptimization reaches. A very large rotation need not lower the energy predicted by a local curvature expansion. New algorithm instances are used when their settings change; `run` locks ordinary settings before execution, including failing execution. As Lesson 3 explained, that is not a guarantee of deep freezing every separately reachable nested object.

## Automated stabilized SCF has a specific policy

`create("scf_solver", "qdk_stabilized")` performs the repeated workflow. Its [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/stabilized_scf.cpp) holds nested `AlgorithmRef` settings for `scf_solver` and `stability_checker`, both native by default. The defaults are five stability cycles, both check flags true, `fail_on_unstable=True`, and `external_instability_action="unrestricted"`.

The native wrapper runs SCF, checks applicable channels, prefers an external unstable direction when both are present, rotates, and reruns SCF. Unlike our manual illustration, it passes the returned direction without an additional exposed amplitude multiplier. When it follows an external direction, its default policy forces subsequent SCF to unrestricted. Once the reference is unrestricted, the wrapper stops requesting the unsupported RHF external channel and checks internal stability.

`max_stability_iterations` has a declared nonnegative bound. With a positive value \(m\), at most \(m\) rotation/rerun cycles follow the initial SCF; a final check evaluates the last result. With zero, the wrapper is plain SCF passthrough and does no stability check. `fail_on_unstable=False` permits return of the last energy/wavefunction even if the requested local stability was not achieved. The return type remains the ordinary SCF pair, not a status-rich stability report; run a final explicit checker if that report is needed.

The alternative action `"rotate_only"` suppresses the wrapper’s explicit switch to unrestricted. It does not make the generated external guess restricted again. A native auto/restricted singlet child can reject that unrestricted guess, so this is not a safe synonym for “remove external instability while remaining RHF.” Also, the default native checker cannot analyze a ROHF result; select a compatible checker or a manual supported workflow rather than assume the composite expands its components’ capabilities.

A concrete configuration example, still unexecuted, is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef

robust = create(
    "scf_solver", "qdk_stabilized",
    method="hf", max_iterations=100, max_stability_iterations=3,
    fail_on_unstable=True,
    scf_solver=AlgorithmRef("scf_solver", "qdk", enable_gdm=True),
    stability_checker=AlgorithmRef(
        "stability_checker", "qdk", max_subspace=80,
        davidson_tolerance=1e-8, stability_tolerance=-1e-4,
    ),
)
robust_energy, robust_reference = robust.run(structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz")
```

Common parent SCF settings are copied to the child after nested construction, so the parent’s `max_iterations` wins over a competing nested override. The parent also supplies check flags and method to a compatible checker. Disabling both checks with positive cycles is not meaningful and will cause the native checker to reject the request.

The optional `"pyscf_stabilized"` implementation is different composition, not an alias for this native wrapper. It calls the PySCF mean-field object’s own `stability` routine, obtains candidate orbital rotations/status, preferentially follows an available external instability, converts to an unrestricted mean-field object when necessary, and reruns `kernel` with the new density. It does not call the separately registered QDK `"pyscf"` stability checker or inherit all that checker’s `nroots`/threshold controls. Its defaults are five cycles, both checks enabled, and failure on unresolved instability; zero cycles is passthrough. Its cycle setting is an integer without the native wrapper’s declared nonnegative bound, so supply a sensible nonnegative value explicitly. The regular adapter’s missing explicit `mf.converged` check is not repaired merely by naming the wrapper “stabilized.”

## A practical diagnostic record for stretched nitrogen

For our 1.85-Å case, first retain the exact geometry, electron count, basis definition, SCF type, method, backend, and configured thresholds. Check the iteration log and retained basis rank before interpreting the last decimal places. If residuals decrease steadily, a larger iteration cap may be justified. If they oscillate, compare the default hybrid with a deliberate alternative or a compatible orbital guess; do not change basis, functional, and optimizer simultaneously and then call the difference a convergence correction.

Next verify numerical consistency by tightening relevant thresholds and comparing converged energies and density-sensitive quantities, rather than assuming a requested tolerance is an error bar. Examine internal stability of a properly converged reference and external stability if the chosen reference and scientific question permit it. Keep the original restricted result when following an unrestricted branch: this is a change in allowed variational space and potentially spin character, not just deletion of a failed file.

The repository’s [stability tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_stability.py) include RHF nitrogen at 1.2 and 1.6 Å in def2-SVP with different internal/external status patterns. The [stabilized-SCF test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_scf.cpp) checks external-priority reoptimization at its own 1.6-Å def2-SVP model. Those are recorded source baselines establishing that these code paths matter; they are not the missing results of our cc-pVDZ 1.85-Å calculation. The standalone documentation workflow uses yet another geometry, 1.4 Å, and is a procedural example rather than our reference.

Finally, report exactly what was established: numerical convergence, the channels and curvature tolerance checked, whether reoptimization changed spin restrictions, and any remaining unresolved status. A stable HF reference remains an approximation. We now have a disciplined starting point for interpreting density and for asking a different question: how the energy changes when the **nuclei**, rather than the orbitals alone, move.
lessons.caveats: Read-only source/test tracing at 97a3ff4f; no calculations or tests run. All mathematical examples are illustrative and other N2 test geometries remain separate. Native stability rejects ROHF/ROKS although native SCF supports ROHF; GDM rejects MPI world_size>1. qdk_stabilized uses unscaled direction and external-first policy; rotate_only may pass an incompatible unrestricted guess to a restricted child. Native zero-cycle wrapper bypasses stability; PySCF no-analysis checker yields stable empty results and stabilized adapter does not add explicit kernel convergence checking. Actual DIIS/GDM switch is below absolute energy threshold. No prior prepared lessons were overwritten.

lessons.title: Moving nuclei and interpreting electron distribution
lessons.body:
# Lesson 7 — Moving nuclei and interpreting electron distribution

## An energy is only one kind of answer

Our fixed-geometry nitrogen calculation answers an energy question at 1.85 Å. It does not yet tell us how a chosen analysis partitions the electrons between atoms, which way the nuclei would be pushed, or where a particular electronic model predicts an equilibrium bond length. Those questions require different quantities and, sometimes, a different calculation.

We will keep three operations separate. **Population analysis** interprets an existing electronic state. **Nuclear differentiation** asks how its fully specified energy model changes with nuclear coordinates. **Geometry optimization** repeatedly uses energies and derivatives to choose new coordinates. None of these operations automatically adds electron correlation or validates the electronic branch it receives.

All examples are unexecuted API illustrations. Source tests are evidence of intended implementation behavior, not calculations run for this lesson. If we relax the N₂ geometry, the result would be a new scientific case, not a replacement for the original fixed 1.85-Å benchmark.

## Atomic populations are a convention for assigning shared density

The electronic density extends across the molecule; it does not arrive with a unique label saying which atom owns each electron. An **atomic population** assigns part of that density to an atom using a specified rule. A **partial charge** is the corresponding nuclear charge minus assigned electron population. Such charges are useful summaries, but are not unique atom-by-atom observables independent of basis and analysis method.

The actual public algorithm is `population_analyzer`. Both the native `"qdk"` implementation and optional `"pyscf"` implementation expose **Mulliken analysis**, selected by `method="mulliken"`. The [native schema](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/population_analysis.hpp) allows only that method. A method name is not an implementation name: `create("population_analyzer", "mulliken")` is not the native factory contract. Do not assume that every population scheme offered by the external PySCF project is exposed through this adapter.

Mulliken analysis uses the AO density matrix \(P\) and overlap matrix \(S\). Let \(A\) denote an atom and \(\mu\in A\) denote basis functions assigned to that atom. Its electron population is

\[
N_A=\sum_{\mu\in A}(PS)_{\mu\mu}
=\sum_{\mu\in A}\sum_\nu P_{\mu\nu}S_{\nu\mu}.
\]

This allocates overlap-associated density between the atoms carrying the basis functions. Summing all atomic populations recovers \(\operatorname{Tr}(PS)\), the total represented electron count. Summing only diagonal entries of \(P\) would ignore the overlap convention and generally be wrong.

As a purely illustrative two-function example, assign one basis function to each of two centers and let

\[
S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.2\\0.2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
P=\frac56\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Each diagonal entry of \(PS\) is one, so the two Mulliken populations sum to two. The trace of \(P\) alone is only five-thirds. These are invented matrices showing the mathematics, not computed H₂ or N₂ data.

For an all-electron calculation the partial charge is \(q_A=Z_A-N_A\), in units of the positive elementary charge. A positive value means fewer assigned electrons than nuclear charge. The molecular sum should agree with the specified total charge when all represented electrons are included. Individual Mulliken values need not behave like nonnegative probabilities, and they can be sensitive to diffuse functions or a changed basis. A large change after basis augmentation can be a partitioning effect rather than a large physical transfer of charge.

## The implementation uses the actual one-electron density, including correlation

A correlated wavefunction need not have an AO density of the simple HF form \(2C_{\mathrm{occ}}C_{\mathrm{occ}}^{\mathsf T}\). Its **one-particle reduced density matrix**, abbreviated 1-RDM, is a compact representation of one-electron information. In an MO basis we denote it by \(\gamma\): diagonal entries are orbital populations, and off-diagonal entries retain coherence between orbitals. Its full construction from many-electron amplitudes belongs to Lesson 9.

For a real restricted orbital representation, the transformation to the AO density is \(P=C\gamma C^{\mathsf T}\). Unrestricted calculations transform alpha and beta blocks separately and add their AO densities. Using only the diagonal occupations in a non-natural MO basis would discard information needed for the population analysis.

The [native analyzer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/population_analysis.cpp) reads the active-space 1-RDM, embeds it at the actual active orbital indices, and restores inactive occupied orbitals. For ordinary restricted electron orbitals those inactive diagonal entries are two; for each unrestricted spin block they are one. It then forms the AO density, multiplies by the overlap matrix, and uses the basis’s AO-to-atom mapping to assign the diagonal contributions.

This supports more than the initial HF determinant, provided the required density information exists. It requires real-valued 1-RDM data in the native implementation, appropriate spin-resolved blocks for unrestricted orbitals, and molecular orbitals carrying both a basis/structure and overlap matrix. Incompatible active-space dimensions or missing data are explicit errors. For `ModelOrbitals`, the native implementation instead reports populations from the site-basis density diagonal; that is a lattice-model interpretation, not atom-centered Gaussian analysis.

The [PySCF adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/population_analysis.py) similarly builds the density from the supplied wavefunction’s 1-RDM, calls PySCF’s `mulliken_pop`, and sums AO populations using PySCF’s atom slices. It returns electron populations, not the partial-charge array returned by a differently named external routine. The [native tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_population_analysis.cpp) specifically check overlap contraction, heteronuclear atom assignment, unrestricted density, correlated off-diagonal density, and inactive-core restoration.

For our existing `reference`, an ordinary API use would be:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create

populations = create("population_analyzer", "qdk", method="mulliken").run(reference)
basis = reference.get_orbitals().get_basis_set()
effective_charges = basis.get_effective_nuclear_charges()
partial_charges = [float(z) - n for z, n in zip(effective_charges, populations)]
```

For the all-electron N₂ case, effective and physical nuclear charges coincide. A density respecting interchange of the two nitrogen atoms should give equal populations; with fourteen represented electrons, that symmetry would imply seven on each. This is a symmetry expectation, not a measured result here.

The effective-charge expression also handles ECP bookkeeping correctly: compare the explicitly represented electron population with \(Z_A^{\mathrm{eff}}\), or equivalently restore removed core electrons before subtracting from physical \(Z_A\). Subtracting only explicit electrons from a heavy atom’s unreduced physical charge would manufacture a spurious large positive charge. Frozen inactive orbitals and ECP-replaced core electrons are separate accounting issues.

## The energy surface has nuclear coordinates as its arguments

Now regard the electronic energy, including the appropriate nuclear/core constant, as a function of all nuclear positions. With \(N_{\mathrm{at}}\) atoms, collect the Cartesian coordinates into

\[
R=(x_0,y_0,z_0,x_1,y_1,z_1,\ldots),\qquad d=3N_{\mathrm{at}}.
\]

A component of the **nuclear gradient** is \(g_a=\partial E/\partial R_a\). It tells us how the energy changes for a small displacement in coordinate \(a\). The corresponding mechanical force is \(F_a=-g_a\): nuclei accelerate downhill in energy, not uphill. Coordinates are in Bohr, energies in Hartree, gradients in Hartree/Bohr.

The **nuclear Hessian** is

\[
H^{\mathrm{nuc}}_{ab}=\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial R_a\partial R_b}.
\]

It is a \(d\)-by-\(d\) matrix, in Hartree/Bohr², describing how one coordinate’s gradient changes when another coordinate moves. It is not the electronic orbital Hessian used in Lesson 6. The latter varied orbitals at fixed nuclei; this one varies nuclei with the electronic calculation defined at each geometry.

For our two-atom case the gradient has six entries and the Hessian is six by six. A diatomic bond scan can be described by one chosen bond-length coordinate, but the Cartesian derivative API still returns all six nuclear components. In an isolated, well-converged calculation translational invariance implies the net force should be nearly zero. This provides a diagnostic, not an excuse to discard a nonzero net force before investigating it.

## The derivative objects preserve the geometry they refer to

[`NuclearGradients`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/nuclear_gradients.hpp) stores atom-major components: x, y, z for atom zero, then x, y, z for atom one. `get_values()` gives the flat vector, `as_matrix()` gives an atom-by-three matrix, and `get_atom_gradient(i)` retrieves one atom. It is a gradient object, so a forces array requires explicit negation.

[`NuclearHessian`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/nuclear_hessian.hpp) stores the matrix in the same coordinate order. `get_matrix()` returns it, and `get_atom_pair_block(i, j)` extracts the three-by-three block coupling atoms \(i\) and \(j\). Both objects retain a `Structure` identifying the geometry. Constructors reject a null structure or incorrect array shape; a correctly shaped matrix is not thereby a physically correct, converged Hessian.

Both support JSON and HDF5 with a serialization version, the associated structure, and explicit units. The [gradient serializer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/nuclear_gradients.cpp) writes `hartree/bohr`; the [Hessian serializer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/nuclear_hessian.cpp) writes `hartree/bohr^2`. File names follow the `nuclear_gradients` and `nuclear_hessian` type suffixes. No files are created in this preparation; this is the persistence contract for later use.

The computational interface is

```python
energy, gradients, hessian, wavefunction = calculator.run(
    structure, charge=0, spin_multiplicity=1,
    seed_or_basis="cc-pvdz", n_inactive_orbitals=0,
)
```

`hessian` and `wavefunction` are optional outputs and may be `None`. Returning a gradient does not imply a Hessian was computed. These names and the keyword `seed_or_basis` come from the [actual Python binding](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/pybind11/algorithms/nuclear_derivative.cpp), rather than an assumed common name shared by every algorithm.

## Analytic derivatives account for moving basis functions

An **analytic gradient** differentiates the mathematical energy expression and its integral ingredients. It does not mean an exact solution of the many-electron problem; an analytic HF gradient remains the derivative of an HF model.

At an accurately stationary variational solution, many first-order orbital-response terms can be eliminated through the stationarity conditions. But the Gaussian basis is attached to moving atoms. Moving a nucleus changes overlap and basis-dependent integrals as well as the explicit nuclear potential. The additional moving-basis contribution is commonly called the **Pulay term**. Keeping just electrostatic attraction derivatives and forgetting basis motion gives the wrong finite-basis force.

For a closed-shell SCF discussion, the gradient has the schematic structure

\[
g_a=\text{one-electron integral derivatives}
+\text{two-electron/XC derivative terms}
+\frac{\partial E_{\mathrm{nuc}}}{\partial R_a}
-\sum_{\mu\nu}W_{\mu\nu}\frac{\partial S_{\mu\nu}}{\partial R_a},
\]

where \(W\) is an energy-weighted occupied density matrix. The formula is a conceptual separation, not a complete replacement for the spin- and functional-dependent implementation.

The native [gradient assembly](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/scf/src/scf/scf_impl.cpp) includes nuclear repulsion, kinetic and attraction derivatives, overlap derivatives contracted with an energy-weighted quantity, ECP derivatives when present, electron-repulsion derivatives, and XC gradients for DFT. **Libint** provides ordinary Gaussian-integral derivatives; **Libecpint** provides ECP derivatives; **GauXC** supplies the native XC-gradient integration boundary. As established earlier, this native XC route uses ExchCXX built-in kernels rather than an assumed direct Libxc call.

The registered analytic implementation is `create("nuclear_derivative_calculator", "qdk")`, with alias `"analytical_gradient"`. Its [current wrapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/qdk_nuclear_derivative.cpp) requires its `energy_calculator` reference to be exactly `scf_solver/qdk`, requires `n_inactive_orbitals=0`, and rejects `compute_hessian=True`. There is no automatic numeric Hessian fallback inside that analytic implementation. It cannot be redirected to `pyscf`, `qdk_stabilized`, or a correlated calculator merely by changing the nested reference.

The wrapper uses native SCF’s analytic-gradient entry point and forwards its method settings. Representative [native tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_nuclear_derivative.cpp) compare analytic and numeric GGA, hybrid-GGA, open-shell hybrid-GGA, and range-separated DFT gradients. Those establish concrete tested paths, not a blanket claim that every reference restriction or every external functional is validated. A returned derivative remains subject to the underlying SCF support and convergence requirements. Analytic second derivatives would require additional electronic-response machinery; this public analytic calculator does not supply them.

## Finite differences trade extra electronic calculations for generality

The default derivative implementation is **`qdk_finite_difference`**, with alias `"numeric"`. It approximates derivatives by evaluating the total energy at displaced structures. The step \(h\) is a nuclear displacement in Bohr, not an SCF mixing factor.

For coordinate direction \(a\), central differences give

\[
g_a\approx\frac{E(R+h e_a)-E(R-h e_a)}{2h},
\]

where \(e_a\) is a unit coordinate vector. The diagonal Hessian element is

\[
H^{\mathrm{nuc}}_{aa}\approx
\frac{E(R+h e_a)-2E(R)+E(R-h e_a)}{h^2}.
\]

For different coordinates \(a,b\), the mixed element uses four doubly displaced geometries:

\[
H^{\mathrm{nuc}}_{ab}\approx
\frac{E_{++}-E_{+-}-E_{-+}+E_{--}}{4h^2},
\]

with, for example, \(E_{+-}=E(R+h e_a-h e_b)\). The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/finite_difference_nuclear_derivative.cpp) computes these expressions directly from energies, reuses the single-coordinate energies for diagonal elements, and writes symmetric off-diagonal pairs. It is not a Hessian obtained by finite-differencing analytic gradients.

`finite_difference_step` defaults to `1e-3` Bohr with a declared allowed range of `1e-8` to `1.0`. For a smooth energy surface the central formulas have truncation error of order \(h^2\). But energy noise is amplified by approximately \(1/h\) for gradients and \(1/h^2\) for Hessians. Reducing the step can therefore make the result worse unless the electronic calculations are sufficiently accurate and stay on a consistent branch.

For illustration, an energy uncertainty scale of \(10^{-8}\) Hartree with \(h=10^{-3}\) Bohr can generate a gradient-noise scale around \(10^{-5}\) Hartree/Bohr and a Hessian-noise scale around \(10^{-2}\) Hartree/Bohr², with coefficients depending on the differences combined. These are order-of-magnitude arithmetic estimates, not error bars produced by the library.

The cost is explicit. With \(d=3N_{\mathrm{at}}\), a gradient uses \(1+2d\) energy evaluations, including the central energy. With a full Hessian this implementation uses \(1+2d^2\) in total. For N₂, \(d=6\), so those counts are 13 and 73. They count complete energy evaluations, not SCF iterations. Each displaced calculation can have its own convergence cost. The [water derivative test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_nuclear_derivative.cpp) checks shapes, finite values, near-zero total gradient, and symmetric numeric Hessian data without implying that every step choice is reliable.

## Which energy methods can finite differences actually call?

The shared derivative settings contain an `energy_calculator` `AlgorithmRef`. Unlike many fixed-type nested settings, this reference is intentionally allowed to change algorithm type. Nevertheless, the [energy-dispatch code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/nuclear_derivative_detail.cpp) handles specific families, not every possible registered algorithm.

For `scf_solver`, it directly calls the selected solver and returns its total energy and wavefunction. The default is `qdk`; an optional registered PySCF SCF implementation can be selected for the numeric route, subject to its own conventions. `orbital_solver` is ignored for this direct SCF path.

For `multi_configuration_scf`, the numeric route supplies reference orbitals and active alpha/beta counts to an MCSCF calculator, such as the available PySCF implementation. For `multi_configuration_calculator`, it first builds a Hamiltonian using the nested `hamiltonian_constructor`, then calls a calculator such as `macis_cas` or `macis_asci`. Those correlated methods are taught later. A coupled-cluster calculator is not silently supported merely because it also reports an energy: unhandled algorithm types raise an explicit error.

The default `orbital_solver` and `hamiltonian_constructor` are native `qdk`. Optional `localize_reference_orbitals=True` acts only on multireference paths and uses a nested localizer, default `qdk_pipek_mezey`, on the current active orbital indices. This is a representation-control step, not a replacement for choosing a scientifically appropriate active space.

`n_inactive_orbitals` subtracts that many doubly occupied orbitals from each spin population to determine active counts. The helper validates positive multiplicity, nonnegative explicit electron count after ECP accounting, compatible charge/spin parity, and that inactive count does not exceed either spin population. The multireference paths currently require positive active counts for both spins. Even when the selected SCF path does not use an active space, invalid inactive-count input is still rejected; for our first examples it is zero.

Seed behavior is especially important for finite differences. The central energy may use an appropriate `Orbitals` or `Wavefunction` seed. Displaced evaluations intentionally regenerate orbitals from a named basis rather than reuse coefficient matrices whose basis centers belong to the undisplaced geometry. `reuse_seed_active_space=True` preserves active/inactive **indices** for multireference evaluations; it does not preserve displaced coefficients or guarantee chemical orbital continuity. This will motivate Lesson 8.

A seed whose basis has the explicit `custom_basis_set` name is rejected for displaced numeric evaluations. Other nonstandard names must actually be resolvable when reloaded. A basis object carrying custom shells but masquerading as a standard name should not be assumed to retain those custom shells after displacement. With an optional SCF backend, numeric derivative validation also needs a basis representation the QDK counting path can understand, not only a name recognized by the external engine.

The default `suppress_child_algorithm_logging=True` temporarily raises the process-global native logger threshold during child energy evaluations. For convergence diagnosis, setting it false preserves the current child logging. That makes a large numeric calculation easier to diagnose without pretending a logging setting changes its physics.

## First obtain derivatives without changing the benchmark geometry

A useful analytic-gradient request for the nitrogen model is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef

analytic = create(
    "nuclear_derivative_calculator", "qdk",
    energy_calculator=AlgorithmRef(
        "scf_solver", "qdk", method="hf", convergence_threshold=1e-9,
    ),
)
energy_at_stretch, gradients, no_hessian, reference_at_stretch = analytic.run(
    structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz", 0,
)
forces = -gradients.as_matrix()
```

The tighter electronic tolerance is a deliberate numerical choice for derivative work, not a new HF approximation. `forces` would have two rows and three columns. No values or force directions are being reported here.

If a Hessian is required, choose a separate numeric calculator:

```python
numeric = create(
    "nuclear_derivative_calculator", "qdk_finite_difference",
    compute_hessian=True, finite_difference_step=1e-3,
    energy_calculator=AlgorithmRef(
        "scf_solver", "qdk", method="hf", convergence_threshold=1e-9,
    ),
)
energy_check, numeric_gradients, nuclear_hessian, numeric_reference = numeric.run(
    structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz", 0,
)
```

These are complete requested operations, not guarantees that this step and tolerance suffice near every electronic instability. Compare numeric gradients with analytic ones where supported and repeat a step-size study before interpreting delicate curvatures. The [release example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/release_notes_v2_0.py) shows the same separation between analytic gradients and numeric Hessians on its own small H₂ example.

## Geometry optimization asks a different scientific question

A **geometry optimization** repeatedly chooses nuclear displacements to reduce the energy or locate a specified saddle point. This differs from a **scan**, where we prescribe a sequence of geometries or bond lengths and evaluate them. It also differs from **dynamics**, where forces, masses, initial conditions, and time integration describe motion. An optimization step is not a physical time step.

Near a candidate geometry, a local quadratic approximation combines the gradient with a curvature model. A minimum-search method moves in a downhill direction and limits the step when the local model is not trustworthy. A transition-state search instead seeks a first-order saddle: one meaningful downhill curvature direction and uphill curvature in the remaining internal directions. It therefore cannot be understood as merely “minimize harder.”

At a stationary geometry the nuclear gradient is small, but classification needs curvature. For an isolated nonlinear molecule, three translations and three rotations produce zero modes ideally; a linear molecule has three translations and two independent rotations. Thus linear N₂ has one internal vibrational mode after removing five rigid-motion directions. Small numerical deviations in those nominal zero modes must not automatically be interpreted as reaction-coordinate instabilities.

For harmonic vibrational interpretation, one forms the mass-weighted matrix \(M^{-1/2}H^{\mathrm{nuc}}M^{-1/2}\), where \(M\) contains each atomic mass repeated for its three coordinates. Its internal eigenvectors describe coordinated motions, and eigenvalues relate to squared harmonic frequencies after unit conversion. A negative internal eigenvalue is associated with an imaginary harmonic frequency. This is the conceptual next analysis of a Hessian, not a claim that the data object automatically computes normal modes, vibrational thermochemistry, tunneling, or reaction rates.

Geometry convergence must also be conditional on a well-defined electronic energy branch. If one displaced SCF point is a different spin-broken solution or an unconverged iterate, its difference from its neighbor need not be a derivative of one smooth surface. A stabilized electronic solver can help find locally stable branches, but switching branches can introduce its own discontinuities. Keep electronic stability and nuclear stationary-point classification separate.

## geomeTRIC supplies the nuclear optimizer; QDK supplies the engine

The available implementation here is the optional **`geometry_optimizer/geometric`** plugin. The C++ factory declares `"geometric"` as its default name but has no built-in concrete optimizer registration; the [plugin](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/geometric/__init__.py) registers it when the external `geometric` package is available. A default name therefore does not prove availability on this environment.

The plugin’s `optimizer` setting defaults to `"tric"`. **TRIC** means translation–rotation–internal coordinates: molecular or fragment translation and rotation are represented explicitly alongside internal bond/angle-like motion, improving the coordinate description for many optimizations. Internal coordinates describe molecular distortions more naturally than independently stepping every x/y/z entry. They change the optimization coordinates, not the underlying energy model.

The adapter accepts the forwarded coordinate-system names `tric`, `tric-p`, `dlc`, `hdlc`, `prim`, and `cart`. Delocalized internal coordinates combine primitive internal-coordinate directions; hybrid schemes combine coordinate descriptions; `cart` uses Cartesian coordinates. The important API distinction is that these are `optimizer` choices passed to geomeTRIC, not separately registered algorithms named `geometric_tric` or `geometric_cart`. Their detailed coordinate construction is external geomeTRIC functionality, not reimplemented in this repository.

The [adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/geometric/geometry_optimizer.py) constructs a geomeTRIC molecule whose stored geometry is in Ångstrom using geomeTRIC’s own `bohr2ang` constant. The custom engine receives optimizer coordinates in Bohr, constructs a new QDK `Structure` preserving element/mass/nuclear-charge information, and calls the configured derivative calculator. It returns a Hartree energy and atom-major Hartree/Bohr gradient to geomeTRIC. It does not negate the gradient into forces because the optimizer asks for an energy gradient.

Final geomeTRIC geometries are converted back from Ångstrom to Bohr using that same external constant; the last engine geometry can be used as a fallback. Using one consistent conversion constant at both boundaries avoids tiny artificial mismatches with cached evaluations. The [plugin tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_geometric_plugin.py) explicitly check the Bohr engine contract and final-coordinate conversion.

The engine retains the original optimization input on repeated calls; it is not a general orbital/basis transport service. A basis-name string, as in our example, avoids assuming an arbitrary original orbital seed or custom basis has automatically followed every new geometry. The selected derivative calculator must be able to rebuild the scientific model at those coordinates.

## The geometry controls and their exact units

The shared settings use a nested `derivative_calculator`, default `nuclear_derivative_calculator/qdk_finite_difference`, `max_iterations=300`, and `compute_hessian=False`. The iteration cap has a declared range from one to one million. This cap counts geometry steps, not the electronic evaluations inside each derivative call.

The geomeTRIC extension supplies these default convergence thresholds:

| Quantity | Setting | Default and unit |
|---|---|---|
| Energy change | `convergence_energy` | `1e-6` Hartree |
| RMS gradient | `convergence_rms_gradient` | `3e-4` Hartree/Bohr |
| Maximum gradient | `convergence_max_gradient` | `4.5e-4` Hartree/Bohr |
| RMS displacement | `convergence_rms_displacement` | `1.2e-3` Å |
| Maximum displacement | `convergence_max_displacement` | `1.8e-3` Å |

RMS means root mean square, a combined measure of many components; the maximum criterion prevents one large component from being hidden by the average. By default geomeTRIC requires the five criteria together. Each exposed threshold has a declared range of zero to one in its stated units. `transition_state=False` selects minimization; setting it true forwards geomeTRIC’s transition-state search flag. `print_level=0` controls external verbosity.

`compute_hessian` has a precise separate meaning. During geometry iterations the adapter sets the derivative calculator’s Hessian flag false. After optimization, if a final Hessian was requested it creates a fresh derivative calculator and evaluates it at the optimized structure. This final reporting option is not a request to use that Hessian at every optimizer step, nor an explicit initial transition-state Hessian input.

Consequently, selecting analytic `qdk` derivatives and also `compute_hessian=True` on the optimizer fails at the final derivative request: the analytic implementation rejects Hessians. Use numeric derivatives for that combined workflow, or optimize with analytic gradients and explicitly request a separate numeric Hessian afterward.

The return contract is `(energy, optimized_structure, hessian, wavefunction)`, with the latter two optional. If a matching final engine evaluation is cached and no Hessian is requested, the adapter reuses its energy/wavefunction; otherwise it evaluates the final geometry again. It does not return a new detailed optimization-history object or an independent convergence certificate. Underlying derivative/optimizer errors remain important; a plausible final geometry alone does not establish a transition state. A missing coordinate payload can fall back to the engine’s last coordinates, so meaningful success interpretation remains tied to the upstream run and requested criteria.

## A controlled relaxation fork, not a silent change of benchmark

Here is a source-backed configuration pattern adapted to our nitrogen variables. It requests analytic gradients during optimization and leaves the original `structure` untouched:

```python
optimizer = create(
    "geometry_optimizer", "geometric",
    optimizer="tric", max_iterations=50, compute_hessian=False,
    derivative_calculator=AlgorithmRef(
        "nuclear_derivative_calculator", "qdk",
        energy_calculator=AlgorithmRef(
            "scf_solver", "qdk", method="hf", convergence_threshold=1e-9,
        ),
    ),
)
relaxed_energy, relaxed_structure, no_hessian, relaxed_reference = optimizer.run(
    structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz", 0,
)
```

This is not an executed result, a recommendation that RHF is adequate for stretched N₂, or a promise of the experimental equilibrium distance. It defines an optimization on a particular model and orbital branch. To classify the resulting stationary point, apply a supported nuclear Hessian calculation and electronic checks separately.

The repository’s [geomeTRIC release example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/release_notes_v2_1.py) instead starts H₂ at 1.4 **Bohr** and uses numeric derivatives with a `1e-2`-Bohr step. Its smoke test compares to an HF/STO-3G reference bond length. Those are a different molecule, basis, and starting geometry, not evidence for our nitrogen equilibrium. The ordinary external optimizer uses working files and logging infrastructure; none of it was invoked in this read-only course preparation.

## What these outputs can and cannot justify

A Mulliken population can explain how one chosen convention partitions density and can help compare related calculations with consistent bases. A nuclear gradient identifies first-order forces on a chosen electronic energy surface. A Hessian describes local nuclear curvature. A converged geometry optimizer can locate a stationary structure within its model and search setup. None alone establishes a full reaction mechanism, a thermodynamic free energy, or a reaction rate.

For the original fixed-geometry QPE problem, we may deliberately keep 1.85 Å because the scientific objective is a difficult stretched-bond electronic energy, not equilibrium optimization. Population and force diagnostics are still useful, but they do not authorize relabeling a relaxed calculation as the same benchmark. The extra classical cost also belongs to any honest end-to-end workflow accounting: 73 energy evaluations for a numeric diatomic Hessian are not one electronic calculation simply because one high-level method returned the result.

We have also encountered a representation problem that will grow along a bond scan. Orbital indices can remain numerically identical while their chemical character changes. The next lesson develops canonical, natural, and localized orbital descriptions so those handoffs become chemically intelligible, without assuming that a rotation automatically preserves every truncated many-electron approximation.
lessons.caveats: Source and tests inspected at 97a3ff4f without execution. Population analyzer exposes Mulliken only; native requires real 1-RDM and proper overlap/basis data. Analytic derivative requires scf_solver/qdk and no inactive orbitals and supplies no Hessian; no automatic fallback. Numeric derivatives call only implemented SCF/MCSCF/MC energy families, reject explicit custom-named bases on displaced evaluations, and preserve seed active-space indices rather than orbital character. Geometry plugin is optional and uses original seed on repeated calls; examples use basis-name strings to avoid claiming general orbital transport. geomeTRIC internals are external; only adapter contracts/options and tests were traced. Final compute_hessian with analytic derivative raises. No normal-mode, thermochemistry, rates, or new nitrogen result is claimed.

lessons.title: Choosing more useful orbitals
lessons.body:
# Lesson 8 — Choosing more useful orbitals

## The same orbital space can be described in different ways

Our original N₂ reference has 28 spatial orbitals in cc-pVDZ. SCF naturally supplies **canonical orbitals**, which diagonalize the effective mean-field operator. These are convenient for orbital energies and perturbative formulas, but they need not be the most useful orbitals for describing bonds, comparing geometries, selecting a reduced model, or constructing compact approximate wavefunctions.

This lesson changes the orbital description, not the geometry. The nitrogen nuclei remain 1.85 Å apart unless an explicitly separate example says otherwise. We will distinguish three goals: spatial localization, diagonalization of one-electron density, and optimization of more specialized representation objectives. A method called a localizer in the registry can serve any of these goals; not all of its outputs are spatially localized.

No localization, density calculation, cube evaluation, or test was executed during preparation. Code excerpts describe supported calls and their source-level limitations. Illustrative matrices are mathematical examples, not nitrogen outputs.

## What an orbital rotation does—and what it does not preserve

Let the columns of \(C\) contain molecular-orbital coefficients in the AO basis, and let \(S\) be the AO overlap. Starting from \(C^{\mathsf T}SC=I\), a real orthogonal rotation \(U\) gives

\[
C^{\prime}=CU,\qquad U^{\mathsf T}U=I,
\qquad {C^{\prime}}^{\mathsf T}SC^{\prime}=I.
\]

The rotated orbitals span the same selected space. They are not new basis functions fitted to the atom, and the AO basis size has not decreased. Consequently, a rotation alone does not reduce the number of electron spin modes or qubits in an unreduced representation.

If \(U\) mixes only occupied orbitals of a determinant, that determinant changes only by the determinant of \(U\), an unobservable overall phase for a unitary transformation. Rotations among unoccupied orbitals leave the occupied determinant unchanged as well. In UHF this applies separately within the occupied alpha and beta spaces. Mixing occupied and unoccupied orbitals generally changes the determinant and its energy; that was the purpose of the stability perturbations in Lesson 6.

A fully represented many-electron state can be expressed in another orbital basis without changing the physics, but its determinant amplitudes must be transformed too. Likewise, an exact complete-active-space calculation is invariant under rotations inside the same complete active space when its Hamiltonian and wavefunction are treated consistently. An **active space** is the subset of orbitals retained for explicit many-electron correlation; inactive orbitals are fixed occupied orbitals, while excluded orbitals lie outside that correlated model. Mixing across those boundaries changes a truncated model unless its definition is changed consistently.

For a one-particle density matrix \(\gamma\) in the MO basis, consistent re-expression is

\[
\gamma^{\prime}=U^{\mathsf T}\gamma U,
\qquad C^{\prime}\gamma^{\prime}{C^{\prime}}^{\mathsf T}
=C\gamma C^{\mathsf T}.
\]

The AO density, and therefore a consistently defined Mulliken population, is unchanged. Keeping old determinant coefficients after changing occupied–virtual orbitals is not this transformation. Neither is retaining old active-space labels while mixing their orbitals with an excluded space.

## The QDK localizer return contract is especially important

The public Python class is `OrbitalLocalizer`, backed by the C++ `Localizer` interface. The call is

```python
transformed_reference = localizer.run(wavefunction, loc_indices_a, loc_indices_b)
transformed_orbitals = transformed_reference.get_orbitals()
```

The result is a `Wavefunction`, not an `Orbitals` object despite some older docstrings. The two index lists select columns to transform. Use sorted, unique, valid zero-based indices. For a restricted common spatial-orbital set the lists must agree. An empty list means no orbitals in that channel, not “use all.”

Crucially, current localizers return a **single Aufbau determinant carrier with updated orbitals**. They do not in general transform and preserve an input CI expansion or coupled-cluster amplitudes. Some methods attach derived, transformed 1-RDM data, but this does not turn the carrier’s single determinant into the original correlated state. Even an empty selection can return such a new single-reference carrier with unchanged orbital coefficients. The [factory helpers and implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/localization.cpp) make that behavior explicit.

Thus a correlated input should be retained. Use the returned orbitals to build a new Hamiltonian and solve the chosen correlated problem in that representation before interpreting new CI coefficients, energies, or entropies. The fact that a transformed 1-RDM is attached is not proof that every higher-order property of the original state survived.

At this revision the native registry provides `qdk_pipek_mezey`, `qdk_vvhv`, `qdk_natural_orbitals`, `qdk_gauge_fixing`, `qdk_active_space_qio`, and the deprecated `qdk_mp2_natural_orbitals`. The optional PySCF multi-method implementation is named **`pyscf_multi`**, not `pyscf`. Use `available("orbital_localizer")` in an ordinary installed environment to discover which are registered. This course has inspected the registrations rather than importing the package.

## Canonical orbitals solve a different optimization problem

Canonical SCF orbitals diagonalize the effective Fock or Kohn–Sham operator. Localization instead chooses a different basis inside an allowed subspace by optimizing a localization objective. A lower localization objective is not a lower HF total energy; for occupied-only rotations the determinant energy is unchanged to numerical accuracy.

A canonical orbital may extend over both nitrogen atoms and have definite molecular symmetry. That is not a flaw. Delocalization can be the cleanest description of the mean-field operator. Localized combinations can instead make bond and atom-centered character easier to see. Degenerate or nearly degenerate orbital energies also make individual canonical columns nonunique or sensitive to small changes in geometry.

After a nontrivial rotation, the original list of orbital energies does not generally diagonalize the transformed mean-field matrix. Native Pipek–Mezey, natural-orbital, and VVHV outputs invalidate orbital energies. The current PySCF localizer adapter copies input energy arrays into its output, so their presence must not be interpreted as proof that the localized columns are canonical. Algorithms requiring canonical orbital energies need a scientifically consistent canonical reference, not merely `has_energies()==True`.

## Pipek–Mezey concentrates an orbital’s atomic populations

**Pipek–Mezey (PM)** localization favors orbitals whose population is concentrated on a smaller number of atoms. For one normalized orbital \(p\), define its Mulliken population on atom \(A\) as

\[
Q_A^p=\sum_{\mu\in A}C_{\mu p}(SC)_{\mu p}.
\]

This is the population of one orbital with unit normalization, not a net atomic partial charge and not a factor-of-two closed-shell electron count. Native PM maximizes

\[
L_{\mathrm{PM}}=\sum_p\sum_A (Q_A^p)^2.
\]

For illustration, an orbital split equally between two atoms contributes \(0.5^2+0.5^2=0.5\); an orbital wholly assigned to one atom contributes one. Maximizing the sum therefore favors concentration under the chosen population rule. Bond orbitals can still extend across two atoms; “localized” does not mean each orbital becomes a delta function on a nucleus.

The [native implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/localization/pipek_mezey.cpp) uses Jacobi, or pairwise plane, rotations. For two orbitals,

\[
\phi_s^{\prime}=\cos\theta\,\phi_s+\sin\theta\,\phi_t,
\qquad
\phi_t^{\prime}=-\sin\theta\,\phi_s+\cos\theta\,\phi_t.
\]

It computes atomic populations and cross-populations, derives candidate rotation angles and objective increases for orbital pairs, applies advantageous rotations, and repeats sweeps. The overlap-times-coefficient matrix is rotated alongside the coefficients, avoiding a full recomputation from scratch for each pair.

The internal stopping controls have defaults `tolerance=1e-6`, `max_iterations=10000`, and `small_rotation_tolerance=1e-12`; the schema requires at least two iterations. `tolerance` is used for objective-change and small proposed angle/increase tests, not an electronic energy accuracy. `small_rotation_tolerance` zeros small intermediate pair coefficients before choosing angles. The internal routine logs whether it converged, but returns its last coefficient matrix rather than throwing solely because the sweep limit was reached.

There is a concrete current limitation: the public `qdk_pipek_mezey` wrapper constructs a fresh internal default settings object rather than forwarding its own configured settings to the iterative routine. Those exposed settings can be stored, but changing them is not honored by this wrapper’s calculation at this revision. We therefore do not present a changed tolerance as a verified control of native PM convergence. The VVHV path below does forward its settings to its internal PM object. This is a source-level behavior to account for, not a request to modify the repository.

Native PM requires the molecular basis, its atom mapping, and AO overlap. It localizes **the selected columns as one group**. It does not automatically split a mixed input list into occupied, inactive, active, or virtual subsets. If preserving the HF determinant is the goal, select occupied and virtual groups separately. If preserving a later frozen-core partition is also important, separate core and valence occupied groups too.

For our original restricted HF `reference`, localizing only its seven occupied orbitals is a valid determinant-preserving illustration:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create

n_alpha, n_beta = reference.get_total_num_electrons()
occupied = list(range(n_alpha))
pm = create("orbital_localizer", "qdk_pipek_mezey")
occupied_localized = pm.run(reference, occupied, occupied)
```

This assumes the original RHF reference, not an unrestricted result from the stability workflow. It changes occupied orbital shapes, not the electron count or molecular geometry. The [native localization tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_localization.cpp) explicitly check metric values, overlap orthonormality, selected-space unitary transformations, and separate occupied/virtual calls.

## Boys, Edmiston–Ruedenberg, and Cholesky offer different meanings of local

The optional implementation is configured, for example, as

```python
boys = create("orbital_localizer", "pyscf_multi", method="foster-boys")
boys_reference = boys.run(reference, occupied, occupied)
```

The [adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/localization.py) dispatches to PySCF’s `lo.PM`, `lo.Boys`, `lo.ER`, or `lo.cholesky_mos`. QDK supplies the converted basis and selected coefficient columns; the external library supplies those localization implementations.

**Foster–Boys** minimizes total orbital spatial spread:

\[
L_{\mathrm{Boys}}=\sum_p
\left(\langle\phi_p|r^2|\phi_p\rangle
-\left|\langle\phi_p|\mathbf r|\phi_p\rangle\right|^2\right).
\]

The first term measures the squared distance distribution and the second removes the squared position of its center. For rotations within a fixed subspace, the sum of the first terms is invariant, so one can equivalently maximize the sum of squared orbital centers. Dipole/moment integrals connect this spatial objective to the coefficient matrices. This can produce compact bond or lone-pair descriptions without relying on Mulliken atom assignments.

**Edmiston–Ruedenberg (ER)** instead maximizes the sum of each orbital’s Coulomb self-repulsion:

\[
L_{\mathrm{ER}}=\sum_p(pp|pp)
=\sum_p\iint
\frac{|\phi_p(\mathbf r)|^2|\phi_p(\mathbf r^{\prime})|^2}
{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r^{\prime}|}\,d\mathbf r\,d\mathbf r^{\prime}.
\]

Concentrating an orbital’s density tends to increase that self-repulsion, making it a localization objective. We are maximizing this auxiliary quantity while not changing the physical occupied determinant under an occupied-only rotation. This is not a proposal to maximize the molecule’s total electron-repulsion energy. ER requires two-electron integral work and is generally more expensive than population- or moment-based localization.

**Cholesky localization**, selected by `method="cholesky"`, is a noniterative alternative based on a rank-revealing factorization of the selected orbital subspace’s coefficient-density/projector representation. Pivoting identifies independent AO-associated directions, and factorization constructs a localized spanning set. Conceptually one factors a matrix built from \(C_{\mathrm{sel}}C_{\mathrm{sel}}^{\mathsf T}\); in the complete-rank case the new factors span the same selected subspace. It is cheaper than optimizing every orbital-pair objective repeatedly, but does not guarantee the optimum of Boys, PM, or ER. This is not Cholesky factorization of the four-index electron-repulsion tensor, which is a different subject in Lesson 12.

For PySCF PM only, `population_method` defaults to `"mulliken"` and accepts `"lowdin"`, `"meta_lowdin"`, and `"becke"` as well. Löwdin analysis assigns populations after symmetric AO orthogonalization; meta-Löwdin is an external modified orthogonalization/atomic-partition scheme; Becke uses smooth atom-centered real-space weights rather than assigning overlap terms solely by AO labels. These change the PM localization criterion. They do not add those methods to the standalone `population_analyzer`, which exposed only Mulliken in Lesson 7.

The adapter defines `occupation_threshold=1e-10`, but its current localization body does not use it to partition the chosen columns. Despite broad docstrings about automatic separation, callers must choose their groups. Its schema also does not forward arbitrary PySCF localization iteration tolerances; external defaults govern the kernel calls shown here.

A small but important input limitation is visible in the current code: the helper’s single-index path returns the full input matrix before the caller copies its first column back to the selected slot. A nonzero singleton selection can therefore copy column zero into that slot rather than act as a no-op. Do not use singleton calls to this adapter as an assumed harmless operation; skip localization of one-column groups at the calling level. This is particularly relevant when separately treating one singly occupied ROHF orbital. Multi-column occupied selections such as the nitrogen example follow the actual localization kernels.

## Natural orbitals diagonalize density, not spatial spread

The 1-RDM introduced in Lesson 7 can be written in many orbital bases. **Natural orbitals** diagonalize it:

\[
\gamma U=U n,\qquad \phi_p^{\mathrm{NO}}=\sum_q\phi_qU_{qp}.
\]

\(n\) is diagonal, and its entries are natural-orbital occupation numbers, often abbreviated NOONs. For a physical electron 1-RDM in a common spatial-orbital basis, spin-traced occupations lie between zero and two; spin-resolved occupations lie between zero and one. Their sum is the corresponding electron count. Natural orbitals need not be spatially localized.

An illustrative matrix

\[
\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.3\\0.3&1\end{pmatrix}
\]

has occupations 1.3 and 0.7 in the equal-weight plus/minus orbital combinations. Off-diagonal coherence in the original basis becomes unequal diagonal populations in the natural basis. This is a density-matrix example, not the two-determinant Hamiltonian from Lesson 2 and not a computed nitrogen density.

For an RHF determinant, the spin-traced 1-RDM has occupations two and zero, so the occupied and virtual natural-orbital subspaces are highly degenerate. Natural-orbital analysis of that determinant alone cannot reveal the correlated occupations it never contained. Fractional occupations from a correlated density can signal that a single paired determinant is inadequate, but the interpretation depends on where the density came from.

In particular, a spin-traced UHF/UKS density can have fractional spatial occupations even though its full spin-orbital state is one determinant. Adding two different spin projectors need not give a spatial matrix with only zero/two eigenvalues. Thus fractional spatial NOONs are not by themselves proof that an exact correlated wavefunction has been obtained. Approximate perturbative density matrices also require physical-consistency checks.

The native **`qdk_natural_orbitals`** implementation has no configurable algorithm settings. Its [actual requirements](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/localization/natural_orbitals.cpp) are stricter than “any occupation vector”: matching alpha/beta active and inactive spaces, identical selected lists exactly equal to the active-space indices, AO overlap, and real spin-dependent active 1-RDM blocks of the correct dimensions. It adds the spin blocks, symmetrizes small numerical asymmetry, diagonalizes the active density, and sorts occupations in descending order. Only the active coefficient columns are replaced.

For unrestricted input, it reconstructs each active spin density in the AO basis and projects both into the selected alpha spatial-orbital span before diagonalization. The output is restricted. If the beta active span is not contained in that target span, this projection is not a guaranteed lossless re-expression of the whole unrestricted active density. Full common-space examples avoid that problem, but matching orbital indices alone does not prove matching spans.

The output invalidates canonical energies and carries rotated spin-resolved and spin-traced 1-RDM data, together with its single-reference carrier. Preserve the original correlated state and re-solve for new correlated amplitudes when needed. The [natural-orbital regression](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_natural_orbital_localizer.py) uses a deliberately spin-broken PBE/UKS N₂ calculation at **2.0 Å** and verifies descending fractional occupations in the full space. That is a test of this capability, not a result for our 1.85-Å HF calculation.

## The older MP2-natural-orbital shortcut is still registered, but deprecated

**`qdk_mp2_natural_orbitals`** constructs a selected-space Hamiltonian and asks MACIS for a density-derived orbital transformation from second-order Møller–Plesset perturbation theory, MP2. MP2 estimates correlation through excitations from a canonical reference, weighted by electron interactions and orbital-energy differences. Near small denominators, such as strongly stretched-bond situations, a perturbative approximation can become unreliable; its natural orbitals are not automatically superior.

The [legacy implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/localization/mp2_natural_orbitals.cpp) requires restricted closed-shell input with orbital energies, matching sorted selections, and both occupied and virtual orbitals in the chosen subset. It constructs integrals, calls `macis::mp2_natural_orbitals`, rotates the selected columns, clears orbital energies, and attaches a spin-traced occupation-density payload. Electron counts come from the input wavefunction, not missing user settings suggested by an old error message.

Its [deprecation guidance](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/localization/mp2_natural_orbitals.hpp) is to use `qdk_natural_orbitals` with a wavefunction that already supplies the MP2 active-space 1-RDM. That separates generation of an approximate correlated density from the generic diagonalization step. A suitable MP2 RDM must be generated or imported separately. The current native dynamical-correlation MP2 calculator returns amplitude storage, not an RDM-bearing state; Lesson 11 explains that boundary.

## VVHV separates useful virtual character from excess flexibility

Virtual orbitals are unoccupied in the reference determinant, not physically irrelevant. They provide directions for excitations and orbital response. In a large flexible basis, however, ordinary localization of the entire virtual space can mix chemically interpretable valence-antibonding directions with many high-flexibility functions. The objective may become poorly tied to the chemical distinction we care about.

**Valence-virtual/hard-virtual separation (VVHV)** uses a minimal basis as a reference vocabulary. Valence virtuals are the part of that compact vocabulary orthogonal to occupied orbitals. Hard virtuals complete the remaining full-basis virtual space. “Hard” is a construction label for extra basis flexibility, not a theorem that these orbitals never matter for chemistry or correlation.

The native implementation is `"qdk_vvhv"`. Its [current call contract](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/localization/vvhv.cpp) requires **all virtual orbital indices**, not all molecular orbitals, in each applicable spin channel. Some header text says all orbitals; the implementation and successful tests pass only the virtual range. It leaves occupied coefficients unchanged. For a restricted reference, the two lists must match; for unrestricted input it constructs each spin’s virtual complement separately. It currently rejects a reduced-rank basis where AO and MO counts differ.

Let \(S_{FF}\) be overlap in the full basis and \(S_{FM}\) cross-overlap between full and minimal basis functions. The construction first represents the minimal functions in the full AO basis by solving a least-squares problem equivalent, in a well-conditioned full-rank case, to

\[
T=S_{FF}^{-1}S_{FM}.
\]

It orthonormalizes this compact representation in the full-basis metric. With occupied coefficients \(C_o\), it projects away occupied components:

\[
T_v=(I-C_oC_o^{\mathsf T}S_{FF})T.
\]

After removing the expected near-null directions and orthonormalizing the remainder, these columns form valence virtuals. This explains the linear algebra: subtract components already represented by occupied orbitals, rather than deciding valence character from an arbitrary virtual energy cutoff.

The current inner iterative localizer is **Pipek–Mezey**, explicitly constructed in the wrapper. It localizes the valence-virtual set. Although an internal class accepts an inner-localizer object, the public settings do not expose a choice of Boys or ER for that role. Occupied localization is a separate call before VVHV, not something the present VVHV wrapper automatically performs.

Hard virtuals are constructed atom by atom and angular-momentum block by angular-momentum block. The implementation builds prototype hard directions, projects atom-centered functions out of the combined occupied-plus-valence-virtual space, aligns the remaining directions with the prototypes, and orthogonalizes them globally. This supplies an AO-linked description of the full complement rather than a freely rotating virtual set with no chemical reference.

`minimal_basis` defaults to `"sto-3g"` and accepts `"sto-3g*"`. `weighted_orthogonalization=True` computes orbital spreads from dipole and quadrupole integrals and weights each hard-virtual column by the inverse of its spread plus `1e-6` before the final orthogonalization. This biases the resulting orthogonal set toward compact directions. The inherited iterative tolerances are forwarded to the inner PM routine on this path. Projection orthogonalizations also use fixed numerical cutoffs and check expected rank separation; some separation problems are warnings, while size/mapping/rank incompatibilities are errors. Neither a completion log nor a successful return proves that a chosen minimal basis defines the best scientific partition.

For nitrogen, the stored STO-3G resource contains two s functions and one p shell per atom: five spatial functions per N, ten for N₂. With seven occupied orbitals, the ideal full-rank count is three valence virtuals and \(28-10=18\) hard virtuals, totaling the original 21 virtuals. These are resource-derived counts, not a new localization result. No spin mode has been removed.

A correctly scoped unexecuted call is:

```python
n_mo = reference.get_orbitals().get_num_molecular_orbitals()
virtual = list(range(n_alpha, n_mo))
vvhv = create("orbital_localizer", "qdk_vvhv", minimal_basis="sto-3g")
partitioned_reference = vvhv.run(occupied_localized, virtual, virtual)
```

The [VVHV tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_localization.cpp) use this occupied-PM-then-virtual-VVHV pattern and test active-space metadata preservation. Preserved metadata means the same indices are stored; if the chosen virtual transformation crosses a later active/excluded boundary, that alone does not preserve the chemical content of a truncated model. Plan the partition and transformation together.

## Natural-orbital degeneracy leaves a gauge choice

A **gauge choice** here means a choice of orbital basis inside a subspace that has no unique individual vectors under the preceding criterion. If several natural occupations are equal, any orthogonal rotation within that block keeps the spin-traced 1-RDM diagonal. The subspace is determined, but its individual orbitals are not.

The native **`qdk_gauge_fixing`** method makes that choice more reproducible and then targets a quantum-representation objective. It requires restricted natural orbitals, real nearly diagonal active 1-RDM data, overlap, and identical valid selected lists. A selection may cover a subset of the active space but cannot split an occupation-degenerate block.

The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/localization/gauge_fixing.cpp) first anchors selected blocks to independent AO-associated directions. It then performs coordinate-descent sweeps over pair rotations within those blocks. Each trial is judged by a mapped coefficient norm

\[
\lambda=\sum_\ell |h_\ell|,
\]

where \(h_\ell\) are coefficients of the mapped active-space Hamiltonian in a qubit-operator expansion. We will derive that expansion later; for now, this is a measure of the size of the operator description, not an electronic energy. The current objective sets the separate core-energy offset to zero and is evaluated before qubit tapering.

The native code builds a reference Hamiltonian once after anchoring, transforms its one- and two-electron integrals for candidate rotations using MACIS utilities, maps them with the native Jordan–Wigner machinery, and sums coefficient magnitudes. Each objective evaluation is therefore substantially more expensive than a small matrix norm. It uses `angle_samples=32` over \([0,\pi)\), followed by scalar golden-section refinement, and accepts rotations only when the objective improves by more than `improvement_tolerance=1e-10` Hartree.

`degeneracy_tolerance=1e-6` controls the allowed occupation spread in each block. `max_sweeps=3` limits coordinate-descent passes; zero requests AO anchoring only. `hamiltonian_constructor` is a nested reference, native `qdk` by default. The settings enforce at least four angle samples, nonnegative sweep count, and finite meaningful tolerances through schema and runtime checks.
