The initial AO anchoring need not improve \(\lambda\) relative to an arbitrary input orientation; the monotonic acceptance rule applies to the following optimization from that anchor. Nor does reducing this one objective prove a lower complete resource estimate: synthesis precision, state preparation, tapering, repetitions, and the chosen quantum algorithm also matter. The method carries transformed 1-RDM information but still does not carry the original CI expansion. The [gauge-fixing tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_gauge_fixing_localizer.py) verify occupation spectra and CASCI energy invariance by rebuilding and re-solving, rather than treating the returned determinant carrier as the correlated answer.

## Quantum-information orbitals use local uncertainty as an objective

The remaining native method, **`qdk_active_space_qio`**, rotates a fixed restricted active space to minimize the sum of single-orbital entropies. QIO means quantum-information orbitals. It is not an active-space selector and does not implement full-space QIO or a method that mixes across the active boundary.

For a spatial orbital, the local occupations are empty, alpha-only, beta-only, and doubly occupied. Let \(n_\alpha,n_\beta\) be its spin populations and \(d\) its double-occupation expectation, which requires two-particle information. The four probabilities are

\[
p_0=1-n_\alpha-n_\beta+d,\quad
p_\alpha=n_\alpha-d,\quad
p_\beta=n_\beta-d,\quad p_2=d.
\]

The local entropy is \(s=-\sum_k p_k\ln p_k\), with zero-probability contributions taken as zero. The [shared entropy helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/orbital_entropy.hpp) uses natural logarithms. The objective is \(\sum_i s_i\) over active orbitals. A rotation changes which orbital subsystems carry uncertainty and correlation; it need not reduce the overall many-electron correlation or localize orbitals in physical space.

The [QIO implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/localization/active_space_qio.cpp) requires real spin-dependent active 1- and 2-RDMs, restricted orbitals with overlap, and matching selected indices exactly equal to the active space. Restricted open-shell input is supported; unrestricted orbitals are rejected. It tests pair rotations using a coarse and then fine angle scan, accepts entropy-reducing moves, rotates working RDM tensors, and accumulates one overall orbital rotation.

Its actual controls are `max_cycles=200`, `convergence_tolerance=1e-10` for sweep-to-sweep entropy-sum change, `coarse_angle_step=0.02` radians, `fine_samples=201`, and `improvement_tolerance=1e-12` for accepting a pair improvement. The coarse step is bounded between `1e-4` and \(\pi/2\), fine samples must be at least four, and the tolerance settings are checked for finiteness. Reaching a cycle limit returns the accumulated transformation; it is not a global entropy-minimum certificate.

Two-particle density storage grows as the fourth power of active orbital count, and repeatedly rotating/inspecting it is not free. The method keeps the input physical state’s density information fixed for the representation search; it does not solve a new correlated eigenproblem after every trial angle. Output contains the transformed orbitals and rotated 1-RDM payloads, generally not diagonal, but not the original correlated coefficients or a retained transformed 2-RDM payload. The [QIO tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_active_space_qio_localizer.py) explicitly run CASCI again before comparing final entropy and energy. That is the correct conceptual handoff, and the full RDM machinery will be taught in Lesson 9.

## See the orbital without mistaking the picture for an observable

A **cube grid** samples a scalar field in a rectangular region of space. For an orbital it evaluates \(\phi_p(\mathbf r)=\sum_\mu C_{\mu p}\chi_\mu(\mathbf r)\); for a density it evaluates the corresponding quadratic expression. An orbital isosurface is a surface at a chosen positive or negative amplitude. Its colors commonly distinguish sign/phase, not positive versus negative electron charge. Changing an orbital’s overall sign changes the picture’s colors but not its one-orbital density.

The native [`CubeGrid` and `CubeGenerator`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/utils/cube_generator.hpp) use Bohr for origin, spacing, and margin. `CubeGrid.from_basis_set` encloses the nuclear bounding box plus a margin; spacing divides each padded extent by the number of intervals. The default grid is 80 points per axis with a 3-Bohr margin. A one-point axis has zero spacing. Axes are Cartesian-aligned, and the backend imposes an `INT_MAX` total-point limit; that limit is not a practical memory recommendation.

The generator translates the basis once and uses GauXC’s **host orbital evaluator**, a different role from its DFT quadrature routines. It supports correctly represented spherical and Cartesian Gaussian basis data; that evaluator capability does not remove the earlier limitations of high-level SCF/adapter Cartesian workflows. Coefficient ordering and normalization must match the basis. For ECP models it samples the explicitly represented density; removed core density is not reconstructed.

A complete no-output-file API illustration for one localized orbital is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data.symmetry import SymmetryLabel, axes
from qdk_chemistry.utils import CubeGenerator, CubeGrid

local_orbitals = occupied_localized.get_orbitals()
basis = local_orbitals.get_basis_set()
alpha = SymmetryLabel([axes.alpha()])
coefficients = local_orbitals.coefficients().block([alpha, alpha])
grid = CubeGrid.from_basis_set(basis, 40, 40, 40, 3.0)
field = CubeGenerator(basis).orbital(coefficients[:, 6], grid)
```

The Python binding returns an array shaped `(40, 40, 40)` here. Column six is a selected localized orbital; after localization it should not automatically be called the highest-energy occupied canonical orbital. No grid evaluation was performed in preparing this lesson, even though this particular lower-level API can return a field without writing a cube file.

`CubeGenerator.density` uses the supplied AO density exactly as given. It does not add a missing spin factor or sum separate spin blocks. Supplying half the restricted total density produces half the density field with exactly the same array shape. The [cube tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_utils_cube_generator.py) compare AO evaluation with PySCF, test that a rank-one density gives the squared orbital, and verify linear scaling of the supplied density matrix.

For file-oriented workflows, `generate_orbital_cubes` writes one zero-indexed file per requested spatial orbital, with separate alpha/beta files for unrestricted orbitals. The Python convenience helper [`generate_cubefiles_from_orbitals`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/cubegen.py) defaults to a 40-cubed grid and can use native or optional PySCF evaluation. Its `output_folder=None` mode returns cube text, but **still creates and removes intermediate files**; it is not a disk-free API. It was not called under this task’s read-only constraints. Full viewer/UI integration is reserved for Lesson 32.

## Choose orbitals for a purpose and check the relevant invariants

For the current nitrogen story, occupied PM orbitals can help interpret the mean-field reference; VVHV can organize the remaining virtual flexibility without throwing it away. A correlated 1-RDM can later produce natural occupations for evidence-based active-space decisions. Gauge fixing and QIO optimize still different objectives. No single orbital set is guaranteed best for every subsequent solver or quantum algorithm.

Useful checks depend on the claim. For a purported rotation within a selected space, verify overlap orthonormality and the selected-space transformation. For occupied-only HF localization, compare the occupied AO density and energy rather than individual column values, which may differ by signs and rotations. For an active-space transformation, preserve its boundaries and re-solve the correlated model before comparing CI energies. For visualization, check grid units, spin factors, and basis ordering before trusting attractive lobes.

Along a bond-stretching scan, orbitals can change sign, exchange order, or rotate inside degenerate subspaces. Localized or AO-anchored descriptions can help maintain chemical interpretation, but the current per-geometry localizers do not guarantee a globally smooth matching of orbitals across geometries. VVHV supplies a minimal-basis reference, not an automatic proof that orbital index twelve denotes the same chemical direction everywhere. Natural-orbital degeneracies are another reason to compare subspaces and character rather than index alone.

Finally, locality can reduce the importance of some long-range integrals or make selected CI amplitudes more compact, but Coulomb interactions remain long ranged and improvements are conditional. A different orbital representation can also make an approximation less compact. Claims of fewer terms, easier state preparation, or lower resource estimates must be tested for the chosen downstream algorithm, truncation, and precision—not inferred merely from the word “localized.”

We now have the vocabulary to separate basis functions, molecular-orbital coefficients, occupation/density information, and determinant amplitudes. The next lesson turns that last distinction into an actual correlated electronic solution: configuration interaction, selected determinant methods, and the reduced density matrices that many of these orbital transformations require.
lessons.caveats: No localization, chemistry import, cube evaluation or test executed. All localizers return Aufbau determinant carriers rather than transformed CI/CC coefficients; special 1-RDM payloads are not full correlated-state preservation. Native PM wrapper currently ignores its configured iterative settings and its kernel may return after nonconvergence. PySCF localizer is pyscf_multi, does not use occupation_threshold for automatic grouping, preserves stale energy arrays, and its nonzero-singleton path can copy column zero; avoid singleton calls. VVHV requires all virtual indices, not all MOs, retains occupied columns, and rejects reduced AO/MO rank. Unrestricted natural orbitals project onto alpha active span; lossless representation is conditional. Gauge objective excludes separate core offset and anchoring is not guaranteed to improve lambda. QIO needs real spin-dependent 1/2-RDM and returns only rotated 1-RDM payloads with carrier. Cube convenience helper output_folder=None still uses intermediate files; lower-level evaluation can be disk-free but was not run. Lesson 11 source tracing clarified the earlier MP2 handoff sentence: qdk_mp2_calculator does not itself produce the RDM required by qdk_natural_orbitals.

lessons.title: Describing interacting electrons classically
lessons.body:
# Lesson 9 — Describing interacting electrons classically

## Optimize the many-electron coefficients, not only the orbitals

At the stretched N₂ geometry, one optimized determinant can remain an inadequate description even after its SCF residual is small and its allowed stability tests pass. Orbitals describe one-electron shapes. Correlation also requires flexibility in how several electrons occupy those shapes together.

We now hold a chosen orbital representation fixed and write

\[
|\Psi\rangle=\sum_{I\in\mathcal D}c_I|D_I\rangle.
\]

\(D_I\) is a Slater determinant, \(\mathcal D\) is the chosen determinant collection, and \(c_I\) is its amplitude. Unlike the MO coefficients \(C_{\mu p}\), these amplitudes describe a many-electron superposition. **Configuration interaction (CI)** optimizes them by solving the Hamiltonian eigenvalue problem in that determinant space.

The same principle underlies full CI, CASCI, selected CI, and the projected solver in this repository. They differ primarily in which determinant space they provide and how they search or diagonalize it. They do not all optimize the orbitals; that is the MCSCF question in Lesson 11.

Our running molecular model remains neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å with 28 spatial orbitals in cc-pVDZ. Nothing in this lesson claims a newly executed calculation. Small matrices are illustrative, and separate molecular examples are explicitly identified.

## Configuration records need an orbital basis and a consistent sector

For an electron spin-half `Configuration`, each spatial-orbital slot has one of the values `0`, `u`, `d`, or `2`: empty, alpha-only, beta-only, or doubly occupied. `Configuration.from_spin_half_string("2du0")` records occupations, not spatial orbital shapes or amplitudes. A determinant acquires its physical meaning only when paired with a particular ordered orbital basis and fermionic ordering convention.

A [`ConfigurationSet`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/configuration_set.hpp) associates a collection of configurations with `Orbitals` and a single-particle sector name such as `"electrons"`. That sector label identifies the kind of particles/basis being represented; it is not itself a constraint fixing electron number or total spin. For active-space calculations, configuration positions refer to the active-orbital ordering, not necessarily to consecutive positions in the full original MO matrix. Inactive filled orbitals are represented through the orbital metadata and Hamiltonian, rather than repeated in every active configuration string.

The [packed representation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/configuration.hpp) uses two bits per spin-half spatial slot, or one bit per slot for a generic bitstring configuration. `capacity()` reflects byte-padded storage; `ConfigurationSet.num_modes()` derives the meaningful non-padded count from its orbitals. Here a spin-half slot can represent two electron spin modes; it is not automatically one occupation qubit. Conversion to MACIS bitsets places alpha occupation in the low half and beta occupation in the high half. A string’s displayed length, packed capacity, active spatial-orbital count, and qubit count must not be treated as synonyms.

The concrete [ConfigurationSet validation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/configuration_set.cpp) checks consistent capacities and, for a nonempty defined active window, sufficient capacity and no occupied overhang. Despite broader header wording, it deliberately omits particle-number and spin-conservation checks. It is also a vector-like collection, not a mathematical set that automatically removes duplicates. Supply unique determinants in the desired electron-number sector yourself.

For fixed alpha/beta counts, the determinant dimension in \(K\) spatial orbitals is \(\binom K{N_\alpha}\binom K{N_\beta}\). We already counted 400 for three alpha and three beta electrons in six spatial orbitals. The full nitrogen count is enormous; a compact bit record does not remove the combinatorial number of such records.

Fixing \(N_\alpha-N_\beta\) fixes a spin projection. It does not uniquely request a total-spin eigenvalue. Even a full determinant calculation in one projection sector can contain several total-spin sectors, and an incomplete selected determinant space may not be closed under total-spin operations. These interfaces take active alpha/beta counts, not a separate guaranteed singlet-targeting instruction. Spin interpretation must be checked rather than inferred only from equal counts.

## Slater–Condon connectivity keeps the matrix structured

Define the CI matrix by \(H_{IJ}=\langle D_I|\hat H|D_J\rangle\). The diagonal is the energy of determinant \(I\); off-diagonal entries couple different occupations. The stationary coefficients satisfy

\[
\sum_J H_{IJ}c_J=Ec_I.
\]

A one-electron operator can remove an electron from one occupied spin orbital and place it in one unoccupied spin orbital: a **single excitation**. A two-electron operator can change at most two occupations: a **double excitation**. Consequently, a Hamiltonian containing only one- and two-electron terms has zero matrix elements between determinants differing by more than two excitations. These are the central **Slater–Condon rules**. The diagonal and connected entries can be evaluated from the molecular integrals without integrating the full many-electron coordinate wavefunction afresh.

The nonzero values include fermionic signs. Creation and annihilation operators are algebraic operations for adding or removing occupation in a specified ordered list of spin orbitals. Passing an operator through an occupied mode changes sign. That bookkeeping expresses antisymmetry; omitting it changes interference and energies, not merely the appearance of the coefficient vector. The bundled [MACIS determinant operations](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/sd_operations.hpp) and [excitation contribution code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/asci/determinant_contributions.hpp) implement these connectivity and sign operations.

An explicitly illustrative two-determinant matrix is

\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}-1.0&-0.1\\-0.1&-0.6\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{Ha}.
\]

The first determinant alone has energy −1.0 Hartree. Optimizing both amplitudes gives a lowest eigenvalue \(-0.8-\sqrt{0.05}\approx-1.0236068\) Hartree. The lowering comes from coherent mixing through the off-diagonal coupling. This is not a molecular result or a repeat of the different toy matrix in Lesson 2.

For an exact Hermitian Hamiltonian and an orthonormal determinant subspace, the lowest projected eigenvalue is variational: enlarging a nested determinant space cannot raise its exact minimum. In practice matrix-element screening and incomplete eigensolver convergence introduce separate numerical approximations. A smaller selected space may also be replaced, rather than enlarged, during selection refinement, so successive reported energies need not decrease monotonically.

## FCI, CASCI, and selected CI reduce different things

**Full configuration interaction (FCI)** includes every determinant with the prescribed particle counts in the finite orbital space. It is exact within that finite model and the specified sector, not exact continuum chemistry. It still carries basis, relativistic/ECP, frozen-core, and other modeling assumptions.

**Complete active space CI (CASCI)** includes every allowed determinant in a selected active orbital space while holding inactive orbitals filled and excluded orbitals outside the correlated treatment. The word complete refers to the active determinant space. Selecting six active orbitals and then solving all 400 determinants for three alpha/three beta electrons is different from selecting 400 determinants spread over 28 active orbitals.

**Selected CI** keeps only chosen determinants from a potentially much larger orbital space. This can target important configurations economically, but sacrifices completeness. **ASCI**, adaptive sampling configuration interaction, selects and refines that determinant list using estimates of missing amplitudes; its name does not mean that this native solver executes a quantum sampling experiment.

The actual [multi-configuration interface](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/mc.hpp) is `run(hamiltonian, n_active_alpha_electrons, n_active_beta_electrons)`, returning `(energy, wavefunction)`. Those counts are active electrons, not automatically the molecule’s full fourteen. The Hamiltonian has an active one-body operator, two-body integrals, and a constant core energy. Native solvers diagonalize the active electronic matrix and add `hamiltonian.get_core_energy()` to the reported result. Do not add that constant a second time or assume it is only physical nuclear repulsion when inactive orbitals or ECPs are present.

## The native complete-space solver and its real limits

The default implementation is **`multi_configuration_calculator/macis_cas`**. The [adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/macis_cas.cpp) requires a restricted Hamiltonian and identical alpha/beta active orbital indices. Restricted means a common spatial-orbital representation; unequal active alpha/beta counts can still describe an open-shell sector. An unrestricted HF result is not accepted directly just because a common API produced it.

MACIS generates alpha occupation combinations, beta combinations, and their Cartesian product. The adapter constructs a `SortedDoubleLoopHamiltonianGenerator` from restricted one- and two-electron integrals. Its sorting exploits determinant connectivity when building matrix elements; it does not change the physical determinant space.

For one determinant the result is its diagonal matrix element with coefficient one. For a determinant dimension at or below `iterative_solver_dimension_cutoff=2000`, the adapter builds a sparse CSR Hamiltonian, converts it to a dense matrix, and calls LAPACK’s symmetric eigensolver. **CSR**, compressed sparse row storage, records nonzero values and their column positions grouped by row. Dense diagonalization stores all matrix entries and computes all eigenpairs even though this API returns only the lowest state.

For larger spaces the complete determinant list still exists, and the selected-CI diagonalization machinery builds a sparse Hamiltonian and runs Davidson. This is not a magic matrix-free FCI method that avoids enumerating all determinants. Memory includes the determinant list, sparse nonzero entries, vectors, and eigensolver workspace.

The true bitset dispatch in [`macis_base.hpp`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/macis_base.hpp) supports active-orbital representation widths up to 2048 spatial slots through successively larger template bitsets. Some older method comments say 128. Neither number is a feasible FCI problem-size promise: a representation may fit one determinant while the required number of determinants is impossible to store.

The [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_mc.cpp) exercise one-determinant cases and force the iterative path on a 441-determinant water/STO-3G space by lowering the cutoff. Those are regression cases, not demonstrations that the full 28-orbital nitrogen problem is cheap.

## Davidson solves the coefficient problem in a small expanding subspace

Given a trial coefficient vector \(c\), its energy estimate is the Rayleigh quotient, \(E=c^{\dagger}Hc/(c^{\dagger}c)\). The residual

\[
r=Hc-Ec
\]

measures failure to satisfy the eigenvalue equation. A small energy change alone is not the same as a small residual.

Davidson maintains several orthonormal trial vectors, projects \(H\) into their span, diagonalizes that small projected matrix, and constructs an improved full-space vector. It then approximately preconditions the residual using the Hamiltonian diagonal:

\[
t_I\approx-\frac{r_I}{H_{II}-E}.
\]

Small denominators are regularized; the new direction is orthogonalized against the current subspace and added if useful. This trades dense full-space diagonalization for repeated sparse matrix–vector products plus small dense eigenproblems.

The [bundled implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/solvers/davidson.hpp) uses double reorthogonalization, a default minimum denominator magnitude of `1e-12`, and an explicit residual-norm stopping test. It calls **sparsexx** for sparse matrix/vector work and **lobpcgxx’s Rayleigh–Ritz helper** for the projected problem. That helper use does not mean the exposed CI solver is a separate LOBPCG algorithm. BLAS/LAPACK provide underlying numerical algebra.

`ci_residual_tolerance` defaults to `1e-6`; its declared range is zero to one, but zero should not be read as a useful guarantee of an exactly zero floating-point residual. `ci_matel_tol` defaults to machine epsilon, approximately `2.2e-16`, and controls sparsification of CI Hamiltonian entries, not selection of determinant amplitudes.

A naming subtlety matters: the QDK setting **`max_solver_iterations=200` is mapped to MACIS `ci_max_subspace`**, the maximum Davidson subspace dimension. In the current non-restarted Davidson implementation this also limits the sequence of expansions, but it is not an independently configurable general iteration budget. The limit is clamped to matrix dimension; failure to converge throws `Davidson Did Not Converge!`. Increasing it uses more full coefficient-sized vectors, not just a few scalar bookkeeping entries. Dense CAS/PMC cases do not use this residual stopping loop.

MACIS is bundled source with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory/University of California origins and Microsoft contributions recorded in its headers. It supplies determinant algorithms and solvers, not a remote service. Its tree contains MPI paths, but the enclosing QDK build configuration disables MACIS MPI in the configured integration, and selected incremental/RDM paths contain additional MPI restrictions. Do not infer that every visible parallel library or every build option participates in every solve.

## A small complete CI handoff, without attempting full nitrogen FCI

The repository’s [MC example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/mc_calculator.py) uses H₂ at 0.740848 Å in STO-3G. Here is that separate small-system pattern with density outputs requested explicitly:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import Ansatz, Structure

h2_structure = Structure.from_xyz("""2
Separate small CI example
H 0.0 0.0 0.0
H 0.0 0.0 0.740848
""")
_, h2_reference = create("scf_solver", "qdk").run(h2_structure, 0, 1, "sto-3g")
h2_hamiltonian = create("hamiltonian_constructor", "qdk").run(h2_reference.get_orbitals())
ci = create(
    "multi_configuration_calculator", "macis_cas",
    calculate_one_rdm=True, calculate_two_rdm=True,
)
h2_energy, h2_ci = ci.run(h2_hamiltonian, 1, 1)
energy_from_density = Ansatz(h2_hamiltonian, h2_ci).calculate_energy()
```

These calls were not executed. In this finite two-spatial-orbital example there are four determinants in the fixed one-alpha/one-beta sector. The final line requests a consistency check using the returned densities, not another optimization. Its energy should agree with the CI result within the applicable numerical conventions and tolerances. We will select a tractable nitrogen active space in Lesson 10 instead of pretending this H₂ calculation solved stretched N₂.

## Projected MC optimizes coefficients on a supplied determinant list

The implementation **`projected_multi_configuration_calculator/macis_pmc`** receives a Hamiltonian and an explicit list of `Configuration` objects. It builds and diagonalizes the Hamiltonian restricted to those determinants, using the same one-determinant/dense/iterative size distinction as CAS. The list is a free input: it may come from a scientific heuristic, a sampled support, or a deliberately constructed excitation set.

For the separate H₂ example, a two-configuration request would be:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data import Configuration

pmc = create("projected_multi_configuration_calculator", "macis_pmc")
selected = [Configuration.from_spin_half_string("20"),
            Configuration.from_spin_half_string("02")]
projected_energy, projected_state = pmc.run(h2_hamiltonian, selected)
```

The result optimizes both coefficients anew. In contrast, `wavefunction.truncate(k)` keeps the largest-magnitude amplitudes and renormalizes the retained vector; it does not rediagonalize the projected Hamiltonian. For a fixed valid subspace, coefficient reoptimization can do no worse than any normalized truncated candidate in that same subspace. The projected solver is therefore not merely a sophisticated spelling of truncation.

The [current projected adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/macis_pmc.cpp) rejects unrestricted Hamiltonians, insufficient configuration capacity and empty determinant lists. Its list validation is not a complete physical-sector or uniqueness validator. Provide unique determinants with consistent active indexing and particle counts. Duplicate records are not independent orthonormal basis functions, even if an input path accepts them. The [PMC tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_pmc.py) establish the projected energy/coefficient interface; they should not be read as permission to ignore those mathematical requirements.

## ASCI estimates which missing determinants are worth adding

In **`macis_asci`**, the variational determinant list evolves. Suppose a current approximation has energy \(E\) and amplitudes \(c_I\). Rearranging the CI equation suggests a missing determinant \(J\) might have amplitude approximately

\[
\widetilde c_J\approx
\frac{\sum_{I\in\mathcal C}H_{JI}c_I}{E-H_{JJ}},
\]

where \(\mathcal C\) is a selected set of important **core determinants**. Here core means search seeds, not frozen core electrons or core orbitals. The denominator measures the candidate diagonal energy relative to the current eigenvalue; near-degenerate candidates can become important. Signed contributions from several parents must be accumulated before ranking because they can reinforce or cancel.

The [contribution kernels](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/asci/determinant_contributions.hpp) generate connected single and double excitations, include fermionic signs, compute diagonal estimates efficiently, and store numerator/denominator contributions. The [search](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/asci/determinant_search.hpp) accumulates repeated candidates and keeps those with large ratio magnitudes. These ratios guide selection; they are not normalized final amplitudes. The chosen list is then rediagonalized to obtain the variational coefficients.

The native [adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/macis_asci.cpp) starts from the canonical HF determinant. Growth increases the target determinant count; refinement repeatedly replaces/searches the list and rediagonalizes at approximately fixed size. If `ntdets_max` is strictly greater than the computed full-CI dimension, the adapter instead invokes the complete-space path. Equality is not that shortcut’s condition. The CAS/PMC dense-size cutoff is not the adaptive ASCI solver’s general dispatch rule.

The important default controls are:

| Control | Current default and meaning |
|---|---|
| `ntdets_max` | `100000`, target variational determinant size |
| `ntdets_min` | `100`, minimum requested growth size, not a guaranteed returned size |
| `core_selection_strategy` | `"percentage"`, choose search seeds by accumulated squared coefficient weight |
| `core_selection_threshold` | `0.95`, target retained search-core weight |
| `ncdets_max` | `100`, limit used by `"fixed"` core selection, not a cap on percentage selection |
| `search_matel_tol` | `1e-8`, screens weighted coupling contributions in the excitation kernels |
| `rv_prune_tol` | `1e-8`, prunes small candidate ratio contributions |
| `grow_factor` | `8.0`, requested multiplicative growth factor |
| `max_refine_iter` | `6`, nominal refinement budget; zero skips refinement |
| `refine_energy_tol` | `1e-6` Hartree, successive refinement-energy stopping threshold |

Percentage selection can require far more than 100 core determinants when weight is diffuse. Thus `ncdets_max=100` does not make the default search cheap in a strongly multiconfigurational state. `just_singles=False` includes doubles; setting it true changes which connected configurations are searched and can omit essential correlation. Search constraint levels partition work; they are not a total-spin setting or a declaration that only that excitation rank exists.

Growth uses a minimum factor of `1.01`, backs off with `growth_backoff_rate=0.5` if the requested size is not achieved, and recovers toward the requested factor using `growth_recovery_rate=1.1`. It can stop when no further growth is achieved. These [growth semantics](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/asci/grow.hpp) are more informative than treating `ntdets_max` as a guaranteed determinant count.

Refinement checks energy changes but retains a separately converged CI solve at each step. The [current refinement routine](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/asci/refine.hpp) can detect an oscillation and diagonalize the union of two determinant sets, extending the iteration budget by a bounded amount. That union can exceed the nominal trial target, so the target is not a hard peak-memory bound. If refinement does not meet its criterion, it throws rather than silently labeling the last list converged.

Warm-starting Davidson is enabled by default. Old coefficients are mapped by determinant identity into the new list and normalized if their retained vector norm meets `min_warm_start_overlap=0.5`. This is an L2 norm threshold, not a fifty-percent retained probability statement. Incremental Hamiltonian construction reuses sufficiently overlapping lists with `min_patch_overlap=0.3`; otherwise it rebuilds. `grow_ci_residual_tolerance=0` means use the refinement tolerance, and positive values allow a looser growth solve. `taper_grow_factor=0` disables the optional reduced final expansion factor.

The matrix-construction strategies `sorted_double_loop`, `residue_arrays`, and `dynamic_bit_masking` organize detection of connected determinants, not different physical Hamiltonians. The default is the sorted double loop. Residue arrays use excitation-deletion patterns and incur per-determinant electron-pair memory; the adapter falls back to the sorted method above sixty active electrons. Dynamic bit masking filters candidate connections using bit patterns; `dynamic_bit_masking_num_masks=0` uses its internal default. Unknown strategy strings currently fall back to the sorted method, so inspect the chosen settings rather than infer a new algorithm from a typo.

`pair_size_max=500000000` concerns stored search contributions and can imply substantial memory; it is not the total determinant target or a process-memory budget. More generous selection thresholds and larger determinant spaces need a deliberate resource plan. Conversely, a sparse state with large retained weight can still miss an energetically important collection of small amplitudes. Selection and refinement thresholds are not certified chemical-error bounds.

Several `pt2_*` controls are exposed from the bundled ASCI settings, but this wrapper’s return path does not execute an additional perturbative PT2 energy-correction stage. Its returned energy is the selected variational result plus the core constant. Also leave `grow_with_rot=False` in the present course workflow: the bundled optional route rotates integral arrays during growth, while this adapter does not return the accumulated orbital transformation with its original orbital object. It should not be presented as a provenance-safe drop-in orbital optimization. Use explicit orbital transformations and consistent Hamiltonian reconstruction instead.

## Reduced density matrices retain what few-electron observables need

A full many-electron state contains vastly more information than is required for a one-electron observable such as density. **Reducing**, or tracing out, the unobserved particles means summing over their possibilities while retaining coherence in the coordinates or orbitals we still observe. It is not choosing the single most likely configuration.

For a normalized \(N\)-electron wavefunction, a coordinate-space 1-RDM can be expressed as

\[
\gamma(x,x^{\prime})=N\int
\Psi(x,X)\Psi^*(x^{\prime},X)\,dX,
\]

where \(x\) includes position and spin and \(X\) stands for the other electron coordinates. Its trace is \(N\), not one, because it represents electron counts. A two-particle RDM analog retains two electron coordinates with a factor \(N(N-1)\), counting ordered electron pairs. In a finite orbital representation, these become matrices/tensors that can be built by summing amplitude products and operator matrix elements between connected determinants.

Use a consistent convention. For the real molecular path here, the one-body density convention can be written \(\gamma_{pq}=\langle a_q^{\dagger}a_p\rangle\). The QDK [two-body convention](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/wavefunction.hpp) is

\[
\Gamma(p,q,r,s)=\langle a_p^{\dagger}a_r^{\dagger}a_s a_q\rangle.
\]

The symbols \(a^{\dagger}\) and \(a\) are the creation/removal operators already used for fermionic signs. A diagonal one-body element is an occupation; a two-body entry describes a pair occupation or pair coherence. For one doubly occupied spatial orbital, the opposite-spin \(\Gamma^{\alpha\beta}_{iiii}\) is one and its spin-traced ordered-pair value is two. In a normalized fixed-N full active-space density, \(\sum_{pr}\Gamma(p,p,r,r)=N(N-1)\).

The spin-dependent accessors return alpha and beta 1-RDM blocks and the `aaaa`, `aabb`, `bbbb` 2-RDM blocks. Spin tracing adds alpha/beta one-body blocks; for two-body data it includes both opposite-spin orientations, with an index-pair transpose where needed. It is not always just doubling one supplied tensor. Public two-body arrays are flattened with the last index fastest: \(pK^3+qK^2+rK+s\). These conventions matter as much as array shape.

For a restricted Hamiltonian, the actual [`Ansatz.calculate_energy`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/ansatz.cpp) contracts

\[
E=E_{\mathrm{core}}+
\sum_{pq}h_{pq}\gamma_{qp}
+\frac12\sum_{pqrs}g_{pqrs}\Gamma_{rspq}.
\]

Here \(g\) is the stored chemist-ordered two-electron tensor, and the explicit pair permutation is the implementation’s indexing convention. For unrestricted storage, same-spin terms carry one-half factors and the combined opposite-spin contribution carries factor one. Follow the matching producer and consumer’s explicit index contractions: a legacy beta-first comment is not a universal storage convention. Lesson 12 traces the native alpha-alpha|beta-beta production and reconstruction paths. Reuse the provided contraction or verify the exact convention before writing a guessed `einsum`. This particular native energy-contraction implementation expects real RDM variants; complex coefficient storage elsewhere does not imply universal complex-property support.

There is a genuine interface-normalization caveat. CAS/ASCI’s shared wavefunction builder multiplies MACIS spin-dependent two-RDMs by two to convert the bundled half-weighted convention to the QDK convention. PMC’s separate eager RDM path stores the raw spin-traced MACIS two-RDM without the same conversion. Therefore eager PMC two-RDM data must not be assumed interchangeable with CAS/ASCI for the above energy formula; verify pair traces and energy consistency before consuming it. Our RDM example deliberately uses CAS. This conclusion comes from the [builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/macis_base.hpp), the projected adapter, and [MACIS RDM contribution factors](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/include/macis/util/rdms.hpp), not a newly run calculation.

## Ask for expensive density and entropy data deliberately

The common MC flags default false: `calculate_one_rdm`, `calculate_two_rdm`, `calculate_single_orbital_entropies`, `calculate_two_orbital_entropies`, and `calculate_mutual_information`. CAS/ASCI’s builder supports the corresponding requested products. A one-RDM block has \(K^2\) entries; a two-RDM block has \(K^4\), and several spin blocks can be required. Computing them also involves determinant-pair connectivity and amplitude products. “The energy converged” does not make all of those properties free.

PMC has a different eager path: requesting either one- or two-RDM allocates and computes both spin-traced densities. It does not use the same shared entropy builder. The normalization warning above and its limited spin-resolved payload are further reasons to inspect capabilities rather than rely on a shared settings class alone.

A single spatial orbital has the four local possibilities from Lesson 8, so its entropy can be computed from spin-resolved 1/2-RDM information. Two-orbital entropy retains the joint subsystem; it generally needs more information than blindly reading a few pair-density entries. The MC entropy path evaluates it from the determinant expansion. The container can also derive mutual information from already available entropy data using \(I_{ij}=s_i+s_j-s_{ij}\), with no extra one-half factor in this implementation. Natural logarithms are used. Request only the properties needed for the next scientific decision.

## A Wavefunction container is a capability contract

[`StateVectorContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/wavefunction_containers/state_vector.cpp) stores determinant records and one coefficient per record, with real or complex coefficients supported as data. Its constructor checks matching coefficient/determinant counts; it does not generally normalize arbitrary user amplitudes automatically. Native MACIS solvers produce real coefficient vectors for their restricted real-integral path.

Single determinants can generate compatible occupation-based RDMs lazily. A general multi-determinant state does not automatically generate every missing RDM when an accessor is called; the required densities need to have been supplied or computed by the producer. Capability methods such as `has_one_rdm_spin_dependent()` and `has_two_rdm_spin_traced()` matter. When a localizer supplies a non-determinantal 1-RDM alongside an Aufbau carrier, the container avoids pretending that missing higher densities can always be manufactured from that carrier. This preserves the caveat from Lesson 8.

The occupation accessors have another concrete nuance: for stored nontrivial RDM data, `get_active_orbital_occupations()` diagonalizes each real spin 1-RDM and returns descending eigenvalues. It does not rotate the attached coefficients at that moment. These spectral occupations must not automatically be assigned to the current non-natural orbital columns as their diagonal populations. For a specific orbital basis use the appropriate 1-RDM diagonal, or explicitly transform to a consistent natural-orbital representation.

[`AmplitudeContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/wavefunction_containers/amplitude_container.hpp), used for MP2/CC-type results, instead stores a reference and excitation-amplitude blocks. It is pure storage: it does not expand those amplitudes into CI determinants or generate RDMs. Determinant-coefficient, occupation, norm, overlap, and RDM-based operations are not generally available on that amplitude state. `contains_determinant` checks the reference support, not an expansion of the correlated exponential. An amplitude-type tag identifies Møller–Plesset or coupled-cluster meaning; it does not turn the amplitudes into normalized state-vector probabilities. We will use this distinction explicitly in Lesson 11.

For normalized, aligned determinant expansions, the overlap is \(\langle\Psi|\Phi\rangle=\sum_I c_I^*d_I\), and pure-state fidelity is its squared magnitude. If inputs are not normalized, divide by the product of squared norms. The current state-vector `overlap` method requires the same determinant count, compatible particle count, and the same orbital object, then takes a coefficient inner product. It does not reconcile different determinant orderings/supports for you. Align the determinants explicitly before treating that number as physical overlap; equal vector lengths alone are insufficient.

Mathematically, truncating a normalized unique-determinant expansion to support of weight \(w=\sum_{I\in\mathcal S}|c_I|^2\) and renormalizing gives fidelity \(w\) with the original. That is a retained-state overlap, not an energy-error bound. The current `truncate` implementation creates a new state without carrying old correlated density payloads. Do not use the size-restricted overlap API on unequal supports as if it performed that derivation automatically.

Serialization preserves the defining records and orbital association, but object identity and physical equivalence remain distinct: `ConfigurationSet` equality uses orbital-pointer identity rather than a complete deep comparison. Full provenance and migration treatment comes later; for now retain the model, active ordering, coefficients, and requested property capabilities together.

## Classical diagonalization after qubit mapping is still classical

The separate `qubit_hamiltonian_solver` interface takes a `QubitOperator` and returns `(ground_energy, numpy_eigenvector)`, not a molecular `Wavefunction`. Its implementations are `qdk_dense_matrix_solver` and default `qdk_sparse_matrix_solver`.

The [Python code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/qubit_hamiltonian_solver.py) materializes the operator matrix. The dense implementation calls a LAPACK-backed full symmetric eigensolver. The sparse implementation constructs a sparse matrix, converts it to sparsexx through the binding, and runs Davidson with `tol=1e-8` and `max_m=20`. It is not a matrix-free operator-action simulation. For \(q\) qubits the vector has \(2^q\) entries, and the dense matrix has \(4^q\) entries; sparsity helps matrix storage without eliminating vector-size growth.

Two limitations are essential. Both implementations currently take the real part of the matrix before solving. They are therefore appropriate only when discarding the imaginary part does not change the Hamiltonian; general complex Hermitian operators are not faithfully handled by this path. Also, these solvers do not expose an electron-number or spin-sector projection argument. They find the lowest state of the supplied qubit operator’s entire represented space, which need not be the target molecular particle sector unless that restriction has been supplied by some other valid construction.

The [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_qubit_hamiltonian_solver.py) cover small real-matrix qubit operators and compare energies/vectors. They establish a useful small-system reference, not quantum execution or advantage. A mapped-operator eigenvector also needs its encoding and mode order before it can be interpreted as electron occupations.

## A correlated approximation can guide the next reduction

We now have several distinct tools. CASCI gives a complete coefficient solution inside a finite chosen active space. ASCI trades completeness for adaptive determinant selection. PMC optimizes on externally supplied support. RDMs and entropy products summarize specific information from those states. Classical qubit diagonalization provides another small-model check after mapping, with its own matrix and sector limitations.

None requires that our production strategy first solve the impossible full nitrogen FCI problem merely to decide what to keep. A carefully chosen preliminary space, a bounded selected-CI calculation, or another justified approximate correlated density can supply diagnostic evidence. Its quality and omissions must be assessed rather than assumed exact. Lesson 10 turns that evidence into an explicit active-orbital and active-electron model, separating omission error from coefficient-solver error and keeping the original molecular question visible.
lessons.caveats: Source/test tracing only at97a3ff4f. No package imports, calculations or tests run. Native CAS/ASCI/PMC use restricted real Hamiltonians and active counts, not a total-spin target. max_solver_iterations maps to Davidson subspace; bitset capacity2048 is not feasibility. Percentage ASCI core selection is not capped by ncdets_max; refinement union may exceed determinant target; no PT2 correction is executed by wrapper. grow_with_rot changes integral representation without returned accumulated orbital transformation and is excluded from teaching workflow. PMC eager two-RDM uses raw half-weighted MACIS data, unlike CAS/ASCI conversion; require normalization/energy checks. ConfigurationSet omits number/spin conservation and uniqueness checks. StateVector overlap needs aligned support/order and same orbital object; general multideterminant RDMs are not all lazy. Occupation accessors diagonalize spin RDM without rotating orbitals. AmplitudeContainer is pure storage and does not supply CI/RDM/norm/overlap. Qubit solvers materialize full matrices, discard imaginary parts, and do not impose electron sector. Lesson12 corrected one sentence that inferred universal mixed-spin beta-first storage from an Ansatz comment; native producer and reconstruction paths use alpha-alpha|beta-beta semantics.

lessons.title: Selecting the active space
lessons.body:
# Lesson 10 — Selecting the active space

## Reduce the orbital problem without losing sight of the chemistry

Lesson 9 gave us methods for optimizing determinant amplitudes. The remaining difficulty is that allowing every occupation of every orbital is usually too expensive. Active-space selection makes a different reduction: choose which orbitals can participate in explicit electron correlation at all.

Our question remains the electronic energy of neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å. The starting cc-pVDZ representation has 28 spatial orbitals and fourteen electrons. Selecting a smaller active space does not shrink the molecule or change its nuclear charge. It changes the many-electron model built from that orbital representation.

We will follow all four registered native selectors and the optional AVAS adapter, then trace the actual nitrogen tutorial. Code is illustrative and unexecuted. Numerical reference values below are attributed to repository tests, not calculations performed during this preparation.

## Active, inactive, and excluded are physical modeling choices

An **inactive orbital** is held occupied in the reference partition—doubly occupied in the restricted paired-electron case used here. An **active orbital** may change occupation across determinants. An **excluded virtual orbital** remains empty in the correlated model. Beware the word virtual: an orbital unoccupied in HF can still be active in CASCI, where excitations populate it.

We will write CAS(\(N_e\)e, \(N_o\)o) for \(N_e\) active electrons in \(N_o\) active spatial orbitals. Separately record \(N_\alpha\) and \(N_\beta\) because the solver takes those counts. For a singlet-like paired sector, CAS(6e,6o) uses three alpha and three beta electrons, giving 400 determinants before further symmetry reductions. Equal counts alone are still not a total-spin certificate.

For our fourteen-electron reference, a CAS(6e,6o) model with four inactive orbitals accounts for eight inactive plus six active electrons. If eighteen of the 28 spatial orbitals are excluded, the bookkeeping is four inactive, six active, eighteen excluded. The original AO/MO data can remain available even though the active Hamiltonian acts on only six spatial orbitals.

Selecting six orbitals and solving every determinant within them is not the same as selecting a few determinants across all 28 orbitals. Both reductions can be used together: selected CI inside a candidate active orbital space is a useful preliminary calculation. Their errors must not be merged into one unexplained “active-space approximation.”

## Frozen electrons still change the active Hamiltonian

We do not merely delete the inactive-electron rows and forget their interactions. For real restricted orbitals, let \(i,j\) label inactive doubly occupied orbitals and \(p,q\) active orbitals. The effective one-body matrix of the frozen-core active model is

\[
h^{\mathrm{act}}_{pq}=h_{pq}
+\sum_{i\in\mathrm{inactive}}
\left[2(pq|ii)-(pi|iq)\right].
\]

The inactive electrons contribute a Coulomb field and exchange, just as occupied electrons did in HF. The constant energy is

\[
E_{\mathrm{core}}=E_{\mathrm{nuc}}
+2\sum_i h_{ii}
+\sum_{ij}\left[2(ii|jj)-(ij|ji)\right].
\]

For an ECP model, the nuclear/core constant and one-body operator must use the effective-Hamiltonian convention already established. The remaining active–active two-electron integrals are retained. Correlation involving changes of inactive occupancy or occupation of excluded orbitals is omitted by this bare active-space model.

The native [Hamiltonian constructor](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/hamiltonian.cpp) implements this through an inactive density, inactive Coulomb/exchange matrices, the inactive Fock matrix, and an inactive energy constant. Its output therefore carries more than a smaller subarray. Later correlated solvers add the stored core constant to the active eigenvalue. This is frozen-core embedding, not the more general correlation-dependent downfolding discussed in Lesson 11.

## What a selector actually returns

The [interface](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/active_space.hpp) is `selector.run(wavefunction)`, returning a new `Wavefunction` with orbital-partition metadata. Native registration provides exactly `qdk_valence`, `qdk_occupation`, `qdk_autocas`, and `qdk_autocas_eos`. The factory default is **`qdk_autocas_eos`**, not the valence selector labeled “default” in some prose. An entropy-based default still needs suitable entropy information; creating it does not make that information exist.

The source file named `entropy_active_space.cpp` implements `qdk_autocas_eos`; it does not register an additional `qdk_entropy` method. The [registration code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/active_space.cpp) is the catalog to follow. The optional PySCF implementation is `pyscf_avas`.

Native selection helpers retain the coefficient representation for metadata-only selections and derive inactive indices from Aufbau occupied positions outside the selected active list. They downselect from the input’s candidate active indices; they do not retrieve an orbital that was already removed from that candidate space. The returned wavefunction is not generally the correlated input restricted with all amplitudes preserved. A one-determinant input has its occupation record projected to the new active ordering. For a multi-determinant input, the helper constructs an Aufbau occupation record and then projects it. Correlated amplitudes and RDM payloads are not propagated as a new correlated solution.

Thus “selected wavefunction” usually means a **model/reference carrier ready for Hamiltonian construction and a fresh solve**. That is consistent with the localizer warning in Lesson 8. Keep the original correlated evidence used for selection and do not present the selector’s single determinant as that evidence itself.

## Manual indices are supported as data, not a separate native selector

If chemical analysis already supplies the exact indices, a new `Orbitals` object can carry explicit `active_indices` and `inactive_indices`. The public [`spin_index_set`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/symmetry.py) helper constructs symmetry-aware index sets from sorted alpha/beta lists.

For illustration only, this specifies a six-orbital partition in the original restricted HF representation:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data import Orbitals
from qdk_chemistry.data.symmetry import spin_index_set

original = reference.get_orbitals()
n_mo = original.get_num_molecular_orbitals()
active = list(range(4, 10))
inactive = list(range(4))
manual_orbitals = Orbitals(
    coefficients=original.coefficients(), energies=original.energies(),
    ao_overlap=original.get_overlap_matrix(), basis_set=original.get_basis_set(),
    active_indices=spin_index_set(n_mo, active, active),
    inactive_indices=spin_index_set(n_mo, inactive, inactive),
)
```

A Hamiltonian constructor can consume `manual_orbitals`; a CASCI solver would separately need the consistent active alpha/beta counts. The same integers applied to natural or localized orbitals can describe a different physical subspace. This manual HF partition is therefore not automatically the tutorial’s final gauge-fixed natural-orbital model, even though its index lists look identical.

Ensure active/inactive indices are disjoint and valid, electron counts fit the selected orbitals, and the chosen spin sector is possible. Creating metadata does not project a correlated state with a guaranteed retained norm or construct all omitted interactions. No index list by itself contains that scientific argument.

## `qdk_valence`: an explicit frontier-window model

The valence selector uses `num_active_electrons` and `num_active_orbitals`, both defaulting to invalid sentinel `-1` until supplied. It requires restricted orbitals carrying orbital energies, positive requested sizes, sufficient candidates, no more active electrons than total electrons, and an even number of electrons left inactive.

Its [actual rule](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/active_space/valence_active_space.cpp) computes the number of inactive pairs as

\[
N_{\mathrm{inactive}}=(N_{\mathrm{total}}-N_e)/2,
\]

then selects a contiguous block in the candidate-index ordering beginning after that offset. It does not scan the numerical orbital energies to discover the best chemical valence subspace. The expected canonical ordering makes this a frontier-window heuristic.

The **HOMO** is the highest occupied molecular orbital and the **LUMO** the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital of a specified reference. The **Fermi level** is a filling boundary or chemical-potential notion; for a small finite molecule, an occupied/unoccupied frontier is the more direct picture. Selecting occupied orbitals near that boundary together with nearby unoccupied partners can capture important bonding/antibonding flexibility, but an energy-neighbor need not be the chemically relevant orbital in a metal complex, diffuse basis, or unusual excited state.

Stored energies are only a structural prerequisite in this implementation, not an independent proof that columns are actually canonical and energy-ordered. Repeated downselection of an already reduced candidate list also follows index/offset rules rather than a universal chemical tracking algorithm. Inspect the returned lists and active counts instead of relying solely on requested sizes. The code’s checks are not a substitute for independently ensuring \(N_\alpha,N_\beta\le N_o\) and appropriate inactive pairing.

The helper `compute_valence_space_parameters(reference, charge)` provides a starting size, not a selector by itself. It estimates valence electrons from element identities relative to smaller noble-gas cores and supplies a period-based orbital count, capped by available orbital space. The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/utils/valence_space.cpp) counts nitrogen as five valence electrons and four valence orbitals, so N₂ suggests **CAS(10e,8o)**. Its optional `include_double_d_shell=True` adds five correlating d-like directions per supported d-block atom to the suggested orbital count; it does not create those functions or prove that their correlation is adequately represented. Elements beyond the implemented period-six range receive a warning. Charges and ECP-derived explicit counts must remain consistent with the chosen reference.

Starting from the original fourteen-electron, 28-orbital RHF reference, the nitrogen tutorial’s valence window is indices 2 through 9, leaving orbitals 0 and 1 inactive. That is a manageable candidate for subsequent analysis, not a claim that all other correlation has disappeared.

## `qdk_occupation`: threshold fractional occupations with the right provenance

The occupation selector uses `occupation_threshold=0.1`. For an occupation \(n_p\), its actual test is

\[
\min\{n_p,|n_p-2|\}\ge t,
\]

where \(t\) is the threshold. For physical occupations in \([0,2]\), this selects \(t\le n_p\le2-t\), including equality. An orbital almost full or almost empty is omitted; a singly occupied or substantially fractional orbital is retained. The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/active_space/occupation_active_space.cpp) requires restricted orbitals, a candidate active space, and an even total electron count. It rejects an empty selection. It does not explicitly impose equality of alpha/beta counts despite some older descriptions calling it strictly closed-shell.

This method needs a meaningful occupation source. A paired HF determinant has only zero/two total occupations, so with the default positive threshold it supplies no evidence for a correlated active space and can select nothing. Fractional occupations from a correlated density may be informative, but fractional spatial occupations from spin-traced broken-symmetry references or uncontrolled approximations need separate interpretation.

There is an important data-convention issue from Lesson 9. The wavefunction occupation accessor used here can return descending eigenvalues of each spin 1-RDM without rotating the attached MO coefficients. The selector then associates those entries with candidate indices. Therefore apply it only when occupation ordering is consistent with the orbital representation—particularly a validated restricted closed-shell natural-orbital representation—or inspect the mapping explicitly. A spectrum alone does not label arbitrary original canonical orbitals. A spin-traced natural basis of a more general open-shell density need not diagonalize both spin blocks separately.

The threshold is a heuristic about one-electron occupation, not a bound on energy lost by omitting a weakly occupied orbital. Many individually small contributions can sum to important dynamical correlation. Nor does a scalar occupation tell us which other orbitals form a coupled bonding or magnetic partner. That motivates entropy-based and chemically targeted approaches.

## Entropy measures uncertainty of an orbital’s occupation

A spatial orbital has four local possibilities: empty, alpha-only, beta-only, or doubly occupied. Write its spin occupations as \(n_\alpha,n_\beta\) and double-occupation expectation as \(d\). Its probabilities are

\[
p_0=1-n_\alpha-n_\beta+d,\quad
p_\alpha=n_\alpha-d,\quad
p_\beta=n_\beta-d,\quad
p_2=d.
\]

The double-occupation quantity comes from the opposite-spin two-particle RDM. The single-orbital von Neumann entropy is

\[
s=-\sum_{k\in\{0,\alpha,\beta,2\}}p_k\ln p_k.
\]

The code uses natural logarithms, so the maximum for four equally likely local states is \(\ln4\), not two bits. Zero entropy means the local occupation is definite. For a pure correlated global state, local uncertainty can reflect entanglement with other orbitals. The value depends on the chosen orbital subsystems: rotating orbitals can change these local entropies without changing the exact full many-electron state.

A deterministic HF occupation gives zero local entropy in its own occupied/virtual orbital description, even if the true molecule would be strongly correlated. A selector cannot infer missing correlation from an approximation that never represented it. The [wavefunction implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/wavefunction.cpp) can compute single-orbital entropy from available real spin-resolved active 1/2-RDMs or use an explicitly supplied entropy payload. Generic complex entropy evaluation is not implemented. Ask the preliminary solver for the necessary data; amplitude-container storage alone does not provide it.

The shared entropy-selection helper requires matching alpha/beta active index lists, one entropy per candidate orbital, and available entropy data. It sorts entropy values together with their actual orbital indices, keeping their identity during ranking. With `normalize_entropies=True`, it divides positive values by their maximum, not by \(\ln4\) and not by the entropy sum. Thus normalized values express relative prominence, while the raw maximum still contains information about the overall scale.

## `qdk_autocas`: a plateau in selected count, not a cluster of ten orbitals

The autoCAS family automates complete-active-space selection using correlated orbital diagnostics. The original native variant `qdk_autocas` uses defaults `num_bins=100`, `min_plateau_size=10`, `entropy_threshold=0.14`, and `normalize_entropies=True`.

The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/active_space/autocas_active_space.cpp) first checks the **raw maximum entropy**. If it is below 0.14, it returns an empty active selection with a warning. This is an algorithmic threshold decision, not proof that HF is quantitatively accurate.

Otherwise it evaluates thresholds \(b_k=k/\texttt{num_bins}\) and counts how many sorted entropies are strictly above each threshold. A **plateau** is a run of adjacent thresholds for which that selected-orbital count stays unchanged. `min_plateau_size=10` means ten threshold bins, not ten selected orbitals. With 100 bins, it asks for a relatively wide interval over which the same candidate count is suggested.

The code identifies sufficiently long plateaus, takes their positive selected counts, and chooses the largest such count. It retains that many highest-entropy orbitals, then sorts the selected physical indices for downstream use. If no qualifying positive count exists, it returns an empty space rather than silently inventing one.

Its `entropy_threshold` is a maximum-entropy gate in this implementation; the later plateau loop does not independently require each chosen orbital’s raw entropy to exceed that setting. Turning off normalization also does not rebuild histogram bins over the raw entropy range: thresholds remain from zero to just below one. Those precise semantics are more useful than interpreting every “entropy threshold” as one universal per-orbital cutoff.

The bin count must be at least two and plateau size at least one. Their resolution affects which gaps count as robust. A broad plateau often indicates a natural-looking separation in this diagnostic, but it is not an error-controlled proof that everything below it is chemically negligible.

## `qdk_autocas_eos`: direct gaps in ranked entropy

EOS is **enhanced orbital selection**, as named in the [repository documentation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/user/comprehensive/algorithms/active_space.rst). The default native selector `qdk_autocas_eos` uses consecutive entropy differences instead of histogram bins. Its settings are `normalize_entropies=True`, `diff_threshold=0.1`, and `entropy_threshold=0.14`.

Let \(\widetilde s_i\) denote the descending entropies after optional normalization. For positive raw maximum \(s_{\max}\), the normalized absolute threshold is \(0.14/s_{\max}\). The [code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/active_space/entropy_active_space.cpp) considers a cut after position \(i\) when

\[
\widetilde s_i>t_{\mathrm{entropy}},\qquad
\widetilde s_i-\widetilde s_{i+1}>t_{\mathrm{diff}}.
\]

It chooses the **largest qualifying prefix**, not necessarily the first or largest gap. After normalization the first test still expresses an absolute raw-entropy condition, because the threshold is divided by the same maximum. The difference threshold, however, then measures a relative gap; with normalization disabled it measures a raw-entropy gap.

For a purely illustrative ranked list \([0.80,0.78,0.60,0.58,0.03,0.02]\), normalization gives approximately \([1,0.975,0.75,0.725,0.0375,0.025]\). With the defaults, cuts after the second and fourth orbitals pass both tests. EOS selects four because that is the largest qualifying count. This is not a nitrogen entropy calculation, and a count of four says nothing by itself about how many electrons remain active; original orbital identities and the inactive partition still determine that.

Unlike the histogram variant, EOS only considers adjacent differences. Equal high entropies with no qualifying gap need not produce an all-orbital selection; no boundary can mean an empty result. A one-candidate list likewise has no adjacent cut. The current EOS code lacks a separate explicit zero-maximum guard before threshold normalization. Treat nonempty meaningful entropy data as a prerequisite and check the result; do not rely on a generic promised exception or assume that absence of a selected space proves absence of correlation.

The [selector tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_active_space.cpp) use controlled synthetic entropy arrays to test normalization, threshold changes, non-contiguous indices, and empty selections. These synthetic records are algorithm tests, not molecular evidence.

## What autoCAS does not do automatically

Neither native autoCAS selector runs an SCF, CASCI, ASCI, or orbital-localization calculation internally. Their settings contain no nested energy solver that creates missing entropies. The workflow supplies a preliminary correlated state. This is important both for cost accounting and for understanding why simply calling the default selector on a paired HF state is not a production active-space strategy.

A conservatively chosen valence candidate can be analyzed by CASCI if small enough. For larger candidates, a bounded ASCI calculation or another justified approximate correlated density can provide preliminary evidence. Those entropies need not be quantitatively exact to suggest relevant orbitals, but their stability under enlarging the determinant support or candidate space should be checked. An omitted orbital outside the preliminary candidate space is invisible to the entropy ranking; the algorithm cannot discover its importance from no data.

The selector’s explicit symmetry guard is matching alpha/beta candidate indices. It does not perform a general total-spin adaptation, enforce every point-group multiplet, or guarantee that a chosen cut preserves complete natural-occupation-degenerate blocks. The inactive helper relies on an Aufbau-style partition. Verify active electron counts, open-shell partners, and required symmetry-related orbitals yourself. The gauge fixer in Lesson 8 can reject a split occupation-degenerate block; that is a separate safeguard, not a property automatically guaranteed by entropy selection.

For practical bookkeeping, choose a meaningful candidate reference once and downselect from it deliberately. Repeatedly applying a size-based selector to an already reduced candidate list is not a universal way to grow or track a chemical space. Preserve a broader reference if you later need to reconsider excluded orbitals.

## AVAS asks a chemically different question

**AVAS**, automated valence active space, selects orbitals by their overlap with target atomic functions. It can start from an appropriate single-determinant reference without first computing correlated entropies. This makes it useful when chemical reasoning identifies a metal d shell, ligand p manifold, or another local target.

Conceptually, let \(\{\chi_\mu^T\}\) span a target atomic-function space with overlap matrix \(S_T\). Its projector is

\[
P_T=\sum_{\mu\nu}|\chi_\mu^T\rangle
(S_T^{-1})_{\mu\nu}\langle\chi_\nu^T|.
\]

AVAS examines matrices such as \(A_{ij}=\langle\phi_i|P_T|\phi_j\rangle\) within occupied and virtual orbital groups. Diagonalizing these projected-overlap matrices creates orbital combinations ranked by target character. Eigenvalues above a threshold identify strongly represented target directions. This is a projection/rotation method, not an energy-ranking rule or an entropy calculation.

The [QDK PySCF adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/active_space_avas.py) delegates that method to `pyscf.mcscf.avas.AVAS`. It exposes `ao_labels=[]`, `threshold=0.2` with a zero-to-one bound, `canonicalize=False`, and `openshell_option=2`. The target labels must be supplied; an empty list raises an error. The external implementation supplies its atomic-reference details; the QDK schema does not expose every upstream AVAS option or an arbitrary new target-basis keyword.

A source-backed input pattern for nitrogen would be:

```python
avas_selector = create(
    "active_space_selector", "pyscf_avas",
    ao_labels=["N 2s", "N 2p"], threshold=0.2, canonicalize=False,
)
avas_reference = avas_selector.run(reference)
```

This requires the optional plugin and a compatible restricted single-determinant input; it was not run and no selected count is promised. Labels have an atom and orbital part, such as `"N 2p"`. The adapter preserves explicit indexed labels and wildcards, and can expand an unindexed element label to match multiple indexed atoms in the converted molecule. A misspelled element/target is not silently replaced by a chemically guessed one.

Unrestricted input is rejected. Restricted open-shell references have explicit options: option two includes singly occupied orbitals in the alpha projection procedure, while option three keeps singly occupied orbitals in the active space. The adapter passes this option upstream rather than enforcing a complete alternative spin theory itself. It has tests on restricted water and ROHF oxygen cases. Its open-shell output is constructed with separate alpha/beta blocks, even when the returned coefficient arrays are equal; check downstream restricted-Hamiltonian requirements rather than assume every solver will accept it unchanged.

AVAS can rotate or canonicalize orbitals and reorder them into inactive, active, and excluded groups. It returns a new single-determinant `Wavefunction` carrier with metadata and invalidated orbital energies, not just a list of the original column indices. Multi-determinant input is not supported by this adapter. For nonstandard or already reduced seeds, verify the returned occupations and partition instead of assuming arbitrary correlated amplitudes were transported through its rotations.

## Follow the actual nitrogen tutorial without losing the correlated state

The [current tutorial workflow](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/tutorial_choose_active_space.py) starts from the same 1.85-Å neutral singlet and native cc-pVDZ RHF reference used in earlier lessons. It then performs these distinct scientific stages.

First, the valence-size helper suggests ten electrons in eight orbitals. `qdk_valence` selects indices 2–9 and a CASCI solver receives active populations five and five. This is \(\binom85^2=3136\) determinants, vastly smaller than full fourteen-electron CI in 28 orbitals.

Second, CASCI is run with `ci_residual_tolerance=1e-10`, `calculate_one_rdm=True`, and `calculate_two_rdm=True`. The density defines a natural-orbital rotation. The tutorial does **not** take the localizer’s returned Aufbau carrier as the correlated answer: it rebuilds the Hamiltonian in those natural orbitals and runs CASCI again. Only then does it read the new representation’s single-orbital entropies.

The essential handoff can be written using the existing restricted nitrogen `reference`:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data.symmetry import SymmetryLabel, axes
from qdk_chemistry.utils import compute_valence_space_parameters

ne, no = compute_valence_space_parameters(reference, 0)
valence = create(
    "active_space_selector", "qdk_valence",
    num_active_electrons=ne, num_active_orbitals=no,
).run(reference)
alpha = SymmetryLabel([axes.alpha()])
indices = list(valence.get_orbitals().active_indices().indices(alpha))
na, nb = valence.get_active_num_electrons()
build_h = create("hamiltonian_constructor", "qdk")
cas = create("multi_configuration_calculator", "macis_cas",
             ci_residual_tolerance=1e-10,
             calculate_one_rdm=True, calculate_two_rdm=True)
valence_energy, valence_ci = cas.run(build_h.run(valence.get_orbitals()), na, nb)
natural_carrier = create("orbital_localizer", "qdk_natural_orbitals").run(
    valence_ci, indices, indices,
)
natural_energy, natural_ci = cas.run(build_h.run(natural_carrier.get_orbitals()), na, nb)
selected = create("active_space_selector", "qdk_autocas_eos").run(natural_ci)
```

These calls are unexecuted. The existing solver objects may be reused with their unchanged locked settings, as explained in Lesson 3. A changed tolerance would require a new configured instance. Neither selector contains the CAS solver; the workflow explicitly owns the preliminary computational cost.

Third, the tutorial inspects the EOS-selected partition and explicitly errors if no active orbitals were selected. Its recorded reference retains indices 4–9, makes 0–3 inactive, and leaves eighteen excluded virtuals. The resulting model is CAS(6e,6o) with active populations three and three.

Fourth, it gauge-fixes the selected complete degenerate blocks while still supplying the **broader correlated natural-orbital state** to the gauge fixer. The returned orbitals still carry the broad input active space, so the workflow explicitly reapplies the EOS active/inactive index sets to a new `Orbitals` object. It then constructs the final reduced Hamiltonian and runs a fresh CASCI solve with the reduced counts. This is a careful separation of evidence, representation choice, model reduction, and coefficient optimization—not a chain of objects all representing one unchanged correlated state.

The [tutorial regression test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_sample_tutorial_gs_qpe.py) records:

| Stage at the tutorial geometry | Recorded reference |
|---|---|
| Native cc-pVDZ RHF | −108.418633697214 Hartree |
| Initial CAS(10e,8o) | −108.778369520882 Hartree; 3136 determinants |
| Natural-orbital CAS(10e,8o) | Same CASCI energy within the test tolerance |
| Refined CAS(6e,6o) | −108.771051792909 Hartree; 400 determinants |

These are source reference values, not newly computed outputs. The test’s optional entropy snapshot has two low-entropy valence orbitals and six above 0.5; the six include two moderately high and four very high entropies. EOS selects the largest qualifying group, not only the four largest entries.
