Exact per-orbital snapshot numbers depend on the reference configuration and should not be generalized to another geometry or basis.

The energy increase from the natural-orbital valence model to the reduced model is approximately **7.318 milliHartree** by subtraction of those recorded references. That quantifies an omission effect relative to this larger candidate model. It is not the full error against exact chemistry, and it is not zero merely because an automated selector found a clean entropy cut.

The separate `examples/qpe_stretched_n2.ipynb` uses **1.270025 Å**. None of its energies, active-space diagnostics, or resource numbers should be merged into this 1.85-Å sequence.

## Assess the reduction as a scientific decision

An active-space proposal should be tested against the intended observable: a relative energy, bond-stretching profile, spin splitting, density feature, or another stated target. Enlarge the candidate orbital set, increase preliminary selected-CI support, vary thresholds, inspect orbital character, and compare to an appropriate larger reference where affordable. A stable entropy cut can be useful evidence, but it is not a certified chemical-accuracy theorem.

Occupation thresholds miss some weak but collectively important dynamical correlation. Entropy methods only see correlation represented in their supplied state and orbital basis. AVAS can miss chemistry outside the specified atomic target. A contiguous valence window can miss energetically separated but chemically essential partners. These are different failure modes; using several diagnostics can expose disagreement without treating their intersection as automatically correct.

Along a geometry path, keeping the same integer indices is not the same as keeping the same physical subspace. Orbitals can exchange order, change character, or rotate within degenerate blocks. A threshold crossing can abruptly change active electron/orbital count and produce a discontinuous model. For a reaction or bond scan, compare orbital overlaps and chemical character and consider a consistent union of relevant subspaces. The current per-geometry selectors do not supply a universal cross-geometry orbital-tracking guarantee. The derivative workflow’s reuse of index metadata likewise does not solve this problem automatically.

Reducing eight active spatial orbitals to six reduces an untapered occupation encoding from sixteen to twelve electron spin modes. But total quantum cost also depends on the Hamiltonian’s coefficients and terms, preparation overlap, precision, repetitions, and encoding. A smaller model may be harder to prepare accurately or may introduce unacceptable chemical error. Resource estimation should compare complete model/workload choices at a common accuracy target, not just qubit counts.

We now know exactly which electrons remain variable, which are held filled, and what source evidence supports the chosen reduction. The next question is how to repair limitations of fixed-orbital CASCI and how excluded-space correlation can influence a smaller model. That leads to MCSCF, dynamical correlation, and the precise effective-Hamiltonian capabilities that this repository actually offers.
lessons.caveats: Source/test tracing only at97a3ff4f; no workflow or scientific calculation run. Native registered selectors are exactly valence/occupation/autocas/autocas_eos; defaultEOS, no separately registered qdk_entropy. Valence uses candidate-index offset, not actual energy sorting. Occupation selector uses spectral occupation accessor so column association must be checked; restricted/even-count restriction differs from older closed-shell wording. Histogram entropy_threshold is raw-max gate; bins remain0..1, and per-plateau raw cutoff is not enforced. EOS rescales absolute threshold by max and chooses largest qualifying adjacent gap, with no separate zero-max guard; no-gap can return empty. Neither selector runs preliminary MC internally or guarantees spin/degenerate-partner closure. Native selector returns projected/Aufbau carrier, not correlated amplitudes. AVAS restricted single-determinant input only; open-shell output compatibility requires checking. Nitrogen10e8o->6e6o energies/counts are recorded tutorial test references at1.85Angstrom and not notebook1.270025Angstrom results.

lessons.title: Refining and reducing the chemical model
lessons.body:
# Lesson 11 — Refining and reducing the chemical model

## Three different ways to improve a reduced calculation

The previous lesson produced a clear active-space model for our fixed 1.85-Å nitrogen problem. A CASCI calculation can optimize every determinant coefficient inside that space and still have two important limitations: its orbitals were chosen elsewhere, and correlation involving excluded orbital occupations is absent.

There are several responses, and they are not interchangeable. **MCSCF** adapts orbitals and determinant coefficients together. **Reference-derived correlation methods**, such as MP2 and coupled cluster, approximate additional electronic correlation around a reference with their own assumptions. **Downfolding** aims to incorporate effects of a larger space into an effective smaller-space Hamiltonian. A smaller active space plus a scalar energy correction is not automatically the same thing as such an effective Hamiltonian.

The repository’s current implementation boundary is important enough to state immediately:

| Interface and implementation | What is actually available here |
|---|---|
| `multi_configuration_scf / pyscf` | Optional PySCF CASSCF engine with a nested QDK MC solver |
| `dynamical_correlation_calculator / qdk_mp2_calculator` | Native restricted/unrestricted MP2 energy and amplitude construction within supported input cases |
| `dynamical_correlation_calculator / pyscf_coupled_cluster` | Optional PySCF CCSD adapter, including tested unrestricted-reference use |
| `effective_hamiltonian_constructor` | Interface and validation support, but no bundled concrete downfolding implementation or default choice |

This is a lesson about those actual methods and contracts, not a promise that every related method in the chemistry literature can be invoked by changing a string. No calculations or tests were executed in preparing it. Any new small numerical example is explicitly illustrative; recorded tests using other geometries remain separate from our 1.85-Å case.

## MCSCF changes the orbitals for the correlated state

HF optimizes orbitals for one determinant. CASCI optimizes coefficients in fixed orbitals. **Multi-configurational self-consistent field (MCSCF)** optimizes both. If the configuration expansion is complete within a specified active space, the usual name is **complete active space SCF (CASSCF)**.

A useful parameterization is

\[
|\Psi(c,\kappa)\rangle=
\sum_{I\in\mathcal D_{\mathrm{active}}}c_I
|D_I(Ce^{\kappa})\rangle.
\]

\(c_I\) are configuration amplitudes, \(C\) the starting MO coefficients, and \(\kappa\) orbital-rotation parameters, represented by an anti-Hermitian matrix so orthonormality is preserved. The energy depends on both sets of variables. Optimizing only \(c\) gives CASCI; allowing appropriate rotations of \(C\) gives MCSCF.

The useful rotations are not all independent physical changes. For a complete active space, rotations wholly inside that active space can be compensated by re-expression of its full CI coefficients. Rotations inside an inactive occupied space or an excluded empty space are likewise redundant for the corresponding state. Rotations mixing inactive, active, and excluded spaces can change the correlated wavefunction available to the approximation. In effect, a fixed number of active orbitals can adapt its shape inside the larger AO/MO span.

This is different from the localization of Lesson 8. A localizer chooses a representation objective inside a specified subspace and usually returns a reference carrier. MCSCF optimizes the electronic energy and performs correlated coefficient solves as the physically relevant orbital subspace changes.

For example, a six-orbital active model in 28 MOs can optimize which six orbital directions best describe its correlated electrons while keeping the active-space size fixed. It has not expanded to full CI over all 28 orbitals. At an ideal variational minimum it can improve on the corresponding fixed-orbital CASCI starting point, but a practical nonlinear iteration can reach different local solutions or fail. A lower final energy is not by itself a global-minimum or correct-state certificate.

## Macro and micro iterations have different jobs

At fixed orbitals, the CI equation gives optimized amplitudes and reduced density matrices. Those densities describe the correlated response needed to form orbital gradients. A proposed orbital rotation changes integrals, which changes the coefficient problem; orbital and CI changes are coupled.

A **macroiteration** updates the larger, self-consistent orbital/coefficient problem with refreshed integral and CI information. **Microiterations** use local response or curvature approximations to make cheaper orbital progress inside that larger cycle. A second-order or augmented-Hessian strategy uses information about orbital energy curvature rather than only the first derivative. These concepts explain why one MCSCF step is much more than a new SCF diagonalization, and why the cost includes repeated integral transformations and correlated subproblems.

The current QDK adapter delegates the actual orbital-update and microiteration machinery to **PySCF’s `mcscf.CASSCF(...).kernel(...)`**. It does not reimplement that optimizer in the Python shim or expose a menu choosing arbitrary first-order, two-step, and augmented-Hessian variants. We should not infer a more detailed upstream algorithm configuration than the adapter actually supplies.

The [`MultiConfigurationScf` interface](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/mcscf.hpp) takes **`Orbitals` and two active electron counts**, returning `(energy, wavefunction)`. Older prose mentioning a Hamiltonian and several algorithm objects as run arguments is not the current signature. The C++ factory has no registered native implementation; its default implementation name is `pyscf`, available through the optional plugin. Bundled MACIS contains MCSCF-related library routines, but their existence is not a separately registered native QDK MCSCF solver.

## Trace the PySCF–QDK CASSCF bridge

The [adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/mcscf.py) requires restricted orbitals and identical alpha/beta active and inactive index sets. Unequal active alpha/beta counts are allowed for an appropriate restricted open-shell problem; the [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_mcscf.py) include both a singlet nitrogen case and an oxygen triplet case with four active alpha and two active beta electrons.

It builds a PySCF mean-field object from the supplied orbitals, occupations, molecular basis, charge, and spin information. It constructs PySCF CASSCF with the number of active orbitals and active electrons. The QDK selection indices are converted to PySCF’s one-based `sort_mo` request, placing the active orbitals into the layout expected by the external optimizer.

The nested setting `multi_configuration_calculator` defaults to `AlgorithmRef("multi_configuration_calculator", "macis_cas")`. The adapter wraps that QDK calculator to look like PySCF’s FCI solver. When PySCF needs a CI solution, it passes active one-electron integrals, two-electron integrals, and a core constant. The wrapper restores full four-index integrals, packages a QDK Hamiltonian over temporary `ModelOrbitals`, and calls the nested MC calculator. Thus **PySCF supplies the orbital optimization and current integrals; MACIS can supply the correlated CI solve**.

The wrapper supplies `make_rdm1` and `make_rdm12` callbacks using the most recently returned QDK wavefunction. It forces `calculate_one_rdm=True` and `calculate_two_rdm=True` on the child before use, regardless of false values in an initial child reference. Its `ci0` parameter is not used as a new CI warm start by this shim. A source comment mentions a two-RDM scaling, but the current callback only reshapes the already supplied QDK tensor; do not apply an extra factor from that comment.

After PySCF reports convergence, the adapter attaches optimized molecular coefficients, energies, basis/overlap information, and the last CI coefficients/determinants to the output. It carries spin-resolved densities when available and falls back to stored spin-traced densities otherwise. Unlike a localizer’s Aufbau carrier, this output is intended to contain the actual correlated solver result in the optimized orbital representation.

There is a layout limitation worth handling deliberately. The adapter sorts/reorders MOs for PySCF, then copies the input active/inactive index lists into its output metadata rather than returning a general inverse permutation. A conventional contiguous inactive-then-active layout, as used in the tutorial, avoids treating arbitrary noncontiguous input indices as automatically preserved identities. Check returned orbital ordering and model consistency when using custom partitions.

## Configure the supported MCSCF workflow, not a hypothetical one

The PySCF MCSCF settings are `max_cycle_macro=50`, `verbose=0`, and the nested MC reference. The outer schema does not expose arbitrary `conv_tol`, `max_cycle_micro`, root-selection, or state-average weights. Child CI controls such as `ci_residual_tolerance` are configured inside the reference and have the semantics from Lesson 9; in particular `max_solver_iterations` controls MACIS’s Davidson subspace.

For the valence reference from Lesson 10, a valid unexecuted pattern is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef

active_orbitals = valence.get_orbitals()
na, nb = valence.get_active_num_electrons()
mcscf_solver = create(
    "multi_configuration_scf", "pyscf",
    max_cycle_macro=50,
    multi_configuration_calculator=AlgorithmRef(
        "multi_configuration_calculator", "macis_cas",
        ci_residual_tolerance=1e-10,
    ),
)
casscf_energy, optimized_ci = mcscf_solver.run(active_orbitals, na, nb)
```

This chooses orbital adaptation of the valence candidate. It does not secretly retain the fixed-orbital final energy from Lesson 10. The same design can start from a different supported contiguous active partition, but the comparison must state which one was optimized.

A selected-CI child such as `macis_asci` can be substituted at the interface, provided its returned state and RDM capabilities satisfy the callbacks. With incomplete selected CI, however, the effective orbital/coefficient model and convergence depend on determinant selection. Smooth, fully variational CASSCF properties should not be transferred uncritically to every selected child, particularly when selected support changes with orbitals.

The adapter explicitly raises if PySCF CASSCF does not converge. It does not promise global optimization or automatic tracking of one electronic root along a reaction coordinate. **State averaging**, which optimizes orbitals for a weighted set of states, is an important general MCSCF concept, but no corresponding state-average/root-control settings are exposed here. Likewise, an ordinary lowest-state MC child is not an excited-state targeting API.

The [standalone documentation example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/mcscf.py) and nitrogen MCSCF test use a **2.0-Å** molecule. They are evidence for the method/interface, not a CASSCF energy baseline for our 1.85-Å case. No such new nitrogen number is reported here.

## Orbital adaptation does not recover all outside-space correlation

“Static” or strong near-degeneracy correlation describes situations where several configurations compete prominently, as in bond breaking. “Dynamical” correlation often describes many smaller amplitude changes by which electrons avoid one another. The distinction is useful but not a sharp separation into two independent physical forces. Both depend on the reference and orbital space.

CASSCF can improve a chosen correlated model by adapting orbitals, but it still omits determinant changes involving excluded orbitals and fixed inactive occupancies. Conversely, a single-reference perturbative or coupled-cluster correction can capture extensive dynamical correlation while failing badly when its reference is qualitatively inappropriate. Neither label is an automatic accuracy ranking.

Do not add a generic MP2 number to a CASCI energy and call it a validated multireference perturbation method. A consistent post-CAS treatment must define its reference, excitation spaces, denominators, and double-counting rules. The actual reference-derived methods below are not general CASPT2, NEVPT2, or multireference coupled-cluster implementations exposed by this repository.

## The dynamical-correlation contract packages a reference and Hamiltonian together

An **`Ansatz`** pairs a Hamiltonian with a reference wavefunction. The [`DynamicalCorrelationCalculator`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/dynamical_correlation_calculator.hpp) consumes that pair and returns

```python
energy, ket_wavefunction, bra_wavefunction = calculator.run(ansatz)
```

The energy is a total energy, not only the correlation increment. A **ket** is the right state representation. The optional **bra** is a left-state representation used by methods whose practical equations are not Hermitian. It is not necessarily just a copy whose coefficients can be complex-conjugated mechanically. Why coupled cluster needs a left representation becomes clear below.

The native factory defaults to `qdk_mp2_calculator`; the optional PySCF registration adds `pyscf_coupled_cluster`. There is not a separate required `coupled_cluster_calculator` registry type for the current plugin. The shared interface is extensible, but each concrete method still has narrower scientific input assumptions.

## MP2 estimates the leading correlation around canonical HF

**Møller–Plesset second-order perturbation theory (MP2)** separates the Hamiltonian into a solvable mean-field part and a residual interaction. It estimates leading corrections assuming the reference is a sensible starting point and the residual mixing is sufficiently small.

Let \(i,j\) label occupied orbitals, \(a,b\) virtual orbitals, and \(\varepsilon\) their canonical orbital energies. For the real restricted spatial-orbital formulation used here,

\[
t_{ij}^{ab}=\frac{(ia|jb)}
{\varepsilon_i+\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_a-\varepsilon_b},
\]

\[
E_{\mathrm{MP2}}^{\mathrm{corr}}
=\sum_{ijab}t_{ij}^{ab}\left[2(ia|jb)-(ib|ja)\right].
\]

The numerator is an electron-repulsion coupling and the denominator is a reference excitation-energy difference. For ordinary occupied-to-virtual gaps the denominator is negative, giving the familiar negative leading correction for a stable conventional reference. Same-spin unrestricted contributions use antisymmetrized couplings; opposite-spin contributions do not contain the same exchange subtraction.

As a purely illustrative contribution, a coupling of 0.1 Hartree and denominator −0.5 Hartree gives amplitude −0.2 and a simple numerator-squared/denominator contribution −0.02 Hartree. If that denominator becomes −0.01 while the coupling remains fixed, the amplitude magnitude becomes ten: the small-correction assumption is no longer credible. These are invented perturbation numbers, not an N₂ calculation.

MP2 uses orbital-energy information in an essential way. A localized or natural-orbital object with no energies cannot simply be inserted into this formula. Nor is a stale copied energy array evidence that the current orbitals diagonalize the needed mean-field operator. DFT or correlated-reference orbitals may be useful elsewhere, but passing them to a routine that assumes canonical HF does not automatically define a justified generalized perturbation theory.

## The native MP2 implementation is an actual solver, but not an RDM producer

The [native implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/mp2.cpp) reads active alpha/beta counts, extracts orbital energies corresponding to active indices, and uses the Hamiltonian’s molecular two-electron tensors to form the correction and amplitudes. Its restricted case requires equal alpha/beta counts. If the Hamiltonian is unrestricted, it evaluates same- and opposite-spin terms separately.

An unequal-spin reference with a restricted Hamiltonian is not a supported RO-MP2 shortcut: the dispatch selects the unrestricted branch, but that branch explicitly requires an unrestricted Hamiltonian. Both spin active spaces must have compatible sizes, populations must fit, and the ordering is assumed to place occupied active orbitals before active virtuals. The public method checks energy availability but does not independently prove all canonical-reference assumptions.

These kernels divide by the excitation denominators directly; they do not apply a general small-gap regularization or guarantee that a pathological denominator produces a clean diagnostic instead of non-finite amplitudes. Strongly stretched nitrogen is exactly a case where perturbative reliability must not be assumed from a returned number.

The calculator has no method-specific convergence/settings schema: MP2 here is direct algebra on supplied integrals, not an iterative CC residual solve. It computes T1/T2 amplitudes eagerly; T1 is zero in its canonical-HF MP2 model. It returns `reference_energy + correlation_energy`, where `reference_energy` comes from `ansatz.calculate_energy()`. Thus the stored core constant is included once in the reference energy, and should not be added again.

Its result is an **`AmplitudeContainer` tagged `MollerPlesset`**, not a determinant expansion. Both ket and bra return slots refer to that same generated amplitude-wavefunction object in this implementation. The generic container nevertheless carries the `NotSelfDual` metadata convention; a duplicate result handle is not a newly computed normalized bra or an overlap calculation.

Most importantly, this native MP2 calculator does **not** produce a one- or two-particle RDM. It therefore cannot directly supply the RDM-bearing state required by `qdk_natural_orbitals`. The deprecated MP2-natural-orbital localizer has its own MACIS density-related computation, but that does not give the general native MP2 amplitude result new capabilities. Suitable MP2 RDM data must be produced/imported through an explicitly supported route. This clarifies the earlier natural-orbital handoff rather than promising an unavailable automatic conversion.

There are producer-specific amplitude details. Restricted MP2 stores a spatial T2 block; it must not be read as three independently antisymmetrized spin tensors merely because getters expose three block positions. The unrestricted same-spin kernel writes independent \(i<j,a<b\) entries into full-sized vectors without filling every antisymmetry-related partner. In the current active-space UMP2 amplitude construction, the beta-beta call also receives the full beta energy vector rather than the extracted active beta vector, so nontrivial active-space amplitude interpretation requires particular care even when the energy path used the extracted energies. The course’s simple MP2 handoff uses a full restricted reference and does not assume interchangeable amplitude layouts across producers.

The [MP2 tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_mp2.cpp) cover restricted and unrestricted energy references, active restricted energy cases, and amplitude serialization. They are not a guarantee of reliability for a strongly correlated N₂ reference or every custom active ordering.

## Coupled cluster uses an exponential, not a truncated CI list

In **coupled cluster (CC)**, the right-hand state is parameterized as

\[
|\Psi_{\mathrm{CC}}\rangle=e^T|\Phi_0\rangle,
\qquad T=T_1+T_2+\cdots.
\]

\(\Phi_0\) is a reference determinant. \(T_1\) generates single excitations and \(T_2\) double excitations. In spin-orbital notation,

\[
T_1=\sum_{ia}t_i^a a_a^\dagger a_i,
\qquad
T_2=\frac14\sum_{ijab}t_{ij}^{ab}
 a_a^\dagger a_b^\dagger a_j a_i.
\]

The amplitudes now solve coupled nonlinear equations rather than just the second-order denominator formula. **CCSD** keeps connected single and double excitation operators, \(T=T_1+T_2\).

The exponential still generates terms such as \(T_2^2/2\), corresponding to simultaneous double excitations on different parts of the system. These are **disconnected contributions**: products of lower-rank cluster effects, not new independent connected quadruple amplitudes. This is why CCSD is not the same as CI restricted to singles and doubles, even though the names mention the same ranks.

For noninteracting fragments with a compatible factorized reference, \(T_A\) and \(T_B\) commute, and \(e^{T_A+T_B}=e^{T_A}e^{T_B}\). This structure underlies standard CC’s **size consistency**: the energy of separated fragments agrees with the sum of separately calculated energies under the corresponding assumptions. It does not rescue a qualitatively wrong reference at bond dissociation.

Standard projective CC introduces the similarity-transformed Hamiltonian

\[
\overline H=e^{-T}He^T.
\]

The reference projection gives the energy, and projections onto single/double excited determinants are set to zero:

\[
E=\langle\Phi_0|\overline H|\Phi_0\rangle,
\qquad
0=\langle\Phi_i^a|\overline H|\Phi_0\rangle,
\qquad
0=\langle\Phi_{ij}^{ab}|\overline H|\Phi_0\rangle.
\]

This transformed problem is generally non-Hermitian because an excitation-only \(T\) is not anti-Hermitian. Standard CCSD energy is not a variational upper bound obtained by minimizing a normalized expectation value. Converged amplitudes can still be physically poor when the single-reference picture fails.

The “UCCSD” wording in these PySCF tests means **unrestricted-reference CCSD**, not the unitary coupled-cluster quantum ansatz \(e^{T-T^\dagger}\). That latter construction is a different method. Also, the current adapter calls CCSD only; it does not expose a perturbative triples CCSD(T) calculation merely because the external PySCF project can perform one in another interface.

## A left-state solution is additional information

For properties and response in projective CC, the useful left representation is commonly written

\[
\langle\widetilde\Psi|=
\langle\Phi_0|(1+\Lambda)e^{-T},
\]

where \(\Lambda\) contains de-excitation amplitudes obtained from additional left/lambda equations. It is not generally the Hermitian conjugate of the stored right-amplitude list. This is why the reference-derived result type has a separate optional bra slot.

The PySCF CC adapter can request that computation with `compute_bra=True`, then checks `converged_lambda`. To retain the returned lambda amplitudes in QDK storage, `store_amplitudes=True` is also needed. Otherwise the external equations may be solved while the returned bra container does not retain their amplitude arrays. A result object’s existence and a stored useful amplitude payload are different facts.

## Trace the current CCSD adapter and its input boundary

The implementation name is **`dynamical_correlation_calculator/pyscf_coupled_cluster`**. The [code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/coupled_cluster.py) constructs `pyscf.cc.CCSD`, applies exposed controls, runs `kernel`, and explicitly checks `pyscf_cc.converged`. It then adds `pyscf_cc.e_corr` to the QDK `Ansatz` reference expectation. Optional lambda equations are solved and checked separately.

For ordinary molecular orbitals, the [conversion helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/pyscf/conversion.py) reconstructs a PySCF SCF-like object from the molecule, basis, orbital coefficients, energies and occupations. It does not perform a fresh SCF optimization in that conversion. The external CC engine then uses its own molecular integral machinery.

This is an important limitation of the apparently broad Hamiltonian input: when molecular coefficient data are available, `hamiltonian_to_scf` reroutes to the orbital conversion and does **not** directly install arbitrary modified one-/two-body tensors from the supplied QDK Hamiltonian. A reduced or downfolded molecular Hamiltonian must therefore not be assumed faithfully consumed by this route. With a reduced active-space reference, PySCF’s full molecular correlation problem and the QDK amplitude container’s active dimensions can also disagree. The supported examples use a consistent full molecular HF reference/Hamiltonian pair.

For coefficient-free model orbitals, the conversion instead constructs a synthetic restricted SCF object containing the supplied one-/two-body integrals, identity overlap, core-energy function, identity MO coefficients, and occupations. That explicit-integral path rejects unrestricted model Hamiltonians, open-shell occupations, and reduced active spaces. It is an interoperability mechanism, not proof that an arbitrary model determinant is a converged canonical HF reference.

The adapter does not implement multireference CC by accepting a correlated `Wavefunction`. Its occupation-based conversion and reference assumptions remain those of the supported single-reference paths. Passing a CASCI state must not be advertised as a valid post-CAS coupled-cluster correction without a separate method and matching theory.

The [PySCF integration tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_pyscf_plugin.py) demonstrate molecular closed-shell CCSD, genuine unrestricted-reference CCSD, and stored amplitude round trips. The synthetic C++ test named for coupled-cluster calculators checks the extensible interface with a mock implementation; it is not a native CCSD solver or a molecular benchmark.

## CCSD settings have concrete names and narrower scope than old prose

The actual exposed controls are `conv_tol=1e-7`, `conv_tol_normt=1e-5`, `max_cycle=50`, `diis_space=6`, `diis_start_cycle=0`, `direct=False`, `async_io=True`, `incore_complete=True`, `store_amplitudes=False`, and `compute_bra=False`.

`conv_tol` and `conv_tol_normt` control PySCF’s energy/amplitude-update convergence criteria; the latter name includes the final `t`. They are not the native SCF orbital residual threshold. `max_cycle` caps the CC iteration, while the DIIS controls determine history size and when extrapolation begins. `direct` and the I/O controls change the external engine’s integral/memory strategy, not the CCSD excitation rank. `incore_complete=True` is an external CC control, not a promise that the entire surrounding workflow performs no file operations.

Older docstrings also mention `frozen`, `max_memory`, and `verbose`, and the method body contains optional lookups for them, but the shipped `PyscfCoupledClusterSettings` constructor does not register these keys. They are not ordinary settable factory keyword controls in this current schema. Inspect settings rather than promise a frozen-orbital or memory-budget feature from documentation alone.

A conventional dense molecular implementation stores T2 data of size roughly \(o^2v^2\), with \(o\) occupied and \(v\) virtual orbitals. Leading contractions commonly scale as \(o^2v^4\), giving the familiar sixth-power cost when both grow with system size. Full integral storage and scratch arrays add substantial memory beyond the amplitudes. These are algorithmic scaling estimates, not timings or measured memory for this environment. Tightening tolerances does not fix reference breakdown; large amplitudes, difficult convergence, and strong near-degeneracy require scientific reassessment.

## Amplitude storage is not a quantum-ready state vector

Both MP2 and CC use [`AmplitudeContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/wavefunction_containers/amplitude_container.cpp), with an `AmplitudeType` specifying whether the amplitudes belong to Møller–Plesset or coupled-cluster theory. The same arrays do not mean the same ansatz: perturbative doubles are not automatically an exponential CC state. The container stores the reference wavefunction, orbitals, and optional T1/T2 blocks, and validates provided sizes/spin-component completeness against the reference active dimensions.

Getters return T1 alpha/beta blocks and T2 in the order opposite-spin, alpha-alpha, beta-beta. The PySCF adapter flattens its arrays for storage. Canonical tensor axis meaning and antisymmetry conventions must be retained alongside these flattened values. A shape check cannot determine whether a supplied spatial or spin-adapted tensor has been interpreted correctly.

The container is pure storage and marks amplitude wavefunctions `NotSelfDual`. It does not build their determinant expansion, normalize them, compute overlaps, or generate reduced density matrices. `norm()` and `overlap()` throw. Availability of a stored reference determinant does not make that determinant the correlated state. The right and lambda results have the same amplitude-type tag, so their role also comes from the return position and calculation provenance.

Consequently, a coefficient-based state-preparation algorithm cannot directly consume a CC result as if `get_coefficients()` returned normalized determinant amplitudes. Nor can `qdk_natural_orbitals`, population analysis, or entropy selection simply generate missing correlated RDMs from it. Those next steps require an explicit implemented conversion/property calculation, not a property-table assumption.

Using the separate small H₂ reference/Hamiltonian pair from Lesson 9, the actual invocation pattern is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data import Ansatz

reference_ansatz = Ansatz(h2_hamiltonian, h2_reference)
mp2_energy, mp2_ket, mp2_bra = create(
    "dynamical_correlation_calculator", "qdk_mp2_calculator",
).run(reference_ansatz)

ccsd = create(
    "dynamical_correlation_calculator", "pyscf_coupled_cluster",
    store_amplitudes=True, compute_bra=True,
)
ccsd_energy, cc_ket, cc_bra = ccsd.run(reference_ansatz)
```

These examples are unexecuted and use the full small-model HF reference, not the truncated/gauge-fixed nitrogen CASCI state. The [dynamical-correlation documentation example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/dynamical_correlation.py) uses a similar H₂ setup with its explicitly specified basis. No native `calculate_one_rdm` flag or CCSD(T) option should be invented for these calls.

## What downfolding would add beyond discarding orbitals

To understand the effective-Hamiltonian interface, partition a larger orbital window \(W\) into retained target orbitals \(P\) and external orbitals \(Q\). In a formal many-electron derivation, use \(\hat P\) and \(\hat Q\) for projectors onto the corresponding retained/excluded many-electron spaces. The orbital-index lists in the API are not themselves these many-electron projection matrices.

Write the Schrödinger equation in blocks:

\[
H_{PP}\Psi_P+H_{PQ}\Psi_Q=E\Psi_P,
\qquad
H_{QP}\Psi_P+H_{QQ}\Psi_Q=E\Psi_Q.
\]

When the relevant inverse exists, eliminate the excluded component:

\[
\Psi_Q=(E-H_{QQ})^{-1}H_{QP}\Psi_P,
\]

\[
H_{\mathrm{eff}}(E)=H_{PP}
+H_{PQ}(E-H_{QQ})^{-1}H_{QP}.
\]

The second term remembers virtual excursions into the excluded space. Simply keeping \(H_{PP}\) discards them. Exact elimination is not free: the result depends on the unknown energy and the inverse of a potentially enormous excluded-space operator. Practical downfolding methods introduce approximations, references, truncation orders, or transformations to make this tractable.

For an illustrative two-state matrix with retained diagonal −1.0 Hartree, excluded diagonal −0.5 Hartree, and coupling 0.1 Hartree, elimination gives the scalar equation

\[
E=-1.0+\frac{0.01}{E+0.5}.
\]

Ignoring the external state gives −1.0; the exact lower eigenvalue is approximately −1.019258 Hartree. Replacing \(E\) in the denominator by −1.0 gives an approximate −0.02-Hartree correction. This is a toy explanation of exclusion-space influence, not an implemented QDK downfolding calculation or a nitrogen correction.

Exact elimination can induce effective three-body and higher-body interactions even when the starting Hamiltonian contains only one- and two-body terms. A method returning the usual molecular constant/one-/two-body representation must explain how such terms are represented or neglected. A smaller orbital count can therefore shift work and error into classical preprocessing rather than simply remove cost.

## The current effective-Hamiltonian capability is an interface, not a solver

At this revision, [`EffectiveHamiltonianConstructor`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/effective_hamiltonian.hpp) defines

```python
effective_hamiltonian = concrete_constructor.run(reference, hamiltonian, p_indices)
```

This is an interface signature, not an executable example selecting a shipped implementation. The [factory implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/effective_hamiltonian.cpp) registers no concrete instances and its default name is empty. The [documentation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/user/comprehensive/algorithms/effective_hamiltonian_constructor.rst) explicitly states the same limitation. No built-in perturbative downfolding order, CC-based decoupling algorithm, or numerical downfolding result can honestly be taught as currently runnable here.

An external/custom implementation could register into this interface, but its presence and scientific assumptions would require separate evidence. The [current tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_effective_hamiltonian.cpp) use a mock that returns an input Hamiltonian to exercise registration and validation. They are not a physical downfolding demonstration.

The interface still defines a useful scientific handoff. Inputs are a reference `Wavefunction`, a `Hamiltonian` over the larger window, and a `SymmetryBlockedIndexSet` of **absolute MO indices** for the target. If a Hamiltonian’s active indices are `[0, 2, 4, 6]`, target `[0, 4]` identifies those actual MOs; `[1, 3]` does not mean “second and fourth active positions.”

The output contract requires the target indices as its active space, preserved original inactive orbitals, method-consistent inactive/empty classification of removed orbitals, a consistent inactive Fock matrix when present, and the folded scalar contribution in the constant energy term. Other excluded-space contributions belong in the returned effective integrals. The reference and selected approximation must decide how to handle occupations and information in the removed space; the interface alone cannot decide those physics.

Common input validation is **opt-in**: base `run` locks settings but does not automatically call `_validate_inputs`. A concrete implementation may invoke that helper, which checks null inputs, compatible AO/MO dimensions and basis hashes, spin restrictions/symmetries, coefficient and energy consistency, and target/reference active windows as subsets of the Hamiltonian window. The helper permits a target not contained in the reference’s own active subset as long as both are within the larger Hamiltonian window; method-specific information requirements remain the implementer’s responsibility. It is not a generic assurance that two rotated but differently represented states can be combined without transforming their tensors.

The base has no common downfolding settings. Therefore there is no legitimate current `order`, `energy_shift`, or `method="..."` keyword to guess. The correct answer to “which downfolding method did this repository use?” is “none through a bundled concrete implementation at this revision,” unless a separately identified implementation has been supplied.

## Keep ECPs, frozen core, orbital optimization, and downfolding distinct

An **ECP** changes the underlying electronic model by replacing selected atomic core electrons with an effective operator. **Frozen-core active-space construction** retains a reference inactive population and its mean-field effect/constant while omitting its excitations. **CASSCF** adapts orbital shapes and coefficients within its chosen many-electron model. **Downfolding** aims to retain effects of a larger excluded space through a modified smaller-space Hamiltonian.

An MP2 or CCSD scalar correlation energy is not, by itself, a new effective Hamiltonian with corrected eigenstates and observables. Adding a full-space correction to a reduced correlated result without a derivation can double count some correlation and miss other terms. Likewise, if an effective Hamiltonian had already folded in \(Q\), subsequently re-correlating that same \(Q\) contribution would need explicit double-counting control.

A fair comparison would keep geometry, basis, particle/spin target, energy reference, and accuracy goal aligned, then compare a bare active model, an orbital-optimized model, and a specifically defined effective model against suitable larger-space evidence. It would include the cost of obtaining the reference and effective integrals, not just the smaller quantum register. Our recorded 1.85-Å CASCI reference cannot be combined with the 2.0-Å MCSCF example or the 1.270025-Å resource notebook as if they were successive stages of one calculation.

## The handoff to integral representation

At this point the model choices are explicit. We can obtain a correlated fixed-orbital state, optimize a supported CASSCF problem through PySCF with native CI, or run supported single-reference MP2/CCSD calculations while respecting their amplitude and conversion boundaries. We also know where the repository provides an extension contract rather than a completed scientific method.

The next lesson changes a different layer: how the Hamiltonian’s one- and two-electron information is stored, transformed, and factorized. Factorization can reduce storage or circuit-construction cost for a chosen operator, but it does not by itself decide which electrons were modeled, recover missing outside-space correlation, or convert an amplitude-only result into a normalized quantum state. Keeping these layers separate is what makes later resource estimates scientifically interpretable.
lessons.caveats: Read-only source/test tracing at97a3ff4f; no imports, solver execution or tests run. MCSCF is optional PySCF CASSCF with nested QDK CI, not a shipped native orbital optimizer; outer settings limited and arbitrary input MO-index permutation is not restored generically. MP2 directly computes amplitudes without RDMs or small-denominator regularization; restricted open-shell dispatch is rejected by unrestricted-Hamiltonian requirement, and active UMP2 beta-beta amplitude energy indexing needs care. AmplitudeContainer is pure storage/NotSelfDual; native MP2 returns same object in ket/bra slots, CC optional lambda result requires store_amplitudes for retained data. PySCF molecular CC conversion rebuilds from orbitals rather than honoring arbitrary reduced/effective tensors; full molecular/reference examples only. Only CCSD is invoked, not triples; frozen/max_memory/verbose not registered despite optional code lookups. Effective-Hamiltonian factory has no concrete implementation; formal P/Q derivation is illustrative, validation opt-in. One directly related Lesson8 sentence corrected to remove implication that native MP2 produces the RDM required by natural-orbital localizer.

lessons.title: Representing and compressing the Hamiltonian
lessons.body:
# Lesson 12 — Representing and compressing the Hamiltonian

## Keep the model fixed while changing its numerical representation

The nitrogen story now has a precisely identified molecular geometry, orbital basis, active-electron partition, and correlated reference strategy. We can ask a new engineering question: how should we store and manipulate the Hamiltonian of that chosen model?

Five operations must remain distinct. An exact change of storage preserves the numerical operator. Truncating a factorization approximates that operator. Selecting active orbitals changes which electron occupations the model permits. Downfolding would incorporate excluded-space effects through a specifically defined effective operator; as Lesson 11 established, its QDK interface currently has no bundled concrete implementation. Qubit encoding, taught in Lesson 14, represents a fermionic operator with qubit operators.

A low-rank tensor is not automatically a better chemical model. It can be a cheaper representation of the same model, or a controlled numerical approximation that needs its own error assessment. It does not restore correlation omitted by a six-orbital active space or repair an inappropriate spin reference.

All API examples in this lesson are unexecuted. Algebraic examples are illustrative, not measured nitrogen factor ranks or energies. We keep the 1.85-Å tutorial separate from the 1.270025-Å notebook and other regression molecules.

## The Hamiltonian contains numbers with several different index meanings

For real spatial orbitals, the one-electron integral \(h_{pq}\) describes kinetic energy and the external potential between orbitals \(p\) and \(q\). In a frozen-core active Hamiltonian it also includes the inactive-electron field. The two-electron integral in **chemist notation** is

\[
g_{pqrs}=(pq|rs)=\iint
\phi_p(\mathbf r_1)\phi_q(\mathbf r_1)
\frac{1}{|\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2|}
\phi_r(\mathbf r_2)\phi_s(\mathbf r_2)
\,d\mathbf r_1\,d\mathbf r_2.
\]

The first pair shares electron coordinate one; the second pair shares coordinate two. **Physicist notation** instead groups a bra pair and a ket pair: \(v_{ijkl}=\langle ij|kl\rangle=(ik|jl)=g_{ikjl}\). Switching between these notations permutes indices; it is not a different Coulomb interaction.

For example, with two orbitals, chemist entry \(g_{0011}\) is the same number as physicist entry \(v_{0101}\). If each four-index array is flattened with its final index fastest, the first entry occupies offset three while the second occupies offset five. Reading the same flat buffer under the wrong notation therefore changes the interpreted Hamiltonian.

The concrete canonical container uses chemist-ordered `(i,j,k,l)` entries with offset

\[
\operatorname{offset}(i,j,k,l)=iK^3+jK^2+kK+l,
\]

where \(K\) is its active spatial-orbital count. The [element accessor](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian_containers/canonical_four_center.cpp) implements that mapping directly; it does not automatically translate an arbitrary caller’s physicist-order request. Some older RST text says physicist notation is the default, so this is a case where implementation matters more than the overview.

Indices in the active integral arrays are **positions within the active list**. If the full MO indices are `[4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]`, active position zero refers to original orbital four. `get_two_body_element(0,0,5,5)` then refers to the first and last orbitals of that active list. Passing original index nine into a six-orbital tensor is not a request for automatic remapping.

## Spin blocks, symmetries, and constants are part of the representation

The common one-body getter returns alpha and beta matrices. The common two-body getter returns three arrays labeled `aaaa`, `aabb`, and `bbbb`. For a restricted common spatial-orbital representation these can share data. For unrestricted orbitals, different alpha/beta coefficients give different same-spin and mixed-spin integrals, even though the underlying Coulomb interaction is spin independent.

The native four-center construction describes its mixed array as \((\alpha\alpha|\beta\beta)\); the Cholesky reconstruction and its dense-equivalence tests use the corresponding left-alpha/right-beta factors. The low-level transformation call can pass beta coefficient blocks first because of its internal layout, so call order is not a reliable statement of returned spin order. The [constructor](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/hamiltonian.cpp), actual flattened access, and matching producer/consumer tests must agree. Do not infer a universal beta-first storage convention from a legacy contraction comment.

For real Coulomb integrals, swapping members inside either orbital pair or exchanging the two pairs gives the familiar permutation symmetries. For complex orbitals some identities require conjugation and are not interchangeable real-array equalities. Antisymmetrized interaction tensors also have different signs and structure. The molecular containers and factorization algorithms traced here store real matrices/vectors; their mathematical assumptions must not be extended automatically to every complex or effective interaction.

`get_core_energy()` is the zero-body constant: it shifts every eigenvalue in the model by the same amount. For an all-active all-electron model it includes nuclear repulsion. With frozen inactive orbitals it includes their energy; with an ECP it uses the appropriate effective-charge convention and ECP one-electron contribution. It is not necessarily “the energy of the nuclei alone.” An inactive Fock matrix, when supplied, records the field of the frozen partition and can have **full MO dimensions**, even when active integrals have smaller dimensions.

`HamiltonianType.Hermitian` or `NonHermitian` is part of the data description. A metadata label is not a proof that every numerical array satisfies every symmetry or that a chosen solver supports non-Hermitian input. The energy and RDM conventions from Lesson 9 remain in force.

## The facade preserves one API while containers choose the storage

[`Hamiltonian`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian.hpp) delegates to a concrete container. `get_container_type()` identifies it, and Python `get_container()` gives access to container-specific information. The shared `get_one_body_integrals`, `get_two_body_integrals`, `get_one_body_element`, `get_two_body_element`, and availability methods are convenient, but their computational costs can differ enormously.

| Container type | Defining two-body representation |
|---|---|
| `canonical_four_center` | Explicit four-index integral arrays |
| `cholesky` | Pair-index-by-auxiliary factors, with optional AO factors |
| `factorized` | Restricted sum-of-squares factors `U`, `W`, and representation identity weights `WB` |
| `sparse` | Explicit nonzero four-index entries, primarily for model Hamiltonians |

These are existing concrete containers, not four interchangeable algorithms that all consume the same constructor arguments. In particular, a sparse model container constructs `ModelOrbitals`; simply moving molecular arrays into it does not preserve all molecular-basis metadata automatically.

The defining data are supplied at construction. The current interfaces do not provide a general “set this one integral in place” workflow like some older setter-oriented prose suggests. Construct a new representation deliberately. Internal lazy reconstruction caches are different from user mutation of the defining operator.

## Canonical four-center storage is simple and expensive

With \(K\) active spatial orbitals, one full two-electron block has \(K^4\) real entries. For the six-orbital model, that is 1296 entries; for the original 28-orbital space it is 614656. Those counts are arithmetic, not measured allocations for a complete calculation. Multiple spin blocks, intermediate transforms, solver matrices and cached properties add other costs.

Real permutation symmetry can reduce the number of independent values, but the canonical container exposes full flattened blocks rather than a universal eightfold-minimal packed tensor. Its symmetry-blocked storage can alias equivalent spin blocks for a restricted representation. That saves duplicated spin data without making every four-index entry disappear.

The advantage is direct lookup and simple contractions. Many established CI and correlation codes naturally consume these arrays. The disadvantage is quartic storage and expensive AO-to-MO transformation or repeated many-index contractions. The fact that a Hamiltonian is small in active orbital count does not imply that its original AO integral construction was equally small.

## Cholesky uses the Coulomb tensor’s pair structure

Combine each pair of orbital indices into one composite index, \(I=(p,q)\), and form the supermatrix \(G_{I,J}=g_{pqrs}\), with \(J=(r,s)\). A **supermatrix** here is just an ordinary matrix whose labels happen to be index pairs.

For the real Coulomb kernel, this pair matrix is positive semidefinite: the Coulomb quadratic form of any real pair-density combination is nonnegative. **Positive semidefinite (PSD)** means \(x^{\mathsf T}Gx\ge0\) for every real vector \(x\). It can have zero eigenvalues, especially because reversed orbital pairs are redundant.

A pivoted Cholesky decomposition approximates

\[
G\approx LL^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 g_{pqrs}\approx\sum_{t=1}^{R}L^t_{pq}L^t_{rs}.
\]

\(R\) is the retained Cholesky rank, not electron count or number of atoms. The factors can be stored as a \(K^2\)-by-\(R\) matrix. The term “three-center” in this container describes two orbital indices plus an auxiliary index; a Cholesky auxiliary need not be a physical third atom or a separately selected chemical basis function.

The algorithm chooses the largest remaining residual diagonal as its next pivot. If previous columns are known and pivot \(k\) has residual diagonal \(D_k\), the next column is

\[
L_I^{\mathrm{new}}=
\frac{G_{I,k}-\sum_{t\in\mathrm{previous}}L_I^tL_k^t}{\sqrt{D_k}},
\qquad
D_I\leftarrow D_I-(L_I^{\mathrm{new}})^2.
\]

The column removes the strongest remaining pair direction; repeated updates shrink the residual. A threshold controls when the remaining diagonal is judged negligible. This is very different from selecting determinants or deleting orbitals: every active orbital can remain present in the factors.

A purely illustrative two-orbital example takes

\[
L^1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

In pair order `(00,01,10,11)`, its vector is `(1,0,0,2)`. The outer product has nonzero entries \(g_{0000}=1\), \(g_{0011}=g_{1100}=2\), and \(g_{1111}=4\), and has rank one. One Cholesky column reconstructs the tensor exactly. These invented values demonstrate structure, not a molecular integral set obtained in this session.

## Construct Cholesky factors directly from molecular orbitals

The registered implementation **`hamiltonian_constructor/qdk_cholesky`** takes `Orbitals`, rather than an already constructed Hamiltonian. Its [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/cholesky_hamiltonian.cpp) evaluates needed AO Coulomb shell blocks through Libint while performing pivoted decomposition. It avoids first storing the complete AO four-index tensor.

The AO factors are transformed to active MOs by

\[
L^{t,\mathrm{MO}}_{ij}=
\sum_{\mu\nu}C_{\mu i}C_{\nu j}L^{t,\mathrm{AO}}_{\mu\nu}.
\]

Unrestricted input uses separate alpha and beta coefficient transforms with a shared auxiliary space. The constructor requires nonempty active spaces, matching alpha/beta active dimensions, and valid basis/index information; it handles noncontiguous selected columns explicitly. Native orbital/basis conversion restrictions from earlier lessons still apply.

Its actual [settings](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/microsoft/cholesky_hamiltonian.hpp) are `cholesky_tolerance=1e-8`, `eri_threshold=1e-12`, `store_ao_cholesky_vectors=False`, and `cholesky_gemm_batch_cols=20`. The first controls the Cholesky residual stopping scale; the second independently screens small integral shell contributions. The implementation raises an excessively small Cholesky tolerance to a floor proportional to the square root of the maximum AO pair rank times machine epsilon. A nominal zero tolerance is therefore not unlimited exact arithmetic.

`cholesky_gemm_batch_cols` controls batching of matrix multiplication work and must be positive; it is not a desired rank or chemistry-error tolerance. `store_ao_cholesky_vectors=True` retains the original AO factors for possible reuse but increases stored data. The actual auxiliary rank after transforming to a smaller active space can be larger than the minimal rank of that active tensor; projection does not automatically recompress the auxiliary list.

The constructor evaluates the one-electron kinetic/attraction terms and adds ECP integrals where present. It also uses its Cholesky factors to build inactive-electron Coulomb/exchange fields and the inactive constant. Consequently, finite Cholesky error can affect the active one-body term and core energy as well as the active two-body tensor. This differs from factoring an already constructed Hamiltonian, which can preserve its existing one-body/constant terms unchanged.

The [Hamiltonian tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_hamiltonian.cpp) cover restricted/unrestricted Cholesky construction and verify the correct effective nuclear constant for ECP-containing AgH. These are source test cases, not calculations run here.

## A factor getter and an integral getter can have very different costs

A `CholeskyHamiltonianContainer` exposes `get_three_center_integrals()` for the alpha/beta factor matrices and `get_ao_cholesky_vectors()` for the optional AO data. These are the useful interfaces when a consumer can work directly with factors.

Its shared `get_two_body_integrals()` interface reconstructs and caches full four-index arrays on first access. More subtly, the current **Cholesky `get_two_body_element` also builds that full cache** before returning one entry. A request that looks like one scalar lookup can therefore trigger quartic memory. The [container implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian_containers/cholesky.cpp) makes this explicit.

Low-rank storage uses roughly \(K^2R\) entries, advantageous when \(R\) is substantially smaller than \(K^2\). It can be less attractive for a tiny active tensor that inherits many AO factors. Once a legacy consumer requests the reconstructed tensor, peak memory may include both the factors and \(K^4\) cache. Native CI methods discussed earlier call dense integral getters, so changing the container alone does not guarantee their full calculation stays low rank.

Other consumers have specialized paths. The current [native qubit mapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/qubit_mapper/qdk_qubit_mapper.py) forwards Cholesky factors to a C++ provider that contracts one pair row at a time, avoiding a dense four-index intermediate. Its sparse path likewise iterates stored entries. This is a concrete algorithmic advantage of a matched consumer, not a universal benefit of the class name. The [equivalence tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_qdk_qubit_mapper_factorized.py) compare those paths term by term for the same underlying integrals.

## Hamiltonian factorization is a separate registered algorithm family

`HamiltonianFactorization` takes an existing `Hamiltonian` and returns a new one. The current [factory](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_factorization.cpp) registers **`double_factorization`** as its default concrete implementation. This is a working registered algorithm, unlike the interface-only effective-Hamiltonian constructor in Lesson 11.

The first stage produces Cholesky columns of the active pair tensor. The second stage treats each column as a symmetric \(K\)-by-\(K\) matrix and diagonalizes it:

\[
L^t_{pq}=\sum_b \epsilon_b^t U^t_{bp}U^t_{bq},
\]

\[
g_{pqrs}\approx\sum_t
\left(\sum_b\epsilon_b^tU^t_{bp}U^t_{bq}\right)
\left(\sum_{b^{\prime}}\epsilon_{b^{\prime}}^t
 U^t_{b^{\prime}r}U^t_{b^{\prime}s}\right).
\]

The rows of \(U^t\) in this storage convention are the fragment eigenvectors. Each \(L^t\) can have positive and negative eigenvalues even though the outer pair matrix \(G\) is PSD. The Cholesky column already contains its magnitude, so the second-stage eigenvalues are used **unscaled**; multiplying by an additional square root of an imagined first-stage eigenvalue would double count scaling.

For the toy diagonal fragment above, the second stage simply gives eigenvalues one and two with the identity rotation. More generally it expresses each two-electron fragment using rotated one-electron directions, useful for later quantum constructions. It does not optimize one common new molecular-orbital basis for the whole Hamiltonian; different fragments have different rotations.

## The exact current truncation semantics

The [double-factorization code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/algorithms/double_factorization.cpp) requires a non-null restricted Hamiltonian with a two-body term. For a dense input it works in the symmetric pair basis of dimension \(K(K+1)/2\), averages the eight real chemist permutations, and performs pivoted Cholesky. It still receives an existing dense \(K^4\) tensor and allocates a reduced-pair matrix whose size is quartic asymptotically. This route is not an on-the-fly AO integral algorithm.

`truncation_threshold` defaults to `1e-12` and applies to the **largest remaining residual diagonal** of that first-stage decomposition. The actual stopping level is at least its floating-point noise floor. It is not a cutoff applied independently to every original integral, every second-stage eigenvalue, or the final energy error. The current second stage diagonalizes all retained Cholesky matrices without an independent inner-rank truncation setting.

The implementation rejects NaN/non-finite tensor data and indefiniteness exposed through a sufficiently negative residual diagonal. A supplied tensor must genuinely have the PSD Coulomb structure needed by Cholesky. A generic Hermitian many-electron Hamiltonian, an antisymmetrized tensor, or a prospective downfolded interaction need not satisfy that pair-matrix condition. Small hidden negative directions can be truncated before a diagonal check exposes them. Averaging permutation symmetry also means an arbitrary nonsymmetric input is modified, not certified correct.

If the input is already a `CholeskyHamiltonianContainer` with the expected shape, the first stage is skipped. The stored factors are consumed directly, **`truncation_threshold` is ignored**, and each stored auxiliary column produces a second-stage fragment. Even redundant stored columns are retained. The [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_double_factorization.cpp) demonstrate this by supplying five columns spanning only rank three and verifying that five fragments are returned, including with an enormous truncation threshold.

An asymmetric stored Cholesky matrix is symmetrized for diagonalization, with a warning for appreciable asymmetry. Discarding all dense-input fragments is an error rather than a valid zero-interaction output. The one-electron arrays, orbital object, core constant, inactive Fock matrix, and Hamiltonian type are otherwise carried over unchanged. Increasing a threshold cannot undo truncation already present in an input Cholesky representation.

## The factorized container is more general than the default factorizer

[`FactorizedHamiltonianContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian_containers/factorized.hpp) stores `U` flattened as `[R,B,K]`, `W` as `[R,B,C]`, and `WB` as `[R,C]`. Here \(R\) counts groups/fragments, \(B\) counts basis rows per group, and \(C\) counts copies per group; this \(C\) is a dimension label, not the earlier MO coefficient matrix.

Define a leaf matrix

\[
M^{tc}_{pq}=\sum_b W^t_{bc}U^t_{bp}U^t_{bq}.
\]

Its reconstructed tensor is

\[
g_{pqrs}=\sum_{t,c}M^{tc}_{pq}M^{tc}_{rs}.
\]

This is a plain sum of outer-product squares. `WB` does not enter the reconstructed two-electron tensor. The general container can hold a double-factorized tensor-hypercontraction-style representation with multiple copies and normalized basis rows; it does not require all those rows to be mutually orthogonal. Thus arbitrary `W` entries should not all be called eigenvalues of a fragment. They are eigenvalues in the particular orthogonal second-stage decomposition produced by `DoubleFactorization`.

That default producer sets \(B=K\), one copy per fragment, `W` to the fragment eigenvalues, and **`WB=0`**. It does not implement a separate nonlinear fitting optimizer that searches all possible general `U/W/WB` tensor-hypercontraction representations. Having a storage format does not imply every fitting method for it is registered.

The [constructor validation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian_containers/factorized.cpp) checks dimensions, finite factors, active-space consistency, and unit norm of each `U` basis row within `1e-8`. Scaling a row requires compensating its `W` values, not silently changing the operator. The container is restricted-only and supports real factors.

`get_u_matrices`, `get_w_matrices`, `get_wb_matrix`, and the rank/basis/copy count getters expose the representation directly. `get_two_body_integrals()` reconstructs a quartic cache. Unlike the Cholesky scalar getter, its `get_two_body_element()` can contract just the requested pair entries from the factors when that cache is absent. `reconstruct_two_body_integrals()` explicitly requests a new full tensor. Those choices should be deliberate.

## Adjusted one-body terms and normalization are not new chemistry energies

The factorized container also supplies `get_h1_prime()` and `get_lambda()` for downstream factor-based operator constructions. They are not replacements for the original stored one-electron integrals or total molecular energy.

Writing \(h\) for the stored one-body matrix and \(w_B^{tc}\) for `WB`, the [implemented adjusted matrix](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian_containers/factorized.cpp) is

\[
h^{\prime}=h
-\frac12\sum_{t,c}M^{tc}M^{tc}
+\sum_{t,c}\operatorname{Tr}(M^{tc})M^{tc}
-\sum_{t,c}w_B^{tc}M^{tc}.
\]

The first correction includes the one-body term produced when products of one-electron operators are converted to properly normal-ordered two-electron interactions. The trace and identity-weight terms belong to the later decomposition convention. The fermionic algebra behind that distinction is developed in Lesson 14; simply treating a numerical square as an already normal-ordered two-electron operator would miss the correction.

The reported normalization is

\[
\Lambda=\sum_j|\operatorname{eig}_j(h^{\prime})|
+\frac14\sum_{t,c}
\left(|w_B^{tc}|+\sum_b|W^t_{bc}|\right)^2.
\]

This is a factorization-dependent algorithmic normalization, not the ground-state energy, not an entropy, and not necessarily the Pauli coefficient norm of a different mapped representation. Its implementation requires a symmetric adjusted one-body matrix and throws if that condition is not met. The separate core energy is not simply another term inserted into this formula.

Changing `WB` leaves the ordinary reconstructed two-electron tensor unchanged while changing the adjusted matrix and normalization. The [factorized-container tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/tests/test_factorized_hamiltonian.cpp) verify that distinction and the exact one-body correction formula. Do not tune representation weights and report a lower \(\Lambda\) as a lower physical energy. These data will matter for sum-of-squares and quantum-walk constructions later, but their circuit and workload costs still need analysis.

## Sparse storage means explicit missing entries, not inferred interactions

The [`SparseHamiltonianContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian_containers/sparse.cpp) primarily supports lattice/model Hamiltonians. It stores a sparse one-body matrix and a map from four-index keys to two-body values. A missing two-body entry is interpreted as zero; the map is not an instruction to fill all orbital permutations automatically. The common restricted constructors alias the same interaction across appropriate spin channels.

Converting a dense two-body array to this map keeps entries whose value is not exactly zero. It is not a user-tunable molecular integral screening algorithm. The dense-to-sparse one-body path uses Eigen’s sparse conversion. If one deliberately drops small nonzero interactions to obtain sparsity, that is an additional approximation whose symmetry and error must be checked. Duplicate operator contributions need to be combined consistently; a map of unique keys is not a substitute for that algebra.

Sparse-specific accessors allow direct iteration over stored data. The base facade still retains dense one-body information, so this implementation is not sparse-only in every array. A full two-body getter lazily allocates a zero-filled \(K^4\) tensor and inserts the stored entries; even a one-body-only model can incur that allocation if a consumer asks for the dense two-body tensor.

`has_two_body_integrals()` checks whether a sparse-map object is present, not whether a materialized tensor has nonzero norm. An absent map and an explicitly supplied empty map can therefore have different availability metadata while representing zero interaction. The general rule is to inspect the concrete contract rather than infer cost or nonzero physics from one boolean.

Sparse storage is attractive when locality or a model definition makes most entries genuinely zero. Low rank is attractive when many dense entries can be expressed through common factors. A tensor can be dense but low rank, sparse but not very low rank, both, or neither. This is why no single container is always the most compact.

## A source-backed representation workflow

Using the consistently selected orbital object from Lesson 10, the following describes three actual native requests without executing them:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create

selected_orbitals = selected.get_orbitals()
canonical = create("hamiltonian_constructor", "qdk").run(selected_orbitals)
cholesky = create(
    "hamiltonian_constructor", "qdk_cholesky",
    cholesky_tolerance=1e-8, eri_threshold=1e-12,
    store_ao_cholesky_vectors=False,
).run(selected_orbitals)
factorized = create(
    "hamiltonian_factorization", "double_factorization",
    truncation_threshold=1e-12,
).run(cholesky)
factors = factorized.get_container()
rank = factors.get_num_ranks()
```

The last threshold does not re-truncate the supplied Cholesky factors. To study the dense-input cutoff, give the factorizer `canonical` instead. Neither example chooses a different active space. The `selected` carrier is used only to supply orbitals, not falsely presented as the correlated CI state whose amplitudes were preserved.

For a small validation problem, compare reconstructed tensors and core/one-body data, or evaluate the same normalized reference against both operators with consistent RDMs. Re-solving CI at matching active counts tests an eigenvalue consequence but may materialize dense tensors and incur substantial cost. The [Python double-factorization tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_double_factorization.py) use explicitly PSD synthetic tensors to check rank and reconstruction; they are not measured nitrogen compression ratios.

Serialization preserves the defining representation through `container_type`: the [loader dispatch](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian.cpp) knows canonical, Cholesky, sparse, and factorized containers and rejects unknown types. Factors, orbital metadata, constants, and versions belong in that record; a lazy dense cache is not the scientific definition. No serialized files were written during preparation.

## Budget factorization error separately from chemistry error

For a fixed normalized state, the energy change caused by integral approximation is a contraction of its density information with changes in the one-body, two-body, and constant terms. Schematically,

\[
\delta E=\delta E_{\mathrm{core}}
+\sum_{pq}\delta h_{pq}\gamma_{qp}
+\frac12\sum_{pqrs}\delta g_{pqrs}\Gamma_{rspq}.
\]

The number and magnitude of these terms matter; a pivot threshold is not automatically an absolute molecular energy error. For Hermitian operators in the same state space, an operator-norm bound on \(\delta H\) bounds eigenvalue shifts, but this implementation does not turn every requested tolerance into that certificate.

A useful assessment varies factorization/screening thresholds while keeping geometry, basis, active partition, spin restriction, and solver precision fixed. Separate reconstruction error from error introduced when one constructs the inactive field with approximate factors. Preserve signs, pair ordering and constants before blaming a discrepancy on rank truncation.

Finally, factorization can lower memory or provide more useful input to a quantum algorithm without proving quantum advantage. A smaller rank may alter a later normalization and circuit decomposition, but the complete cost also includes fragment rotations, state preparation, precision, shots/repetitions, and error correction. Before analyzing those costs, we need a concrete vocabulary for the quantum registers and operations that will consume these representations.
lessons.caveats: No numerical factorization, chemistry imports, tests or file output executed. Concrete storage/accessor paths are chemist ordered despite older RST physicist-default claim. Native mixed block described/tested alpha-alpha|beta-beta; do not infer beta-first storage from legacy contraction comment. qdk_cholesky builds AO factors on demand; its scalar integral accessor still materializes full tensor. Double factorization restricted/PSD; dense input symmetry is averaged and cutoff applies only first pivoted stage; stored Cholesky vectors bypass cutoff and retain redundant auxiliaries. Second stage keeps all eigenvalues, B=K,C=1,WB=0. Factorized general rows are unit normalized but not required mutually orthogonal; no separate general DFTHC fitting optimizer registered. WB affects h1_prime/lambda but not reconstructedg. Sparse container is model oriented, does not infer missing permutations and can materialize quartic dense caches. Factorization thresholds do not certify chemical accuracy.

lessons.title: Learning the quantum computer vocabulary
lessons.body:
# Lesson 13 — Learning the quantum computer vocabulary

## From a chemical state to a quantum register

We have described electronic states, selected a molecular model, and examined Hamiltonian representations. Before translating electrons into qubits, we need to understand what a quantum program actually manipulates. The next few ideas explain the Q# operations already present in this repository rather than asking us to treat circuit diagrams as unexplained symbols.

A quantum circuit is not a picture of electrons moving between atoms. It is a program acting on an abstract quantum register whose states have been assigned a meaning. The physical device implementing that register is a later hardware/error-correction question. Our six-active-electron nitrogen model does not automatically mean six qubits; an occupation encoding of six spatial orbitals has twelve spin modes before any symmetry reduction.

All circuit examples and arithmetic in this lesson are illustrative or read from source tests. No QDK import, compilation, simulation, measurement, or resource estimate was executed while preparing the course.

## A qubit has amplitudes, not two simultaneously readable classical values

A classical **bit** takes a value zero or one. A **qubit** is described by a normalized vector in a two-dimensional complex state space. Choose the computational basis

\[
|0\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
|1\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

A pure qubit state has the form

\[
|\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle,
\qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1.
\]

The complex amplitudes \(\alpha,\beta\) play the same mathematical role as amplitudes in our determinant expansions, although the basis labels now refer to qubit values. Their squared magnitudes give probabilities of computational-basis measurement. They are not two classical answers that can both be read out.

For example, the illustrative state \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}|0\rangle+\tfrac{i}{2}|1\rangle\), with \(i^2=-1\), gives outcome zero with probability three-quarters and outcome one with probability one-quarter. The imaginary factor does not make an imaginary probability. It carries phase information that can matter when amplitudes later interfere.

Multiplying the entire state by the same unit-magnitude factor \(e^{i\phi}\) gives an unobservable **global phase**. Multiplying only one component changes a **relative phase**, which can affect subsequent measurements after suitable operations. This distinction is central to phase-estimation circuits and to getting signs right in fermionic mappings.

## Gates are linear, reversible transformations

An ideal quantum **gate** is represented by a unitary matrix \(U\):

\[
U^{\dagger}U=I.
\]

The dagger means transpose plus complex conjugation. Unitarity preserves normalization, and the inverse operation is \(U^{\dagger}\), also called the **adjoint**. Measurement is different: it produces classical information and generally changes the state irreversibly from the perspective of the register alone.

The elementary **Pauli gates** are

\[
I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

`I` changes nothing. `X` exchanges zero and one. `Z` preserves computational-basis populations but changes the sign of the one component. `Y` both exchanges the basis values and adds phase: \(Y|0\rangle=i|1\rangle\) and \(Y|1\rangle=-i|0\rangle\). A minus sign in an amplitude is not a third classical measurement outcome.

The **Hadamard gate**, written `H` in circuit code, is

\[
H_{\mathrm{gate}}=\frac1{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

It sends zero to the equal-plus superposition \(|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\), and one to \(|-\rangle=(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\).
