The subscript reminds us that this `H` gate is not the molecular energy operator \(\hat H\). In general an energy matrix is not itself a unitary gate; an algorithm constructs suitable unitaries or embeddings from it.

The repository’s [state-preparation utilities](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/StatePreparation.qs) use `X` to set occupied basis bits and `H` to prepare uniform superpositions. Their meaning is concrete matrix action, not a shorthand for solving a chemistry problem.

## Worked interference: a phase change becomes a different outcome

Follow this ideal one-qubit sequence without measuring between gates:

\[
|0\rangle\xrightarrow{H}
\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}
\xrightarrow{Z}
\frac{|0\rangle-|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}
\xrightarrow{H}|1\rangle.
\]

Immediately after the `Z`, a computational-basis measurement would still look fifty-fifty. The final `H` combines amplitudes: contributions to zero cancel and contributions to one reinforce. That is **interference**. Without the `Z`, applying `H` twice returns zero instead.

A coherent superposition is therefore not merely a classical mixture of “zero half the time, one half the time.” A fifty-fifty mixture has lost the relative phase information. Applying `Z` does not change that mixture, and applying `H` still leaves a fifty-fifty computational-basis distribution. The coherent and mixed cases can have the same immediate measurement probabilities but different responses to subsequent gates.

An illustrative Q# program using the same gate syntax is:

```qsharp
operation InterferenceExample() : Result {
    use q = Qubit();
    H(q);
    Z(q);
    H(q);
    return MResetZ(q);
}
```

This is teaching code, not a function claimed to exist in the repository. `use` allocates a qubit, and `MResetZ` measures in the Z basis and resets the qubit to zero. In the ideal mathematical model its result is `One`. No run was performed here.

## Phase and rotation gates require explicit conventions

A phase gate such as \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)\) changes relative phase without changing immediate Z-measurement probabilities. The commonly named \(T\) gate is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\); this `T` is a gate name, not the kinetic-energy matrix from Lesson 5.

Use the standard rotation convention

\[
R_P(\theta)=e^{-i\theta P/2},
\]

where \(P\) is a Pauli matrix and \(\theta\) is an angle in radians. For example,

\[
R_z(\theta)=
\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\theta/2}&0\\0&e^{i\theta/2}\end{pmatrix}.
\]

A phase operation \(\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})\) differs from this by a global phase. That can be harmless for an isolated operation but not necessarily after making the operation controlled.

The chemistry repository uses Q# **`Exp`**, not a blind substitution of a coefficient into `Rz`. The [Pauli-exponential code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/PauliExp.qs) calls:

```qsharp
Exp(paulis, -coeff, systems);
```

The [matrix-equivalence test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit_mapper.py) checks the resulting term operation against \(e^{-i\,\mathrm{coeff}\,P}\). In the rotation convention above, that corresponds to \(R_P(2\,\mathrm{coeff})\), not \(R_P(\mathrm{coeff})\). The minus sign and factor of two are thus fixed by the concrete source/test contract, rather than guessed from a gate’s name. The external QDK standard library implements the primitive `Exp`; its internal compiler/runtime source was not reviewed here.

Gate order matters. If code applies operation one and then operation two, the state is multiplied by \(U_2U_1\). The repository’s sequential-composition helper follows precisely that chronological order. We will derive full Hamiltonian simulation formulas later; the immediate lesson is not to conflate an energy coefficient, an evolution angle, and a rotation-gate argument.

## Registers use tensor products

A **register** is an ordered collection of qubits. Two qubits have four computational-basis states, and \(q\) qubits have \(2^q\). The joint state space is a tensor product, meaning we combine all basis possibilities and multiply amplitudes for independent subsystems.

For the following derivation write kets in the displayed order \(|q_0q_1\rangle\). Then

\[
(a|0\rangle+b|1\rangle)\otimes(c|0\rangle+d|1\rangle)
=ac|00\rangle+ad|01\rangle+bc|10\rangle+bd|11\rangle.
\]

A gate acting on one subsystem is extended by the identity on the other. For example, \(X\otimes I\) in this displayed order flips the first listed qubit and leaves the second alone. A tensor-product matrix has a block structure; \(X\otimes I\) has identity blocks off diagonal and zero blocks on the diagonal. It is not the elementwise product of two matrices.

Actual software interfaces may print tensor factors in a different order. We will track that explicitly rather than silently switching which end of a bitstring means qubit zero.

## CNOT creates correlations coherently

The **controlled-NOT**, written `CNOT` in Q# and often `cx` in OpenQASM, has a control qubit and a target qubit. On basis states,

\[
\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin{\oplus}a\rangle,
\]

where \(\oplus\) is exclusive-or, addition modulo two. The target flips when the control is one; the control is not measured. Linearity extends this action to a superposition.

The repository’s [binary-encoding utilities](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/BinaryEncoding.qs) explicitly apply `CNOT(qs[control], qs[target])`, as well as X, SWAP, and double-controlled X operations, to manipulate encoded occupation information. These are coherent register transformations, not conditional statements based on reading a hidden classical value.

Starting from zero-zero, apply `H` to the first qubit and CNOT from first to second:

\[
|00\rangle\longrightarrow
\frac{|00\rangle+|10\rangle}{\sqrt2}
\longrightarrow
|\Phi^+\rangle=\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]

This is a **Bell state**. It is entangled: it cannot be written as a tensor product of two pure one-qubit states. If the product formula above had nonzero `00` and `11` amplitudes but zero `01` and `10`, its factors would have to be both nonzero and zero in incompatible ways. The joint information cannot be assigned to two independent state vectors.

Each individual Z measurement is random, but the joint outcomes are equal: `00` or `11` ideally. A classical mixture of those same two outcomes reproduces that Z correlation, so that measurement alone does not establish quantum coherence. Measuring both qubits in X instead distinguishes them: the Bell state retains equal-outcome correlation, whereas that classical mixture gives all four X-basis combinations equally often.

Entanglement does not enable faster-than-light communication. A local measurement result remains random, and local statistics cannot reveal another party’s freely chosen action without the appropriate shared comparison. Correlation is not controllable signaling.

CNOT also does not clone an arbitrary unknown qubit. On \(|+\rangle|0\rangle\) it makes the Bell state, not \(|+\rangle|+\rangle\). Known computational-basis information can be copied reversibly, but arbitrary unknown amplitudes cannot be copied by that same operation.

## Controlled-U makes phase observable between branches

A general controlled operation is

\[
\operatorname{C}U=
|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+
|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes U.
\]

On a control superposition it coherently combines a branch that does nothing and a branch that applies \(U\):

\[
|+\rangle|\psi\rangle\longrightarrow
\frac{|0\rangle|\psi\rangle+|1\rangle U|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]

If \(U\) is replaced by \(e^{i\phi}U\), the one branch now gains a relative phase. A phase that was global for an isolated system operation becomes observable through control interference. This is why a scalar Hamiltonian energy offset cannot be dropped casually in a controlled evolution without accounting for its phase or restoring it consistently in interpretation.

The [controlled Pauli-exponential source](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/ControlledPauliExp.qs) uses

```qsharp
Controlled Exp([control], (paulis, -coeff, systems));
```

The [controlled matrix test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_controlled_circuit_mapper.py) compares to the block-diagonal controlled-U formula above. This directly checks both which branch acts and the sign convention. We are not yet deriving phase-estimation bit extraction; we are learning the coherent controlled operation it will require.

## Adjoint, controls, and ordinary classical code are different capabilities

Q# uses an `operation` for routines that can act on qubits, and a `function` for classical computation/construction. `Qubit[]` is an array of qubit handles. `Result[]` is an array of classical measurement results. `Unit` is a return type meaning no classical value is returned; it is not a unit of energy.

An operation declared `is Adj + Ctl` exposes adjoint and controlled variants. `Adjoint op` requests its inverse; `Controlled op` requests a coherent controlled version. The [composition helpers](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/CircuitComposition.qs) build these callable forms and adapt a control-register operation to a single-control-qubit signature. The declared callable capability matters: not every source helper exposes every modifier just because some gates in its body are unitary.

Ordinary irreversible assignments cannot simply be promoted into coherent computation. A reversible implementation of a classical function typically preserves its input and writes an answer into another register, for example \(|x\rangle|y\rangle\mapsto|x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle\). Overwriting many distinguishable inputs with the same value would not have a unitary inverse.

Classical assignments and loops are still useful around quantum operations. In Q# source, constructing an array of measurement results or looping over known coefficient parameters is classical control. It does not place the Python/Q# integer variables themselves into quantum superposition. A branch on a measured `Result` is **classical feedback**, different from `Controlled op` acting on an unmeasured qubit.

## Ancillas must be prepared, used, and cleaned up

An **ancilla** is an auxiliary qubit used for a computation rather than directly representing the target electronic occupation. A circuit may have an occupation register, a control/readout qubit, address registers, and scratch/work ancillas. They all cost space while alive, but their roles differ.

A work register often becomes entangled with the system while computing an intermediate value. Simply ignoring it does not restore a clean system state; it can destroy interference when viewed only on the system. **Uncomputation** coherently reverses the work after its result has been used, returning the scratch register to its known initial state when the algorithm’s assumptions hold.

Q#’s `within { ... } apply { ... }` pattern performs the setup, the body, then the adjoint of the setup. The repository’s `MakeSharedAncillaOp` uses this pattern to prepare and restore trailing shared ancillas. The enclosed operation must respect the intended ancilla contract; an arbitrary destructive operation is not magically repaired by running the preparation backward.

The binary-encoding helpers also accept pools of initially zero ancillas and document which are restored before return. Reusing a cleaned ancilla can reduce peak width even though the algorithm performed many work operations. Measurement-based cleanup is another implementation strategy, but it can change which adjoint/control capabilities a routine exposes. We will treat detailed state-preparation tradeoffs later rather than assuming every helper is one generic unitary black box.

## Measurement returns samples, not the whole amplitude vector

A computational-basis measurement of one qubit returns zero or one with the corresponding squared-amplitude probabilities. Measuring a general Pauli observable returns an eigenvalue sign, conventionally represented by `Zero` for +1 and `One` for −1. Measuring in X or Y means asking a different observable, often implemented through a basis change and a computational measurement.

Measurement generally changes the joint state. For the Bell example, observing zero on one qubit conditions the partner to zero in that measurement basis. Repeating that measurement immediately on the same state is not another independent sample of the original preparation. A **shot** normally means reprepare the intended initial state, execute the circuit, and obtain a fresh set of outcomes.

The repository’s [`MeasureInBasis`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/MeasurementBasis.qs) calls `MResetX`, `MResetY`, or `MResetZ` for the chosen basis and resets qubits. For a Pauli-I position it performs `Reset` but appends no measurement result. Thus the returned result-array length can be smaller than the register width. It is a destructive readout/cleanup operation, not a state-preserving observation of all amplitudes. `MakeMeasurementCircuit` checks that the basis array matches the declared register size before preparation and readout.

Repeated shots estimate probabilities and expectation values statistically. An ideal Bell experiment does not guarantee exactly fifty `00` and fifty `11` results in one hundred shots. Finite-sample uncertainty remains even with noiseless gates. Noise and qubit loss introduce additional issues that are not the same as this ordinary sampling uncertainty.

## Indexing conventions must be attached to the data

The written ket order in our two-qubit derivations was \(|q_0q_1\rangle\). The repository’s standardized executor bitstrings instead place the first returned bit at the **right-hand end** after conversion. The [result-processing code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_executor/qdk.py) reverses the raw result array while making its string.

The [executor test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit_executor_qdk.py) makes this concrete: X on qubit zero of a two-qubit register gives raw results `One, Zero`, but the standardized count key is `"01"`. The same physical register assignment can therefore be written `|10⟩` in a q0-first explanatory ket and `"01"` in the result format. That is ordering, not a physical disagreement.

A little-endian integer convention assigns significance \(2^j\) to bit/qubit \(j\). A big-endian displayed ordering gives the leftmost listed bit the greatest significance. The [dense-preparation tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_state_preparation_dense.py) explicitly handle Q# state-dump ordering, where the first allocated qubit is the most significant bit of the dense dump index. The [Python preparation builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/dense_pure_state.py) uses a reversed `rowMap` to bridge its determinant-derived amplitude indexing to the Q# preparation.

Do not declare “QDK is always big endian” or “everything is little endian.” The interface matters: a state dump, an array of qubit handles, a Pauli label, and an executor count key can use different display/index conventions. Keep the conversion explicit, especially when not every qubit is measured.

## A concrete Circuit and execution handoff

The [executor tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit_executor_qdk.py) contain the following Bell-circuit structure in OpenQASM. The adapted example below shows the actual QDK Chemistry data/algorithm contract but was not executed:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import Circuit

bell = Circuit(qasm="""
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c[0] = measure q[0];
c[1] = measure q[1];
""", num_qubits=2)
executor = create("circuit_executor", "qdk_sparse_state_simulator", seed=42)
results = executor.run(bell, shots=100)
counts = results.bitstring_counts
```

The ideal possible outcomes are `00` and `11`; no actual counts are being reported. The circuit explicitly measures, so the executor has classical results to return. A preparation-only operation returning `Unit` is not automatically a sampling program returning bitstrings.

[`CircuitExecutorData`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/circuit_executor_data.py) contains count data, `total_shots`, executor identity, and optional execution metadata. Loss-affected outcomes, when an applicable noise model produces them, are separated into `loss_bitstrings` using `L`. Clean counts alone then need not sum to total shots. Full execution/noise policy is a later chapter; here the key distinction is between a prepared state, a returned classical sample, and metadata describing how it was produced.

## Circuit representations are descriptions at different stages

[`Circuit`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/circuit.py) can hold OpenQASM text, QIR, a Q# circuit representation, or Q# factory data together with a composable operation. **OpenQASM** is a language for quantum programs. **QIR**, quantum intermediate representation, is a lower-level compiler interchange representation. **Q#** is the programming language used for many repository circuit routines. Changing formats is not itself execution on hardware.

A Q# factory stores a program and classical parameters from which a representation can be compiled when needed. `qsharp_op` is the callable used for composition; by itself it is not one of the constructor’s sufficient stored representations. The constructor requires QASM, QIR, a Q# circuit representation, or factory data. Conversion availability is also not universal: some QIR-to-QASM/Qiskit paths need the optional Qiskit integration.

The public data object resists ordinary attribute reassignment, but `get_qir()` can internally cache compiled QIR derived from its factory. This is a compiler-artifact cache, not a cached quantum state. Supplying several representations also does not independently prove they mean the same program; keep them tied to a consistent producer.

The known `num_qubits` field records the width of the register on which the supplied operation acts. **Internally allocated scratch qubits are not included in that declaration.** A compiler/resource estimate can therefore report a different peak width. `CircuitMetadata.num_phase_gradient_ancillas` describes special reusable trailing ancillas; it requires a declared width and cannot exceed that width. Their detailed preparation comes later, but even now we can see why one integer is not a complete physical-resource report.

## QDK Chemistry composes routines; the external QDK supplies the language runtime

The repository contains Q# source for state preparation, Pauli exponentials, controlled operations, measurement wrappers, and composition. It imports primitive gates and operations such as `PreparePureStateD`, `Exp`, and measurement/reset helpers from the external QDK standard library. Python’s [`QSHARP_UTILS` context helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/__init__.py) loads those chemistry utilities through a shared `qdk.Context`, created lazily. An isolated context can also be created when explicitly needed.

Operations composed together need compatible context ownership. A **target profile** limits which program capabilities the compiler accepts; it is not a complete choice of physical qubit technology or error-correcting code. The helper’s default profile is `Adaptive_RIF`; the Base-profile path loads only its supported subset of chemistry sources. None of those contexts was instantiated for this preparation.

`BeginEstimateCaching` in some repeated Q# wrappers is a resource-estimation facility. It helps the estimator handle repeated identical subroutines; it does not mean a physical device can apply an expensive unitary once and reuse the resulting unknown state for free. Repetition still belongs in the logical workload.

## Simulation, sampling, and resource counting are different computations

A **state-vector simulator** represents a quantum state on a classical computer and updates its amplitudes. A generic \(q\)-qubit vector has \(2^q\) complex amplitudes. As an illustrative storage model, complex128 amplitudes alone require sixteen GiB at thirty qubits. That is not a measurement of QDK’s implementation memory and excludes overhead.

Sparse-state simulation can exploit a state with few nonzero computational-basis amplitudes, but gates can rapidly grow that support. Special **Clifford** circuits—whose gates map Pauli operators to Pauli operators under conjugation—admit other efficient classical descriptions. H, S, and CNOT are examples; arbitrary rotations are not automatically in that class. The full-state executor exposes `type` choices `cpu`, `gpu`, and `clifford`, but a selectable value does not prove a corresponding device exists or that an arbitrary circuit is suitable for the Clifford backend.

The registered default executor is `qdk_sparse_state_simulator`; `qdk_full_state_simulator` uses the external QDK QIR simulation path. Both return measurement data through the executor interface. Their implementations are classical validation/execution backends, not evidence that a quantum device solved the molecule.

A physical quantum state is also not a cheap readable database of all \(2^q\) amplitudes. Reading it produces samples; learning a generic state requires many suitably chosen repeated preparations and measurements. Generic state preparation itself can be expensive. Useful quantum algorithms exploit problem structure and extract a chosen observable or phase, rather than compute every determinant energy and read all answers in parallel.

Resource counting asks yet another question: how many operations and qubits a program requires under a chosen compilation/cost model. `Circuit.estimate()` delegates supported Q# factory or QASM representations to external QDK estimation. `get_qre_application()` adapts available representations to the alternative `qdk.qre` interface. These are alternatives, not mandatory consecutive stages, and neither is a new chemistry calculation or a physical execution.

## Count the right things before discussing hardware

**Gate count** counts operations in a specified gate set. **Depth** counts sequential layers under a specified parallel scheduling/connectivity model. **Width** is the number of simultaneously live qubits. A circuit with many operations can reuse a small clean ancilla, while a short-depth implementation may use more concurrent work qubits. These are distinct tradeoffs.

A high-level `Exp` or rotation is not necessarily one cheap physical gate. It can decompose into many simpler operations, and synthesizing arbitrary rotations to a chosen precision changes later resource counts. Fault tolerance then encodes logical qubits and implements those operations with physical qubits and error-correction cycles. We defer those hardware/QEC models rather than invent a fixed number of physical qubits per chemical electron.

For a simple occupation-basis initializer of our six-active-electron, six-spatial-orbital model, one would allocate twelve occupation qubits and apply X to the six occupied spin-mode positions. That follows the repository’s single-reference preparation loop. It explains why six X operations do not imply only six system qubits, and why the eight inactive electrons are not another eight occupation qubits in that reduced model. Later state-preparation methods may require additional ancillas or different structure.

We now have the vocabulary to read a coherent circuit without mistaking amplitudes for probabilities, controls for measurements, or metadata widths for physical machines. The next lesson assigns electron occupations and fermionic signs to these registers by translating the Hamiltonian into Pauli and Majorana-based qubit representations.
lessons.caveats: Foundational mathematics and source/test tracing only; no QDK import, circuit compilation, simulation, counting or resource estimate executed. Gate rotation convention distinguished from actual Exp(paulis,-coeff) calls and matrix tests. Ket display order, Q# dense dump order, raw Result array and reversed executor count strings are not assumed identical. num_qubits excludes internally allocated scratch; metadata is not physical-qubit count. Q# primitives/compiler/runtime and simulation internals are external boundaries, not reviewed implementations. Circuit conversions depend on available representation and optional tools. Simulator choices are not hardware availability or quantum advantage; physical QEC costs deferred.

lessons.title: Translating electrons into qubits
lessons.body:
# Lesson 14 — Translating electrons into qubits

## The same chemistry, a different language

Our nitrogen molecule has not changed. It is still neutral, singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å. The original cc-pVDZ model had 28 spatial molecular orbitals. The active-space workflow studied earlier produced a six-electron, six-spatial-orbital model, with three active alpha and three active beta electrons. That reduced chemical model, not the complete 28-orbital problem, will now be translated into qubit operators. The separate notebook at 1.270025 Å remains a different calculation.

A **fermion-to-qubit mapping** specifies how an electronic state and every operator acting on it are represented by qubits. It does not select a better basis, recover omitted correlation, or solve the Schrödinger equation. With an exact, compatible mapping, the same model has the same predictions in different coordinates. Numerical screening during mapping is a separate approximation.

For the ordinary mappings in this lesson, six spatial orbitals mean twelve spin-orbital modes and twelve occupation-register qubits. There are still six active electrons. Neither number includes scratch or phase-estimation registers. Had we mapped the full 28-spatial-orbital model without reduction, the occupation register would instead have 56 qubits.

This distinction becomes concrete in the repository’s [nitrogen mapping tutorial](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/tutorial_map_n2_to_qubits.py): it constructs a Hamiltonian from the selected orbitals, explicitly creates a `MajoranaMapping`, maps the active operator, retains the core-energy scalar separately, and validates in the appropriate electron-number sector. We will unpack that sequence rather than treat mapping as a mysterious conversion command. No tutorial, mapper, or test is being executed in this lesson.

## From coordinates to occupations

In **first quantization**, one describes a fixed number of electrons using their coordinates and spin variables. Antisymmetry is a condition on the many-electron wavefunction: exchanging two electrons changes its sign. A determinant is one way to enforce it.

In **second quantization**, one first chooses an ordered list of one-electron modes, such as spin orbitals, and describes which modes are occupied. The underlying physics has not been quantized twice. The language has changed from named particle coordinates to occupation numbers and operations that change them.

With \(M\) spin-orbital modes, an occupation basis state is

\[
|f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{M-1}\rangle,
\qquad f_j\in\{0,1\}.
\]

Here \(f_j\) says whether mode \(j\) contains an electron. The exclusion principle permits at most one electron in a particular spin orbital. Two electrons of opposite spin may occupy the same spatial orbital because they occupy different modes.

The space containing all these occupation states is **Fock space**. It contains sectors with zero, one, two, and more electrons. This is not the SCF Fock matrix, which was an effective one-electron operator. The similar names refer to different objects.

A twelve-mode occupation register has \(2^{12}=4096\) basis states. The sector with three alpha electrons in six alpha modes and three beta electrons in six beta modes has only

\[
\binom{6}{3}\binom{6}{3}=400
\]

states. These are illustrative combinatorial counts for the recorded active-space size, not a newly computed molecular result. An untapered qubit Hamiltonian ordinarily acts on all 4096 states. The mapping does not automatically remove the other electron sectors, and fixing alpha/beta populations does not by itself enforce a particular total-spin eigenvalue.

The ordering is part of the definition. We use

\[
|f_0,\ldots,f_{M-1}\rangle
=(a_0^\dagger)^{f_0}\cdots(a_{M-1}^\dagger)^{f_{M-1}}|\mathrm{vac}\rangle.
\]

The vacuum \(|\mathrm{vac}\rangle\) has no occupied modes. The dagger denotes an adjoint. The operator \(a_j^\dagger\) creates occupation in mode \(j\), and \(a_j\) removes it. These are mathematical building blocks; a number-conserving molecular Hamiltonian does not manufacture net electrons.

Define the preceding-occupation count \(P_j=\sum_{k<j}f_k\). Then

\[
a_j|f\rangle=(-1)^{P_j}f_j
|f_0,\ldots,0_j,\ldots\rangle,
\]

\[
a_j^\dagger|f\rangle=(-1)^{P_j}(1-f_j)
|f_0,\ldots,1_j,\ldots\rangle.
\]

The factors \(f_j\) and \(1-f_j\) enforce empty/occupied restrictions. The sign encodes fermionic exchange. It is not an optional cosmetic phase: different paths between determinants interfere, so inconsistent signs change matrix elements and energies.

Consider the hand-worked four-mode state \(|1,0,1,0\rangle\), written in increasing mode order, not as a software bitstring. Removing the electron from mode 2 crosses one preceding occupied mode, giving \(-|1,0,0,0\rangle\). Creating in mode 3 crosses two and gives \(+|1,0,1,1\rangle\). Creating in already occupied mode 2 gives zero.

The two-mode state \(|1,1\rangle\) makes the algebra especially visible: \(a_1a_0|1,1\rangle=|0,0\rangle\), whereas \(a_0a_1|1,1\rangle=-|0,0\rangle\). Operators act rightmost first. Their sum vanishes. In general the **canonical anticommutation relations** are

\[
\{a_p,a_q\}=0,\qquad
\{a_p^\dagger,a_q^\dagger\}=0,\qquad
\{a_p,a_q^\dagger\}=\delta_{pq}I.
\]

The braces mean \(\{A,B\}=AB+BA\); \(\delta_{pq}\) is one when the indices agree and zero otherwise. A correct mapping must preserve these relations, or their appropriate even-operator relations inside an encoded subspace.

## Writing the operator without losing a factor or an index

Let \(K\) denote the active spatial-orbital count. Let \(p,q,r,s\) run over local active indices from zero to \(K-1\), and \(\sigma,\tau\) denote alpha or beta spin. For the real, spin-conserving molecular integral paths considered here, write

\[
H_{\mathrm{model}}=E_{\mathrm{core}}I+H_{\mathrm{active}},
\]

\[
H_{\mathrm{active}}
=\sum_{pq,\sigma}h^\sigma_{pq}a^\dagger_{p\sigma}a_{q\sigma}
+\frac12\sum_{pqrs,\sigma\tau}g^{\sigma\tau}_{pqrs}
 a^\dagger_{p\sigma}a^\dagger_{r\tau}a_{s\tau}a_{q\sigma}.
\]

Here \(h\) contains the one-electron terms, including the effect of frozen inactive electrons when applicable. The raw, **not antisymmetrized**, Coulomb integral is in chemist order:

\[
g^{\sigma\tau}_{pqrs}=(p_\sigma q_\sigma|r_\tau s_\tau).
\]

The first pair belongs to electron coordinate 1 and the second to coordinate 2. The factor one-half accounts for the two ways of ordering the electron pair in this unrestricted sum. Formulas using antisymmetrized integrals often have a factor one-quarter and different index labels. They are not interchangeable array conventions.

The real restricted implementation shares spatial orbitals and integral blocks between spins. The unrestricted implementation keeps distinct alpha, beta, and mixed blocks. The mixed `aabb` tensor has the alpha pair on the left and beta pair on the right; exchanging whole pairs constructs the opposite-spin ordering. This matches the current producer/mapper paths, not every older explanatory comment in the repository.

Local active index 0 means the first entry of the selected active list. In our refined model it can correspond to full molecular-orbital index 4. Feeding the full index 4 where a local index 0 is required describes the wrong matrix element.

The native mapper uses excitation operators \(E^\sigma_{pq}=a^\dagger_{p\sigma}a_{q\sigma}\) and the identity

\[
a^\dagger_{p\sigma}a^\dagger_{r\tau}a_{s\tau}a_{q\sigma}
=E^\sigma_{pq}E^\tau_{rs}-\delta_{\sigma\tau}\delta_{qr}E^\sigma_{ps}.
\]

That subtraction explains an otherwise surprising implementation detail: the restricted engine folds a two-electron contraction into its effective one-body matrix before mapping. It is algebraic bookkeeping, not an additional chemical approximation. See the [native mapping engine](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/majorana_map_engine.cpp).

Most importantly, the ordinary `qubit_mapper/qdk` path deliberately maps **only** \(H_{\mathrm{active}}\). Its Hamiltonian-taking C++ entry point sets the supplied scalar to zero. Nuclear repulsion and frozen-inactive contributions remain in `hamiltonian.get_core_energy()`. ECP effects, if present in a different model, have already entered its chosen integrals/constants; mapping does not add another universal ECP correction. Our nitrogen example is all-electron before freezing the selected inactive orbitals.

There may nevertheless be an identity Pauli term in the output: mapping occupation operators generates one. That identity coefficient is not a substitute for the omitted core scalar. The [core-energy test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_qdk_qubit_mapper.py) uses one-body integrals that produce an identity coefficient of 1 and a separately supplied core energy of 5; it asserts that the mapped identity coefficient remains 1. Lower-level array-based C++ overloads can accept a nonzero scalar, which explains why their tests look different.

## Pauli arithmetic: the target language

A **Pauli word** is a product of \(I,X,Y,Z\), with at most one factor on each qubit. Operators on different qubits commute because they act on different tensor factors. Operators on the same qubit do not: \(XY=iZ\), but \(YX=-iZ\); \(X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I\).

For example,

\[
(X_0Z_1)(Y_0X_1)
=(iZ_0)(iY_1)=-Z_0Y_1.
\]

This illustrative multiplication shows why merely XOR-ing letter labels is insufficient: phases must also be accumulated. The repository’s native [Pauli implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/pauli_operator.cpp) merges sparse words by qubit index and implements these cyclic and anticyclic signs explicitly.

A qubit operator has the form

\[
H_q=\sum_t c_tP_t,
\]

where \(t\) labels terms, \(P_t\) is a Pauli word, and \(c_t\) its coefficient. The individual Pauli words are Hermitian. After identical words have been combined, their coefficients must be real for a Hermitian Hamiltonian. Complex intermediate coefficients are normal during multiplication; surviving imaginary coefficients cannot simply be discarded on the assumption that all input is valid chemistry.

Two repository objects serve different purposes. `PauliOperator.X(0)` constructs a symbolic Pauli expression. Products and sums build expression trees; `.distribute()` expands products of sums, `.simplify()` performs Pauli arithmetic and combines terms, and `.prune_threshold(epsilon)` removes small terms. This is useful for deriving or constructing small operators. `QubitOperator`, in contrast, wraps an operator **representation container**. Its Pauli-decomposition form holds dense string labels and a coefficient array, plus encoding, ordering, grouping, and optional tapering metadata. A different sum-of-squares container does not automatically expose a Pauli list.

There is an important explicit text-convention boundary. `PauliOperator.to_canonical_terms(4)` puts qubit 0 on the **left**. `QubitOperator` labels put qubit 0 on the **right**. The expression \(X_0Z_2\) is therefore `XIZI` in the first interface and `IZIX` in the second. The [model-Hamiltonian conversion helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/model_hamiltonians.py) actually reverses canonical strings when crossing that boundary. Explicit index positions are more reliable than the overloaded word “little-endian.”

This instructional excerpt follows that implementation; it is not executed here:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data import PauliOperator, QubitOperator
import numpy as np

expr = PauliOperator.X(0) * PauliOperator.Z(2)
terms = expr.simplify().to_canonical_terms(4)
operator = QubitOperator(
    pauli_strings=[label[::-1] for _, label in terms],
    coefficients=np.array([complex(coefficient) for coefficient, _ in terms]),
)
```

This arbitrary spin operator has no claimed fermionic encoding. Attaching the text `jordan-wigner` would not prove it was derived from a particular fermionic Hamiltonian.

The current [Pauli container](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/qubit_operator/containers/pauli_decomposition.py) validates matching term counts, nonempty equal-length labels, and valid Pauli characters. Addition concatenates terms rather than simplifying them; `equiv` combines duplicates for comparison. `is_hermitian` checks each stored coefficient, so duplicate imaginary terms that cancel should be combined before relying on that check. `get_real_coefficients` explicitly discards imaginary parts. Its property named `schatten_norm` computes the sum of absolute **stored coefficients**; it is not the general matrix Schatten trace norm. Duplicates can therefore affect that reported quantity.

The [wrapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/qubit_operator/__init__.py) preserves a historical `qubit_hamiltonian` wire-format identifier even though the current class is `QubitOperator`. Serialization should preserve the actual container and encoding metadata, not just an informal printed list.

## Jordan–Wigner: making the fermionic sign visible

In Jordan–Wigner encoding, qubit \(j\) stores occupation \(f_j\). A local lowering operator is \((X+iY)/2\), and a local raising operator is \((X-iY)/2\). Neither alone knows how many lower-index modes are occupied. The missing factor is a string of Z operators:

\[
a_j=\left(\prod_{k<j}Z_k\right)\frac{X_j+iY_j}{2},
\qquad
a_j^\dagger=\left(\prod_{k<j}Z_k\right)\frac{X_j-iY_j}{2}.
\]

Each preceding occupied qubit contributes a minus sign because \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\). Thus the Z string implements precisely \((-1)^{P_j}\). Empty products, such as for mode 0, mean identity.

Multiplying the raising and lowering expressions gives the number operator

\[
n_j=a_j^\dagger a_j=\frac{I-Z_j}{2}.
\]

This returns zero on an empty mode and one on an occupied mode. The Z prefixes cancel. For a real hopping term between \(p<q\), the result is

\[
a_p^\dagger a_q+a_q^\dagger a_p
=\frac12\left(X_pZ_{p+1}\cdots Z_{q-1}X_q
+Y_pZ_{p+1}\cdots Z_{q-1}Y_q\right).
\]

“Hopping” here means moving occupation between modes; molecular orbitals need not be localized sites. The interior parity string remains when the modes are nonadjacent. Its length illustrates the tradeoff: direct occupation storage is simple, but some mapped operators reach across many qubits.

A hand-worked one-spatial-orbital model ties everything together. Let its one-body integral be \(\epsilon\), its Coulomb integral \(U\), and its two spin modes be alpha and beta. Then

\[
H_{\mathrm{active}}=\epsilon(n_\alpha+n_\beta)+U n_\alpha n_\beta,
\]

\[
H_q=\left(\epsilon+\frac U4\right)I
-\left(\frac\epsilon2+\frac U4\right)(Z_\alpha+Z_\beta)
+\frac U4 Z_\alpha Z_\beta.
\]

The half in the original two-electron sum has not halved the final opposite-spin interaction: both spin orderings contribute. With illustrative values \(\epsilon=-1\), \(U=0.4\), and \(E_{\mathrm{core}}=0.1\), the Pauli coefficients are \(-0.9,0.4,0.4,0.1\). Empty, singly occupied, and doubly occupied active states have energies 0, −1, and −1.6 before adding the core scalar. The doubly occupied total is −1.5. These numbers are toy arithmetic, not nitrogen energies or executed outputs.

## Why the API calls the encoding a MajoranaMapping

Define two Hermitian operators for each fermionic mode:

\[
\gamma_{2j}=a_j+a_j^\dagger,
\qquad
\gamma_{2j+1}=-i(a_j-a_j^\dagger).
\]

They satisfy \(\{\gamma_j,\gamma_k\}=2\delta_{jk}I\), and

\[
a_j=\frac{\gamma_{2j}+i\gamma_{2j+1}}2,
\qquad
a_j^\dagger=\frac{\gamma_{2j}-i\gamma_{2j+1}}2.
\]

These are **Majorana operators** as a mathematical decomposition of ordinary fermionic operators. Their use does not imply that the eventual processor uses physical Majorana devices.

For Jordan–Wigner, the even Majorana is the preceding Z string followed by X, and the odd Majorana is the same string followed by Y. The two-mode factory table, in rightmost-qubit-zero labels, is exactly `IX`, `IY`, `XZ`, `YZ`. The [factory implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/majorana_mapping_factories.cpp) constructs those sparse words directly, and [Python Majorana tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_majorana_mapping.py) assert that reference table and its anticommutation algebra.

A **bilinear** contains two Majoranas. The common primitive is \(B_{jk}=i\gamma_j\gamma_k\), for distinct indices. It is Hermitian for a valid Majorana representation. In particular, \(B_{2j,2j+1}=-Z_j\) for Jordan–Wigner, so \(n_j=(I+B_{2j,2j+1})/2\).

The [MajoranaMapping data class](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/majorana_mapping.cpp) precomputes all upper-triangle bilinears. `mapping.majorana(k)` returns a sparse word when individual Majoranas are available. `mapping.bilinear(j,k)` returns a complex coefficient and sparse word; reversing its arguments changes the sign. Equal indices are deliberately rejected by that bilinear accessor. Products of bilinears suffice for this even, number-conserving Hamiltonian, allowing the engine to support some encodings that do not expose individual Majoranas.

## The native mapping method, step by step

The algorithm family is `qubit_mapper`; its default implementation is `qdk`. The separate `MajoranaMapping` argument is required. There is no need to mutate an encoding-name setting on the mapper. Its two numerical settings are `threshold=1e-12` and `integral_threshold=1e-12`, both doubles. See the [Python adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/qubit_mapper/qdk_qubit_mapper.py) and [factory contract](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/qubit_mapper/qubit_mapper.py).

First, the adapter gets \(K\) from the active one-body matrix and requires `mapping.num_modes == 2*K`. It determines the restricted/unrestricted strategy from the orbitals. It maps the untapered base if the supplied mapping carries tapering metadata, then handles reduction afterward.

Second, the native engine expands excitation operators through Majorana bilinears. Restricted input permits spin summation and real eightfold Coulomb symmetry; unrestricted input keeps distinct spin channels and combines opposite-spin contributions using whole-pair exchange. This is not a general complex spin–orbit or spin-flipping Hamiltonian interface: the present integral entry points consume real arrays and these spin-conserving structures.

Third, it multiplies Pauli words using **binary symplectic storage**. This simply means storing two bit masks: X sets an X bit, Z sets a Z bit, Y sets both, and I sets neither. XOR combines the masks, while a separate phase calculation tracks powers of \(i\). A hash table accumulates all contributions with the same Pauli word. Intermediate complex values are retained.

Fourth, `threshold` is applied to the **accumulated final coefficient**, not to each fractional contribution to that coefficient. The engine retains magnitudes greater than or equal to this threshold. This matters because many individually small terms can add constructively, and larger ones can cancel. `integral_threshold` is different: it screens input integrals, or the contracted effective one-body entries on the restricted path, before their contributions are accumulated. Late Pauli screening does not undo earlier integral screening. The equality convention also differs between individual input loops; do not build a scientific error specification around the exact threshold boundary.

Finally, sparse words are rendered using the mapping’s full qubit width and returned with complex coefficient storage, `encoding=base_mapping.base_encoding`, and `fermion_mode_order=BLOCKED`. A name is descriptive metadata for this native engine: the actual Pauli/bilinear data determines the transformation. Ordinary `.run` locks algorithm settings as explained in Lesson 3; configure thresholds before the call.

The implementation supports up to 1024 qubit positions through its packed-word dispatch and rejects zero-qubit maps. This is an implementation capacity, emphatically not a claim that constructing a dense 512-spatial-orbital molecular operator is cheap. A generic two-electron tensor still has quartic-size work, and the accumulated Pauli sum can itself be large. Precomputing all bilinears adds quadratic-in-mode-count table overhead, with additional word-length storage. If positive screening removes every term, the current wrapper reaches a Pauli container that rejects an empty term list; a completely screened operator is not automatically padded to a zero operator.

Container choice affects preprocessing memory. Canonical input supplies dense two-electron arrays. Cholesky input is contracted one pair-index row at a time without reconstructing the whole four-index tensor. Generic factorized input falls through to dense getters on this ordinary Pauli route. Sparse input has a restricted-only fast path that canonicalizes stored entries under real eightfold Coulomb symmetry. Unlike the sparse container’s literal getter semantics, this **consumer** supplies symmetry partners. Conflicting values at distinct symmetry-related positions are not averaged into a repaired tensor: the canonical position, or a deterministic selected partner, wins. Use physically consistent sparse data rather than exploit that selection rule. Negative/out-of-range sparse indices are rejected.

The [factorized-storage mapper tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_qdk_qubit_mapper_factorized.py) compare Cholesky and sparse paths with appropriate dense references. Those are source-defined checks, not tests run here. Storage efficiency does not eliminate the cost of the resulting operator or guarantee equivalent behavior for arbitrary nonsymmetric arrays.

For error accounting, a removed Pauli contribution \(\Delta H=\sum_t d_tP_t\) obeys \(\|\Delta H\|\leq\sum_t|d_t|\), where the norm is the operator norm and every Pauli word has norm one. Thus many small dropped coefficients can matter collectively. This bound addresses that truncation only; it is not an automatic chemical-accuracy guarantee covering active-space choice, integral factorization, or the wrong symmetry sector.

## Parity and Bravyi–Kitaev: changing what a qubit stores

Jordan–Wigner stores occupations directly. **Parity encoding** instead stores cumulative parity:

\[
b_j=f_0\oplus f_1\oplus\cdots\oplus f_j.
\]

Here \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two: two ones add to zero. The inverse is \(f_0=b_0\), \(f_j=b_{j-1}\oplus b_j\). No information has been lost. Counting ones in the encoded bitstring now does not count electrons.

For a hand-worked example, the increasing-mode occupation vector \(f=(1,0,1,0)\) becomes \(b=(1,1,0,0)\). Its displayed rightmost-qubit-zero bitstring is `0011`, whereas the Jordan–Wigner string was `0101`. Both describe the same two occupied modes under different decoding rules.

CNOT gates can compute these cumulative XORs reversibly. For two modes the parity mapping is obtained by conjugating the Jordan–Wigner operators by CNOT from qubit 0 to qubit 1. The source test checks the resulting Majorana labels `XX`, `XY`, `XZ`, `YI`. For more modes, the factory builds the corresponding X tails explicitly. Parity makes some global occupation parity information local, but changing an occupation can require updating many stored parity bits; it is not uniformly more local than Jordan–Wigner.

**Bravyi–Kitaev**, abbreviated BK, balances occupation and parity information using a tree. A **Fenwick tree** stores parity over selected ranges so that both queries and updates touch logarithmically many ranges rather than every preceding or following mode. The native factory computes parity, update, and remainder sets and uses them to choose Z and X factors in each Majorana image.

For four modes, the standard BK occupation encoding is

\[
b_0=f_0,\quad b_1=f_0\oplus f_1,\quad b_2=f_2,\quad
b_3=f_0\oplus f_1\oplus f_2\oplus f_3.
\]

Its inverse is \(f_0=b_0\), \(f_1=b_0\oplus b_1\), \(f_2=b_2\), and \(f_3=b_1\oplus b_2\oplus b_3\). Our illustrative \(f=(1,0,1,0)\) therefore becomes \(b=(1,1,1,0)\), displayed as `0111`. Three encoded ones still describe two electrons. These inverse relations agree with the four-mode number-operator Z products exercised in the [mapper tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_qdk_qubit_mapper.py) and the exact labels checked by the [Qiskit interoperability tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_interop_qiskit_qubit_mapper.py).

The native `bravyi_kitaev` factory constructs on the next-power-of-two tree and removes out-of-range indices for non-power-of-two mode counts. `bravyi_kitaev_tree` uses a recursively balanced tree over the actual mode count. The two variants can differ, particularly away from powers of two; their names must not be interchanged merely because both contain “BK.”

Neither ordinary parity nor ordinary BK reduces the untapered qubit count below the mode count. They change Pauli support and state encoding. Shorter words can reduce some circuit costs, but term structure, hardware connectivity, state preparation, and the simulation algorithm still matter. Under an exact Clifford change of basis, Pauli words are permuted up to signs, so even their combined coefficient absolute-sum need not improve when their lengths do.

A **Clifford unitary** maps every Pauli word to another Pauli word, possibly with a sign, under conjugation. H, S, and CNOT generate familiar examples. If \(C\) converts encoding A to encoding B, the consistent transformations are

\[
|\psi_B\rangle=C|\psi_A\rangle,
\qquad H_B=CH_AC^\dagger.
\]

Changing only the operator or only its label is not that transformation. More general custom choices can also alter determinant-relative phases, not just the binary occupation labels.

## What mappings are actually available

The native factories at this revision include more than the older JW/BK-only overviews suggest:

| Python construction | What is supplied |
|---|---|
| `MajoranaMapping.jordan_wigner(M)` | Occupation encoding, with M qubits |
| `MajoranaMapping.parity(M)` | Cumulative-parity encoding, with M qubits |
| `MajoranaMapping.bravyi_kitaev(M)` | Standard Fenwick-style BK table |
| `MajoranaMapping.bravyi_kitaev_tree(M)` | Balanced-tree BK table |
| `MajoranaMapping.parity(M, symmetries)` | Parity table plus two-qubit-reduction metadata |
| `MajoranaMapping.symmetry_conserving_bravyi_kitaev(M, symmetries)` | BK-tree table plus two-qubit-reduction metadata |
| `MajoranaMapping.verstraete_cirac(lattice)` | Graph-oriented bilinear encoding with auxiliary qubits and stabilizers |

The Python symmetry argument is a `Symmetries` object carrying alpha/beta counts; it is not the two positional integer arguments used by the corresponding C++ overload. The [bindings](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/pybind11/data/majorana_mapping.cpp) define that boundary. Reduction factories require appropriate even mode counts and valid populations. Their table and `num_qubits` still describe the **pre-taper** basis; the mapper later reduces the operator. How the selected symmetry sector makes that legitimate belongs to Lesson 15, not to an assumption that BK alone “saves two qubits.”

Verstraete–Cirac is a distinct graph-oriented tradeoff, not a free molecular compression option. Its concrete factory requires at least three lattice sites, identifies graph edges nonadjacent in the chosen site sequence, introduces auxiliary fermionic modes, and dresses relevant bilinears with auxiliary stabilizers. A **stabilizer** here is an operator whose chosen eigenvalue specifies the physical encoded subspace. The factory provides bilinears, not an individual-Majorana table, and can use more qubits than physical modes. The native engine adds auxiliary-sector penalty terms when these stabilizers are present. Its full enlarged-space spectrum is therefore not simply the original molecular spectrum with fewer letters. Preparing the intended subspace and tracking those terms are additional obligations; ordinary nitrogen mapping does not need this route.

There is also `qubit_mapper/sum_of_squares`, a representation-specific method rather than another general encoding. Its current implementation requires a `FactorizedHamiltonianContainer`, an untapered mapping labelled Jordan–Wigner, and the matching doubled mode count. It returns structured factors instead of an ordinary Pauli decomposition. Unlike the ordinary Pauli mapper, its metadata energy shift includes the core constant. The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/qubit_mapper/sum_of_squares.py) also has a different `threshold` meaning: it screens small one-body eigenvalues in that construction. We reserve its operator and circuit derivation for the later sum-of-squares lesson; thresholds and energy offsets must not be transferred between these two methods by name alone.

## Custom tables: flexible does not mean automatically valid

`MajoranaMapping.from_table(table, name=...)` accepts two sparse Pauli words per fermionic mode. Each word is a sorted list of `(qubit_index, operator_code)` pairs, with X=1, Y=2, Z=3 and absent factors interpreted as identity. `from_bilinears(num_modes, bilinears, name=...)` instead accepts coefficient/word pairs for every \(j<k\), ordered row by row through the upper triangle. For \(M\) modes that is \((2M)(2M-1)/2\) bilinears. The number of encoded qubits is inferred from the highest referenced qubit, not forced to equal the mode count.

The actual constructor guards include nonempty/even table size, positive mode count for the bilinear form, and the required number of bilinear entries. Accessors check ranges; asking for individual Majoranas of a bilinear-only map fails. **The constructor does not perform a general proof of canonical anticommutation or a complete validation/normalization of arbitrary sparse-word algebra.** Sorted, well-formed words and a mathematically valid encoding remain the author’s responsibility. A custom name is not evidence of correctness.

For Majorana-atomic tables, there is a compact independent algebra check. Represent words by binary masks \((x,z)\). Two words anticommute when

\[
x\cdot z^{\prime}+z\cdot x^{\prime}=1\pmod 2.
\]

The dot products count overlapping mask bits; this is the symplectic parity test. Distinct Majoranas must anticommute and each must square to identity. The repository tests explicitly multiply factory words and check those relations. Bilinear-only encodings instead need their appropriate product relations and any physical-subspace constraints; checking that the vector has the right length cannot establish them. The common engine’s name-independent dispatch is valuable precisely because it lets a validated custom representation reuse the chemical operator machinery.

## Optional libraries and the order of operations

The `openfermion` and `qiskit` mapper variants are optional plugins, not native implementations hidden behind aliases. They use **`mapping.base_encoding` as a string selector and ignore the supplied table**. A manually built table with a misleading standard name can therefore produce a different result from the native engine without a mismatch error. Use factory-generated mappings when comparing backends.

The [OpenFermion plugin](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/openfermion/qubit_mapper.py) supports base names `jordan-wigner`, `bravyi-kitaev`, and `bravyi-kitaev-tree`; it does not expose a parity branch here. Its [conversion code](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/openfermion/conversion.py) constructs an interleaved spin-orbital interaction tensor with the appropriate integral permutation and one-half factor, reindexes those fermionic tensors into blocked order, then calls the external transform. It subtracts the core scalar that OpenFermion initially included. Native and plugin outputs thus follow the same ordinary active-energy convention. Compression and tolerances inside the external library are an additional boundary, not these plugins’ own `threshold` settings.

The [Qiskit Nature plugin](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/qubit_mapper.py) supports `jordan-wigner`, `bravyi-kitaev`, and `parity`. It builds an `ElectronicEnergy`, obtains its second-quantized operator, and invokes the selected external mapper. For unrestricted input it transposes the mixed `aabb` tensor to the `bbaa` arrangement expected by Qiskit’s `h2_ba` argument. It does not add the QDK core scalar. Neither plugin has a general arbitrary-Majorana-table implementation. Their dense getter conversions can also materialize tensors that the native Cholesky mapper avoids.

One optional-plugin pattern is therefore `create("qubit_mapper", "qiskit").run(active_hamiltonian, mapping)` with a supported factory mapping and the plugin actually installed. This is a source-backed calling pattern, not a claim that the dependency is available in this environment. The [OpenFermion tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_interop_openfermion_qubit_mapper.py) and Qiskit tests contain conditional registration and coefficient-comparison checks. A stale test description claiming BK-tree has no native equivalent does not override the current native factory.

A further practical limit is that external conversion can infer width from surviving nonidentity terms. In particular, the OpenFermion converter removes zero terms and derives width from the highest retained qubit index; zero and identity-only operators are not robust full-width placeholders through that path. Always verify expected width rather than assume metadata carries unused modes through every library.

## Keeping the state and the Hamiltonian in the same encoding

Three concepts must remain separate: **mode order**, **binary encoding**, and **string display order**. Native molecular mapping uses blocked modes, alpha first and beta second. Interleaved mode order alternates alpha and beta. Parity/BK say how the ordered occupations become encoded bits. Rightmost-qubit-zero says how those bits or Pauli letters are printed. The [FermionModeOrder enum](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/enums/fermion_mode_order.py) describes the first distinction only.

`QubitOperator.to_interleaved(K)` currently permutes Pauli-string positions and marks the result interleaved. It requires width `2*K`. It is a **wire permutation** of an already mapped operator, not a general decode/reorder/re-encode transformation and not a fermionic-sign correction. It does not recompute BK trees or prove compatibility with a freshly remapped interleaved fermionic problem. Reordering canonical fermionic creation operators can introduce occupation-dependent signs; arbitrary wire swaps are not automatically that reordering. A consistent wire permutation can be used if the state and every consumer are transformed accordingly, but the OpenFermion plugin instead reorders fermionic tensors before mapping when establishing its blocked convention.

Current ordinary `state_prep` implementations prepare occupation-basis states and label their circuits `jordan-wigner`. The [base scattering helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/state_preparation.py) constructs a dense index by adding each determinant occupation bit at its corresponding power-of-two position. It does not accept a `MajoranaMapping` and silently convert to BK. Particular state-preparation methods also have coefficient-type and size restrictions, which we will examine in Lesson 16. Internal “binary encoding” compression in a sparse-state synthesis algorithm is not, by its name alone, Bravyi–Kitaev fermionic encoding; that construction expands back to its declared output basis.

The [encoding_validation module](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/encoding_validation.py) is now deprecated. Its retained `validate_encoding_compatibility` facade emits a warning, requires both encoding strings, and compares those strings. It does **not** compare mode order, active-orbital identity, width, custom tables, determinant phases, or full tapering provenance. It is not a mathematical compatibility proof, nor a promise that every consumer automatically calls it. The explicit mapping workflow improves clarity, but cannot make those obligations disappear.

For our continuing nitrogen story, the dependable baseline is therefore the selected active orbitals, a blocked Jordan–Wigner Hamiltonian, and a compatible occupation-basis state preparation. A different encoding is entirely legitimate, but the state must be transformed too. Relabelling a circuit as BK leaves every gate unchanged and does not perform the required conversion.

## Following the nitrogen trace and knowing what it validates

The tutorial’s core mapping excerpt is short because the preceding choices carry its meaning:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import MajoranaMapping

# active_hamiltonian was constructed from the selected, gauge-fixed orbitals.
n_spatial = active_hamiltonian.get_one_body_integrals()[0].shape[0]
mapping = MajoranaMapping.jordan_wigner(num_modes=2 * n_spatial)
mapper = create("qubit_mapper", "qdk", threshold=1e-10, integral_threshold=1e-14)
qubit_hamiltonian = mapper.run(active_hamiltonian, mapping)
core_energy = active_hamiltonian.get_core_energy()
```

Those are the tutorial’s actual screening choices, not the defaults. This excerpt is instructional only. Its output is an **operator**, not an executed circuit, an eigenstate, or an energy measurement.

The tutorial subsequently validates the transformation by forming the sparse Pauli matrix, selecting only indices whose low six occupation bits contain three alpha electrons and high six bits contain three beta electrons, and diagonalizing that 400-state sector. It adds `core_energy` to the active eigenvalue and compares with the same selected-space CASCI energy. This tests representation consistency for the chosen model; it does not validate that choosing six orbitals was chemically sufficient.

That sector mask is correct for blocked Jordan–Wigner occupations. Applying the same count-of-ones mask to parity or BK bits would choose a different space. Those encodings require decoding occupations or projecting with appropriately transformed number operators. Similarly, the full-register lowest eigenvalue need not be the physical six-electron state.

`QubitOperator.to_matrix` uses a [complex-preserving Pauli matrix utility](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/pauli_matrix.py). Dense matrices cost \(4^q\) entries for \(q\) qubits; its sparse construction also enumerates \(2^q\) register states and has explicit index-capacity limits. This is a small-system check, not a scalable way to validate every large target. It is distinct from the classical qubit-solver wrappers discussed earlier, which can discard imaginary parts and do not enforce the physical electron sector. We have inspected the tutorial and tests, not run either validation route here.

We now have the central translation contract: preserve the chemical model and its constants, define an ordered fermionic space, preserve its signs in the operator algebra, attach an honest encoding description, and prepare states in that same description. **Qubit mapping** performs this operator translation. **Circuit mapping** will synthesize gates for a chosen operation derived from the operator. **Tapering** will reduce a symmetry sector under additional conditions. None is a synonym for the others.

The next lesson uses those distinctions to remove qubits only where a known symmetry makes the reduction legitimate. We will not throw away an apparently unused bit merely because its printed value happens to be zero in one determinant.
lessons.caveats: No imports or scientific/circuit/test execution. Native mapping consumes real spin-conserving integral structures, applies integral screening before final accumulated Pauli threshold, and excludes core energy on the ordinary Hamiltonian-taking route. Sparse mapper supplies symmetry partners unlike literal container getters. Explicit custom-map constructors do not prove canonical anticommutation. Pauli expression canonical strings and QubitOperator labels have opposite index direction. Ordinary state_prep remains Jordan-Wigner; deprecated compatibility facade checks encoding strings only. to_interleaved is a wire permutation, not a general fermionic remapping. Optional plugins dispatch by encoding name, not supplied tables; OpenFermion conversion infers width from surviving terms. Verstraete-Cirac requires a physical codespace and auxiliary penalties. SOS uses separate energy-shift/threshold semantics. Earlier Lesson9 mixed-spin wording was corrected to follow actual alpha-pair/beta-pair producer/consumer paths.

lessons.title: Using symmetry without changing the question
lessons.body:
# Lesson 15 — Using symmetry without changing the question

## A smaller calculation must still answer the same question

Our target remains neutral, singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å. The selected six-spatial-orbital model has three active alpha and three active beta electrons. Lesson 14 translated its operator into twelve occupation qubits without claiming that every state of those qubits describes the intended molecule.

Symmetry now offers two different kinds of saving. We can organize classical arrays so that independent sectors are stored and processed separately. We can also sometimes remove qubits whose values are fixed **after an appropriate encoding transformation**. These are not the same operation. Neither licenses choosing a lower-energy state with the wrong electron count or spin.

A useful engineering rule is to name the constraint before using the saving. “These two arrays share restricted-spin storage” is a data statement. “The state has three alpha electrons” is a particle-sector statement. “This encoded Z operator has eigenvalue minus one” is a qubit-sector statement. They can be related, but none substitutes for the others.

This lesson follows the native symmetry vocabulary, its Python bindings, and the actual tapering path at revision `97a3ff4f`. The general mathematical derivation is explicitly distinguished from capabilities shipped in this implementation. No symmetry search, matrix diagonalization, circuit compilation, or test is being executed.

## What a symmetry preserves

A **symmetry operation** changes the description of a system while leaving the relevant physics unchanged. For a Hamiltonian \(H\) and a unitary symmetry operation \(U\), this means \(UHU^\dagger=H\). Equivalently, \(U\) commutes with \(H\): \([H,U]=HU-UH=0\).

A **group** is a collection of operations closed under composition, including an identity and inverses, with associative composition. A **representation** describes those abstract operations as matrices acting on states. We need these words because a molecule’s geometric rotations, an electron-number phase rotation, and a Pauli string on qubits are quite different objects even when all are called symmetries.

A conserved observable \(Q\) satisfies \([H,Q]=0\). Its eigenvalue can label a **sector**: the set of states with that value. To see why sectors decouple, let \(Q|a\rangle=q_a|a\rangle\) and \(Q|b\rangle=q_b|b\rangle\). Then

\[
0=\langle a|[Q,H]|b\rangle
=(q_a-q_b)\langle a|H|b\rangle.
\]

If \(q_a\ne q_b\), the Hamiltonian matrix element must vanish. States in those different sectors cannot mix under this Hamiltonian. This is a stronger reason for a zero than a coefficient happening to be numerically small.

For our spin-conserving electronic model, the number operators \(N_\alpha\) and \(N_\beta\) commute with the Hamiltonian. Their sum is the active electron number \(N\); their difference gives spin projection \(S_z=(N_\alpha-N_\beta)/2\) in units where \(\hbar=1\). Electron number has integer eigenvalues, although its associated phase operations \(e^{i\theta N}\), for continuous angle \(\theta\), form a continuous symmetry. There is no contradiction between discrete electron counts and a continuous symmetry group.

Particle-number **parity** retains less information: \((-1)^N\) is plus one for even counts and minus one for odd counts. Three alpha electrons and five alpha electrons have the same alpha parity. Preserving parity therefore does not select exact electron number.

Total spin is another distinction. A total-spin eigenstate has \(S^2\) eigenvalue \(S(S+1)\) and multiplicity \(2S+1\). Fixing \(S_z=0\) permits a singlet but also the zero-projection components of higher-spin states. An unrestricted determinant can additionally mix total-spin components. Neither equal alpha/beta counts nor an alpha/beta storage label proves a singlet.

The **molecular point group** consists of spatial transformations, such as rotations, reflections, or inversion, that preserve a fixed nuclear geometry. Orbitals may transform in its irreducible representations, the elementary independent pieces of a representation. In an abelian group, operations commute and irreducible representations can be one-dimensional; nonabelian groups can require multidimensional pieces. These concepts explain familiar orbital labels and degeneracies. They do not establish that the current software automatically discovers or exploits every such label. Geometry distortions, external fields, or a changed model can also break a symmetry that was valid elsewhere along a path.

## The two symmetry APIs have different jobs

The native single-particle vocabulary lives in [`data/symmetry/symmetry.hpp`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry.hpp), with [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry.cpp) and a [Python facade](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/symmetry.py). Its current `AxisName` enumeration contains **Spin only**. There is no populated point-group axis in this vocabulary at this revision. A broad container design is not evidence of a general point-group finder, irreducible-representation solver, or spin-adapted CI implementation.

`SpinValue` stores twice a spin-projection label. `axes.alpha()` carries +1 and `axes.beta()` −1. `axes.spin(two_s, equivalent=True)` constructs the allowed labels from `-two_s` to `+two_s` in steps of two. For electron spin use `two_s=1`, not a molecular singlet multiplicity. `axes.spin_value(two_ms)` and `SpinValue(two_ms)` can carry other integer values; an appropriate axis determines whether a value is admissible. Such a label is data, not a calculation of a many-electron spin eigenstate.

A `SymmetryAxis` contains its name, admissible labels, and an `equivalent` flag. Here **equivalent** means the labels may share numerical storage, as restricted alpha/beta molecular-orbital coefficients can. It does not mean the two spin states are physically identical. A `SymmetryProduct` collects the axes for an index slot. A `SymmetryLabel` supplies one value per axis and serves as a hashable addressing key. An empty product and empty label represent an axis-free quantity. Current loader dispatch recognizes the spin kind; inventing a point-group tag in JSON does not extend the implementation.

Separately, [`data.Symmetries`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/symmetries.py) is a small Python container for **active-space** alpha/beta counts. It exposes `n_alpha`, `n_beta`, `n_particles`, and `sz`; `from_wavefunction` reads `get_active_num_electrons()`, and `from_ansatz` reads the bundled wavefunction. It does not discover symmetry by inspecting the Hamiltonian matrix.

A particularly important naming limit is `Symmetries.spin_multiplicity`: the implementation returns `abs(n_alpha - n_beta) + 1`. That is a count-derived convention, equal to \(2|S_z|+1\), not a measurement or proof of \(S\). For a general state, total spin is not determined by these two counts. Use the property with that qualification rather than silently interpreting `1` as certified singlet character. The [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_symmetries.py) verify the formula; they do not establish a general spin-purity theorem.

## A spin-blocked array you can actually interpret

A **tensor** is an indexed array; rank is its number of index slots, not its numerical matrix rank. A symmetry-blocked tensor associates a label tuple with a dense block. Each slot also has an **extent**, the number of indices available for a particular label.

For example, a spin-diagonal one-body operator in two spatial orbitals has a 2×2 alpha block and a 2×2 beta block. In a restricted representation those blocks can share the same numerical matrix. This source-backed instructional example follows the [Python storage tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_symmetry_blocked_tensor.py):

```python
import numpy as np
from qdk_chemistry.data import symmetry as sym

spin = sym.SymmetryProduct([sym.axes.spin(1, True)])
a = sym.SymmetryLabel([sym.axes.alpha()])
b = sym.SymmetryLabel([sym.axes.beta()])
extents = {a: 2, b: 2}
h = np.array([[-1.0, 0.2], [0.2, 0.5]])  # illustrative entries

blocks = sym.SymmetryBlockedTensorRank2(
    [spin, spin],
    [extents, extents],
    [((a, a), h)],
)
alpha_block = blocks.block((a, a))
beta_block = blocks.block((b, b))
```

This code is not executed here. Both returned blocks describe the same illustrative matrix under restricted storage. `num_blocks()` counts the two accessible keys, not necessarily two independent allocations. The mixed `(a,b)` block has not been supplied. A dense `.block(...)` request for an absent block raises; it does not silently allocate a zero matrix.

For unrestricted storage, construct `axes.spin(1, False)` and supply independent alpha and beta blocks. Restricted storage cannot be used as a trick to merge genuinely different matrices. The actual [common storage implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry_blocked.hpp) activates spin-partner aliasing when every slot has an equivalent spin axis. It flips the spin values simultaneously across all slots. It checks compatible extents and requires explicitly supplied partners to share backing storage. The operative rule is in that implementation; older comments requiring identical `SymmetryProduct` object identity are not the current test in the code.

An **alias** is another key referencing the same immutable backing block. It is not a transpose, complex conjugate, index permutation, or newly computed matrix. In particular, sharing `(alpha,alpha,beta,beta)` and its spin-flipped partner does not itself tell a consumer how a four-index Coulomb tensor should be contracted. The chemist-order and mixed alpha-pair/beta-pair conventions from Lessons 12–14 still apply.

The exported dense families are `SymmetryBlockedTensorRank1` through `Rank4`, with corresponding `...Complex` variants. Rank 1 uses a vector; rank 2 a matrix; rank 3 stores a producer-chosen matrix reshaping of three indices; rank 4 is flat packed. The [shape validator](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry_blocked_tensor.hpp) checks exact rank-1/rank-2 extents and the rank-3 total product. For rank 4 it requires a nonempty flat vector but deliberately leaves packing length to the producer. A successful constructor is therefore not a universal guarantee that an arbitrary rank-4 vector has the desired integral layout.

Complex storage permits complex values. It does not make every Hamiltonian constructor, RDM contraction, or solver complex-capable. That familiar container-versus-consumer distinction remains essential.

## Index sets, counts, sparse maps, and contractions

`SymmetryBlockedIndexSet` associates each label with a sorted, unique list of indices in a declared universe. This is how active or inactive orbital selections can carry separate spin channels. The Python helper `spin_index_set(num_modes, alpha, beta, equivalent=True)` builds one. Its `num_modes` is the orbital universe size **per spin channel** in this helper, not an instruction to allocate that many physical qubits.

For a restricted six-orbital selection inside the original 28-spatial-orbital model, the conceptual lists can both be `[4,5,6,7,8,9]`, with universe size 28. Those are full-space MO identities. The active Hamiltonian subsequently uses local positions 0–5. For unequal spin selections use non-equivalent storage; the helper’s default `equivalent=True` is not an invitation to alias unequal lists. The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry_blocked_index_set.cpp) checks strictly increasing indices and bounds. It does not diagnose whether those indices retain the same chemical character at another geometry.

`SymmetryBlockedScalarCount` stores a scalar count per sector, for example alpha=3 and beta=3. Counts need not have the same storage equivalence as orbital coefficients: a restricted-open-shell calculation can share spatial orbitals but have unequal alpha/beta populations. Use non-equivalent axes for independent counts.
