Its [scalar implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry_blocked_scalar.hpp) computes unit extents internally because the payload is one scalar per label, not a selected-index vector.

`SymmetryBlockedSparseMapRank4` maps a sector label tuple to a map of local four-index tuples and real values. Its `.get(labels, indices)` returns zero when an entry **or the entire block** is absent, unlike the dense `.block` accessor. It validates stored index bounds at construction. `num_entries()` counts entries through accessible block keys, so aliases are included in that count. These are the actual [sparse-map semantics](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry_blocked_sparse_map.hpp), not a general rule that every missing chemistry quantity means zero.

Why does blocking save work? If a matrix is block diagonal, a multiplication can be performed independently in each block. Two blocks of size \(K\) require two dense matrix products of rough cubic cost, instead of one size-\(2K\) product that spends work on known zeros. This is an illustrative scaling comparison, not a timing claim. Savings depend on the consumer actually honoring the blocks.

For a one-particle density matrix \(\gamma\), an orbital change within a sector has the familiar form \(\gamma^{\prime}=U^\dagger\gamma U\), where \(U\) describes the basis rotation in that sector. Density and integral contractions must sum over the matching spin blocks, using their actual index order and conjugation rules. The blocked storage classes do not provide an automatic general tensor-algebra compiler, point-group Clebsch–Gordan machinery, or arbitrary orbital transformation simply because labels are present. A rotation mixing sectors must transform the symmetry representation as well; old labels cannot be retained blindly.

Serialization records the rank/scalar specialization, per-slot symmetry metadata, extents, and groups of keys sharing a stored block. The [tensor loader](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/symmetry/symmetry_blocked_tensor.cpp) restores that shared structure, and existing tests check real/complex ranks and aliases. Prefer the matching loader over manually stripping labels back into an unlabeled tuple. This is an identity-preservation issue, not merely file-format decoration. We have read those tests without writing or round-tripping any files.

## From conserved quantities to removable qubits

Now turn from classical array organization to a qubit Hamiltonian \(H_q=\sum_t c_tP_t\). A Pauli symmetry \(S\) is a Hermitian Pauli operator with \(S^2=I\) that commutes with the Hamiltonian. Its possible eigenvalues are +1 and −1. The two-element structure is called a **Z₂ symmetry**; it is a mathematical parity-like group, not necessarily a single-qubit Z gate in the original encoding.

The **centralizer** of the Hamiltonian’s Pauli terms is the set of Pauli words commuting with all of them. Lesson 14’s binary masks offer a way to find it. Represent a candidate word by \((x,z)\) and each Hamiltonian term by \((x_t,z_t)\). Commutation requires

\[
x_t\cdot z+z_t\cdot x=0\pmod 2
\]

for every retained term. These are linear equations over **GF(2)**, the arithmetic of zero and one with addition given by XOR. Binary Gaussian elimination can find independent solutions. Independence means one generator is not a product of the others.

That is a general mathematical recipe, not a current `find_all_symmetries` API in this repository. The shipped tapering path examined here uses known particle parities in particular encodings; it does not expose a general Hamiltonian centralizer search, commuting-generator selection, and arbitrary Clifford-synthesis pipeline.

Even in a general implementation, a nullspace basis is not yet the final answer. Selected generators must commute with one another to admit simultaneous sector eigenvalues. Their phases must be tracked: binary masks alone do not distinguish a Pauli word from its negative. A product generator’s eigenvalue must equal the product of its constituent signed eigenvalues. Treating dependent generators as independent could remove too many degrees of freedom.

A **Clifford unitary** maps Pauli words to Pauli words, up to signs, under conjugation. For an independent commuting generator set, one can seek a Clifford \(C\) with \(CS_jC^\dagger=Z_{q_j}\), absorbing any minus sign consistently into the sector value. This is a special transformation, not a property of every unitary. In the transformed Hamiltonian, each removable position then carries only I or Z when the symmetry is exact. Substituting \(Z_{q_j}=s_j\), with \(s_j=\pm1\), removes that qubit **within the chosen sector**.

## A two-qubit tapering example by hand

Take the illustrative operator

\[
H=aZ_0+bZ_1+cX_0X_1,
\qquad S=Z_0Z_1.
\]

The coefficients \(a,b,c\) are arbitrary real toy parameters, not molecular integrals. Every term commutes with \(S\). Let \(C\) be CNOT with control 0 and target 1. Conjugation gives

\[
CSC^\dagger=Z_1,
\qquad CHC^\dagger=aZ_0+bZ_0Z_1+cX_0.
\]

In the \(S=s\) sector, remove qubit 1 and obtain

\[
H_s=(a+s b)Z_0+cX_0.
\]

Its two eigenvalues are \(\pm\sqrt{(a+s b)^2+c^2}\). The plus and minus sectors generally have different spectra. Taking the minimum from one sector is not the same as solving the original four-dimensional problem, and selecting the wrong sector changes the question.

For label interpretation, QubitOperator strings place qubit 0 on the right: the original terms are `IZ`, `ZI`, and `XX`. The transformed terms are `IZ`, `ZZ`, and `IX`. Substituting the left-position Z associated with qubit 1 produces exactly the one-qubit expression above. Do not use the opposite canonical-string direction from `PauliOperator` without conversion.

Write state kets here as \(|q_1q_0\rangle\). An even-parity trial state \(u|00\rangle+v|11\rangle\) becomes \(|0\rangle_1\otimes(u|0\rangle_0+v|1\rangle_0)\) after this CNOT. Qubit 1 is known to be zero and can be removed. An odd-parity state instead has that qubit fixed to one. A superposition spanning both parities leaves it correlated with the rest and cannot be replaced by a single fixed eigenvalue without changing the state.

The example also exposes an observable constraint. An observable that changes the selected parity connects different sectors. Its within-sector projection can be zero even when cross-sector transition matrix elements are physically meaningful. Tapering the Hamiltonian does not justify using every original observable unchanged.

## What the current tapering code really does

[`TaperingSpecification`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/tapering.hpp) records `qubit_indices` and matching `eigenvalues`. Construction checks equal lengths, distinct indices, and values restricted to +1 or −1. It does not contain the Hamiltonian, an automatically discovered generator set, or a general Clifford circuit. Without a register width, the standalone constructor cannot check whether all its indices fit that register.

Its two specialized factories are `symmetry_conserving_bravyi_kitaev` and `parity_two_qubit_reduction`. The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/tapering.cpp) requires an even mode count \(M\ge4\) and each spin population at most \(M/2\). It chooses positions

\[
q_\alpha=M/2-1,\qquad q_{\mathrm{total}}=M-1
\]

and values \(s_\alpha=(-1)^{N_\alpha}\), \(s_{\mathrm{total}}=(-1)^{N_\alpha+N_\beta}\). These positions encode the two parities in the supported blocked parity and balanced BK-tree conventions. They are not arbitrary positions that work in an untransformed Jordan–Wigner Hamiltonian.

The public source-backed workflow bundles this specification into a mapping:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import MajoranaMapping, Symmetries

symmetries = Symmetries(n_alpha=3, n_beta=3)
mapping = MajoranaMapping.parity(12, symmetries)
tapered_hamiltonian = create("qubit_mapper", "qdk").run(active_hamiltonian, mapping)
```

This is an unexecuted pattern assuming the matching six-spatial-orbital active Hamiltonian. The alternative `MajoranaMapping.symmetry_conserving_bravyi_kitaev(12, symmetries)` uses BK-tree as its base, not the standard Fenwick BK variant. Both descriptions have pre-taper table width 12 and specify removal of qubits 5 and 11 with eigenvalues −1 and +1. The mapped output has ten problem qubits. The count reduction follows the factory contract; no nitrogen spectrum has been computed here.

A crucial remaining dimension is \(2^{10}=1024\). That is larger than the 400-state exact `(3,3)` electron sector. Each six-bit spin block has 32 odd-parity strings, so the paired odd-alpha/odd-beta parity space has \(32\times32=1024\) states. It also includes other odd spin populations. The [non-power-of-two SCBK test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_qdk_qubit_mapper.py) correctly compares against the union of matching-parity sectors, not just one fixed population. Number-conserving evolution of a correctly prepared fixed-population state can remain in its smaller physical sector, but the tapered operator alone does not enforce that preparation.

Each mapper strips the tapering metadata, maps the base encoding, then calls the shared [Python taper helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/qubit_mapper/qubit_mapper.py). That helper interprets qubit positions using rightmost-qubit-zero labels, substitutes the specified value for Z, deletes the relevant characters, combines identical remaining words, and keeps combined magnitudes strictly greater than a hard-coded `1e-12`. That final cutoff is additional to the native mapper’s configurable screening. It can introduce a tiny extra approximation and does not inherit an arbitrarily tighter mapper threshold.

The helper checks duplicate/out-of-range positions, valid signs, matching list lengths, and that at least one qubit remains. It provides an explicit zero identity term if nothing survives. But it **does not reject X or Y on a supposedly removable qubit**: it skips that whole Pauli term. Mathematically this is consistent with taking the diagonal sector projection \(PHP\). If the Hamiltonian actually couples sectors, however, it is not a spectrum-preserving symmetry reduction. Thus a specification is not a certificate of commutation. Standard factory assumptions and source tests matter; arbitrary user-written metadata must not be trusted as proof.

The internal `_taper_qubits` and `_taper_result` helpers are not general public promises to transform arbitrary states or circuits. The [Majorana tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_majorana_mapping.py) cover expected signs, invalid populations/mode counts, base-versus-tapered metadata, and serialization. Mapper tests check the specialized conserved Z positions and reduced spectra. We have inspected these checks, not executed them.

## Choosing and carrying the sector

A known reference can determine a symmetry eigenvalue when it is actually an eigenstate of that symmetry. For a Jordan–Wigner determinant, a Z-string eigenvalue is the product of −1 over occupied positions in the string. For a superposition, all components must belong to the same sector, with phases treated consistently. A Pauli string containing X or Y generally moves a determinant to another configuration, so its expectation cannot be read from a count-of-ones rule.

For a normalized state and a Hermitian Pauli symmetry, \(|\langle S\rangle|=1\) certifies a definite ± sector in exact arithmetic. An intermediate expectation, such as zero, is not an instruction to choose the plus sector. `Symmetries.from_wavefunction` merely reads count information from the wavefunction API; it does not perform all such expectation or variance checks on arbitrary custom states. The determinant/configuration containers’ own validation limits from Lesson 9 remain relevant.

After choosing the sector, the trial state, state-preparation circuit, Hamiltonian, observables, and later controlled evolution must share the transformed and reduced convention. Current ordinary state-preparation methods return Jordan–Wigner occupation circuits. There is no automatic promise in this tapering workflow to convert and taper an arbitrary such circuit. For parity or BK-tree reduction, derive the appropriate state transformation and remove only known fixed positions; alternatively retain the untapered Jordan–Wigner baseline until the state path is validated.

Setting `Circuit.encoding` to a reduced encoding name does not implement those gates. The deprecated encoding-compatibility facade checks strings only. Matching strings cannot prove matching active orbitals, mode order, removed positions, eigenvalues, or phases. Likewise `to_interleaved` is a wire permutation, not a replacement for reconstructing a differently ordered fermionic encoding.

The ordinary mapper still leaves `get_core_energy()` outside the Pauli operator. A Clifford change and a parity substitution do not make nuclear repulsion or frozen-core energy disappear; add the same scalar once in total-energy comparisons. An identity coefficient created during tapering is part of the active operator, not permission to double count that core scalar.

The graph-oriented Verstraete–Cirac mapping from Lesson 14 is a related but distinct use of constraints. Its auxiliary stabilizers define a physical codespace in an enlarged register, and the engine supplies penalty terms. Those auxiliary constraints are not automatically identical to chemical electron-number parity. The correct subspace, state loading, and energy bookkeeping must accompany that representation too.

## What the savings mean downstream

Removing two problem qubits reduces a generic dense state-vector dimension by four. It can reduce certain gate and storage costs. It does not necessarily remove two qubits from every peak circuit width: control registers, coefficient-loading registers, shared phase-gradient ancillas, and internal workspaces remain. Physical error-correction overhead is a further layer that this calculation has not estimated.

There can also be costs: finding or verifying generators, applying a basis transformation, adapting observables, reconstructing state preparation, and maintaining consistent sectors along geometries. Near a crossing, the lowest state in one symmetry sector may stop being the state of interest. Symmetry labels are valuable precisely because they let us track that distinction instead of silently following the global minimum.

For our nitrogen story, symmetry-blocked classical data and fixed `(3,3)` populations are immediately useful. The specialized parity reductions are real operator capabilities, but a fully reduced workflow still needs a matched state path. We will therefore keep the well-defined untapered occupation encoding as the main state-loading baseline while learning what each preparation method actually does. The next lesson asks how to obtain a useful, affordable trial state without pretending that knowing the desired symmetry means knowing the desired eigenvector.
lessons.caveats: No execution or file writes. Populated native symmetry axis is Spin only; no general point-group discovery/centralizer/Clifford tapering search exposed in the inspected pipeline. Symmetries.spin_multiplicity is count-derived, not S2 certification. Actual spin aliasing tests every slot equivalence rather than object identity despite older comments. Rank4 packed shape is producer-defined; dense missing block raises but sparse get returns zero. Specialized tapering fixes alpha/total parity, not exact electron numbers. Helper skips X/Y terms rather than validating commutation and applies its own1e-12 cutoff. No automatic arbitrary state/circuit tapering; core scalar remains separate. General GF2/Clifford and toy spectra are explanatory derivations, not executed native features.

lessons.title: Loading a useful trial state
lessons.body:
# Lesson 16 — Loading a useful trial state

## The state we want and the state we can afford

We have an active Hamiltonian for stretched nitrogen: neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å, reduced from the original 28-spatial-orbital cc-pVDZ model to a six-electron, six-spatial-orbital model. Its ground eigenstate is the scientific target, but knowing the operator does not mean knowing that eigenstate’s amplitudes.

A **trial state** is a state we can construct with available classical information and a practical circuit. A Hartree–Fock determinant is cheap but may poorly describe stretched bonds. A selected-CI state can improve the overlap without solving the full original problem. A complete CASCI state in a small active space is a useful reference, but an exact classical solution of every large proposed target is not a scalable prerequisite for quantum computation.

State preparation has two costs: obtaining the classical description and implementing that description coherently. Four hundred nonzero CI coefficients are not four hundred free physical instructions, and a list of amplitudes in memory is not a quantum state already loaded into a processor.

This lesson traces every current registered `state_prep` family, plus the identity helper and the sparse method’s optional binary compression. It also separates chemical trial-state loading from coefficient-index preparation for block encodings. These routines share some software interfaces but do not all produce the same kind of output state. All examples are unexecuted prose; existing source tests are evidence of intended behavior, not tests run here.

## Ansatz, coefficients, and the alignment contract

An **ansatz** usually means a chosen form of approximate state. In this repository, [`data.Ansatz`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/ansatz.hpp) has a concrete narrower meaning: it bundles a `Hamiltonian` with a `Wavefunction`. It is not necessarily a parameterized quantum circuit or a variational optimizer.

The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/ansatz.cpp) validates the pairing. If both objects share the same orbital object, it accepts that identity directly. Otherwise it compares MO/AO dimensions, restricted/unrestricted status, alpha/beta active and inactive indices, orbital coefficient matrices, and available orbital energies. Coefficient-matrix differences are compared against machine epsilon in the norm used there; available energies use `1e-12`. Two bases spanning mathematically equivalent spaces but differing by rotations or phase choices are not automatically reconciled. This is deliberate alignment checking, not automatic orbital transport.

`Ansatz.calculate_energy()` is implemented despite a stale header note suggesting future implementation. It requires available RDMs and contracts them with integrals, adding the core energy. The current implementation uses real RDM variants and has specific restricted/unrestricted block contracts. It cannot turn arbitrary stored CC amplitudes into an expectation value by wishful thinking. The projected-MC eager spin-traced two-RDM normalization caveat from Lesson 9 also still matters: do not use that particular payload as an unchecked energy-contraction reference.

For state preparation, the relevant description is normally

\[
|\psi\rangle=\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}c_j|D_j\rangle,
\qquad \sum_j|c_j|^2=1.
\]

Here \(D_j\) is a determinant in one specified orbital/mode ordering, \(c_j\) its complex amplitude, and \(\mathcal S\) its **support**, the set of nonzero components. **Sparsity** means that support is small relative to all occupation bitstrings. Its usefulness depends not only on the number of determinants but also on the relationships among their bits.

A signed coefficient is not a probability. For real amplitudes, minus signs affect interference. For complex amplitudes, relative phases matter too. Replacing all coefficients with their absolute values generally changes the state, even though direct occupation measurements give the same probabilities.

Only containers exposing actual determinant coefficients can feed these wavefunction loaders. `AmplitudeContainer` stores cluster amplitudes, not a ready determinant expansion; localizers and active-space selectors often return determinant carriers rather than the original correlated coefficients. Obtain a compatible correlated state in the selected, possibly transformed orbitals before treating it as the trial CI state.

## Overlap, truncation, and reoptimization

For normalized states, **fidelity** means squared overlap,

\[
F=|\langle\psi_{\mathrm{target}}|\psi_{\mathrm{trial}}\rangle|^2.
\]

Some source tests name the unsquared overlap magnitude “fidelity”; we will keep the squared definition and identify what a test actually checks. Overlap requires consistent orbital basis, determinant identities, signs, and encoding. The wavefunction container’s overlap routine has its own ordering/pointer restrictions; equal vector lengths are not sufficient evidence of matching determinant bases.

If a normalized expansion is truncated to a chosen support \(T\), its retained probability mass is \(w=\sum_{j\in T}|c_j|^2\). Renormalization divides retained coefficients by \(\sqrt w\). The new state has fidelity \(w\) with the original expansion, provided determinants are orthonormal and alignment is unchanged. This is not automatically fidelity \(w\) with the unknown exact ground state.

The `Wavefunction.truncate` operation selects and renormalizes amplitudes. It does not solve for better amplitudes in the chosen support. A projected multiconfiguration calculation instead forms the Hamiltonian in that selected determinant space and solves its eigenproblem, as taught in Lesson 9.

A hand-worked example separates them. Suppose a selected two-determinant subspace has

\[
H_T=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

A truncated-and-renormalized trial vector \((3,1)/\sqrt{10}\) has expectation −0.6 in these illustrative energy units. Reoptimizing the coefficients gives \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) and eigenvalue −1. No determinants were added; their mixing was improved. This is a toy matrix, not a nitrogen result and not an executed PMC calculation.

For a Hermitian model and a normalized state, the variational expectation is bounded below by that model’s ground energy. It need not be an eigenvalue: a state spread over eigenstates has their probability-weighted average energy. Enlarging a nested variational determinant space cannot raise its exactly optimized minimum, but it can increase preprocessing and loading cost, and does not guarantee a better end-to-end resource tradeoff.

If an ideal coherent phase-estimation procedure acts on a trial state \(\sum_k a_k|E_k\rangle\), it identifies the eigenstate branch \(k\) with weight \(|a_k|^2\), subject to its phase resolution. Under that idealized experiment, ground-state branch probability equals ground-state overlap weight. The repository’s iterative bit-estimation circuits can freshly prepare a state for each bit/shot. Their full bit-string success probability is not generically “the fidelity”: fresh eigenstate mixtures, finite precision, feedback, and repeated sampling must be accounted for. We will derive that distinction in the phase-estimation lesson.

## The offered loaders and their real inputs

The [registry](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/registry.py) registers `dense_pure_state`, `sparse_isometry`, `qrom`, and `alias_sampling`; the default is `sparse_isometry`. The optional Qiskit plugin adds `qiskit_regular_isometry`. `sparse_isometry_gf2x` is a deprecated alias, not a separate modern method. `identity_state_prep(num_qubits)` is a helper returning a circuit, not a registered algorithm that accepts a wavefunction.

The [common state-preparation interface](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/state_preparation.py) takes a `Wavefunction` and returns a `Circuit`. That common signature must not hide output semantics: `alias_sampling` returns a coefficient-index PREPARE oracle with entangled workspace, not a clean arbitrary molecular trial state.

The common dense scattering helper obtains active determinants and their coefficients. The register width is `configuration_set.num_modes() * determinant.bits_per_mode()`. For the ordinary spin-half spatial-orbital configurations, there are two bits per spatial mode, alpha in the lower half and beta in the upper half. Synthetic compressed subspaces use one-bit-per-mode configurations. The helper places each coefficient at the integer formed from its determinant occupation bits; it does not assume coefficient-list position equals basis index. Duplicate indices are added in this helper.

That helper rejects empty coefficients, non-negligible imaginary parts, and widths above 32, and produces a real vector of length \(2^q\). The 32-qubit guard is a sanity boundary, not a feasible-memory recommendation: \(2^{32}\) eight-byte real amplitudes alone occupy 32 GiB. There is no cheap route through this helper for a generic sparse 56-qubit nitrogen state. QROM and alias sampling currently use the same dense scattering helper, so their names do not remove that classical allocation.

## Dense pure-state preparation

[`dense_pure_state`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/dense_pure_state.py) is the simplest native Q#-backed loader. It scatters a real wavefunction into the full occupation vector and constructs a `StatePreparationParams` record with a reversed `rowMap`, the amplitude vector, no expansion operations, and the register width. It returns a Q# callable and factory with `encoding="jordan-wigner"` and known `num_qubits`.

The repository’s [`StatePreparation.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/StatePreparation.qs) calls external `Std.StatePreparation.PreparePureStateD` on the subregister selected by `rowMap`. The reversal reconciles its vector/register convention with occupation-bit indices; it does not reverse the physical meaning of alpha and beta. Existing [dense-loader tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_state_preparation_dense.py) compare prepared vectors, single determinants, and energies with sparse isometry.

The Python helper itself does not explicitly normalize the scattered vector despite broad wording in its method docstring. Loading behavior beyond the adapter is delegated to the standard-library operation. Supply a valid normalized, finite nonzero target rather than relying on a blanket claim of validation or repair. The native dense class adds no precision or transpiler settings of its own.

Conceptually, dense state loading can recursively split amplitude norm between branches. If a prefix has total probability \(p\), of which \(p_0\) lies in its zero-child, a Y rotation can allocate amplitudes proportional to \(\sqrt{p_0/p}\) and \(\sqrt{1-p_0/p}\). Repeating down a tree gives general amplitude loading. This explains the exponential generic information cost, but it is not a claim that we reviewed the external standard-library decomposition line by line.

An **isometry** preserves inner products from an input space into an output space. Preparing one state maps a known reference vector to that state; a quantum implementation extends that action to a unitary on a complete space, possibly with clean workspace. It does not need to implement an arbitrary unknown unitary supplied as an exponentially large matrix. Nevertheless a completely arbitrary dense target contains exponentially many independent parameters.

## The optional Qiskit regular isometry

[`qiskit_regular_isometry`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/regular_isometry.py) converts the wavefunction to a dense complex statevector, asks Qiskit’s `StatePreparation` to synthesize it, optionally transpiles it, and exports OpenQASM 3. This is an external Qiskit synthesis contribution, not a second native Q# implementation.

Its settings are `transpile=True`, `transpile_optimization_level=0`, and `basis_gates=["x","y","z","cx","cz","id","h","s","sdg","rz"]`. The adapter additionally applies repository passes `MergeZBasisRotations`, `RemoveZBasisOnZeroState`, and `SubstituteCliffordRz`. These are state-preparation-specific simplifications, not justification to remove such gates from arbitrary unknown-input unitaries.

The [conversion helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/conversion.py) preserves complex coefficients and normalizes when its norm is above `1e-15`. It allocates \(2^q\) complex amplitudes without the native helper’s explicit 32-qubit guard. Duplicate determinant entries are assigned rather than summed on this path. Use unique, valid determinant support instead of assuming all loaders repair duplicates identically.

The circuit is returned with QASM and Jordan–Wigner encoding, but without an explicitly supplied `num_qubits` field in this adapter. Conversion/building consumers must handle that declared-width limitation rather than assume every method returns identical metadata. Dense complex support here does not imply sparse isometry accepts complex input: the sparse parent checks for real coefficients before delegating.

## Sparse isometry: compress the support, load, then expand

The default [`sparse_isometry`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/sparse_isometry.py) exploits the bit patterns of the supported determinants. Build a binary matrix with one row per qubit and one column per determinant. The entries say which occupation bits are one. Coefficients remain aligned with columns throughout; ordinary floating-point row reduction is not the transformation being applied to amplitudes.

A CNOT from row \(u\) to row \(v\) replaces row \(v\) by its XOR with row \(u\). An X gate complements one row. Both are reversible operations on bitstrings. If two rows have identical patterns, a CNOT zeros one. If a row is all ones across the support, X zeros it. Binary Gaussian elimination then finds independent rows and records the CNOTs that eliminated dependent patterns. Removing zero rows at this stage means those qubits are known to be zero **in the transformed supported state**, not that their physical modes have been deleted from the Hamiltonian.

The implementation performs duplicate-row removal, all-ones-row removal, GF(2) elimination, zero-row removal, and an additional guarded diagonal/staircase reduction when its structural test permits it. It tracks the retained row map and operations. This is affine compression: the X translations augment linear XOR transformations. The retained width is related to the affine span of the supported bitstrings, not simply the real matrix rank or the number of determinants.

For a hand-worked example, suppose support contains only the increasing-qubit-order bit vectors `0000` and `1111`, with amplitudes \(\sqrt{0.8}\) and \(\sqrt{0.2}\). All four rows of the support matrix agree. Three CNOT eliminations can leave one independent row. Load \(\sqrt{0.8}|0\rangle+\sqrt{0.2}|1\rangle\) on that qubit and reverse the three CNOTs to reconstruct the four-qubit state. The final circuit still acts on four problem qubits. The saving was a one-qubit dense-loading stage, not an alteration of the chemical model.

For \(d\) determinants and retained width \(r\), the support matrix costs roughly \(qd\) bits in principle, though the Python implementation uses byte-valued arrays and other bookkeeping. The reduced amplitude vector has \(2^r\) entries. Even modest support can have a large affine span, so this method is not guaranteed cheap merely because \(d\ll2^q\).

The ordinary path places each coefficient at its reduced determinant index, normalizes the nonzero reduced vector, constructs a synthetic one-bit-per-mode wavefunction, and delegates dense loading. Its `dense_state_prep` setting defaults to `AlgorithmRef("state_prep","dense_pure_state")`. It then reverses the recorded GF(2)+X operations to restore the original register. Default expansion gates are Clifford X and CNOT gates. Creating the synthetic wavefunction is a software representation of compressed bits, not inventing a new molecule or a smaller physical active space.

The native nested dense factory is composed in Q# using its parameters; this avoids a callable-capturing-callable limitation in adaptive code generation. A nested Qiskit loader is composed via QASM/QIR and Qiskit. A custom child circuit carrying only a prebuilt Q# circuit object is rejected if it cannot enter either composition path. The parent’s [`dense_state_prep` contract](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/sparse_isometry.py) is therefore more specific than “any algorithm in the family works.”

There is no exposed support-pruning threshold in the sparse parent. Its comments mentioning filtering do not implement automatic top-determinant selection. Remove zero coefficients, merge duplicate determinants, select the desired support, and verify normalization beforehand. Duplicate columns can otherwise overwrite coefficients during reduced scattering; an all-identical multi-entry support can produce a zero-rank error. Non-negligible imaginary coefficients are rejected even when the nested loader is complex-capable.

For one determinant, the sparse method bypasses dense loading and applies X on each occupied bit. The actual Q# body uses `bitStrings[i]` on `qs[i]`; a contradictory helper docstring about reversing the input does not describe its behavior. A normalized single determinant’s overall sign is physically global and is not retained by this shortcut. A zero-amplitude “single determinant” should not be supplied as a state. Our six-electron occupation determinant needs six X gates on twelve problem qubits, not six qubits or a zero-cost identity operation.

## Optional binary compression and its non-Clifford price

The sparse method’s `binary_encoding=False` setting enables a second, best-effort route when changed to true. It first obtains forward row-echelon form, then compares the remaining row count with \(\lceil\log_2 d\rceil\). It takes this route only when the latter is strictly smaller; otherwise it falls back to ordinary sparse isometry.

This compression is **not** Bravyi–Kitaev fermionic encoding. It assigns compact binary labels to the finite supported determinant set, loads amplitudes on those labels, and expands back to the same Jordan–Wigner output register.

The [_binary_encoding_utils implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/_binary_encoding_utils.py) first compresses pivot columns from a unary/staircase form to binary. It then processes remaining columns in batches, using Toffoli operations and lookup blocks called PUI blocks in the code to clear sparse indicator rows. A **Toffoli** is a NOT controlled on two bits; unlike the default X/CNOT expansion it is not Clifford. A recorded bijection keeps compact labels matched to original coefficient columns. The synthesizer verifies that non-dense rows are zero and its mapping covers the columns.

`include_negative_controls=True` permits controls conditioned on a bit being zero as well as one. The implementation promotes fixed control patterns and can split batches into power-of-two chunks when its lookup-cost estimate favors that. Smaller dense width can therefore trade arbitrary rotations for Toffolis, lookup tables, and workspace. The winner depends on those costs, not only on a new label count.

`measurement_based_uncompute=False` is the other control. When enabled, selected lookup branches use `Std.Intrinsic.AND` and its adjoint instead of a fully unitary Toffoli uncompute. The [Q# binary expansion](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/BinaryEncoding.qs) borrows known-zero qubits from an ancilla pool formed from unused transformed rows, returns them clean, and allocates helpers if that pool is insufficient. Mid-circuit measurement with corrective feedback can reduce non-Clifford work while preserving the intended logical action. It is not measurement of the final chemical occupations.

The target profile matters. The adapter warns that a Base profile cannot use the intended measurement-based path and relies on unitary uncomputation there; adaptive profiles can lower it to measurement and feedforward. Existing [binary-state tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_state_preparation_binary_encoding.py) check reduced CCZ counts, added measurements, QIR/Qiskit control flow, and output-state independence from measurement outcome. Those are source checks, not new measured savings here. The binary composition advertises `Adj`, not automatically `Ctl`; adjointable does not mean every arbitrary outer-controlled use is supported.

`create_dense(wavefunction)` returns only the dense-loading component embedded in the same full-width register, omitting expansion. It is for component costing. It is generally **not** the full requested trial state. Subtracting additive logical gate counts from matched full/component estimates can isolate expansion work; subtracting total physical resource estimates need not have the same meaning because scheduling and error correction are nonlinear.

## QROM: loading a fixed classical table into rotations

**QROM**, quantum read-only memory in these circuits, means a reversible circuit implementing a lookup table known at circuit construction. It is not a free, universal hardware QRAM device. A lookup correlates an address register with table output, and that temporary output must subsequently be uncomputed.

[`state_prep/qrom`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/qrom_state_prep.py) is a real signed-amplitude loader. It scatters the target over the full \(2^q\) occupation vector, checks finite coefficients and squared coefficients and rejects an all-zero vector, then uses `rotation_bit_precision=10` by default, with the exposed range 1–30. Rescale extreme data rather than regard these checks as a complete safeguard against every possible overflow in a later probability sum.

The [Q# implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/QROMStatePrep.qs) explicitly implements a Shende–Bullock–Markov-style probability tree. At a node with total mass \(p\) and left-child mass \(p_L\), it forms \(\theta=\arccos\sqrt{p_L/p}\); zero-mass nodes get zero angle. It needs a rotation \(R_y(2\theta)\) to distribute the amplitudes. For precision \(b\), it stores the integer

\[
x=\operatorname{Round}\!\left(\frac{2^b\theta}{2\pi}\right)\bmod2^b.
\]

The phase-gradient rotation routine implements \(R_y(4\pi x/2^b)\), matching that convention. Thus quantization changes the prepared amplitudes by a controlled numerical approximation, not by an electron-space reduction. Ignoring wrap-equivalent angles, nearest rounding bounds the individual rotation-angle error by \(2\pi/2^b\); errors across many rotations still require a total state/error budget.

The circuit fixes the most significant occupation bit first, using already fixed prefix bits as lookup addresses for later rotations. It reverses slices explicitly where the little-endian table-lookup interface requires it. Magnitude rotations alone would lose coefficient signs, so a separate sign table is loaded into a scratch sign bit; Z applies the required sign phase, and the lookup is undone. The [signed-amplitude tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_state_preparation_qrom.py) check mixed signs, all-negative vectors, zero entries, and determinant-index placement.

The repository’s [`SelectSwap.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/SelectSwap.qs) splits an address between selection and a swap network. More swap bits mean more parallel scratch data words but fewer select addresses. Passing −1 asks the helper to search its internal integer cost model for a split. The no-swap select model is linear in table length; swap, scratch, and erasure terms change the tradeoff. Do not turn an abstract lookup into a unit-cost oracle, or interpret that internal logical estimate as a measured hardware runtime. The total fixed table and the bare Python dense allocation remain potentially exponential.

## Reusable phase-gradient ancillas

A **phase-gradient state** of \(b\) qubits has amplitudes

\[
|\phi_b\rangle=2^{-b/2}\sum_{k=0}^{2^b-1}e^{-2\pi i k/2^b}|k\rangle.
\]

Adding integer \(x\) modulo \(2^b\) leaves this state unchanged except for phase \(e^{2\pi i x/2^b}\). Condition the addition appropriately and that phase is kicked back onto a target qubit. This makes an integer-valued angle register useful for rotations without synthesizing a completely new arbitrary rotation at every lookup.

[`PhaseGradient.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/PhaseGradient.qs) prepares the gradient using X and an adjoint QFT, performs addition through an external QDK arithmetic primitive, and uses basis changes for its Y rotation. QFT means quantum Fourier transform. The standard-library QFT/adder internals are external-team contributions, not code we claim to have reviewed here. The routine’s documented cost model excludes preparing and unpreparing the gradient itself.

The QROM setting `allocate_phase_gradient=True` makes the callable self-contained: allocate the gradient internally, prepare it, use it, and unprepare it. Its declared `num_qubits` is then just the target-state width, and `num_phase_gradient_ancillas` is zero because no gradient is expected from the caller. Internal allocation still contributes to actual peak logical width.

With `allocate_phase_gradient=False`, the callable expects `[state register | gradient register]`. It declares `num_qubits=q+b` and `CircuitMetadata(num_phase_gradient_ancillas=b)`. The caller must initialize the trailing gradient and preserve it across compatible subroutines. It must not include that nonzero gradient in a reflection intended to test whether ordinary ancillas are all zero. Metadata identifies the sharing contract; it does not prepare the gradient by itself.

There is a subtle export boundary: the associated standalone factory always allocates and prepares its own gradient because an exported circuit has no caller to lend one. Costing the factory and costing a composed callable with a shared gradient answer different questions. Existing tests explicitly distinguish those declared widths. Reuse can amortize preparation **within one composed execution**, not across independently initialized jobs without a maintained quantum state.

Precision limits such as 30 bits are engineering bounds. A comment that an angle grid is “below chemical accuracy” is not a proof about total molecular energy error, long controlled evolutions, or noisy preparation.

## Alias sampling: the same marginal distribution is not the same pure state

[`state_prep/alias_sampling`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/alias_sampling.py) accepts real **nonnegative** wavefunction coefficients, squares them after dense determinant-index scattering, and passes those weights to Q#. It rejects negatives, non-finite values, overflow on squaring/summing, and all-zero weights. Its `bits_precision` defaults to 10 with range 1–30.

For normalized target amplitudes \(c_j\ge0\), the target marginal probabilities are \(p_j=c_j^2\). The result is generally

\[
\sum_j\sqrt{\widetilde p_j}|j\rangle|g_j\rangle,
\]

where \(g_j\) is workspace or **garbage** correlated with the index, and \(\widetilde p\) approximates \(p\). Tracing out that workspace does not in general yield the pure state \(\sum_j c_j|j\rangle\). Correct occupation probabilities alone cannot establish correct interference or ground-state overlap.

The [Q# alias implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/AliasSamplingStatePrep.qs) first discretizes probabilities into \(L2^\mu\) integer units, where \(L\) is table length and \(\mu\) the precision. It floors each allocation, distributes leftover units by largest fractional remainder with deterministic ties, and ensures zero weights do not gain population. The resulting per-entry probability error is bounded by \(1/(L2^\mu)\) in the intended discretization; the [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_state_preparation_alias.py) check that bound and zero-weight behavior.

Walker-style alias construction then assigns each table position a keep count and an alternate index, pairing underfilled and overfilled probability bars. Coherently, the circuit prepares a uniform index, a uniform \(\mu\)-bit comparison value, loads `(keep, alternate)` through QROM, compares the value with keep, and conditionally swaps the index with its alternate. The flag/comparison/lookup registers retain the information needed for reversibility. They are not harmless classical notes one can discard.

Named registers total \(2\lceil\log_2L\rceil+2\mu+1\): index, alternate storage, comparison bits, keep storage, and flag. Lookup/swap implementations can add more scratch. In this Python wrapper, \(L\) is the full scattered occupation-vector length, not automatically the sparse determinant count. A sparse two-entry wavefunction at indices 0 and 3 is explicitly scattered to four weights in a source test.

This is useful as **PREPARE** in a linear-combination-of-unitaries, or LCU, block-encoding construction, where SELECT acts on the index and PREPARE-adjoint is part of the coherent structure. Even there, unpreparing the garbage is not a claim that every branch deterministically returns all workspace to zero after an arbitrary SELECT. The useful zero-ancilla block is extracted by the construction we will derive later.

To load an LCU distribution proportional to \(|w_j|\) through this particular Python wavefunction adapter, the supplied nonnegative amplitudes must be proportional to \(\sqrt{|w_j|}\), because it squares them. Signs of LCU coefficients belong in the matching SELECT action. Separate conditional Q# alias helpers do carry sign bits and conditional/free-rider data for specialized builders; that does not lift the public `alias_sampling` adapter’s nonnegative restriction.

The Q# code uses a phase-safe ancilla-free uniform preparation for non-power-of-two lists, because PREPARE-adjoint must work after phases have been imprinted, not only on the pristine state it first prepared. This is another reason an apparently cheaper preparation shortcut may be invalid as a reusable coherent subroutine.

## Identity preparation, useful code patterns, and complete cost

[`identity_state_prep(q)`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/state_preparation/identity.py) wraps an empty repeated Pauli sequence. It leaves the input register unchanged. On fresh zeroed qubits it therefore leaves the vacuum bitstring, not a six-electron nitrogen determinant. It does not inspect a wavefunction or load a desired state for free. The helper currently supplies neither encoding metadata nor an explicit `num_qubits` field to `Circuit`, although its factory records target indices. Builders requiring those fields cannot infer a chemistry contract from the word identity.

For the continuing untapered Jordan–Wigner story, a source-backed, unexecuted pattern is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef, Ansatz

# trial_wavefunction contains valid real CI coefficients in the selected orbitals.
trial = Ansatz(active_hamiltonian, trial_wavefunction)
prep = create(
    "state_prep", "sparse_isometry",
    dense_state_prep=AlgorithmRef("state_prep", "dense_pure_state"),
    binary_encoding=False,
)
state_circuit = prep.run(trial.get_wavefunction())
```

Changing the nested reference to `qiskit_regular_isometry` requires the optional plugin; its transpilation knobs belong on that nested reference, not a fictional global state-preparation setting. Enabling binary compression is a tradeoff to evaluate on actual support, not an unconditional improvement. A QROM alternative is `create("state_prep", "qrom", rotation_bit_precision=10).run(trial_wavefunction)` under its real-amplitude and dense-width limits.

A fair comparison includes classical CI/support selection, preprocessing tables and bit matrices, dense loading, expansion, sign/phase handling, all scratch allocation, gradient initialization, adjoints, and every repetition the enclosing algorithm requires. It also distinguishes logical rotations from the fault-tolerant gates used to approximate them. Adding determinants may improve overlap enough to save trials, or may cost more in loading than it saves. No single overlap or gate-count number establishes that balance.

For our nitrogen baseline the state register remains twelve qubits even when a sparse loader uses a much smaller dense subregister. A tapered ten-qubit operator from Lesson 15 cannot consume this state circuit without a matched transformation. A localizer’s one-determinant carrier cannot replace the correlated CI state by retaining its old filename. And a coefficient-loading oracle with entangled garbage cannot stand in for a clean trial state because its marginal histogram looks right.

We can now ask the next engineering question precisely: given a state-preparation subroutine and a mathematical Hamiltonian operation in compatible representations, how does the repository assemble them into actual circuits and interchange formats? That is the subject of Lesson 17.
lessons.caveats: No imports, compilation, estimation, tests or scientific execution. Dense native/QROM/alias scatter full2^q real arrays with32-qubit guard; sparse path has no automatic support selection or general complex support and duplicate scattering differs from common helper. Qiskit regular accepts complex dense data but returns QASM without explicit declared width. Identity is a helper, not free chemistry state preparation, and omits encoding/declared width. Binary compression restores JW and is Adj-only at Q# composition boundary; measurement uncompute depends on target profile. Alias sampling carries entangled garbage and is not a clean arbitrary trial-state loader; Python adapter squares nonnegative amplitudes. QROM precision is not a chemical-error guarantee; shared-gradient callable and standalone export have different ownership/cost contracts. Ansatz energy requires actual compatible real RDMs; prior PMC normalization caveat retained.

lessons.title: Turning mathematical operations into circuits
lessons.body:
# Lesson 17 — Turning mathematical operations into circuits

## One workflow, several different translations

The nitrogen story now contains several objects that must not be confused. A chemical Hamiltonian encodes the selected orbital/electron model. A qubit operator represents that Hamiltonian in an encoding such as blocked Jordan–Wigner. A trial-state preparation circuit loads an approximation to a desired eigenstate. None of these, by itself, specifies the full quantum algorithm.

A further decision is needed: which mathematical operation should a quantum circuit implement? Time evolution, a block encoding, and a quantum walk are different operations derived from the same Hamiltonian. The repository represents their plans with `UnitaryRepresentation`, then uses a circuit mapper to produce a `Circuit`. An enclosing algorithm composes state preparation, controls, those operations, measurement, and possibly feedback. Compilation produces an interchange representation for execution or resource counting.

Thus the chain is chemical model → qubit operator → unitary plan → circuit subroutine → algorithm composition → compiled program → a chosen consumer. A **fermion-to-qubit mapper** does not synthesize all the gates, and a **circuit mapper** does not choose a chemically accurate active space. Maintaining these separate responsibilities makes numerical error, representation mistakes, and missing external capabilities easier to locate.

This chapter teaches the concrete circuit contracts at revision `97a3ff4f`. Product-formula error analysis and block-encoding spectral derivations follow in Lessons 18–19; provider execution and physical resource estimation come later. We are reading source and tests, not compiling or executing any circuit here.

## What a unitary plan contains

A unitary matrix \(U\) satisfies \(U^\dagger U=I\), so its action preserves state norm and is reversible. An **operator exponential** is defined by the matrix power series, just as an ordinary exponential is defined for a scalar. For Hermitian \(H\),

\[
U(t)=e^{-iHt}
\]

is unitary. In atomic units, time \(t\) and energy combine to give a dimensionless phase. A circuit generally implements an approximation to this exponential rather than calculating a dense exponential matrix first.

[`UnitaryRepresentation`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/unitary_representation/base.py) wraps a concrete container. Its supported serialization dispatch recognizes `pauli_product_formula`, `lcu`, `lcu_walk`, and `sossa_block_encoding`. Abstract `UnitaryContainer`, `BlockEncodingContainer`, and `QuantumWalkContainer` interfaces are not additional concrete executable methods.

[`PauliProductFormulaContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/unitary_representation/containers/pauli_product_formula.py) stores an ordered `step_terms` list, positive integer `step_reps`, problem width `num_qubits`, and `scale`. Each `ExponentiatedPauliTerm` holds a dictionary from qubit index to Pauli letter and an `angle` \(\theta\), meaning the factor \(e^{-i\theta P}\). It is not an instruction to apply \(R_z(\theta)\). `scale` is evolution-time metadata for converting a measured phase back to an energy; the circuit mapper consumes the already computed term angles and does not multiply them by `scale` again.

The constructor rejects noninteger, boolean, zero, and negative repetition counts. Other payloads still need a valid producer: this is not a complete physical validation of every Pauli index, time, or coefficient. Reordering terms can change the approximate unitary when they do not commute. The current `reorder_terms` helper also reconstructs the container without forwarding `scale`, restoring its default 1.0; do not lose phase-to-energy metadata while experimenting with ordering. `combine` checks equal width and compatible scale, expands repetitions, and fuses adjacent identical Pauli factors, not arbitrary nonadjacent terms.

An [`LCUContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/unitary_representation/containers/block_encoding.py) stores precomputed PREPARE data and a `Select` description. LCU means **linear combination of unitaries**. PREPARE is an ancillary index-state preparation, not the chemical trial-state preparation. SELECT lists operations activated by integer index values, with associated ± signs. `ControlledOperation.ctrl_state` is that index value; its `operation` is a Pauli label with qubit 0 on the right. `power` describes repeated use of the block operation.

An [`LCUWalkContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/unitary_representation/containers/quantum_walk.py) wraps an LCU block encoding and an ancilla reflection to define a walk step. Its scale is a normalization used for the walk’s nonlinear phase-to-energy relation, not the evolution time of a product formula. The container’s `eigenvalue_from_phase` methods therefore differ between families. Applying the product-formula decoder to a walk phase is not an interchangeable implementation choice.

[`SOSSABlockEncodingContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/unitary_representation/containers/sossa.py) carries outer and conditional inner PREPARE data, rotation tables, structural register layout, normalization, and scalar metadata for **sum-of-squares spectral amplification**, abbreviated SOSSA. It represents a specialized block encoding, not a precomposed generic controlled walk. The distinction determines which mapper and phase-estimation builder can consume it.

## Deriving a Pauli exponential as gates

For a Pauli word \(P\), \(P^2=I\), so its exponential simplifies to

\[
e^{-i\theta P}=\cos\theta\,I-i\sin\theta\,P.
\]

We can implement this without constructing that matrix. First rotate every nonidentity factor into the Z basis. For X use H. For Y apply \(S^\dagger\) followed by H. For Z do nothing. Let the combined basis change be \(B\), so \(BPB^\dagger\) is a product of Z factors.

Next accumulate the parity of the participating qubits into one of them using a CNOT ladder. For illustrative \(P=X_0Y_2Z_3\), after the basis changes use CNOT(0,2), then CNOT(2,3). The last qubit holds the XOR of the participating bits. A rotation \(R_z(2\theta)=e^{-i\theta Z}\) on it applies the correct phase to each even/odd parity branch. Undo the CNOT ladder and then undo the basis changes.

If \(V\) denotes that parity network, the whole expression is

\[
U=B^\dagger V^\dagger R_z(2\theta)V B.
\]

Operators on the right act first. With \(w\) nonidentity factors, the straightforward ladder uses \(2(w-1)\) CNOTs plus local basis changes and one rotation. This is a logical construction with unrestricted connectivity, not a hardware layout or an exact gate count promised for every compiled `Exp`. Routing, cancellation across adjacent factors, rotation synthesis, and target conventions can change the realized count.

The repository’s native Q# mapper does not explicitly write that ladder in Python. [`PauliExp.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/PauliExp.qs) calls the external primitive as `Exp(paulis, -coeff, systems)`. The [matrix test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit_mapper.py) compares the result with \(e^{-i\theta P}\). The minus sign and factor-of-two distinction from conventional axis rotations are therefore source-backed. The standard-library decomposition itself remains an external QDK compiler/runtime boundary.

Terms execute in list order. If the list is X then Z, the state is acted on by X’s exponential first, so the resulting matrix is \(e^{-i\theta_Z Z}e^{-i\theta_X X}\). The test explicitly constructs matrices in that order. Changing notation to a product symbol must not silently reverse it.

An empty Pauli map can represent identity. Its factor \(e^{-i\theta I}\) is a global phase for an uncontrolled state evolution, but not necessarily disposable in the enclosing algorithm. The ordinary chemical qubit mapper excluded the core-energy scalar before this stage. Keep that scalar in the classical energy bookkeeping, or deliberately include it with the appropriate phase convention; do not both add it to the operator and add it again to the reported energy.

## Direct control: why phase bookkeeping suddenly matters

A controlled operation is

\[
C(U)=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes U.
\]

The control-zero branch is unchanged; the control-one branch receives \(U\). Replacing \(U\) by \(e^{i\phi}U\) changes the phase **between those branches**, even though it changed only a global phase in an isolated uncontrolled use. This is why controlled Hamiltonian operations need stricter equivalence checks than statevector comparisons that fit away any overall phase.

For an ordered product of factors, controlling every factor with the same control gives the controlled ordered product exactly. A useful construction can run basis changes and parity computation unconditionally, control only the central rotation, and then undo the basis/parity work. On the disabled branch those surrounding operations cancel. The repository uses [`Controlled Exp`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/ControlledPauliExp.qs) rather than manually asserting that every gate name should gain another control.

The algorithm names are `circuit_mapper/pauli_sequence` and `controlled_circuit_mapper/pauli_sequence`; both are defaults within their respective families. The [ordinary mapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_mapper/pauli_sequence_mapper.py) accepts only a Pauli product-formula container, creates the per-term Q# Pauli arrays, repeats the step, and declares the problem-register width. It has no additional synthesis-tolerance settings of its own.

The [controlled mapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/controlled_circuit_mapper/controlled_pauli_sequence_mapper.py) supports one control. The common settings are `control_indices=[0]` and `target_indices=[]`, where an empty target list auto-fills the lowest noncontrol indices to the required width. Explicit targets must have the right length, contain no duplicates, and not overlap controls. Duplicate controls are rejected. Supply sensible nonnegative indices; these checks are not a full proof that every possible standalone layout is supported.

There is a concrete layout limit: the direct controlled-Pauli **standalone Q# factory** allocates `Length(systems)+1`, not one plus the maximum requested index. Compact layouts such as control 0 and targets 1,2 work. A sparse layout such as control 2 and targets 3,4 can be accepted when constructing the `Circuit` yet exceed that factory’s allocation when compiled. The existing explicit-layout test checks construction, not compilation of that sparse case. The composable callable instead receives a control qubit and a target array directly. Do not treat those two interfaces as identical allocation promises.

Controlled mapper results currently do not declare `num_qubits` or encoding in their returned `Circuit`, unlike the ordinary Pauli mapper’s known width. The unitary plan and enclosing builder retain part of the layout knowledge. Source tests of matrix action and source tests that merely return a `Circuit` establish different things.

## A small complete construction pattern

This unexecuted example uses a two-qubit toy operation rather than constructing or expanding the nitrogen molecule again:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data.unitary_representation.base import UnitaryRepresentation
from qdk_chemistry.data.unitary_representation.containers.pauli_product_formula import (
    ExponentiatedPauliTerm,
    PauliProductFormulaContainer,
)

plan = UnitaryRepresentation(
    PauliProductFormulaContainer(
        step_terms=[ExponentiatedPauliTerm(pauli_term={0: "X", 1: "Z"}, angle=0.2)],
        step_reps=1,
        num_qubits=2,
        scale=1.0,
    )
)
circuit = create("circuit_mapper", "pauli_sequence").run(plan)
controlled = create(
    "controlled_circuit_mapper", "pauli_sequence", control_indices=[0]
).run(plan)
```

The first circuit implements \(e^{-0.2iX_0Z_1}\); the second embeds the same logical two-qubit operation on target positions 1 and 2 of a compact three-qubit standalone layout. It does not estimate an energy. `scale=1.0` is explicit decoding metadata, not a second multiplier applied to the angle. Both calls require the installed QDK runtime to construct their Q# callables; neither has been run here.

An actual chemical time-evolution builder would choose the term list and step repetitions from the Hamiltonian and its approximation settings. The [repository usage example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/circuit_mapper.py) shows that division of responsibility. Its separate hydrogen geometry is not our 1.85 Å nitrogen baseline.

## Controlling by swapping with a vacuum register

`controlled_circuit_mapper/cswap_pauli_sequence` offers a different cost tradeoff. Rather than controlling every exponential, it adds a system-sized scratch register initialized to \(|0\cdots0\rangle\). Controlled SWAP gates exchange the system with this register when the control is one. The **uncontrolled** repeated evolution acts on the scratch register, and the swaps are undone. For \(n\) target qubits this uses an additional \(n\)-qubit register and two layers of \(n\) controlled swaps. The repetition loop is inside the sandwich, so those two swap layers cover the whole repeated evolution.

This only works coherently when the all-zero register is an eigenstate of the **actual ordered product**:

\[
U|0\cdots0\rangle=e^{i\phi_0}|0\cdots0\rangle.
\]

Without a phase correction, control zero acquires \(e^{i\phi_0}\) while control one receives \(U\). The [Q# implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/ControlledSwapPauliExp.qs) applies `R1(vacuumPhase, control)`, where \(R_1(\phi)=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\phi})\), making the result \(e^{i\phi_0}C(U)\) on the clean-scratch subspace. It skips this correction only below its small `1e-12` phase threshold.

Particle-number conservation of the exact fermionic Hamiltonian is not enough. A split product formula can leak the computational vacuum if cancellation partners are separated by noncommuting factors. The [Python validator](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/controlled_circuit_mapper/controlled_swap_pauli_sequence_mapper.py) groups contiguous mutually commuting strings, tracks off-diagonal amplitudes by the bit pattern they flip, and checks that those contributions cancel. It uses \(i^{n_Y}\) for the phase of a Pauli string acting on zero, preserving Y signs. Diagonal I/Z terms contribute the known phase \(-\sum_j\theta_j\).

The setting `vacuum_preservation_tolerance=1e-9` is a total budget over flipped supports and all repetitions; the per-step allowance divides by `step_reps`. It is not an instruction to throw away each small intermediate coefficient separately. This is a sufficient structured test, not an arbitrary dense-matrix proof accepting every unitary that happens to fix zero.

A contiguous equal-weight XX/YY pair cancels its action on the vacuum, whereas interleaving a noncommuting Z term can invalidate that argument. The `vacuum_annihilating` term grouper is the source-backed way to arrange suitable Hamiltonian terms before a compatible product-formula builder. The mapper validates rather than blindly trusting the grouping name. A tapered encoding’s all-zero state need not mean fermionic vacuum, so tapering can invalidate the shortcut even for an originally number-conserving problem.

The [CSWAP tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_controlled_swap_circuit_mapper.py) check clean-scratch matrix blocks, phase correction, repetitions, valid cancellations, and rejected leakage. Its standalone factory sizes from the maximum requested index, unlike the direct controlled-Pauli factory. Its callable advertises `Adj`, not a general further-controlled capability. This method can reduce controlled-rotation overhead at the expense of width and swaps; neither resource is universally cheaper.

## PREPARE–SELECT–PREPARE-adjoint

The next native family is `prepare_select_prepare`, available under both `circuit_mapper` and `controlled_circuit_mapper`. Its accepted inputs are LCU containers or LCU-walk containers, not Pauli product formulas and not arbitrary subclasses with a promising name.

Let \(A\) denote PREPARE and \(S\) denote SELECT. The block circuit is

\[
B=A^\dagger S A.
\]

Chronologically it prepares the coefficient index, applies the indexed operation, then unprepares. It acts on the system **and** all the ancillary qubits needed by the coefficient loader. The Hamiltonian appears in a designated matrix block, rather than the complete circuit simply being \(H\), which is generally not unitary. Lesson 19 will explain why the normalization and selected block reproduce the desired operator.

The [PSP mapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_mapper/psp_mapper.py) constructs SELECT directly from the container’s control states, Pauli strings, and sign phases. Its `prepare` setting defaults to `AlgorithmRef("state_prep","dense_pure_state")`. It invokes the child on the container’s coefficient wavefunction, requires a Q# callable and a positive declared width, and ensures that width covers the SELECT index. A loader such as alias sampling can need more ancillary qubits than its index width, so the mapper uses the child’s actual declared width rather than just a logarithm of term count.

This path rejects a PREPARE circuit requesting a caller-owned phase-gradient suffix: the PSP mapper does not supply that sharing contract. Use a self-contained compatible loader. The special no-PREPARE branch uses a no-op with zero index width for an appropriate singleton operation. It is not free loading of a nontrivial distribution. Qiskit-only or otherwise noncomposable PREPARE circuits cannot be embedded merely because they belong to the same family.

[`Select.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/Select.qs) applies a Pauli word conditioned on an integer index and explicitly implements the sign phase of a negative coefficient. In the zero-index-qubit case it uses an identity rotation to retain a minus sign as global phase, so the sign survives a later outer control. This is a concrete example of why identity phases cannot always be optimized away.

The [`PrepSelPrep.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/PrepSelPrep.qs) controlled specialization runs PREPARE and its adjoint **unconditionally** and controls only SELECT. On control zero, \(A^\dagger A=I\); on control one, the desired block circuit remains. This is valid even though a naive “control every gate” construction would cost more. It relies on the stated inverse and workspace contracts.

For an LCU walk, the mapper then applies the reflection \(R=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I\) on the whole block-ancilla register and produces \(W=RB\). The reflection includes coefficient-loader workspace, not just SELECT’s index bits. Its Q# implementation has explicit global/sign corrections, and a controlled walk also controls the reflection. The [controlled PSP tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_controlled_psp_mapper.py) examine both the normalized Hamiltonian block and the expected walk phases.

The current [controlled PSP wrapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/controlled_circuit_mapper/controlled_psp_mapper.py) requires exactly one control at index 0. Its layout is fixed to control followed by system and block ancillas; it does not honor arbitrary inherited `target_indices` as a remapping facility. It repeats according to the top-level container power. Do not independently nest arbitrary powers in the wrapped block and assume they all multiply: these mappers rebuild their step from PREPARE/SELECT data. Use builder-produced consistent plans.

## SOSSA wiring is a separate contract

`circuit_mapper/sossa` accepts only `SOSSABlockEncodingContainer` with `power==1`. It produces the uncontrolled block \(B=U^\dagger\mathrm{Ref}_B U\), not a complete controlled quantum walk. No registered controlled mapper in this batch accepts that container. The current intended outer consumer is the unary phase-estimation builder, which supplies its own reflection schedule. Calling the ordinary `pauli_sequence` default on SOSSA data is an error, not an automatic fallback.

The [mapper settings](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_mapper/sossa_mapper.py) are `outer_prepare_algorithm=AlgorithmRef("state_prep","alias_sampling")`, `inner_prepare_algorithm="controlled_alias_sampling"`, `select_algorithm="qrom_phase_gradient"`, `rotation_bit_precision=10`, and `coefficient_bit_precision=10`. The inner alternative is `direct`; the SELECT alternative is `direct`. Precision settings expose 1–30 bits. These choices trade table loading, arithmetic, rotations, and scratch, not the active electron count.

The outer child is configured by available settings: the parent sets its alias precision and disables internal gradient allocation when the child offers those controls. This is an example of explicit parent override of nested settings, not a guarantee that a supplied child setting always wins. The child must return a Q# callable and declared width.

The mapper handles outer index/workspace, inner index/comparison pieces, sign and generator information, two spin-selection ancillas, and an optional trailing shared gradient. “Free-rider” data here means classical generator metadata loaded alongside the index, not costless chemistry. A reserved free-rider region without its table is rejected. If outer PREPARE and SELECT both use the shared gradient, their widths must agree.

The [Q# block implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/SOSSAWalk.qs) allocates some inner lookup/free-rider scratch internally and uncomputes it. The public declared width includes the system, retained outer/inner reflection registers, spin ancillas, and gradient suffix, but not all such scratch. The suffix is excluded from zero-register reflections because it holds the nonzero phase-gradient state. The callable advertises `Adj`; the standalone factory initializes its own gradient and resets registers at the end. That standalone exported program is not simply a pure unitary matrix on the callable’s argument register.

Existing [SOSSA tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit_mapper_sossa.py) cover algorithm combinations, signed/general-angle blocks, multiple ranks/copies, and declared/shared register sizes. Their full-block fixtures test more than matching a state up to global phase. None of those tests was executed here, and they are not physical device benchmarks.

## Circuit is a bundle of capabilities, not a universal conversion promise

[`Circuit`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/circuit.py) can hold OpenQASM text, QIR, a native QDK Q# circuit object, or Q# factory data, plus an optional composable `qsharp_op`. The constructor needs at least one of the first four representations. A callable alone is not sufficient. The `qsharp` parameter denotes a circuit representation object; it is not an arbitrary source-code string to be parsed automatically.

`QsharpFactoryData(program, parameter)` stores a callable entry point and its classical arguments. The implementation invokes `program` with `*parameter.values()`: **dictionary insertion order is positional argument order**. Key names are descriptive and do not provide keyword binding at that call boundary. Factory dictionaries must therefore be built in the exact signature order. The Pauli mapper’s descriptive dictionary names differing from the Q# parameter names work because their order agrees.

A composable operation acts on qubits supplied by its caller. A factory usually allocates a standalone register and applies the operation. For controlled factories that fresh control begins at zero; a separate experiment must prepare it appropriately to observe the enabled branch. A circuit diagram is yet another view. It does not replace the original callable or turn a diagnostic rendering into a composable state-preparation routine.

`num_qubits` is declared argument-register width when known. It is optional, and internal scratch is excluded. `CircuitMetadata.num_phase_gradient_ancillas` defaults to zero, must be nonnegative, requires a known width if nonzero, and cannot exceed it. The field states a sharing expectation; it neither initializes the gradient nor expresses a physical-qubit requirement. Constructor validation does not parse all supplied representations and prove their widths or semantics agree.

The object resists normal attribute reassignment, but lazy conversions cache internal artifacts. A cached Qiskit circuit is the same mutable object returned on subsequent calls; make a copy before modifying it for a separate experiment. “Immutable container” does not guarantee deep immutability of every returned third-party object.

## The exact conversion paths

`get_qir()` first returns existing QIR. Otherwise it compiles a Q# factory in its owning context and caches that result. With only QASM, it invokes the external OpenQASM compiler using `OutputSemantics.OpenQasm` and **TargetProfile.Base**; this fallback is not a request to use whatever adaptive profile happens to be active elsewhere. That QASM-only compilation result is not cached in the same branch.

`get_qasm()` returns stored QASM first. If none exists but QIR or a factory is available, it goes through QIR-to-Qiskit conversion and Qiskit’s OpenQASM 3 exporter. It requires the optional conversion dependencies and does not store the returned text as a new canonical source. A Q# circuit object by itself is not sufficient for that route.

`get_qsharp_circuit(prune_classical_qubits=False)` returns a stored native circuit object, otherwise asks the factory’s owning context for a circuit view, otherwise uses the external OpenQASM circuit converter. It has no direct QIR-only branch. Pruning applies to the factory-derived view; it is not a promise to delete those qubits from a semantically equivalent physical computation.

`get_qiskit_circuit()` returns its cached result if present, otherwise prefers QIR/factory over QASM. The QIR route uses the repository’s PyQIR-based converter; QASM-only uses Qiskit’s parser. It warns when classical bits appear under a non-Base active context, but that warning does not repair unsupported control flow. Supplying conflicting QASM and QIR can therefore make different getters return different programs. Consistency is a producer obligation, not a constructor theorem.

**QIR**, quantum intermediate representation, is an LLVM-based compiler interchange format: a low-level language for instructions, registers/results, and classical control flow.
