It is not a target device’s pulse schedule and does not choose an error-correcting code. A device/provider/compiler stack must implement the remaining lowering. Likewise OpenQASM is a program interchange language, not a guarantee that every importer understands every language feature.

Serialization currently stores QASM when present, QIR when available or factory-compilable, encoding, width, and shared-gradient metadata. It does not serialize the Python callable/factory as a reusable live closure. A reloaded QIR-only circuit may still be convertible to Qiskit or consumable by an appropriate QIR executor but no longer supplies the Q# operation needed by a native composition builder. A Q#-object-only circuit has no equivalent serialized executable path in these methods. Even content hashing of a factory can trigger compilation. “Inspect this object” is not always equivalent to a pure source read, which is why none of these operations was invoked during this authoring session.

## Contexts, profiles, and reversible composition

The repository’s [Q# context utilities](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/__init__.py) lazily create a shared context, defaulting to `Adaptive_RIF`. `create_qsharp_context` creates a fresh one; `set_qsharp_context` changes the process-wide choice, and `use_qsharp_context` temporarily overrides it on the current thread. Factory methods use the owning context attached to their program when present. Mixing callable objects from unrelated contexts is not a safe substitute for loading everything into one composition context.

A **target profile** states which program features the compiler may use. Base supports a more restricted circuit model; the repository loads a selected subset of its Q# utility files for it. That subset includes ordinary state preparation, Pauli/PSP circuits, and basic phase-estimation components, but excludes QROM/phase-gradient/SOSSA utility files. Choosing Base is therefore not a universal workaround for an adaptive conversion warning. The Base helper also stages a reduced source project internally; no context creation or staging was performed here.

An adjoint reverses a unitary action. Q# `Adj` and `Ctl` are capabilities in the operation type, not properties automatically attached to every `Circuit`. The ordinary `PauliExp` wrapper returns a plain `Qubit[] => Unit` operation in this source, even though its mathematical factors are unitary; use the dedicated controlled mapper for its supported controlled form. The generic sequential helper similarly returns a plain operation, whereas repeated/controlled composition helpers require `Adj + Ctl`. Binary and SOSSA routines advertise their narrower adjoint capability explicitly.

[`CircuitComposition.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/CircuitComposition.qs) offers sequential application, repetition, a controlled-operation adapter, conversion from a control-array interface to a single-control interface, and shared-ancilla initialization wrappers. Its repeated helper contains estimator caching markers. Those markers reuse analysis work; they do not remove repeated physical operations from the requested algorithm.

The `within { A } apply { B }` form means compute \(A\), apply \(B\), then uncompute \(A\). This is why loading a lookup word and later clearing it can preserve coherence without measurement of the chemical data. Where an implementation intentionally uses measurement-based uncomputation, classical feedback and a compatible profile become part of the circuit contract. Resetting arbitrary entangled workspace is not a substitute for uncomputation.

## Qiskit interoperability: useful, but not arbitrary QIR

The [QIR converter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/_interop/qir.py) reads entry-point attributes for required qubit/result counts, resolves indexed QIR qubit/result handles, and forwards supported gates into a Qiskit `QuantumCircuit`. Handlers include Pauli/H/S/T gates and adjoints, axis rotations, controlled Pauli gates, SWAP, two-qubit XX/YY/ZZ rotations, Toffoli, measurement, and reset. Angles are extracted as numerical constants and passed in the corresponding rotation convention, not arbitrary symbolic runtime expressions.

Its control-flow walker is important. It can preserve direct measurement-result-conditioned branches with supported immediate joins as Qiskit `if`/`if_else` blocks. It rejects loops, unsupported branch structure, branch conditions not directly reading a measurement result, and entry points without a body. Equivalent source programs can lower to different classical-expression forms, only some of which it recognizes. The [interop tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_interop_qiskit_qir.py) verify a guarded X remains conditional and explicitly test an unsupported condition. Do not infer universal adaptive-program support from one successful measured-AND conversion, or a blanket unsupported-instruction guarantee from a broad module docstring alone.

The [transpiler helpers](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/_interop/transpiler.py) merge Z-axis regions, replace special-angle rotations with Clifford/T gates or Pauli gates, and remove diagonal operations on qubits known to start at zero. Their settings and assumptions matter. For example, `SubstituteCliffordRz` recognizes numerical multiples of \(\pi/4\) with a default machine-epsilon comparison tolerance and skips symbolic parameter expressions. Its name includes T, which is not itself Clifford. Replacing \(R_z(\pi/2)\) by S is only equal up to a global phase unless that phase is accounted for; the direct replacement does not record a compensating phase. That can be harmless for standalone state preparation or a matched prepare/unprepare pair but is not a license to control the replacement as if its full unitary phase were identical. The zero-state-removal pass likewise is not valid for arbitrary unknown input.

The [circuit-analysis utilities](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/_interop/circuit.py) compute depth, gate counts, and heuristic idle/classical/quantum role labels. Their drawing helper can omit wires, measurements, and gates incident on filtered wires. That produces a simplified visualization, not a proof of equivalent evolution or a reduction in QEC resources. A register classified as classical for one initialization may be quantum in a different coherent use.

Noise conversion is separate again. The [noise adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/_interop/noise_model.py) builds Qiskit Aer depolarizing errors from a supplied error profile and gate arity; it explicitly rejects qubit-loss support in that adapter and unsupported gate/error types. A noiseless representation conversion neither supplies realistic calibration data nor validates a device model. We will treat execution/noise in the dedicated later lesson.

## How the enclosing algorithm uses the subroutines

The native [iterative phase-estimation builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/circuit_builder/iterative_builder.py) expects usable Q# operations for both trial-state preparation and controlled unitary. If they are absent, it raises rather than automatically using arbitrary QIR or a rendered circuit; a separate Qiskit builder serves that plugin route. Its compact control/system layout and width checks are part of the contract. A standalone subroutine factory is not already a complete phase-estimation experiment.

The [unary builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/circuit_builder/unary_phase_estimation_builder.py) instead takes an LCU walk or SOSSA block, obtains a unit-power block circuit, and owns a reflection/query schedule. It requires the mapper to declare width, removes shared-gradient bits from the reflected zero-ancilla count, checks agreement if the state and block both request gradients, and requires a nonempty reflection register. It initializes shared ancillas through a supplied operation rather than pretending metadata itself is a quantum action. Detailed query schedules and success probabilities remain for later chapters.

These builders demonstrate why chemical, encoding, callable, and width compatibility must all hold simultaneously. The unitary representations do not carry a complete automatic proof that an arbitrary input trial state has matching orbital identities or the same tapering sector. Most circuit mappers also do not propagate an encoding label into their returned `Circuit`. Retain the provenance explicitly; a missing label is not permission to pair unrelated states and operators.

## Two different resource-estimation consumers

`Circuit.estimate()` uses factory-derived logical counts and the external estimator, or an OpenQASM estimation path. It raises for a QIR-only or native-circuit-object-only instance. If a result reports a different logical width from the declared argument width, the method logs that difference; it does not rewrite the declaration to a physical-qubit number.

`Circuit.get_qre_application()` is an **alternative** adapter for the optional `qdk.qre` application interface. It chooses a Q# application for factory data, otherwise an OpenQASM application, otherwise a QIR application. That permits a QIR-only route the older `.estimate()` method does not support. It is not a mandatory second step after `.estimate()`. The [Circuit tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit.py) encode those different capabilities.

The external resource-estimation and quantum-error-correction teams supply later models of logical error budgets, gate synthesis, codes, factories, scheduling, and physical devices. At this layer, a circuit contains logical operations and allocation structure. A shorter logical circuit is promising input to that analysis, not an already established reduction in physical cost.

For our nitrogen workflow, the output of this lesson is therefore a carefully specified subroutine contract: which mathematical operation, on which register, with which angles, phases, workspace, representation, and supported consumers. We have not made the active-space approximation more accurate, and we have not run the algorithm. We have made the path from its mathematics to its circuits explicit enough that the next lessons can compare actual time-evolution and block-encoding methods without hiding the engineering between them.
lessons.caveats: No compilation/imports/tests/execution/files. Native Pauli angle convention and chronological ordering traced to Q# calls/tests; actual Exp decomposition external. Direct controlled-Pauli standalone allocation supports compact layouts but can fail accepted sparse high indices; controlled results omit declared width. CSWAP requires vacuum-preserving ordered blocks and phase correction. PSP controls SELECT only, rejects external gradients, controlled version fixes control0 and ignores inherited target remapping. SOSSA unit-power uncontrolled Adj-only block; unary consumer owns reflection, no generic controlled mapper. Circuit getters have differing priorities/dependencies/caches; factory dict argument order is positional; serialization loses live callable. QASM-to-QIR fallback fixedBase, current default contextAdaptive_RIF with limitedBase sources. QIR importer supports particular direct-result branch forms, not all adaptive/QIR programs. Some transpiler replacements are only equivalent up to global phase. get_qre_application and estimate are alternative consumers with different QIR-only capability. Pauli reorder_terms currently resets scale metadata.

lessons.title: Simulating time evolution
lessons.body:
# Lesson 18 — Simulating time evolution

## Turning energy into a phase

We still want the electronic physics of neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å, in the chemical model selected earlier. Its ordinary qubit Hamiltonian describes the active operator, with the nuclear/frozen-inactive core scalar retained separately. A trial-state preparation circuit supplies an initial state. What should happen next depends on the question: estimate an eigenenergy, or follow the evolution of an initial state.

For a time-independent Hermitian Hamiltonian, the evolution operator is

\[
U(t)=\exp(-iHt/\hbar).
\]

The reduced Planck constant \(\hbar\) converts energy times time into phase. The repository’s atomic-unit convention takes \(\hbar=1\), so its formulas use \(e^{-iHt}\). The parameter `time` is simulated physical time in the model’s units, not seconds of hardware wall-clock runtime. A longer simulated time can require more gates and tighter synthesis, but those are derived costs, not the value of `time` itself.

If \(H|E_k\rangle=E_k|E_k\rangle\), then \(U(t)|E_k\rangle=e^{-iE_kt}|E_k\rangle\). This is how energy becomes a phase. In a superposition of eigenstates, the relative phases change with their energy differences; that produces real dynamics. A controlled evolution makes an eigenphase observable relative to a control-zero branch, supplying the central ingredient for later phase estimation.

Adding \(E_{\mathrm{core}}I\) multiplies an uncontrolled evolution by \(e^{-iE_{\mathrm{core}}t}\). That global phase is unobservable in isolated state dynamics but becomes relative under control. The ordinary mapping route deliberately leaves the core scalar outside the Pauli operator, so its measured active energies require the corresponding classical addition once. Do not remove other identity terms without tracking their phases and then assume a controlled circuit is unchanged.

This lesson covers the actual fixed-Hamiltonian builders. Explicitly time-dependent Hamiltonians and propagators belong to the later dynamics lesson. No evolution, scientific calculation, circuit compilation, or test is being executed here.

## Why one exponential becomes many

Write the represented qubit Hamiltonian as

\[
H=\sum_{j=1}^{L}h_jP_j,
\]

where \(P_j\) is a Pauli word, \(h_j\) a real coefficient, and \(L\) the number of listed terms after the relevant screening. Since \(P_j^2=I\), one factor has the exact form

\[
e^{-i\theta P_j}=\cos\theta\,I-i\sin\theta\,P_j.
\]

Lesson 17 showed how basis changes, a parity network, a rotation by \(2\theta\), and uncomputation implement such a factor. The remaining problem is that the exponential of a sum is generally not the product of exponentials.

The **commutator** \([A,B]=AB-BA\) measures whether the order of two operations matters. Commuting operators have a common compatible action and can be exponentiated separately without this splitting error. Anticommuting Pauli words produce \([h_jP_j,h_kP_k]=2h_jh_kP_jP_k\), with norm \(2|h_jh_k|\). The complex phase in \(P_jP_k\) matters. The [Pauli commutator utility](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/pauli_commutation.py) uses the native accumulator for products and reverses its canonical labels into the QubitOperator string convention.

As a toy model, take \(H=X+Z\) on one qubit. Because \([X,Z]=-2iY\), X evolution followed by Z evolution is not exact combined evolution. The exact expression is

\[
U(t)=\cos(\sqrt2t)I-i\frac{\sin(\sqrt2t)}{\sqrt2}(X+Z).
\]

A first-order step instead executes X then Z, whose matrix is \(e^{-i\delta Z}e^{-i\delta X}\). Its short-time expansion contains a leading commutator contribution absent from the target. This is an analytic toy illustration, not a molecular or simulator result.

The distinction between chronology and written multiplication remains important: a list of gates is executed first-to-last, while matrices acting on a column state multiply rightmost-first. The builders return chronological `ExponentiatedPauliTerm` lists. Their `angle` already means the coefficient in \(e^{-i\theta P}\); the circuit mapper’s Q# call uses `Exp(paulis,-angle,systems)`.

## Trotter and Suzuki product formulas

Split total time into \(N\) slices of size \(\delta=t/N\). The first-order Lie–Trotter formula executes each term for \(\delta\) per slice. For two terms \(A\) and \(B\), chronological A then B gives

\[
U_1(t)=\left(e^{-i\delta B}e^{-i\delta A}\right)^N.
\]

The local error begins at order \(\delta^2\); repeated unitary slices give a leading total scale proportional to \(t^2/N\), with commutator-dependent constants. If all terms commute, the product is exact apart from numerical/synthesis errors and coefficient screening.

Second-order **Strang splitting** uses a palindrome: A for half a slice, B for a whole slice, A for half a slice. Its symmetry cancels the leading asymmetric error:

\[
U_2(t)=\left(e^{-i\delta A/2}e^{-i\delta B}e^{-i\delta A/2}\right)^N.
\]

For many groups it sweeps forward with half times, applies the last group at full time, and sweeps back. The leading local error is cubic, and the leading total scaling is \(|t|^3/N^2\). This does not mean “twice as accurate” for a fixed gate budget: one second-order slice contains more factors.

The native [`trotter` builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/time_evolution/trotter.py) supports order 1, order 2, and any positive even integer above 2, despite an older settings comment saying only first order. Higher orders use Suzuki recursion:

\[
S_{2k}(t)=S_{2k-2}(u_kt)^2
S_{2k-2}((1-4u_k)t)S_{2k-2}(u_kt)^2,
\qquad
u_k=\frac1{4-4^{1/(2k-1)}}.
\]

Here \(u_k\) sets the fractional time of each subformula. Some fractions are negative, meaning inverse-time substeps, not negative physical runtime. Each recursion multiplies the unmerged schedule length by roughly five. The implementation merges consecutive entries for the same group before expanding them into Pauli rotations. Higher order can save slices while increasing per-slice length and classical schedule construction.

The algorithm family is `hamiltonian_unitary_builder`, whose default is `trotter`. Relevant defaults are `time=0.0`, `order=1`, `num_divisions=0`, `target_accuracy=0.0`, `error_bound="commutator"`, and `weight_threshold=1e-12`. Zero time means identity evolution; it is not a sensible phase-to-energy decoding interval. A positive explicit division count is a floor; nonpositive values fall back to one slice when automatic selection is disabled. A positive target accuracy activates the selected step estimator, and the larger of manual and automatic counts wins. Nonpositive target accuracy disables automatic selection in the builder, although calling the error helper directly with a nonpositive accuracy raises.

All these builders require a Pauli-decomposition QubitOperator, not an SOS container. Trotter checks coefficient Hermiticity to its threshold, then uses real coefficients above that cutoff. The returned `PauliProductFormulaContainer` contains a single step list, `step_reps`, `num_qubits`, and `scale`. Constructing it neither simulates the state nor synthesizes the final gates.

## Grouping is a mathematical assumption, not just a label

The [shared time-evolution base](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/base.py) consumes an existing `FlatPartition` or `LayeredPartition`; without one, each listed Pauli term is its own group. It materializes subgroup operators, removes empty groups, and sorts outer groups by their number of subgroups. A flat partition therefore follows its stable group ordering, while a layered partition can be reordered by this rule.

Within each subgroup, the code emits separate Pauli exponentials through a helper named `_exponentiate_commuting`. That helper does not itself verify commutation. Exact subgroup exponentiation and the nominal Suzuki order require the intended compatible grouping assumptions. A manually attached partition containing noncommuting terms is not repaired or promoted into an exact group exponential. Layers are a scheduling structure, not proof that their combined group commutes.

Error helpers generally inspect the screened original term list rather than reconstructing and certifying every grouped schedule the builder may produce. Especially for order-dependent second-order constants or unusual layered groups, preserve and check the actual schedule instead of treating a partition strategy string as a proof of the requested order.

This also constrains the CSWAP controlled mapper from Lesson 17. Its computational vacuum must be preserved by the **ordered finite product**, not only by the unsplit chemical Hamiltonian. Randomizing or regrouping terms can destroy cancellation partners that made the shortcut valid.

## What the Trotter accuracy helpers actually compute

An **operator norm** measures the largest vector amplification of an operator; for a unitary difference it bounds worst-case state-vector error. A dimensionless target \(\epsilon\) for \(\|U-\widetilde U\|\) is not an energy tolerance in Hartree.

Define the screened coefficient absolute-sum \(\Lambda=\sum_j|h_j|\). The actual [`trotter_steps_naive`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/time_evolution/trotter_error.py) implementation, for order \(p\), returns at least one and otherwise the ceiling of

\[
2\Lambda^{1+1/p}|t|^{1+1/p}\epsilon^{-1/p}.
\]

For first order this is \(2\Lambda^2t^2/\epsilon\). Some older prose omits that factor two; source tests pin the implemented formula.

For first-order commutator selection, define

\[
C_1=\sum_{j<k}\|[h_jP_j,h_kP_k]\|.
\]

The code uses \(N=\max(1,\lceil C_1t^2/(2\epsilon)\rceil)\). For the standard first-order term splitting, the corresponding commutator estimate follows the familiar norm bound. It detects exact commutation and can therefore be much smaller than a coefficient-only estimate.

For second order, the utility explicitly sums surviving nested commutators:

\[
C_2=\sum_i\sum_{j,k>i}\|[H_k,[H_j,H_i]]\|
+\frac12\sum_i\sum_{j>i}\|[H_i,[H_i,H_j]]\|,
\quad H_i=h_iP_i,
\]

and chooses \(N=\max(1,\lceil\sqrt{C_2|t|^3/(12\epsilon)}\rceil)\). For higher supported even order \(p\), it sums all nonvanishing nested commutators of length \(p+1\), bounding each by \(2^p\prod|h_j|\), then uses the ceiling of \((C_p|t|^{p+1}/\epsilon)^{1/p}\).

The work needed for these estimates matters: the first-order sum is quadratic in term count, the second-order sum cubic, and the generic higher-order helper explicitly enumerates \(L^{p+1}\) index tuples. Choosing an advanced bound can itself dominate classical preprocessing. These are the code’s implemented planning formulas; an asymptotic higher-order theorem or a finite test set is not a universal certificate for every possible grouping, recursion length, threshold, and time. In particular, the helper does not track a full schedule-specific remainder for arbitrary hand-supplied partitions.

For the illustrative \(H=X+Z\), \(t=1\), and \(\epsilon=0.1\), the code formulas give \(\Lambda=2\), \(C_1=2\), and \(C_2=6\). Thus the first-order commutator and naive choices are 10 and 80 slices, and the second-order choices are 3 and 18. These are hand substitutions into the documented implementation formulas, not executed accuracy measurements. The [error tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_trotter_error.py) and [evolution tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_time_evolution_trotter.py) contain formula checks and small-matrix comparisons. A step count alone does not establish chemical accuracy.

Standalone bound helpers call real-coefficient accessors and should be given already validated Hermitian input. They are not substitutes for checking an arbitrary complex operator. Coefficient screening also means their target concerns a screened model, not every term originally present.

## Repeating a unitary versus rescaling its time

Shared settings `power=1` and `power_strategy="repeat"` determine how a requested power is represented. Under `repeat`, the builder constructs its approximation for time \(t\) once and multiplies its repetition count by the power \(m\). Under `rescale`, it constructs an approximation at time \(mt\) instead. These agree for exact evolution but need not agree for a finite approximation or random sampled schedule.

Automatic step selection under `repeat` is based on the base time, not an automatically tightened total-error budget for all \(m\) uses. If each base unitary differs by at most \(\epsilon_0\), telescoping gives a bound \(m\epsilon_0\) for repeated unitary uses. Long phase-estimation powers therefore matter. Under `rescale`, a positive target accuracy makes the helper see the longer time, potentially selecting many more divisions/samples.

The output `scale` is the effective time supplied to construction: base time for repeat, multiplied time for rescale. A raw phase from a powered circuit cannot be decoded by ignoring the power and modular phase branches. Likewise `reorder_terms` currently resets scale metadata, as noted in Lesson 17. Validate phase conversion alongside circuit schedules, not after an unexplained energy discrepancy. Use valid positive powers for these intended workflows; shared power resolution is not a comprehensive independent input validator.

## qDRIFT: importance sampling the terms

[`qdrift`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/time_evolution/qdrift.py) replaces a deterministic sweep by random draws. It samples term \(j\) with probability

\[
p_j=|h_j|/\Lambda
\]

and applies, for every draw, the factor

\[
\exp\!\left[-i\,\operatorname{sign}(h_j)\frac{\Lambda t}{N}P_j\right].
\]

Large coefficients are selected more often rather than assigned proportionally larger angles in each draw. Every sampled angle has the same magnitude, with the coefficient sign retained. Expanding one random step to first order shows its mean generator equals the desired Hamiltonian divided among the \(N\) steps. Finite random fluctuations and noncommuting higher-order terms remain.

Defaults are `num_samples=100`, `target_accuracy=0.0`, `error_bound="campbell"`, `weight_threshold=1e-12`, `seed=-1`, `merge_duplicate_terms=True`, and `commutation_type="general"`, plus the common time/power settings. A nonnegative seed initializes NumPy’s generator reproducibly; −1 uses nondeterministic initialization. The generator is recreated when building, not embedded as a quantum random sampler in the output. Executing the same constructed circuit repeatedly reuses that compiled sequence.

The [`qdrift_samples_campbell`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/time_evolution/qdrift_error.py) helper uses

\[
N\ge\left\lceil2\Lambda^2t^2/\epsilon\right\rceil.
\]

A positive target activates it; `num_samples` remains a manual floor and must be positive. The default floor of 100 can therefore dominate a smaller automatic result. Sampling and the norm calculation screen the same coefficient list. The sampling helper additionally returns an empty list when the remaining norm is below `1e-14`, a separate very-small-operator cutoff. Identity terms can participate in sampling too; their phases should not be dropped without considering control.

Duplicate fusion is exact **within the sampled unitary**: it collects consecutive mutually commuting runs and combines identical Pauli words by adding angles. Distinct commuting words remain separate, and it does not cross noncommuting boundaries. `commutation_type="qubit_wise"` is a stricter alternative to general Pauli commutation. This optimization changes the emitted rotation count, not the number of random draws used in the sample-count prescription.

The crucial qualification is the error metric. The Campbell prescription concerns the **averaged quantum channel**: average the density-matrix transformations \(\rho\mapsto U_\omega\rho U_\omega^\dagger\) over independently sampled random circuits \(\omega\). A channel describes how states and their probabilities evolve; its diamond-distance metric also considers inputs entangled with a reference system. A small error of that averaged channel is not the same claim as small coherent operator error for one fixed sampled circuit.

The [qDRIFT tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_time_evolution_qdrift.py) explicitly average channel representations over seeds and allow a finite-sampling tolerance. They do not assert every sampled circuit has operator error at most the requested epsilon. A single sample can fluctuate on a scale resembling \(\Lambda|t|/\sqrt N\), rather than the averaged-channel \(\Lambda^2t^2/N\) scale. Controlling and powering one fixed sample for QPE does not magically invoke the averaged-channel theorem. Energy phases, repeat/rescale choices, and randomness across circuit builds need a separately justified algorithmic analysis.

For \(H=X+Z\), the sampling probabilities are one-half each. With \(N\) draws, each angle is \(2t/N\); the particular count and order of X and Z draws vary. This toy example shows both why the mean generator is right and why an individual schedule is not exact. A fixed seed makes experiments reproducible, not scientifically exact.

## Partially randomized evolution: a heavy head and a light tail

[`partially_randomized`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/time_evolution/partially_randomized.py) divides the screened, magnitude-sorted terms into a deterministic head \(H_D\) and a random tail \(H_R\). Its `weight_threshold` has a different meaning from Trotter/qDRIFT: it is the **head/tail split**, not the removal tolerance. Terms at or above a nonnegative split threshold are deterministic. The separate `tolerance=1e-12` screens small terms away.

With default split value −1, the implementation chooses the top ten percent by integer term count, at least one. For a single surviving term, it remains deterministic. Any negative split value enters this automatic branch in the implementation. The default is not a chemical orbital threshold or a fraction of cumulative coefficient weight.

Other defaults are `trotter_order=2`, `num_random_samples=100`, `seed=-1`, `merge_duplicate_terms=True`, and `commutation_type="general"`. Only deterministic order 1 or 2 is supported. Unlike Trotter and qDRIFT, this settings class offers no `target_accuracy` auto-budgeting helper and no `num_divisions` time-slicing control.

Order 1 emits a full-time deterministic sweep followed by the tail samples. Order 2 emits a forward half-time deterministic sweep, the full-time randomized tail, and the reverse half-time deterministic sweep. Tail sampling uses \(\Lambda_R=\sum_{j\in R}|h_j|\), not the full norm. Existing term partitions are not consumed by this method; magnitude sorting and its own sequence construction determine the order.

For a toy \(H=X+0.1Z+0.05Y\), split threshold 0.5, time 0.2, and five tail draws, the second-order sequence begins and ends with an X factor of angle 0.1. The central random angles have magnitude \((0.1+0.05)0.2/5=0.006\). There are seven factors before any duplicate fusion. The [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_time_evolution_partially_randomized.py) check this head/tail structure and related norm/seed behavior; the numbers here are explanatory arithmetic.

This can be attractive when a few large terms dominate and a long tail has small total weight. But increasing tail samples does not remove the fixed deterministic splitting error of the outer sweep. Nor does a second-order outer palindrome turn one sampled tail into a deterministic second-order approximation with a universal operator-norm bound. The cited partially randomized phase-estimation research motivates the method; the current adapter does not implement a complete theorem-driven choice of split, time subdivisions, and full QPE error budget. Do not infer such a guarantee from a complexity formula in its docstring.

## Zassenhaus: correcting the noncommuting product

Zassenhaus takes a different route: begin with exponentials of the pieces, then add exponentials of commutators that correct the mismatch. For generators \(A\) and \(B\), a formal product is

\[
e^{t(A+B)}=e^{tA}e^{tB}e^{t^2C_2}e^{t^3C_3}\cdots,
\]

\[
C_2=-\tfrac12[A,B],\qquad
C_3=\tfrac16[A,[A,B]]+\tfrac13[B,[A,B]].
\]

“Nesting” means taking the commutator of an operator with an already formed commutator. These higher terms account for order-sensitive interactions between the pieces. For quantum evolution the primitive generators are \(-iH_j\); their factors of \(-i\) must be retained when converting a correction to a real Pauli rotation angle.

For the toy choice \(A=-iX\), \(B=-iZ\), the second correction is \(C_2=-iY\). The written product through that correction is \(e^{-itX}e^{-itZ}e^{-it^2Y}\). Its chronological circuit applies the Y correction first, then Z, then X. That is not the same chronological order as the first-order example earlier. The current [`zassenhaus` builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/time_evolution/zassenhaus.py) explicitly reverses its assembled factor list to preserve the required multiplication convention.

Default order is 2. Other defaults mirror Trotter’s time, power, division, accuracy, error-bound, and coefficient-threshold settings, with an additional `term_grouper=AlgorithmRef("term_grouper","commuting")` used when decomposing noncommuting correction exponents. Order 1 delegates to first-order Trotter. The current generic code accepts integer orders at least 2 through symbolic generation; it is not hard-capped at order 4 despite the older module summary. The inspected numerical convergence tests principally cover orders 2–4, while symbolic tests include degree 5. Higher acceptance is not a practical scaling or comprehensive validation guarantee. There is also no live automatic optimal-order search in the inspected execution path despite broad introductory prose suggesting one.

[`utils/zassenhaus_generation.py`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/zassenhaus_generation.py) is an in-memory symbolic generator, not a file-generation step we need to run. It uses exact rational `Fraction` coefficients, antisymmetry to canonicalize commutators, and a dependency-ordered directed acyclic graph of shared subexpressions. A DAG is a graph whose arrows have no cycles, so children can be evaluated before parents. An LRU cache of up to 128 symbolic plans reuses structures for the same leaves/order; coefficient- and time-dependent Pauli calculations are separate.

The builder evaluates nested commutators with Pauli arithmetic, skips ones whose constituent operators all commute, and caches repeated evaluations. For a degree-\(n\) correction it multiplies the symbolic coefficient by \(i(-i)^n\) to express the exponent as \(-i\) times a Hermitian Pauli operator, then uses time \(t^n\). If a correction itself contains noncommuting terms, it selects an internal order \(\lceil(p+1)/n\rceil-1\) for requested outer order \(p\), recursively decomposing where necessary. Merely listing its terms once would not always preserve the desired overall order.

A final optimization merges equal Pauli rotations only by moving past commuting neighbors, with a final angle cutoff `1e-15`. Correction screening at `weight_threshold` and this angle cutoff are additional numerical approximations. Nested commutators can create many new words and grow rapidly with order and group count; cached symbolic dependencies do not make the underlying Pauli expansion or subgroup combinations free.

## Zassenhaus error estimates are leading-remainder estimates

The [`zassenhaus_error` helpers](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/time_evolution/zassenhaus_error.py) inspect the first omitted exponent \(C_{p+1}\). The commutator-aware route combines its actual Pauli coefficients after cancellation and uses their absolute-sum as an upper bound \(\beta\) on that exponent’s norm. It selects

\[
N=\max\left(1,\left\lceil(\beta|t|^{p+1}/\epsilon)^{1/p}\right\rceil\right).
\]

The naive route replaces the nested operator norms by coefficient-norm estimates and a symbolic coefficient absolute-sum \(\kappa_{p+1}\), giving the analogous expression with \(\beta=\kappa_{p+1}2^p\Lambda^{p+1}\). A provided symbolic-plan dictionary must contain the omitted degree; otherwise it raises. The public helpers reject nonpositive accuracy or order and incompatible containers.

These formulas capture the **leading local omitted exponent** and its expected small-step scaling. They do not sum a rigorously bounded infinite remainder at arbitrary time, fully certify each internal correction split, or automatically account for a different grouped leaf decomposition in every use. A zero leading estimate can mean that leading term vanishes, not a generic proof that all higher terms and implementation truncations vanish. Treat the result as a source-defined planning estimate requiring convergence/error validation, not a universal all-orders chemical guarantee.

The [Zassenhaus tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_zassenhaus.py) verify symbolic coefficients, small-matrix convergence slopes near the expected order, optimizations, and particular model/molecular fixtures. Those tests support the implemented mechanism. We have read them, not rerun them or promoted their finite cases into an unrestricted theorem.

## Choosing a method and an error budget

| Builder | Concrete attraction | Principal obligation |
|---|---|---|
| `trotter` | Transparent deterministic term schedule; Suzuki orders available | Control slice error, schedule assumptions, and factor count |
| `qdrift` | Sample many-term Hamiltonians by coefficient importance | Distinguish averaged-channel bounds from one coherent compiled unitary |
| `partially_randomized` | Keep a dominant head deterministic and sample the tail | Budget both fixed splitting and random error; no automatic complete tolerance solver |
| `zassenhaus` | Explicit commutator corrections can improve small-step order | Pay classical/gate growth and validate leading-remainder estimates |

For a compact unexecuted use pattern:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create

builder = create(
    "hamiltonian_unitary_builder", "trotter",
    time=0.2, order=2,
    num_divisions=4, target_accuracy=1e-3,
    error_bound="commutator", weight_threshold=1e-12,
    power=1, power_strategy="repeat",
)
plan = builder.run(qubit_hamiltonian)
circuit = create("circuit_mapper", "pauli_sequence").run(plan)
```

Here `qubit_hamiltonian` must be the intended Hermitian Pauli operator in the same encoding as the trial state. Four is a manual minimum, not necessarily the final slice count. The numerical choices illustrate API semantics; they are not a recommended nitrogen production budget or an executed result.

Keep errors in compatible units. Chemical basis/active-space/DFT-versus-wavefunction choices concern the physical model. Integral factorization and Pauli screening change the represented Hamiltonian. If that change is bounded by \(\|\Delta H\|\), exact evolutions can differ by up to \(|t|\|\Delta H\|\). Product-formula and rotation-synthesis errors instead concern the implemented unitary. Trial-state infidelity and finite-shot statistical error are other contributions, not automatically covered by `target_accuracy`.

For normalized states, a unitary-error bound \(\epsilon\) bounds the resulting state-vector error; an observable expectation can then change by up to roughly \(2\|O\|\epsilon\). Phase-to-energy conversion additionally involves time, modular branches, and eigenstate identification. Do not add a dimensionless circuit epsilon directly to a Hartree chemical error or label a simulation norm bound an energy confidence interval.

A sensible engineering comparison holds the represented Hamiltonian, target state/sector, total algorithmic objective, and error metric fixed, then counts complete controlled operations, repeated state loading, scratch, and synthesis precision. The longest QPE powers can dominate that accounting. For random methods, specify whether randomness is frozen in one compiled unitary, redrawn across jobs, or part of a justified partially randomized protocol.

Time evolution is therefore a method with explicit contracts, not a single black-box “simulate” button. The next lesson studies another route to exposing Hamiltonian information: place a normalized operator inside a larger unitary and use quantum-walk phases rather than a direct approximate time exponential.
lessons.caveats: No imports/execution/tests/circuits or files. Trotter naive formula includes factor2 omitted by some prose; group helpers trust commutation and sort layered outer groups. Generic high-order bound enumerates L^(p+1) tuples; not a universal schedule certificate. Repeat power does not tighten base accuracy for all repetitions. QDrift Campbell epsilon is averaged-channel, not a fixed controlled-unitary guarantee; compiled sequence reused by repeats. Partially randomized has no target_accuracy/num_divisions controls and ignores term partitions; deterministic splitting error persists as tail sampling grows. Zassenhaus accepts generic orders>=2, tests chiefly2..4; no actual optimal-order search. Omitted-exponent norm is a leading-remainder estimate with separate screening/internal splitting limitations. Core scalar and scale/power phase bookkeeping remain separate.

lessons.title: Block encoding and quantum walks
lessons.body:
# Lesson 19 — Block encoding and quantum walks

## A Hamiltonian need not be exponentiated directly

The time-evolution builders in Lesson 18 approximate an exponential of a fixed Hamiltonian. They are not the only way to expose its eigenvalues to a quantum algorithm. Another route embeds a normalized Hamiltonian into a larger unitary, then builds a walk whose phases encode the Hamiltonian spectrum through a known nonlinear relation.

Our chemical target remains neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å in the selected active-space model. This new representation does not restore discarded virtual orbitals, replace cc-pVDZ with a complete basis, or correct a poor trial state. It changes the quantum algorithm used for the represented operator.

We will first derive ordinary Pauli LCU block encoding and its walk, then trace the repository’s factorized sum-of-squares route. The latter is concrete implemented functionality, but it has a specialized circuit and phase-estimation interface. It must not be mistaken for a generic controlled version of the ordinary LCU walk. No circuits, factorization, simulation, or resource estimates are executed in this lesson.

## What “a block of a unitary” means

An **ancilla** is a working register in addition to the system register describing the electronic state. Let \(B\) be a unitary on both. It block-encodes \(H/\alpha\) when

\[
(\langle0|_a\otimes I)B(|0\rangle_a\otimes I)=H/\alpha.
\]

Here \(|0\rangle_a\) means all the designated ancillas are zero, and \(\alpha>0\) is a normalization. A subblock of a unitary cannot have operator norm greater than one, so \(\alpha\ge\|H\|\) is necessary for this exact form. The complete unitary is not the Hamiltonian; it contains additional blocks needed to preserve norm and reversibility.

Applied to a normalized system state, it has the structure

\[
B|0\rangle_a|\psi\rangle
=|0\rangle_a H|\psi\rangle/\alpha+|\mathrm{outside}\rangle,
\]

where the second term is orthogonal to the all-zero ancilla subspace. If the ancillas were measured and only zero outcomes retained, the success probability would be \(\|H|\psi\rangle\|^2/\alpha^2\). The surviving system state would require normalization. Thus “implement a block encoding” does not mean deterministically apply the generally nonunitary \(H\) to every input.

A quantum-walk algorithm can instead use that larger unitary coherently, without measuring those ancillas after each application. Understanding this distinction prevents a mistaken postselection cost model and the equally mistaken claim that a unitary circuit directly outputs all Hamiltonian information.

## LCU: put coefficient magnitudes in PREPARE and signs in SELECT

Let

\[
H=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}h_jP_j,
\qquad \lambda=\sum_j|h_j|.
\]

For real coefficients, define signed unitaries \(V_j=\operatorname{sign}(h_j)P_j\). Pauli words are unitary and Hermitian. Since \(\|P_j\|=1\), the triangle inequality gives \(\|H\|\le\lambda\). The normalization can be larger than the actual operator norm, sometimes substantially.

PREPARE, denoted \(A\), loads

\[
A|0\rangle_a=\sum_j\sqrt{|h_j|/\lambda}\,|j\rangle_a.
\]

These are amplitudes, not probabilities. SELECT applies the signed Pauli word conditioned on the index:

\[
S=\sum_j|j\rangle\langle j|\otimes V_j.
\]

The complete block unitary is \(B=A^\dagger S A\). Projecting the ancillas onto zero on both sides gives

\[
\langle0|_a B|0\rangle_a
=\sum_j\frac{|h_j|}{\lambda}V_j
=H/\lambda.
\]

The two square-root amplitudes, from prepare and unprepare, multiply to the required magnitude. Negative signs must survive in SELECT. Omitting them would block-encode another Hamiltonian with all-positive coefficients.

For a hand-worked example, take \(H=0.6X-0.4Z\). Then \(\lambda=1\), PREPARE amplitudes are \(\sqrt{0.6}\) and \(\sqrt{0.4}\), and SELECT applies X on address zero and −Z on address one. For system \(|0\rangle\), the all-zero-ancilla branch is \(-0.4|0\rangle+0.6|1\rangle\), with probability \(0.16+0.36=0.52\) if measured. This is illustrative arithmetic, not a molecular or executed circuit result.

## The current LCU builder and its numerical boundaries

The registered method is `hamiltonian_unitary_builder/lcu`. Its [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/block_encoding/lcu.py) accepts a Pauli-decomposition QubitOperator and checks Hermiticity. Settings are `power=1`, `quantum_walk=False`, and `tolerance=1e-12`. Here tolerance is the minimum acceptable coefficient L1 norm, not a requested block-encoding error and not a universal per-term truncation setting.

The builder counts terms to choose an index width, constructs a one-bit-per-mode **synthetic** wavefunction for the PREPARE amplitudes, and constructs a `Select` object containing integer control states, Pauli labels, signs, and system/index dimensions. These synthetic modes are coefficient-address bits, not extra chemical orbitals. With `quantum_walk=False`, the result wraps an `LCUContainer`; with true, it wraps an `LCUWalkContainer` with `scale` set to the coefficient absolute-sum. Both still require a circuit mapper.

A zero coefficient norm is rejected by default. Non-Hermitian complex coefficients are rejected by the container’s Hermiticity check; allowed negligible imaginary components are not a general complex non-Hermitian block-encoding capability. Combining duplicate Pauli labels before building is useful: otherwise the list length and coefficient absolute-sum can be needlessly enlarged, even when terms cancel.

There is a concrete screening subtlety. The norm and initial term count use stored coefficients, whereas PREPARE/SELECT construction calls `get_real_coefficients()` with its own default `1e-12` per-term filter. Tiny filtered entries can therefore leave a normalization or address-width mismatch relative to the retained list. At a sufficiently small total scale, an accepted norm can coexist with an empty filtered list. For a precision-controlled workflow, combine and screen an explicitly chosen operator first, budget that change, and make the norm and retained term list consistent rather than assuming the LCU tolerance controls all screening.

For a singleton, the builder constructs a zero-mode PREPARE wavefunction. That represents zero necessary address bits, but the generic default dense loader has a minimum declared width of one; abstract minimum address size and actual mapped ancillary allocation are not always identical. The PSP mapper also contains a no-PREPARE branch, but do not infer it is automatically used for every singleton constructed by the current LCU builder.

The [LCU tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_block_encoding_lcu.py) check square-root amplitudes, signs, address widths, zero-norm rejection, serialization, and particular full-block actions. They are source evidence, not tests run here. The block builder does not know an ordinary molecular `core_energy`: its input is the qubit operator. The active energy from the standard molecular mapping still needs the separately retained scalar added once.

## PREPARE may have workspace, and that changes the circuit contract

A realistic PREPARE can act on index bits and workspace. Alias sampling, for example, prepares \(\sum_j\sqrt{p_j}|j\rangle|g_j\rangle\), with garbage correlated with the index. That does not prepare a clean molecular trial state, as Lesson 16 emphasized. It can nevertheless be a valid LCU PREPARE if SELECT acts on the correct index and PREPARE-adjoint acts on the **entire** register afterward. The zero-ancilla block then uses the marginal probabilities \(p_j\).

With finite alias precision, those probabilities become \(\widetilde p_j\), so the represented block changes accordingly. Exact cleanup and the right sign phases still matter. Correct marginal probabilities alone do not establish that an arbitrary state-preparation routine has a usable adjoint after SELECT has imprinted phases.

The [PSP mapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_mapper/psp_mapper.py), registered as `circuit_mapper/prepare_select_prepare`, builds these subroutines with a nested `prepare` AlgorithmRef, defaulting to `dense_pure_state`. It requires a Q# callable, a declared width covering the SELECT index, and no externally owned phase-gradient suffix. A self-contained QROM loader may be appropriate; a shared-gradient variant is explicitly rejected by this mapper. A QASM-only child is not automatically interchangeable with a composable Q# operation.

The mapped register is `[system | all PREPARE ancillas]`. Alias sampling can increase the second portion far beyond the address width. SELECT uses only the leading index portion, while unprepare and the walk reflection must account for the necessary workspace. The controlled PSP variant supports one control at position zero and controls only SELECT, leaving PREPARE/unprepare unconditional. Its Q# specialization makes the control-zero branch cancel to identity. The [controlled mapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/controlled_circuit_mapper/controlled_psp_mapper.py) does not provide arbitrary inherited target-index remapping.

QROM means a circuit for fixed classical lookup data, not a unit-cost physical QRAM promise. Alias comparisons, lookup words, signs, phase-gradient initialization where used, and uncomputation all contribute to the final resource count.

## Why a walk has two phases for one energy

For the ideal signed-Pauli SELECT, \(S=S^\dagger\) and \(S^2=I\). Therefore \(B=A^\dagger S A\) is also a Hermitian unitary. Define the reflection about the zero-ancilla subspace,

\[
R=2\Pi-I,\qquad \Pi=|0\rangle\langle0|_a\otimes I,
\]

and the walk \(W=RB\). A reflection leaves the specified subspace unchanged and negates its orthogonal complement. The repository’s [`PrepSelPrep.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/PrepSelPrep.qs) implements this order, including sign/global-phase corrections needed under outer control.

Let \(H|E\rangle=E|E\rangle\), put \(\mu=E/\lambda\), and define \(|a\rangle=|0\rangle_a|E\rangle\). For \(|\mu|<1\), there is a normalized orthogonal companion \(|b\rangle\) such that

\[
B|a\rangle=\mu|a\rangle+\sqrt{1-\mu^2}|b\rangle.
\]

Because \(B\) is a Hermitian involution, it acts within the two-dimensional span as

\[
B=\begin{pmatrix}\mu&\sqrt{1-\mu^2}\\\sqrt{1-\mu^2}&-\mu\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
W=\begin{pmatrix}\mu&\sqrt{1-\mu^2}\\-\sqrt{1-\mu^2}&\mu\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The walk eigenvalues are

\[
e^{\pm i\arccos(E/\lambda)}.
\]

This derivation explains the essential extra space. The raw unextended electronic eigenstate is not generally itself a single walk eigenstate. Even \(|0\rangle_a|E\rangle\) lies in an enlarged invariant subspace and typically decomposes into the two walk eigenphase branches. At the endpoints the companion construction degenerates appropriately. A notebook shorthand writing one walk phase directly on a raw chemical state must not replace this contract.

If phase estimation measures fraction \(\varphi\), the [LCU-walk container](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/unitary_representation/containers/quantum_walk.py) reconstructs

\[
E=\lambda\cos(2\pi\varphi).
\]

The two branches \(\varphi\) and \(1-\varphi\) give the same energy. This is not the linear \(-\mathrm{angle}/t\) decoder for time evolution. Powers introduce their own modular ambiguity and must be handled by the phase-estimation schedule, not ignored in a standalone decoder call.

An ideal block and walk can expose the spectrum without Trotter splitting error for the represented Hamiltonian. Integral truncation, coefficient screening, imperfect PREPARE probabilities, rotation synthesis, finite phase resolution, trial overlap, and physical noise remain. “No Trotter error” does not mean “exact chemistry” or “automatically lowest total cost.”

## From the factorized Hamiltonian to squares

The factorized route uses the matrices from Lesson 12 rather than expanding every contribution into a long Pauli sum. Use \(K\) active spatial orbitals, ranks \(R\), basis rows \(B_f\), and copies \(C_f\). We use subscripts on the last two symbols to avoid confusing the basis count with the block unitary \(B\).

For each rank/copy pair, define

\[
M^{rc}_{pq}=\sum_b w_b^{rc}u_{bp}^r u_{bq}^r,
\qquad
D_{rc}=\sum_{pq,\sigma}M^{rc}_{pq}a^\dagger_{p\sigma}a_{q\sigma}.
\]

Each real row \(u_b^r\) is unit normalized, but different rows need not be orthogonal in the general factorized container. The two-electron tensor is reconstructed as \(g_{pqrs}=\sum_{rc}M^{rc}_{pq}M^{rc}_{rs}\). In operator form, normal ordering introduces a one-body correction:

\[
H_{\mathrm{model}}=E_{\mathrm{core}}I+\widehat h_1
+\frac12\sum_{rc}\left(D_{rc}^2-\widehat{(M^{rc})^2}\right).
\]

A hat here means the corresponding spin-summed one-body operator. The subtraction follows from anticommuting annihilation and creation operators; squaring a one-body operator is not purely a two-electron interaction.

The container also carries identity weights \(w_B^{rc}\). They do not change the reconstructed integral tensor, but they change the square decomposition and its normalization. Put \(q_{rc}=w_B^{rc}-\operatorname{tr}M^{rc}\), and define

\[
F_{rc}=D_{rc}+q_{rc}I,
\]

\[
h_1^{\prime}=h_1-\frac12\sum_{rc}(M^{rc})^2
+\sum_{rc}\operatorname{tr}(M^{rc})M^{rc}
-\sum_{rc}w_B^{rc}M^{rc}.
\]

Completing the square gives \(\widehat h_1^{\prime}+\frac12\sum F_{rc}^2\), with the corresponding scalar subtraction. This is a representation identity before numerical truncation, not an effective Hamiltonian that removes more electrons.

Diagonalize the real symmetric \(h_1^{\prime}\). A positive eigenvalue \(v\) contributes \(v n\), expressible as \((\sqrt v\,a)^\dagger(\sqrt v\,a)\). A negative eigenvalue \(-v\), with \(v>0\), can instead be written \(v(1-n)-v\), using a hole generator \(\sqrt v\,a^\dagger\). **Hole** here means absence of occupation in that rotated mode. There are two spin channels, hence two copies of the negative-mode scalar subtraction.

With these explicit generator definitions, the positive shifted operator is

\[
H_{\mathrm{gap}}=\sum_{r,\sigma}O_{r\sigma}^\dagger O_{r\sigma}
+\frac12\sum_{rc}F_{rc}^2,
\qquad H_{\mathrm{model}}=H_{\mathrm{gap}}+E_sI,
\]

\[
E_s=E_{\mathrm{core}}-2\sum_{v_r<0}|v_r|
-\frac12\sum_{rc}\left(w_B^{rc}-\sum_b w_b^{rc}\right)^2.
\]

The factor one-half on the spin-free squares belongs to these definitions. Alternatively one can absorb it into a generator \(F_{rc}/\sqrt2\). Omitting it while retaining the same stored weights changes the Hamiltonian. The independent matrix constructions in the [SOSSA tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_phase_estimation_sossa.py) and [full-block tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit_mapper_sossa.py) make this normalization concrete.

## The actual sum-of-squares data and mapper

The current class is [`SumOfSquaresContainer`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/qubit_operator/containers/sum_of_squares.py), wrapped in `QubitOperator`, not an assumed additional `SumOfSquaresOperatorContainer` API. It stores `RotatedPaulis` blocks containing rotation-angle rows, complex coefficient rows, and small Pauli label sets, plus dimensions and `energy_shift` metadata. `.to_matrix()` deliberately raises `NotImplementedError`; an ordinary Pauli representation must be rebuilt for a small direct matrix reference.

The registered [`qubit_mapper/sum_of_squares`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/qubit_mapper/sum_of_squares.py) requires a `FactorizedHamiltonianContainer`, matching \(2K\) modes, and untapered Jordan–Wigner mapping. Its validation checks the mapping name/count/tapering rather than proving an arbitrary custom table is canonical JW; use the factory mapping.

Its `threshold=1e-12` screens eigenvalues of \(h_1^{\prime}\), not final Pauli coefficients. Screened modes retain their outer-register slots with zero amplitude. Positive and screened slots precede negative slots. Negative tolerance and NaN are rejected; valid numerical data and a physically appropriate factorization remain prerequisites.

The one-body coefficient rows are \(\sqrt{|v|}(1,\pm i)/2\), weighting X and Y in the rotated frame. The plus sign describes a particle annihilation generator and the minus sign a hole creation generator. For the spin-free term,

\[
F_{rc}=w_B^{rc}I-\frac12\sum_{b,\sigma}w_b^{rc}\widetilde Z_{b\sigma}^{r}.
\]

The stored two-body coefficient row is therefore the **negative** basis weights followed by the identity weight. Coherent spin selection supplies the explicit half in that expression. The mapper’s `energy_shift` includes the original core scalar. Do not add `core_energy` again after a decoder that already adds this shift.

Rotation rows encode unit vectors through \(K-1\) neighboring **Givens rotations**, two-coordinate rotations that successively eliminate vector components. The Python routine works from the bottom using `arctan2` and a hypotenuse update, preserving signs and quadrants. These rotations describe which orbital combination the simple X/Y/Z generator acts on; they are not a list of independently sampled physical orbitals.

The direct source-backed input route is native double factorization from Lesson 12, whose output has basis count \(B_f=K\), copies \(C_f=1\), and zero identity weights. General factorized containers with other dimensions can also feed this route when their data satisfies the contract, but there is no separately registered general nonlinear DFTHC fitting optimizer in the repository. Factorization can be truncated; its model error must still be accounted for. Abstract effective-Hamiltonian/downfolding interfaces from Lesson 11 do not supply a missing concrete preprocessing method here.

## SOSSA’s normalization and amplitude tables

The registered `hamiltonian_unitary_builder/sossa` means **Sum of Squares Spectral Amplification**, as stated in the [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hamiltonian_unitary_builder/block_encoding/sossa.py). It requires a sum-of-squares container labelled blocked Jordan–Wigner. It validates the fixed one-body slot count and X/Y particle/hole relation, real Z/identity spin-free coefficients, their dimensions, and positive finite normalization.

There are \(X_o=K+RC_f\) outer generator slots. In the actual code, a one-body coefficient row has absolute-sum \(\sqrt{|v_r|}\), and the builder’s outer weight is \(c_r=\sqrt{2|v_r|}\), including the two-spin factor. A spin-free outer weight is

\[
c_{rc}=\frac{|w_B^{rc}|+\sum_b|w_b^{rc}|}{\sqrt2}.
\]

The outer PREPARE amplitudes are \(c_x/\sqrt{2\Lambda}\), where

\[
\Lambda=\frac12\sum_x c_x^2
=\sum_r|v_r|+\frac14\sum_{rc}\left(|w_B^{rc}|+\sum_b|w_b^{rc}|\right)^2.
\]

This matches the factorized normalization convention of Lesson 12 for the retained data, not necessarily the ordinary Pauli coefficient norm \(\lambda\). A docstring formula that omits the explicit two-spin factor must not override the implemented outer-weight calculation and its tests.

The inner table has shape `[K + R*C_f, B_f + 1]`. One-body slots use a delta at inner index zero. Spin-free rows contain `sign(weight)*sqrt(abs(weight))` for the stored negative-Z and identity weights. Inner PREPARE squares/normalizes magnitudes; SELECT reads the sign separately. Zero rows receive a harmless fallback entry because their outer amplitude is zero, not because a new generator was inserted into the Hamiltonian.

One-body angles have shape `[K,K-1]`; the operator’s spin-free angles have shape `[R*B_f,K-1]`. The builder repacks SELECT angles to `[R*(B_f+1),K-1]` in basis-major/rank-minor address order, padding the identity basis with zero rotations. “Free-rider” bits record generator type and rank alongside an index. Their table is required when the layout reserves them. Structural dimensions affect actual lookup widths, not just printed summaries. The [builder tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_block_encoding_sossa.py) check weights, slots, sign relations, and missing-table failures.

## The specialized circuit and its walk spectrum

The SOSSA circuit mapper returns a Hermitian, self-inverse block operation whose selected block is

\[
A_{\mathrm{signal}}=H_{\mathrm{gap}}/\Lambda-I.
\]

For an energy \(E\), its signal eigenvalue is \(\mu=(E-E_s)/\Lambda-1\), in the interval [−1,1] for the valid ideal represented construction. An outer reflection completes the associated walk, with paired phases

\[
e^{\pm i\arccos((E-E_s)/\Lambda-1)}.
\]

The [`SOSSABlockEncodingContainer.eigenvalue_from_phase`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/unitary_representation/containers/sossa.py) consequently uses

\[
E=2\Lambda\cos^2(\pi\varphi)+E_s
=\Lambda(1+\cos(2\pi\varphi))+E_s.
\]

This is neither the ordinary LCU decoder nor a time-evolution decoder. It describes the phase of the **completed walk**, not an arbitrary eigenphase of the standalone block. Both paired branches give the same energy. The shifted energy window is \(0\le E-E_s\le2\Lambda\).

The optional builder settings `reference_ground_state_energy` and `reference_energy_gap` both default to NaN, meaning unset, and are mutually exclusive. The first is a total model energy including core; the second is the distance \(E_{\mathrm{gap}}=E_{\mathrm{gs}}-E_s\). This “gap” is not the excitation gap between ground and first excited states.

They supply an optional effective normalization

\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{gap}}(2\Lambda-E_{\mathrm{gap}})}.
\]

It reflects the local phase-to-energy sensitivity: \(|dE/d\theta|=\Lambda|\sin\theta|\) at that reference energy. It is useful for algorithmic precision/resource planning, not an extra measured energy. The code requires the supplied reference gap strictly inside \((0,2\Lambda)\); endpoints, out-of-window inputs, and supplying both settings raise. Without a reference, block construction is still possible, but accessing `lambda_eff` raises. The phase decoder itself uses \(\Lambda\) and \(E_s\), not a fabricated default for the missing reference. A classically affordable estimate can be supplied with its uncertainty; exact prior knowledge of an intractable ground state is not presumed.

## A small square-completion check

Take a one-spatial-orbital toy with one-body integral −0.3, Coulomb integral 0.8, zero core scalar, one normalized basis vector, weight \(w=\sqrt{0.8}\), and identity weight zero. Normal ordering gives \(h_1^{\prime}=0.1\). With \(n=n_\alpha+n_\beta\),

\[
H_{\mathrm{gap}}=0.1n+\frac{0.8}{2}(n-1)^2,
\qquad E_s=-0.4.
\]

Empty, singly occupied, and doubly occupied active states therefore have shifted energies 0.4, 0.1, and 0.6; adding the shift gives 0, −0.3, and 0.2, which agrees with \(-0.3n+0.8n_\alpha n_\beta\). The normalization is \(\Lambda=0.1+0.8/4=0.3\), so the signal eigenvalue of a singly occupied state is \(0.1/0.3-1=-2/3\). Substituting its walk phase into the SOSSA decoder returns −0.3.

This is hand arithmetic demonstrating factors and shifts. It is not nitrogen, not a run of the factorizer, and not an execution of the SOSSA circuit. It shows why losing either the one-half in the square or the scalar shift would produce a scientifically different answer.

## Where the generator cost is paid

The [SOSSA circuit mapper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_mapper/sossa_mapper.py) defaults to outer alias sampling, inner conditional alias sampling, and QROM/phase-gradient SELECT, with coefficient and rotation precision both 10 bits. Inner `direct` and SELECT `direct` alternatives are available. The parent sets applicable child alias precision and external-gradient ownership; nested settings do not universally override parent decisions.

SELECT computes spin-selection flags, conditionally swaps spin blocks, rotates the selected orbital combination toward a designated mode, applies the simple Majorana-derived action, and uncomputes the rotation/spin selection. In the direct [Q# path](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/SOSSAWalk.qs), a neighboring Givens step uses a CNOT sandwich around a neighbor-controlled \(R_y(2\theta)\). It acts in the one-excitation subspace and leaves zero/double occupation unchanged. Rotating every orbital as an independent one-qubit gate would not have that number-preserving action.

The phase-gradient path loads angle words and implements the same neighboring action using arithmetic. Its Givens angle quantization uses \(x=\operatorname{Round}(2^b\theta/(4\pi))\) modulo \(2^b\), because its decomposition needs uncontrolled half-angle rotations; this differs from the probability-tree QROM loader’s angle convention in Lesson 16. Negative modular values are handled explicitly. The routine checks finite/range-compatible angles, and branch-specific measurement erasure requires the matching phase correction for what was actually loaded.

[`SelectSwap.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/SelectSwap.qs) trades selection size against swap-network scratch, and can use measurement-based erasure with phase fixups. It also chooses whether free-rider data should be loaded separately or carried in repeated inner lookups using its logical cost model. This is real scheduling/lookup logic, not evidence that every selected option minimizes complete hardware cost.

[`UnaryIteration.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/UnaryIteration.qs) constructs one address indicator at a time using reversible AND recursion rather than allocating a permanent one-hot flag for every table entry. For non-power-of-two tables, unused address states can route to valid subtrees; the classical erasure mirror deliberately reproduces that routing. Padding and phase fixups are part of the coherent implementation, not irrelevant indexing details.

The circuit remains an **uncontrolled, Adj-only, unit-power block**. `circuit_mapper/sossa` rejects other powers. The current unary QPE builder owns the outer reflection and query schedule; ordinary iterative/standard controlled mappers do not accept SOSSA as a generic controlled walk. Full unary scheduling belongs to Lesson 21.

Its declared register includes the system, retained outer/inner reflection registers, two spin ancillas, and a shared phase-gradient suffix where needed. Additional inner lookup/free-rider scratch is allocated internally. The gradient must be initialized by the composing caller and excluded from zero-ancilla reflections. The standalone factory instead initializes its own gradient and resets outputs for cleanup. Neither structural container width nor callable argument width equals a physical-qubit estimate.

Independent full-block tests explicitly convert their interleaved classical matrix basis into the Q# blocked convention, including the fermionic permutation sign, not just reversing a bitstring. This validates the target operator across that stated basis change. It does not prove that an arbitrary trial state with a matching text encoding label is aligned automatically. Retain the orbital, mode-order, and phase conventions from Lessons 14–17.

## Comparing the two routes fairly

Ordinary Pauli LCU needs the signed coefficient list, its norm \(\lambda\), the index distribution, and a valid PREPARE/SELECT circuit. Factorized SOSSA needs \(h_1^{\prime}\), ranks/bases/copies, signed generator weights, rotations, \(\Lambda\), the scalar shift, and optional reference data for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\). A smaller factor count can reduce lookup structure without guaranteeing a smaller normalization or cheaper complete circuit. A smaller normalization can help phase resolution while still requiring expensive generators.

For an unexecuted ordinary route:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef

walk_plan = create(
    "hamiltonian_unitary_builder", "lcu", quantum_walk=True, power=1
).run(qubit_hamiltonian)
walk_circuit = create(
    "circuit_mapper", "prepare_select_prepare",
    prepare=AlgorithmRef("state_prep", "dense_pure_state"),
).run(walk_plan)
```

For the specialized route, assuming `factorized_hamiltonian` is already the intended real factorized active model:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data import MajoranaMapping

k = factorized_hamiltonian.get_one_body_integrals()[0].shape[0]
mapping = MajoranaMapping.jordan_wigner(2 * k)
sos_operator = create("qubit_mapper", "sum_of_squares").run(factorized_hamiltonian, mapping)
sos_plan = create("hamiltonian_unitary_builder", "sossa", power=1).run(sos_operator)
sos_block = create("circuit_mapper", "sossa").run(sos_plan)
```

The second result is a block, not a ready interchangeable controlled phase-estimation circuit. Neither snippet supplies a chemistry trial state or a complete workload. Optional QDK runtime/arithmetic and later resource-estimation/QEC models are external contributions; their internals were not reviewed or run here.

A fair comparison keeps the same chemical model, target sector, desired energy uncertainty, and state-preparation assumptions, then includes coefficient/factor preparation, all lookup and rotation precision, control/reflection requirements, repeated uses, and final readout. Bare Pauli LCU needs the ordinary core scalar added separately; SOSSA’s decoder already includes it through \(E_s\). Do not compare differently shifted energies or differently truncated Hamiltonians and call the difference a quantum algorithm improvement.

We now have two ways to turn Hamiltonian information into coherent operations. Before deriving complete phase-estimation protocols, we next examine the simpler measurement task: estimating the expectation of an observable on a prepared trial state, including exactly what finite shots and term grouping do to the reported uncertainty.
lessons.caveats: No execution/imports/factorization/circuits/tests/files. LCU stored norm/count and get_real_coefficients per-term screening differ; tolerance is minimum L1, not total-error control. Singleton abstract zero address bits can still map through minimum-one-bit dense loader. Alias garbage is valid only with complete PREPARE/adjoint block contract. Walk phases occur in enlarged invariant subspaces, not on raw unextended electronic states. SOS squares use one-half SF square with explicit F definition; outer one-body weights include sqrt2 spin factor. SOS energy_shift includes core; decoder returns total model energy. SOSSA blockedJW only, unit-power uncontrolled Adj-only block, unary owns reflection. General nonlinear DFTHC fitting optimizer absent; factorization/threshold errors remain. lambda_eff optional reference-derived distance-to-shift quantity, not excitation gap or measured value. Basis permutation signs appear in independent full-block tests.

lessons.title: Measuring energies and other quantities
lessons.body:
# Lesson 20 — Measuring energies and other quantities

## An expectation value is not automatically an eigenvalue

We can now prepare a trial state and construct circuits associated with a Hamiltonian. Before building a full phase-estimation experiment, there is a more direct task: estimate the expectation value of an observable on that state.

An **observable** is represented by a Hermitian operator. Its eigenvalues are possible ideal measurement outcomes, while its expectation is their probability-weighted mean. For state \(|\psi\rangle\), the energy expectation is

\[
\langle H\rangle_\psi=\langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle.
\]

If \(|\psi\rangle\) is an energy eigenstate, this equals its eigenvalue. Otherwise it averages different eigenenergies. A successful measurement of a sparse trial state therefore validates the prepared state’s energy expectation, not a claim that the full CASCI ground energy has been obtained.

Our continuing target remains neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å. Its selected six-electron, six-spatial-orbital model is distinct from the original 28-orbital cc-pVDZ model and from other notebooks’ geometries. The ordinary mapped operator contains active terms; the core scalar stays outside it. Those modeling choices do not disappear when measurement begins.

The current registered expectation-estimator implementation is `expectation_estimator/qdk`. It uses explicit measurement circuits, a configurable circuit executor, and classical processing of counts. We inspect those implementations and tests here without running any simulation, measurement, or scientific workflow.

## Why measuring occupation bits once is insufficient

A computational-basis measurement reports occupation bits in the Jordan–Wigner interpretation. For a qubit, outcome bit zero means Z eigenvalue +1 and bit one means −1. Consequently the number operator \(n=(I-Z)/2\) has the expected empty/occupied outcomes. This interpretation must be transformed for parity/BK encodings; bit count is not universally electron count.

A general mapped Hamiltonian is

\[
H_q=\sum_j h_jP_j.
\]

Its Pauli words can contain X and Y as well as Z. A Z-basis occupation measurement does not reveal the X/Y coherence needed for all of those expectations. Nor does one shot reveal an expectation value: it samples one random outcome according to the **Born rule**, whose probabilities are squared amplitudes in the chosen measurement basis.

A **shot** means preparing the same intended state again and performing the selected measurement experiment. Repeated shots approximate the corresponding probability distribution. They do not read out the entire quantum state, and the measurement generally disturbs the state rather than leaving an unknown trial state available for free reuse.

For a Pauli word, the eigenvalue is ±1. Measure each nonidentity position in its indicated basis and multiply the single-qubit ±1 outcomes. Equivalently, for the recorded bits belonging to the word, return \((-1)^{\text{number of ones}}\). Identity positions contribute +1 and need not be measured.

For X, a Hadamard before Z measurement implements the X basis. For Y, apply \(S^\dagger\) **then** H before Z measurement. If that basis-change matrix is \(B=HS^\dagger\), then \(B^\dagger ZB=Y\). Reversing that order or using S instead of its adjoint changes the observable or its sign. The Qiskit fallback in the [estimator implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/expectation_estimator/qdk.py) uses exactly `sdg` then `h` for Y.

The native Q# [`MeasurementBasis.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/MeasurementBasis.qs) instead calls external `MResetX`, `MResetY`, or `MResetZ`. Identity positions are reset without appending a result. These primitives and the runtime are external QDK contributions; the repository wrapper is what we have reviewed.

## Bitstrings, masks, and omitted identity positions

QubitOperator Pauli labels place qubit 0 on the right. Measurement results contain only measured positions, compressed into a smaller register. The estimator reconstructs a mask for each term on those compressed positions; it does not directly interpret every returned bit position as the original qubit index.

For example, a group basis `XIZ` measures qubit 2 in X and qubit 0 in Z, leaving qubit 1 unmeasured. The result has two bits. The mask for `IIZ` uses the compressed bit corresponding to qubit 0; the mask for `XII` uses the one corresponding to qubit 2. A three-character Pauli label and a two-character result string are therefore consistent, not a missing-data error.

The code sorts measured qubit indices, assigns contiguous mask positions, parses binary strings or strings beginning with `0x` as hexadecimal integers, and obtains each term’s sign from mask-and-outcome parity. It normalizes by the sum of the returned count frequencies. Unsupported formats and an empty total count raise. Its [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_expectation_estimator.py) explicitly check compressed masks, binary/hex formats, X/Y basis construction, and zero-count failures.

A returned histogram is still only data about one measurement basis. It does not contain the original complex amplitudes. Relative phase is learned indirectly through appropriately chosen basis measurements, not extracted as an extra column next to every occupation string.

## Grouping measurements: two meanings of “commuting”

If two Pauli words are **qubit-wise commuting**, then at every position their nonidentity letters agree. Identity can coexist with any letter.
