Such words share a basis made only from independent one-qubit basis changes. For example, `IZ` and `XZ` share the basis `XZ` and can be estimated from the same shots.

**Global commutation** is less restrictive. XX and YY commute because they anticommute at two positions and the two signs cancel. But one local basis cannot simultaneously be X and Y on either qubit. Their common eigenbasis requires an entangling transformation, such as a suitable Bell-basis circuit, rather than just independent H/S gates.

This distinction is decisive in the current software. The expectation estimator supports one local Pauli basis per measured group. It does not provide a general joint-diagonalization circuit for arbitrary globally commuting groups. Attaching a global-commuting partition therefore does not automatically produce a measurement saving.

The [`term_grouper` family](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/term_grouper/base.py) returns a **new** QubitOperator with partition metadata; it does not mutate the input or execute measurements. It rejects non-Pauli representations. Its default is `commuting`, which is useful for evolution but is not the universally safe default for this measurement estimator. Choose `qubit_wise_commuting` explicitly for a local-basis measurement workflow.

The actual bundled strategies are `commuting`, `qubit_wise_commuting`, `identity`, and `vacuum_annihilating`. The optional NetworkX plugin adds `nx_commuting` and `nx_qubit_wise_commuting`. These names denote different grouping methods, not six expectation-estimation algorithms.

## How the graph-coloring methods group terms

The native [commuting groupers](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/term_grouper/commuting.py) build a **noncommutation graph**. Each vertex is a Pauli term, and an edge joins a pair that cannot share the requested kind of group. A graph coloring assigns different colors to connected vertices; terms with the same color form a valid group.

The native algorithm visits terms in input order and puts each into the first existing group with no conflicts, or opens a new group. This greedy first-fit rule is deterministic for a fixed ordered input, but it need not minimize the number of groups. It compares pairs, costing roughly quadratic term-count work and potentially quadratic graph storage, with Pauli-label comparisons adding a width factor.

The [NetworkX variants](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/networkx/term_grouper.py) call external greedy DSATUR coloring. DSATUR selects according to saturation degree, the number of distinct colors already present among neighbors. It can improve a grouping but remains a heuristic, not a proof of minimum colors, minimum variance, or minimum hardware runtime. The [conditional plugin loader](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/networkx/__init__.py) registers those variants only when its dependency is available; no installation or availability test is being performed here.

`commuting` and `nx_commuting` use global Pauli commutation. Their qubit-wise counterparts use the stricter local criterion. None of those graph-coloring decisions uses the prepared state’s covariance matrix or an optimal shot-allocation calculation. A group count is a useful structural metric, not a complete statistical cost estimate.

The [`identity` grouper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/term_grouper/identity.py) means the identity **transformation of the grouping problem**: it puts every term into its own singleton group. It does not select only Pauli-I terms, replace the Hamiltonian by identity, or remove small coefficients.

## Vacuum-annihilating groups are for a different purpose

The [`vacuum_annihilating` grouper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/term_grouper/vacuum_annihilating.py) has `tolerance=1e-9`. It groups terms by the positions they flip and by the parity of their Y count. Acting on the all-zero computational state, a term contributes

\[
h_jP_j|0\cdots0\rangle=h_j i^{n_Y}|b_F\rangle,
\]

where \(F\) is its X/Y support. Only terms reaching the same bitstring can cancel. Separating even/odd Y parity makes the grouped terms mutually commuting and separates real from imaginary vacuum amplitudes for real coefficients.

The implementation requires finite real coefficients and finite nonnegative tolerance. It first checks each bucket’s total cancellation, then cuts it at exactly zero running sums rather than approximate prefixes that could strand an uncancelled remainder. Diagonal I/Z terms form an unconstrained phase group. It retains every term and returns a partition; it does not subtract their expectation values from a general chemical trial state.

Its main use is preserving the all-zero **workspace** eigenstate in the CSWAP control construction, not measuring the nitrogen trial state, which has six active electrons and is not computational vacuum. XX and YY can be in one such group but are not qubit-wise commuting; this expectation estimator will not jointly measure them with local basis changes. The [partition tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_term_partition.py) verify these distinctions, cancellation rules, invalid coefficients/tolerances, and input preservation.

If an expectation is exactly known for a specifically prepared state, it can in principle be added classically. An identity coefficient is the simplest state-independent example. A vacuum-annihilating sum has zero expectation on the vacuum, not on every state. Deleting it from an operator because of one reference state is not an operator identity, and changing the state, noise model, or observable can invalidate that shortcut.

## Partition metadata and actual estimator support

[`FlatPartition`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/term_partition.py) stores groups of integer indices into a QubitOperator’s Pauli list. `LayeredPartition` stores group → layer → term indices for hierarchical scheduling. `strategy` is a descriptive string; it is not a proof that the terms have the named property. The QubitOperator constructor checks coverage of its terms exactly once, but it does not derive commutation from a label. Use nonempty valid groups; an empty group can otherwise become an invalid empty operator when materialized.

The current estimator consumes **FlatPartition** groups as measurement groups and verifies local-basis compatibility when constructing each basis. It does not whitelist strategy names: a globally labelled group that happens to be QWC can work, while a group containing XX and YY raises. It does not automatically recolor or split that invalid flat group. An unsupported partition subtype, including LayeredPartition, is ignored and the estimator falls back to measuring each term individually.

With no partition, it also measures each term individually. Attaching a partition is therefore a real control over circuit generation, not cosmetic metadata. A partition optimized for evolution need not be suitable for measurement.

Groupers preserve the operator coefficients, label ordering, encoding string, and fermion-mode-order field. However, the current commuting, identity, and NetworkX constructors omit an existing tapering specification when constructing their output, whereas the vacuum-annihilating grouper explicitly carries it. Keep the original sector/tapering provenance rather than assume every new object copies all metadata. The represented Pauli arrays may be unchanged while important workflow context is no longer attached.

## What one estimator call does

The [public contract](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/expectation_estimator/expectation_estimator.py) is

```python
energy_result, measurement_data = estimator.run(
    circuit,
    qubit_hamiltonian,
    total_shots,
    noise_model=None,
)
```

The circuit prepares one fixed state; the operator supplies the observable. Parameterized/unbound circuit sweeps are not implemented by this call. Despite the class name referring to energy, it can estimate other valid Hermitian Pauli sums, such as an appropriately encoded particle-number operator or a correlation observable. Their units follow their coefficients; a particle-number expectation is not measured in Hartree.

The only estimator setting is a nested `circuit_executor`, defaulting to `AlgorithmRef("circuit_executor","qdk_sparse_state_simulator")`. Other compatible executors can be selected, such as the native full-state simulator or optional Qiskit Aer backend. The estimator does not become an analytic exact expectation evaluator when the executor uses a full-state simulator: this path still obtains finite-shot counts. Backend seeds control reproducibility, not a guarantee of physical accuracy or statistical independence beyond the experiment’s assumptions.

First the estimator requires a Pauli-decomposition container and resolves measurement groups. Its own input checks do not provide a complete general Hermiticity validation: ensure the observable has finite real combined coefficients. In particular the identity-only path takes the real part of the coefficient sum, so passing an imaginary “observable” is not a supported way to estimate a non-Hermitian operator.

Next it removes **identity-only groups** from execution and adds their coefficient sum as an exact offset. If an identity term shares a nonidentity group, it can remain there, contributing expectation one and variance zero from the same data. The routine does not otherwise screen small coefficients or automatically detect all state-specific deterministic terms. If every group is identity-only, it returns the exact sum with zero reported variance and no circuit shots.

For each remaining group, it creates a new measurement circuit. If the supplied circuit has a Q# callable, the wrapper allocates a register of the observable’s width, applies that callable, and uses the native measurement-basis routine. It does not automatically supply extra caller-owned phase-gradient ancillas from metadata. A trial callable requiring such a suffix must be adapted with the proper ownership contract before this path can measure it.

Without a Q# callable, the estimator uses optional Qiskit conversion, checks that the circuit width equals the Pauli-label width, appends local basis rotations and a compact classical measurement register, and returns QASM. This fallback does require Qiskit, even when the eventual chosen executor is a QDK simulator. Existing measurement/classical-control structure and extra workspace need to satisfy that conversion/composition path; a rendered circuit or arbitrary QIR object is not an automatic compatibility guarantee.

## `total_shots` is a budget request with integer rounding

Let \(G\) be the number of nonidentity measurement groups. The code requires `total_shots >= G` and assigns

\[
n_g=\left\lfloor\frac{\text{total_shots}}G\right\rfloor
\]

to **each** group. It does not distribute the remainder, weight allocation by coefficients, estimate variances adaptively, or optimize state-preparation cost. The requested executions therefore total \(G\lfloor\text{total_shots}/G\rfloor\), which can be smaller than the supplied number. This rule is independent of the executor’s random seed.

One circuit-executor call is made per group, with `shots=n_g` and `noise=noise_model`. Every shot includes fresh state preparation and the group’s basis measurement. Fewer groups can reduce separate circuit programs, but does not automatically reduce the chosen total shot budget or total uncertainty. Read `measurement_data.shots_list` for allocations and sum each returned count dictionary for usable observed shots.

[`CircuitExecutorData`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/circuit_executor_data.py) distinguishes clean bitstring counts, total requested/executed shots, and separate loss bitstrings. The expectation estimator currently consumes only clean `bitstring_counts` and does not propagate all executor metadata or loss records into its MeasurementData. Statistics normalize by the observed count sum, which can differ from the allocation after loss. That is effectively a conditional-survival estimate, with possible postselection bias; an empty clean count set raises. More shots do not automatically remove that bias.

## Means, quantum variance, and variance of an estimator

For a Pauli outcome random variable \(X\in\{-1,+1\}\), let its true expectation be \(m\). Since \(X^2=1\), its single-shot variance is \(1-m^2\). For \(n\) independent identically prepared shots, the sample mean \(\widehat m\) has variance

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m)=\frac{1-m^2}{n}.
\]

The estimator computes \(\widehat m\) from count-weighted parity signs and reports the plug-in estimate

\[
\widehat v=\frac{1-\widehat m^2}{n}.
\]

This is a variance estimate **of the mean**, not the single-shot quantum variance. It is slightly downward-biased at finite sample size. For \(n>1\), the corresponding unbiased sample-variance estimate of the mean uses \((1-\widehat m^2)/(n-1)\). The current implementation uses \(n\), not \(n-1\).

The intrinsic quantum energy variance is a different quantity,

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\psi(H)=\langle H^2\rangle_\psi-\langle H\rangle_\psi^2.
\]

An exact eigenstate has zero intrinsic energy variance. Yet separately measuring its noncommuting Pauli components can produce noisy sample means. For the ground eigenstate of the illustrative \(X+Z\), each individual Pauli expectation is \(-1/\sqrt2\), so each single-term measurement has variance one-half even though the state’s exact energy is sharp. Estimating the energy by separate Pauli measurements therefore still costs shots.

The current returned `energy_variance` is calculated as

\[
V_{\mathrm{reported}}=\sum_j |h_j|^2\widehat v_j.
\]

That matches a diagonal, independent-term approximation to the variance of the energy estimator. It is not a computation of \(\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2\), not a certified error bound, and not automatically a confidence interval.

## Grouped shots introduce covariance the current result omits

When two terms use the same shots, their estimated means can be correlated. For a group, the correct variance of the weighted sample-mean estimator includes

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat E_g)=\frac1{n_g}
\left[\sum_j h_j^2\operatorname{Var}(X_j)
+2\sum_{j<k}h_jh_k\operatorname{Cov}(X_j,X_k)\right].
\]

**Covariance** measures whether two quantities fluctuate together or oppositely. It can increase or decrease the total depending on the state and coefficient signs. The current estimator does not calculate those cross terms, even though grouped count dictionaries contain enough joint outcome information to estimate them.

As a hand-worked counterexample, measure Z on both qubits of the Bell state \((|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2\), and estimate \(H=Z_0+Z_1\). Suppose an illustrative 100-shot histogram has 50 `00` and 50 `11`. Each Pauli mean is zero and its reported mean variance is 0.01, so the code’s diagonal sum is 0.02. But the per-shot energy score is always +2 or −2. Its plug-in mean variance is \(4/100=0.04\). Ignoring the positive covariance understates the variance by a factor two in this example.

One way to process the raw data correctly is to assign each group outcome \(b\) a score \(Y_g(b)=\sum_{j\in g}h_jx_j(b)\), then compute its weighted first and second moments and divide the score variance by the number of shots. This is a mathematical post-processing prescription, not a claim that the current `qdk` estimator already performs it. An unbiased finite-sample version applies the appropriate sample correction. Independent groups’ estimator variances can then be summed under the independence assumptions.

The usual large-sample standard error is the square root of the estimator variance. A two-sided normal approximation such as mean ±1.96 standard errors additionally assumes adequate sampling and approximately normal mean errors; it is not guaranteed for small counts, rare events, drift, correlated shots, or systematic noise. Zero observed variance is especially deceptive: one shot or a short run with all identical outcomes does not prove the true failure probability is zero. The result’s summary printing a plus/minus square root does not remove these qualifications.

## A complete toy estimate, including rounding and offsets

Consider the ungrouped illustrative operator

\[
H_q=0.3I+0.6X-0.4Z.
\]

Request 101 shots. Identity is handled classically; the two remaining groups receive 50 shots each, so only 100 shots are allocated. Suppose X-basis outcomes are 40 plus and 10 minus, while Z-basis outcomes are 15 plus and 35 minus. Then

\[
\widehat m_X=0.6,\qquad\widehat m_Z=-0.4,
\]

\[
\widehat E_q=0.3+0.6(0.6)-0.4(-0.4)=0.82.
\]

The code’s plug-in mean variances are \(0.64/50=0.0128\) and \(0.84/50=0.0168\). Because these two terms were measured in separate groups, the diagonal aggregation gives

\[
V_{\mathrm{reported}}=0.6^2(0.0128)+0.4^2(0.0168)=0.007296,
\]

with square root about 0.0854 in the toy energy units. If an independently retained core scalar were 0.2, total energy would be 1.02 with the same sampling variance, assuming the scalar is exact. All counts and coefficients here are illustrative, not generated by a simulation or taken from nitrogen.

This example separates four ideas: an exact identity contribution, a requested versus allocated shot count, a noisy active-operator expectation, and an independently added core scalar. It does not claim 0.0854 is a certified total chemical uncertainty.

In principle, with known per-group score variance \(V_g\), equal-cost shots are allocated optimally roughly in proportion to \(\sqrt{V_g}\). For independently measured individual terms this becomes \(|h_j|\sqrt{1-m_j^2}\). Those variances may require pilot samples, and unequal circuit costs change the optimization. The current estimator does none of this automatically; there is no exposed adaptive-allocation setting to turn on. A graph-coloring heuristic alone cannot promise statistically optimal savings.

## Returned data, units, and what survives serialization

The [actual result classes](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/estimator_data.py) are `EnergyExpectationResult` and `MeasurementData`. The first stores `energy_expectation_value`, `energy_variance`, `expvals_each_term`, and `variances_each_term`. The last two are lists of arrays organized by measured group, with entries in that group’s term order. They are not automatically flat arrays indexed like the original complete Hamiltonian.

Pauli expectations and their mean variances are dimensionless. The weighted energy expectation has the coefficients’ units, and its aggregated variance has squared units. The identity-only shortcut returns empty per-term arrays because no measurements were made. The summary’s count label should not be used to infer the original total Pauli count from the length of a group-list field.

MeasurementData pairs measured group Hamiltonians with bitstring-count dictionaries and allocated `shots_list`. In mixed identity/nonidentity runs, identity-only groups are omitted from that measurement list; the offset is already included in the numerical energy result, but is not a separately named MeasurementData field. Retain the original operator and core scalar if you want to reconstruct the full calculation later. The all-identity shortcut instead retains its resolved Hamiltonian groups but has empty counts/shot lists.

Both classes have JSON/HDF5 methods and tests. The numerical result stores its scalar/array statistics. MeasurementData serialization is narrower than full QubitOperator serialization: it stores Pauli labels and coefficients for each group, counts, and shot allocation, but not their full encoding/tapering/partition provenance. Its JSON path also uses raw `coefficients.tolist()` rather than the package’s complex-array encoding; a complex NumPy dtype can yield Python complex values that ordinary JSON dumping cannot serialize, even when imaginary parts are zero. HDF5 stores coefficient arrays directly. These are current format limits, not a reason to silently discard physical complex data. None of those file methods was called here.

The [result-class tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_energy_expectation_result.py) and [measurement-data tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_estimator_data.py) check particular payloads and round trips. Such structural tests do not certify covariance-aware uncertainty, all dtype cases, or preserved chemical provenance.

## Following the supplied workflow without overinterpreting its output

The [quickstart](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/quickstart.py) selects the top two determinants from a CASCI wavefunction, then runs `projected_multi_configuration_calculator` on that support. This reoptimizes coefficients; it is not merely deleting small amplitudes and keeping the old energy. It prepares the returned sparse state, maps the matching active Hamiltonian, groups it by `qubit_wise_commuting`, and compares measured total energy with the sparse projected reference `E_sparse`.

The [state-preparation notebook](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/state_prep_energy.ipynb) follows the same benchmarking logic and prints a square root of `energy_variance`. Its prose and plus/minus display must be read with the current covariance and finite-sample qualifications above. It is a separate source example, not newly executed nitrogen data. A classical reference already known for a small state is useful for validating state loading; the benchmark itself is not proof of quantum advantage over that classical reference calculation.

For the continuing nitrogen baseline, an unexecuted pattern is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef

# trial_circuit prepares the intended state in the same blocked JW active basis.
measurable = create("term_grouper", "qubit_wise_commuting").run(qubit_hamiltonian)
estimator = create(
    "expectation_estimator", "qdk",
    circuit_executor=AlgorithmRef("circuit_executor", "qdk_sparse_state_simulator", seed=42),
)
result, data = estimator.run(trial_circuit, measurable, total_shots=10000)
total_energy = result.energy_expectation_value + active_hamiltonian.get_core_energy()
allocated_shots = sum(data.shots_list)
usable_shots = sum(sum(counts.values()) for counts in data.bitstring_counts if counts is not None)
```

The shot count is illustrative, not a recommended converged budget. `result.energy_variance` remains the implementation’s diagonal plug-in quantity. For grouped results, use the raw outcomes and the covariance formula before interpreting a standard error. The code measures only the supplied Pauli observable. SOS structured operators are rejected by this estimator; their separate shifted block-encoding spectral contract must not be treated as another Pauli measurement offset automatically.

## What more shots can and cannot fix

Sampling uncertainty can decrease with repeated valid preparations, approximately as the inverse square root of shot count under the usual assumptions. It cannot repair an incorrect basis, a too-small active space, a DFT model used as though it were the intended interacting Hamiltonian, a wrong electron sector, lost coefficient signs, or a mismatched tapered state/operator. Those are different errors.

Noise changes the prepared/measured distribution. Survival postselection, drift, and systematic readout errors can bias the estimate even when a plug-in variance is tiny. The current estimator forwards an optional noise profile; it does not implement a general error-mitigation, confidence-calibration, or loss-correction procedure. Backend/provider behavior and richer noise treatment belong to the execution lesson.

Complete resource accounting includes state preparation for every group and every shot, basis changes, measurement/reset, classical processing, and any circuit conversion or synthesis needed by the executor. Reducing group count or reporting a small statistical variance is not the same as reducing physical-qubit overhead.

Finally, expectation estimation and phase estimation answer different questions. Pauli sampling estimates an average energy of the prepared state. Ideal phase estimation samples eigenvalue branches, with trial-state overlap and finite resolution determining their outcomes. We now have the operator, state-loading, circuit, and statistical vocabulary needed to derive the repository’s full phase-estimation methods without mistaking one kind of result for the other.
lessons.caveats: No measurements/simulation/imports/tests/files executed. Estimator supports Pauli decomposition and QWC-compatible FlatPartition groups; non-QWC flat groups raise, LayeredPartition ignored with individual-term fallback. Default term_grouper is globalcommuting, not always measurement-compatible. Equal floor shot allocation drops remainder; statistics normalize clean observed counts. energy_variance is diagonal plug-in variance of estimated means, omits within-group covariance and uses n not n-1; printed sqrt is neither intrinsic Var(H) nor certified confidence interval. Identity-only groups skipped, core scalar separate. No automatic general Hermiticity validation; identity branch takes real part. Shared-gradient trial callables not automatically accommodated. Most groupers omit tapering metadata except vacuum strategy. MeasurementData serialization loses full operator provenance and raw complex dtype can break JSON; loss/executor metadata not propagated. Quickstart compares projected sparse-state energy, not automatically full CAS ground energy.

lessons.title: Reading energies through phase estimation
lessons.body:
# Lesson 21 — Reading energies through phase estimation

## The phase belongs to an eigenstate, not necessarily the ground state

Pauli sampling in Lesson 20 estimated the expectation of an observable on a prepared state. Quantum phase estimation, or **QPE**, instead estimates an eigenphase of a chosen unitary. If that unitary encodes a Hamiltonian spectrum, a phase can be converted into an energy. QPE does not inherently select the lowest energy, identify the correct electron sector, or make an approximate chemical model exact.

Our continuing problem is neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å, reduced from the 28-spatial-orbital cc-pVDZ model to the selected active model. The ordinary Pauli route still separates the core scalar; the SOSSA route has already included it in its energy-shift metadata. A trial state supplies overlap with desired eigenstates, not a guarantee that every run returns the ground state.

This chapter separates three layers: the mathematical QPE experiment, the repository’s circuit builders, and its classical orchestration/decoding algorithms. That distinction is especially important for iterative QPE, whose current implementation repeatedly prepares the system rather than preserving one collapsed eigenstate throughout all bits. Nothing is executed here; source tests and tutorial settings are attributed evidence, not new results.

## Phase kickback in one control qubit

Suppose \(U|u\rangle=e^{2\pi i\varphi}|u\rangle\), where \(\varphi\) is a phase fraction measured in turns. Start a control in \(|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\). A controlled U gives

\[
\frac{|0\rangle+e^{2\pi i\varphi}|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\otimes|u\rangle.
\]

The system eigenstate factors out, but its eigenphase has become a relative phase of the control. This is **phase kickback**. A final H and Z measurement give probability \((1+\cos2\pi\varphi)/2\) for zero. Applying \(U^r\) changes the phase to \(r\varphi\) modulo one. Repeated powers expose different binary digits or finer phase structure, but their implementation cost is real.

Write an exactly representable phase as \(\varphi=0.b_1b_2\cdots b_m\), meaning \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}b_j2^{-j}\). The symbols MSB and LSB mean most- and least-significant bit. They describe numerical place values, not automatically physical qubit positions.

For time evolution \(U(t)=e^{-iHt}\), the fraction is

\[
\varphi=(-Et/2\pi)\bmod1.
\]

The minus sign is the convention used by the repository’s Pauli product formulas. Energies separated by \(2\pi/t\) have the same phase. These are **aliases**: physically different values indistinguishable from this one periodic signal. More phase bits refine the measured fraction but do not by themselves remove that energy ambiguity.

The product-formula container chooses a principal angle in \((-\pi,\pi]\) and returns \(-\mathrm{angle}/t\). It does not automatically search every physically possible energy branch. A known spectral bound, an energy shift, or a prior interval narrower than one alias period is needed to identify the intended branch. For example, a coefficient bound \(|E|\le\lambda\) permits \(|t|\lambda<\pi\) to keep the spectrum away from the wrap boundary. A very conservative bound can require many bits for fine energy precision. Zero evolution time cannot be used to decode energy.

## Standard QPE: Fourier analysis of controlled powers

A quantum Fourier transform, or **QFT**, changes between an integer basis and phase-pattern basis. In ideal standard QPE, an \(m\)-qubit phase register starts in a uniform superposition over \(M=2^m\) integers. Controlled powers produce

\[
\frac1{\sqrt M}\sum_{x=0}^{M-1}e^{2\pi i x\varphi}|x\rangle|u\rangle.
\]

The inverse QFT converts that phase progression into a distribution over integers \(y\). Its amplitude is

\[
a_y=\frac1M\sum_{x=0}^{M-1}e^{2\pi i x(\varphi-y/M)}.
\]

If \(M\varphi\) is an integer, the ideal distribution is concentrated there. Otherwise amplitude spreads over nearby bins with finite tails. This **spectral leakage** is finite-resolution behavior, not necessarily hardware noise. Bin spacing is \(2^{-m}\) in phase fraction and \(2\pi/(|t|2^m)\) in a local unaliased time-evolution energy scale. Bin width is not a confidence interval.

For a superposition \(\sum_k c_k|u_k\rangle\), the coherent experiment entangles the phase register with eigenstate-dependent phase distributions. Under ideal sufficient resolution, a complete shot selects an eigenstate branch with weight \(|c_k|^2\). Closely spaced phases can remain unresolved; finite-bin measurement need not project onto one unique eigenvector. The user-facing orchestration can also summarize many shots rather than retain each collapse result.

The registered orchestration method is `phase_estimation/qdk_standard`. It has `shots=3` by default. The corresponding native builder is separately registered as `qpe_circuit_builder/qdk_standard`. Its settings include `num_bits=-1`, requiring an explicit positive value, the nested unitary builder, the controlled mapper, and `measure_phase=True`.

A real configuration trap is visible in the [standard orchestration source](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/standard_phase_estimation.py): its settings inherit the base `qdk_iterative` builder reference and do not replace it with the standard builder. Configure `qpe_circuit_builder=AlgorithmRef("qpe_circuit_builder","qdk_standard",...)` explicitly. Otherwise the orchestration’s builder-type check fails. Registry names at two different layers are not automatic mutual configuration.

The [native standard builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/circuit_builder/standard_builder.py) constructs one controlled operation for each power \(2^{m-1},\ldots,1\), associates them with its phase wires, and returns a single-element circuit list. [`StandardPhaseEstimation.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/StandardPhaseEstimation.qs) prepares the system once, Hadamards the phase register, applies the powered operations, and calls the external inverse QFT. The final factory measures the phase register and resets remaining qubits.

Do not infer final bit significance solely from a wire’s power before the inverse QFT. The Q# routine returns measurements in its wire order and the executor applies its result-string convention. The public result is interpreted as an MSB-first binary fraction. Existing [standard-QPE tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_phase_estimation_standard.py) use nonpalindromic references such as phase 13/16 and expected string `1101`, preventing a casual double reversal from appearing correct only by accident. We have not reviewed the external QFT implementation or executed those tests.

The measurement-free `qsharp_op` is adjointable for coherent composition. Setting `measure_phase=False` changes the standalone factory’s phase-readout behavior, but that factory still resets its allocated register at the end. Use the composable operation, not a discarded standalone output, when a later algorithm needs coherent phase tags.

The orchestration executes the one circuit for the configured shots, selects the most frequent complete bitstring, converts it to a fraction, and returns one `QpeResult`. It does not return the whole phase histogram in that object. A count tie follows the existing dictionary order through Python `max`; this is not a physics-based branch decision. Empty surviving counts cause a failure at dominant-bin selection. A modal phase can correspond to whichever eigenstate has the largest observed weight, not necessarily the ground state.

## Iterative QPE: the actual feedback recurrence

The default orchestration method is `phase_estimation/qdk_iterative`, with `shots_per_bit=3`, default `qpe_circuit_builder/qdk_iterative`, and default sparse-state executor. The [iterative builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/circuit_builder/iterative_builder.py) has `num_bits=-1`, `phase_correction=0.0`, and `num_iteration=-1`. A negative iteration selects all bit circuits; a nonnegative one selects that zero-based iteration. Positive bit count and an in-range iteration are required.

The first executed iteration uses \(U^{2^{m-1}}\) and resolves the **least-significant** bit of an exactly \(m\)-bit eigenphase. Later iterations proceed toward the MSB. The Q# circuit applies H to the control, applies an Rz feedback correction, applies the already-powered controlled unitary, applies H again, and measures/resets the control. The sign convention follows the actual [Q# routine](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/IterativePhaseEstimation.qs), not an assumed generic IQPE formula.

Let \(F\) be the stored feedback angle, initially zero. The [orchestration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/iterative_phase_estimation.py) sends correction \(-F\), obtains one bit by majority vote, and updates

\[
F\leftarrow F/2+\pi b/2.
\]

After all bits, it returns phase fraction \(F/\pi\) and reverses the execution-order bit list into MSB-first order. Ties choose zero because zero wins when its count is greater than or equal to the count of one. If loss leaves both counts absent, this comparison also chooses zero; the algorithm does not separately diagnose that as a no-data bit. Noise/loss handling therefore needs care beyond reading a plausible-looking final bitstring.

For the illustrative eigenphase \(5/8=0.101\), three iterations use powers 4,2,1. The first phase is \(\pi\) modulo \(2\pi\), yielding bit 1 and \(F=\pi/2\). The next phase is \(\pi/2\), canceled by \(-F\), yielding bit 0 and \(F=\pi/4\). The final relative phase is \(5\pi/4-\pi/4=\pi\), yielding bit 1 and final \(F=5\pi/8\). The numerical bitstring is `101`. This is hand arithmetic in the ideal eigenstate case, not a simulator output.

Building all iteration circuits with one fixed `phase_correction` is useful for inspection or component costing. It does not know the feedback produced by a future run. The orchestration updates correction and iteration settings between measurements and calls the builder’s implementation for the selected iteration; it does not execute a prebuilt all-zero-feedback list as if it were adaptive QPE.

## Fresh preparation changes the success story

Textbook iterative schemes can recycle a phase ancilla while retaining the same physical system state across bits. The current QDK Chemistry bit circuit does something more specific: it allocates a fresh register, runs the supplied state preparation, measures the phase control, and resets the system/ancillas. The executor repeats that circuit for each shot. The Python algorithm then builds and runs the next bit’s fresh circuit.

For a true eigenstate this is an efficient-width way to gather bit evidence. For a trial superposition, different shots and bits can encounter different spectral components. A concatenated result need not have the same distribution as a complete coherent standard-QPE shot.

Consider a toy trial with equal weights on exact eigenphases 0 and 3/4, using two bits and one shot per bit. Coherent standard QPE would ideally return `00` or `11`. In the fresh-state implementation, the first, least-significant bit can be zero from the phase-zero component. With zero feedback, a fresh phase-3/4 component at the next iteration gives a random control bit because its relative phase is \(3\pi/2\). A one outcome then creates `10`, corresponding to 1/2—neither original phase. This hybrid outcome is possible without noise or Hamiltonian approximation. It is a consequence of repreparation plus feedback built from potentially different components.

More shots per bit can reduce ordinary bit-sampling error under suitable single-eigenstate conditions, but do not turn that mixture protocol into the coherent-collapse experiment. For an odd three-shot majority and independent wrong-bit probability \(p\), the wrong majority probability is \(3p^2-2p^3\). In a real adaptive sequence, the bit distribution depends on prior feedback and the state mixture; treating every bit as having the same independent error probability is another assumption.

Thus neither “ground fidelity F” nor “use about 1/F complete trials” is a blanket success formula for this implementation. Repeated complete IQPE runs, examining their full distribution, and validating the protocol on an appropriate model are meaningful; interpreting every bitstring as an eigenvalue sampled with ground overlap weight is not generally justified. The [iterative tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_phase_estimation_iterative.py) include carefully prepared eigenstate benchmarks and specific noncommuting cases, not a theorem for every trial mixture.

## Shared nested settings and the unitary being estimated

The [common circuit-builder base](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/circuit_builder/base.py) defaults to `hamiltonian_unitary_builder/trotter` and `controlled_circuit_mapper/pauli_sequence`. It explicitly sets the requested power on each newly resolved unitary builder and forces the mapper’s control index to zero. Those are parent overrides. Changing a nested reference’s power/control setting does not necessarily override the enclosing QPE schedule.

The standard and iterative builders must estimate powers of a consistent unitary. With deterministic `power_strategy="repeat"`, the powers repeat the same base approximation when the builder inputs agree. With `rescale`, the builder recompiles at a longer simulated time; a finite product formula need not equal a power of the previously built approximation. The enclosing phase-estimation interpretation then needs an error analysis, not just a matching nominal time.

Random builders add another trap. Fixed-seed qDRIFT with repeat may reproducibly construct the same sampled base product and repeat it, but its averaged-channel bound still does not certify the coherent eigenphases of that one product. With the default nondeterministic seed, separately rebuilt bit/power circuits can instead use different sampled base products. They are not automatically powers of one common U at all. Partial randomization has related finite splitting and consistency obligations.

The common native builder derives extra unitary ancillas from the **unitary container’s** structural width, not by inspecting every generated controlled circuit. A coefficient loader that adds alias-sampling workspace beyond that structural LCU width is not automatically accommodated by standard/iterative composition. The unary builder has a different, explicit mapper-width contract. Likewise the state-preparation width check only rejects a known width greater than the passed register; it does not prove exact equality, encoding identity, spin sector, or orbital alignment.

The controlled-Pauli standalone high-index allocation limit and CSWAP vacuum-preserving ordered-block requirement from Lesson 17 still apply. Native QPE uses compact control/system layouts. A tapered operator needs a correspondingly transformed trial state. Common state-preparation or mapper class ancestry is not a universal compatibility certificate.

## Unary QPE: a signed query schedule, not a unary-sized phase register

The registered orchestration and builder names are both `qdk_unary` in their respective families. The orchestration defaults to `shots=3`, `resolve_positive_branch=False`, and its matching unary builder. The [builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/circuit_builder/unary_phase_estimation_builder.py) defaults to an LCU unitary builder with `quantum_walk=True`, an uncontrolled `prepare_select_prepare` circuit mapper, `num_queries=-1`, and `compute_capacity=-1`. An explicit positive query count is required.

Unary here refers to sequential one-hot **address iteration**, not allocating one permanent phase qubit for every query. With \(p\) block queries, there are \(p+1\) reflection slots, addressed by

\[
m=\lceil\log_2(p+1)\rceil
\]

phase qubits. The implementation computes this as the positive query count’s bit length. For example, seven queries need three phase bits, while eight queries need four. Queries need not be a power of two. A conflicting positive `num_bits` setting is warned about and ignored; `num_queries` determines the register.

The phase register is prepared in a zero-padded **cosine-window** state, implemented with amplitudes proportional to

\[
\sin\left(\frac{\pi(j+1)}{p+2}\right),\qquad j=0,\ldots,p.
\]

This smooth weighting suppresses spectral tails compared with a rectangular uniform window. Padding outside the valid slot range must remain zero because invalid address values can route to the wrong slot through the unary-iteration helper. It is not harmless unused register space.

The schedule uses a self-inverse block encoding B and an outer reflection R. It applies p blocks and omits exactly the reflection selected by the phase address. On slot j, the resulting action is the signed walk power \(W^{p-2j}\), with \(W=RB\). The [Q# schedule](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/UnaryPhaseEstimation.qs) controls the reflection/slot behavior rather than requiring a generic controlled version of B. That is why an Adj-only SOSSA block can fit this protocol while it cannot be passed to the ordinary controlled-QPE mapper.

The address-dependent phase changes by twice the walk eigenphase between slots. After inverse QFT, the measured fraction is related to the walk phase by \(y=\pm2\varphi\bmod1\). This doubled-phase alias is central to the decoder; it is not a minor bit-order correction.

## Unary decoding needs prior branch information

The [unary orchestration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/phase_estimation/unary_phase_estimation.py) folds conjugate bins and combines their counts. For a measured y it computes \(f=\min(y,(-y)\bmod1)/2\). `resolve_positive_branch=True` chooses canonical walk fraction f; false chooses \(1/2-f\). It then selects the most populated canonical bin, breaking ties toward the smaller canonical fraction, and reports both mirror energy candidates.

For ordinary LCU, \(E=\lambda\cos(2\pi\varphi)\). The two candidates are E and −E. Default false chooses the nonpositive **signal** branch; it cannot infer from the data alone that the desired state actually belongs there. The implementation’s default is not a universal ground-state oracle.

For SOSSA, \(E=\Lambda(1+\cos2\pi\varphi)+E_s\). The ambiguity is instead between energies reflected around \(E_s+\Lambda\): \(E\) and \(2(E_s+\Lambda)-E\). The flag chooses the lower or upper half of that shifted signal band, not necessarily negative or positive total molecular energy. Use physically justified reference/bound information to choose a branch, and account for uncertainty near its dividing point.

Because conjugate bins are folded, `phase_fraction` and `bitstring_msb_first` in the unary result describe the chosen representative bin; they need not be the literal most frequent original shot string. `canonical_phase_fraction` is the decoded walk phase, and `raw_energy` is computed from that canonical phase. The [unary tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_phase_estimation_unary.py) explicitly check merged conjugate counts, deterministic ties, and the doubled-phase relationship.

Increasing p sharpens the finite window but cannot recover the discarded sign/half-band information without extra knowledge. A suggested query-scaling formula in the settings description, involving normalization and desired energy error, is planning guidance; the builder does not automatically solve a complete chemical/phase/statistical budget from an epsilon setting.

## Unary representation, ancillas, and execution limits

The builder accepts an LCU **walk** container or a SOSSA block-encoding container; a bare LCU container without the walk interpretation is rejected. For LCU it extracts/rebuilds a unit-power block and warns when supplied powers are ignored. SOSSA must already have unit power. The mapper must return a Q# callable and declared width, with a nonempty ancillary region for the outer reflection.

Shared phase-gradient metadata is handled explicitly here. State preparation and the block may each request a trailing gradient; if both do, their widths must agree. The builder initializes it once around the schedule, appends it only to consumers expecting it, and excludes it from zero-ancilla reflection. Inner scratch allocated inside B is still additional to the declared argument register. Physical QEC overhead is not represented by these widths.

`compute_capacity=-1` keeps logical qubits in compute. A positive value requests the QDK resource-estimation memory/compute placement model with least-recently-used scheduling, and the Python builder warns that placement counts may be inaccurate. Zero or values below −1 raise. This setting is not proof that a physical quantum memory device or a particular hardware deployment exists.

There is also an explicit current backend limit: unary orchestration permits only the executor named `qdk_sparse_state_simulator`. Recursive Q# unary iteration threads a callable through the recursion and is not lowered to QIR by the current path. The full-state QIR executor and Qiskit executors are therefore rejected by name, even if other parts of the same workflow can use them. Construction and supported logical-count interpretation are different capabilities from exporting/deploying a general QIR program. The source tests exercise particular interpreter and counting paths; no such execution was performed here.

## Optional Qiskit circuit builders

The optional plugin supplies `qpe_circuit_builder/qiskit_standard` and `qiskit_iterative`, while the orchestration remains the corresponding `phase_estimation/qdk_standard` or `qdk_iterative` algorithm. Their [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/phase_estimation_circuit_builder.py) builds Qiskit circuits and exports QASM rather than native composable Q# operations.

Qiskit standard QPE probes the compiled controlled circuit for workspace width, prepares the phase register with H gates, applies increasing powers on its phase wires, and calls external `synth_qft_full(..., inverse=True)`. Its `qft_do_swaps` setting defaults true. Turning swaps off changes output ordering and is not compensated by a new generic decoder in this orchestration; preserve the tested setting unless you explicitly adapt and validate the convention.

The Qiskit standard path checks that state-preparation width equals the system width. The iterative plugin composes prepared and controlled circuits as gates, which requires appropriate gate-convertible, effectively unitary subcircuits; arbitrary adaptive measurement-bearing preparations cannot simply become a gate. Extra decomposition ancillas and QIR-to-Qiskit control-flow restrictions still apply. These are optional external synthesis/conversion contributions, not alternative physical hardware guarantees.

## What QpeResult does and does not store

[`QpeResult`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/qpe_result.py) stores `method`, phase fraction and angle, canonical phase fraction and angle, `raw_energy`, candidate `branching`, optional `resolved_energy`, optional MSB-first bits/string, and optional metadata. The factory normalizes phase fractions modulo one and calls the supplied container decoder on the canonical fraction.

For standard and iterative orchestration, canonical phase equals the measured/assembled fraction, branching defaults to the single decoded energy, and resolved energy remains unset. Those methods do not enumerate all time-evolution aliases using a chemical energy interval. For unary, both mirror candidates are supplied and the branch flag sets resolved energy. The word “raw” does not mean untouched data in every method: it is still a decoder output from the canonical phase.

The current orchestrators do not populate complete shot histograms, per-bit counts, all generated circuits, state-overlap diagnostics, or confidence intervals into this result. Optional metadata is merely available storage. If those details are needed for auditing, retain execution data or a surrounding workflow record explicitly. The main tutorial does exactly that for repeated complete IQPE runs.

JSON/HDF5 preserve these result fields, with metadata serialized as JSON where appropriate. They do not serialize the decoder callable or prove which Hamiltonian, orbital model, approximation settings, core shift, and trial state produced a number. Keep that provenance with the result. Unknown/malformed metadata is not a recovered physical interpretation.

For ordinary Pauli time evolution or ordinary LCU, add the separately omitted molecular core scalar once to the decoded active energy. For SOSSA, the decoder already adds the shift containing that scalar. Adding it again would double count it. Statistical spread across runs, finite-bit resolution, approximation errors, and chemical model errors must be reported separately rather than bundled into an unexplained plus/minus number.

## The nitrogen tutorial is deliberately reference-guided

The main [IQPE tutorial](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/tutorial_run_iqpe.py) reuses the 1.85 Å mapping/trial-state workflow. Its defaults are six phase bits, three shots per bit, twenty complete runs, and seeds starting at 42. It uses first-order Trotter with one base division and repeated powers, and the native iterative orchestrator with a full-state simulator.

Its time-selection routine first considers \(t_{\mathrm{bound}}=\pi/\lambda\), then uses a **known selected-space reference energy** to choose a finite phase-grid point and adjust time so that grid energy sits one milliHartree above the reference. This is explicitly circular validation input. It demonstrates implementation and finite-grid behavior; it is not a production strategy for discovering an unknown ground energy or proof that a generic six-bit calculation is accurate to one milliHartree.

The surrounding tutorial repeats complete runs with consecutive seeds, stores each bitstring/energy/error/runtime record, and requires a unique modal complete bitstring when summarizing. That outer aggregation is not a hidden `num_trials` setting of the base IQPE algorithm. The separate notebook at 1.270025 Å remains a different molecular baseline; its resource/circuit results must not be substituted into this story.

For the tutorial’s declared m=6 and three-shot bit votes, each complete run performs 18 state preparations/bit shots and \(3(2^6-1)=189\) base-unitary applications when counting repeated powers. Twenty complete runs therefore imply 360 bit shots and 3780 base-unitary applications before expanding each base step into Pauli gates. These are arithmetic workload counts from source settings, not observations from an executed session. The largest one-bit circuit alone is not that complete workload.

## A bounded configuration pattern

This source-backed pattern is unexecuted. Assume `qubit_hamiltonian` is a validated nonzero Hermitian Pauli operator and `trial_circuit` is a compatible clean preparation in the same untapered active encoding:

```python
from math import pi
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef

coefficient_bound = qubit_hamiltonian.schatten_norm
base_time = pi / (2 * coefficient_bound)
qpe = create(
    "phase_estimation", "qdk_iterative",
    shots_per_bit=3,
    qpe_circuit_builder=AlgorithmRef(
        "qpe_circuit_builder", "qdk_iterative",
        num_bits=6,
        unitary_builder=AlgorithmRef(
            "hamiltonian_unitary_builder", "trotter",
            time=base_time, order=2, num_divisions=4,
            power_strategy="repeat",
        ),
        controlled_circuit_mapper=AlgorithmRef("controlled_circuit_mapper", "pauli_sequence"),
    ),
    circuit_executor=AlgorithmRef("circuit_executor", "qdk_sparse_state_simulator", seed=42),
)
# In an authorized execution environment: result = qpe.run(trial_circuit, qubit_hamiltonian)
```

The bound-based time avoids relying on the known nitrogen energy to select a phase-grid target. It does not certify a six-bit energy tolerance, four-division Trotter accuracy, or adequate trial-state overlap. Those choices are explicit illustrative limits that must be refined for a real accuracy objective.

## Comparing variants without hiding the work

Standard QPE uses m phase qubits and one state preparation per complete shot, but all controlled powers must be coherent within that shot. Iterative QPE uses one phase control per bit circuit, yet repeats preparation and uses classical feedback; the longest controlled power remains \(2^{m-1}\). Fewer phase qubits does not mean shallow evolution or near-term noise tolerance. Unary uses a logarithmic phase-address register plus an arbitrary-length block/reflection schedule, and a specialized doubled-phase decoder with prior branch selection.

All variants also need system qubits, representation-specific ancillas, internal scratch, and later physical error correction. Count every powered operation, every PREPARE/SELECT/reflection or Pauli step, rotation precision, state preparation, measurement/reset, shot, complete trial, and classical build/post-processing stage. Randomization consistency and shared-ancilla ownership belong in that accounting.

QPE is therefore a carefully defined spectral experiment, not an energy-reading instruction that ignores state quality and implementation details. The next lesson examines two related tools: overlap-sensitive Hadamard tests and coherent success amplification, including why a finite-resolution phase filter is not a free exact-ground-state oracle.
lessons.caveats: No executions/imports/tests/files. Standard orchestration inherits iterative builder default and needs explicit standard reference. Native width check not complete encoding proof; common extra-ancilla sizing uses container not full generated workspace. IQPE fresh prep each bit/shot, majority ties/no-data favor0, no generic whole-run ground-fidelity distribution; all-bit construction lacks future adaptive feedback. Powered random builders must represent sameU; averaged-channel guarantees insufficient. Unary signed schedule measures doubled phases, folds counts, needsprior signalhalf/sign; SOS branch is relative shiftedband notphysicalenergyzero. Unary orchestration only qdk_sparse_state_simulator duecurrentrecursiveQ#QIRloweringlimit. QpeResult lacksfullhistograms/decoderprovenance; standard/iterative no generalaliasresolver. Tutorial timealignment isknown-referencevalidation, notunknownenergy strategy. Ordinarycore separate/SOScore included.

lessons.title: Overlap tests and success amplification
lessons.body:
# Lesson 22 — Overlap tests and success amplification

## An energy number does not describe the whole state

Two trial states can have similar energy expectations but different overlaps with the desired eigenstate. Two time-evolution circuits can agree on occupation probabilities yet differ in relative phase. After learning expectation estimation and QPE, we need tools that reveal coherent overlap information and, under specific assumptions, increase the probability of a desired outcome.

The continuing chemistry problem is neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å in the selected active model. These methods do not change that model or supply a missing exact ground-state oracle. Their benefit depends on the trial state, the definition of success, the cost of testing success, and the validity of reversible circuit composition.

This lesson first derives the Hadamard test, then amplitude amplification, and finally the repository’s QPE-based subspace-marking oracle. The last has an important exact-phase-grid restriction: its current temporary-ancilla design is not a general robust off-grid spectral filter. All examples and calculations here are source-backed descriptions or hand-worked toys, not executions.

## The complex quantity measured by a Hadamard test

Let a compatible state-preparation operation produce \(|\psi\rangle\), and let \(U\) be a unitary. Define

\[
z=\langle\psi|U|\psi\rangle.
\]

This number can be complex. Its magnitude measures how much the evolved state overlaps the original; its phase carries information not visible in a simple probability comparison. For time evolution, \(z(t)=\sum_k|c_k|^2e^{-iE_kt}\) when \(|\psi\rangle=\sum_k c_k|E_k\rangle\). Thus it depends on the energy distribution, not only on its mean or its minimum.

Prepare a control in \(|+\rangle\) and apply controlled U. The joint state becomes

\[
\frac{|0\rangle|\psi\rangle+|1\rangle U|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]

The control’s X expectation is \(\operatorname{Re}z\), and its Y expectation is \(\operatorname{Im}z\). Accordingly,

\[
P_X(0)=\frac{1+\operatorname{Re}z}{2},\qquad
P_Y(0)=\frac{1+\operatorname{Im}z}{2},
\]

where zero means the +1 eigenvalue of the selected control observable. Two separate measurement ensembles are needed to estimate both components. One shot cannot reveal the complete complex overlap.

The sign of the imaginary part depends on the precise controlled-U and measurement conventions. The repository’s [`HadamardTest.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/HadamardTest.qs) uses H, then the supplied controlled operation, then `MResetX` or `MResetY`. Its [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_hadamard_test.py) compare the Y result with the **positive imaginary part** of \(\langle\psi|U|\psi\rangle\), not its negative.

A local decomposition of Y measurement would apply \(S^\dagger\) followed by H before Z measurement. A different S/S-dagger convention changes the sign. For an illustrative eigenstate with \(U|\psi\rangle=e^{-i\pi/4}|\psi\rangle\), the X expectation is \(1/\sqrt2\) and Y expectation is \(-1/\sqrt2\). This is analytic phase arithmetic, not a measured molecular result.

The Q# routine resets the system before measuring the control. An unconditional local reset of the system preserves the reduced state of the control, so this does not change the overlap statistic. It does mean the system is not returned for reuse. Each shot starts with state preparation again.

## Counts, errors, and state-to-state overlaps

For either basis, the estimated component is \((n_0-n_1)/(n_0+n_1)\). Under independent repeated shots, a component with true mean m has sample-mean variance \((1-m^2)/N\), at most \(1/N\). A plug-in estimate and finite-sample confidence qualifications follow the discussion in Lesson 20. Zero observed variance does not prove perfect accuracy, and coherent circuit approximation or noise can bias the mean independently of shot count.

The two parts may be combined into \(\widehat z=\widehat x+i\widehat y\). Its magnitude squared is not automatically an unbiased fidelity estimate, and \(|z|^2\) here is the overlap between \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(U|\psi\rangle\), not necessarily the ground-state fidelity. Always state which states are being compared.

For two pure states prepared by unitary extensions \(A_\psi\) and \(A_\phi\), their overlap can in principle be written

\[
\langle\phi|\psi\rangle=\langle0|A_\phi^\dagger A_\psi|0\rangle.
\]

That suggests a Hadamard test of a composed unitary, but it requires a realizable adjoint, consistent ancillas, and correct relative phases. A nonunitary density object, CC amplitude container, or arbitrary pair of wavefunction files cannot simply be passed to this interface as an overlap oracle. The shipped high-level Hadamard method accepts a `UnitaryRepresentation`, not two Wavefunctions or an arbitrary second Circuit in place of U. A supported representation/mapper or an explicitly engineered compatible unitary is still needed.

A global phase of a standalone U becomes a relative control-branch phase and changes z. The up-to-global-phase circuit rewrites discussed in Lesson 17 are therefore not automatically safe before adding control. An overall global phase of the complete controlled experiment is different and does not affect its probabilities.

## The actual Hadamard-test workflow

The registered algorithm is `hadamard_test/qdk`; the separately registered builder is `hadamard_test_circuit_builder/qdk`. The [orchestrator](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hadamard_test/hadamard_test.py) uses that builder by fixed name rather than exposing a general nested builder-selection setting.

Its settings are `test_basis="X"`, `controlled_circuit_mapper=AlgorithmRef("controlled_circuit_mapper","pauli_sequence")`, and `circuit_executor=AlgorithmRef("circuit_executor","qdk_full_state_simulator")`. X and Y are the supported basis choices; Z is rejected. The run signature is `run(state_preparation_circuit, unitary, shots)`, requiring a Circuit, a UnitaryRepresentation, and a positive integer shot count.

The [builder base](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hadamard_test/circuit_builder/base.py) sets control index zero on the nested controlled mapper. The [native builder](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hadamard_test/circuit_builder/qdk_builder.py) requires Q# callables for preparation and controlled evolution and creates a Q# factory on `[control | target register]`. It does not automatically convert a QASM-only preparation into a composable Q# operation.

Its target width is `unitary.get_num_qubits()`. For a Pauli product formula this is the system width. For a block encoding it includes structural block ancillas, and the state preparation is handed that enlarged register. A chemical state loader expecting exactly the system-only width is not universally compatible. A loader adding workspace beyond the unitary container’s structural width is not automatically accommodated either. There is no explicit shared-gradient ownership logic or complete encoding/orbital compatibility proof in this builder.

The default Pauli mapper therefore has a clear supported pattern: first build a time-evolution `UnitaryRepresentation`, then test its overlap on a compatible state. Other configured mappers retain their own limits, including CSWAP vacuum preservation and PSP layout/workspace assumptions. Merely changing the AlgorithmRef does not prove an arbitrary block/SOSSA unitary is supported.

The high-level run returns `CircuitExecutorData` directly: count dictionaries, shot information, and executor data, not a precomputed complex number or an EnergyExpectationResult. It has no `noise` argument in its own run signature and does not forward a noise profile. To study an explicitly noisy test through available executor support, construct the circuit with the builder and invoke a compatible executor separately; that is a different workflow, not an undocumented high-level parameter.

A source-backed, unexecuted usage pattern is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef

# trial_circuit and unitary_plan already satisfy the same register/encoding contract.
real_test = create(
    "hadamard_test", "qdk", test_basis="X",
    circuit_executor=AlgorithmRef("circuit_executor", "qdk_full_state_simulator", seed=42),
)
# In an authorized execution: counts = real_test.run(trial_circuit, unitary_plan, shots=1000).bitstring_counts
# Repeat with a separately configured test_basis="Y" to estimate the imaginary part.
```

The [repository example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/hadamard_test.py) builds the target evolution before calling this method. Its hydrogen example and the water test fixture are not the stretched-nitrogen baseline. Their references compare with the same constructed finite product-formula unitary, not a claim of exact arbitrary molecular propagation.

## Amplification needs a precisely defined good subspace

An amplitude-amplification problem starts with a preparation \(A|0\rangle=|\psi\rangle\) and a **good subspace**, represented by a projector \(\Pi_G\). The success probability is

\[
p=\langle\psi|\Pi_G|\psi\rangle.
\]

The good subspace may mean a flagged computational pattern or a specified spectral region. It is not necessarily one ground eigenvector. A predicate must distinguish good from bad coherently, without revealing which branch occurred.

Write the normalized state as \(|\psi\rangle=\sin\theta|G\rangle+\cos\theta|B\rangle\), with \(p=\sin^2\theta\). The normalized good and bad components span a two-dimensional plane. Define reflections

\[
R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I,
\qquad S_G=I-2\Pi_G.
\]

Applying the good reflection and then the prepared-state reflection rotates the state in this plane. With these conventions, after k rounds the good probability is

\[
p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).
\]

Different texts attach an overall minus sign to a differently defined reflection; the physical probability formula does not justify dropping relative phases inside the implementation. The repository’s actual order follows the two reflections defined above.

For a hand-worked example, \(p=1/4\) means \(\theta=\pi/6\). One round gives success one; two rounds return it to one-quarter. This is **overshooting**: more rounds are not always better. If p is unknown, choosing rounds requires an estimate or an additional robust strategy. This implementation supplies fixed integer rounds, not automatic amplitude estimation, fixed-point amplification, or a general unknown-success scheduler.

For small known p, the first maximum occurs at a round count of order \(1/\sqrt p\). Rejection sampling would need order \(1/p\) independent preparations to obtain one success under its assumptions. The quadratic statement counts ideal oracle uses; an expensive coherent predicate, adjoint, or state preparation can erase its practical advantage.

## How the generic implementation realizes the reflections

The algorithm `amplitude_amplification/qdk_base` takes `state_prep_oracle: Circuit` and `good_state_oracle: Circuit`. The [only numerical setting](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/amplitude_amplification/amplitude_amplification.py) is `rounds=1`; zero is allowed and negative rounds raise. It returns a Circuit, not an executed probability estimate.

The preparation callable must have the action \(A\) on its declared argument register and a valid adjoint. The good-state callable has the form `(register, flag)`, flipping the flag if the register is good. A simple example in the [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_amplitude_amplification.py) uses a multi-controlled X to mark the all-ones basis state. That custom predicate is explicit Q# logic, not a newly registered generic “find my target state” method.

[`AmplitudeAmplification.qs`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/qsharp/src/AmplitudeAmplification.qs) reflects about the prepared state by applying \(A^\dagger\), reflecting about all-zero, and applying A. It reflects about good states by computing the flag, applying Z to the flag, and uncomputing the flag. The initial A is executed once, and each round adds one \(A^\dagger\) and one A. Thus the literal preparation/adjoint count is \(2k+1\), with two flag-oracle uses per round before any compiler simplification.

The Python wrapper checks that both Circuits contain Q# callables, but does not mathematically prove their unitarity, clean-workspace action, adjoint correctness, or encoding agreement. The Q# operation types require `Adj`. A measured circuit, unsupported callable capability, or dirty released ancilla cannot be made reversible merely by naming it an oracle.

The amplified Circuit’s factory measures the whole amplified register. Its `qsharp_op` exposes the same preparation/amplification without measurement for further composition. The returned Circuit currently omits explicit width, encoding, and shared-gradient metadata; preserve those contracts externally rather than treating the output as self-describing for every downstream consumer.

The input preparation’s declared width is used when available. Otherwise the wrapper attempts a resource estimate and reads its logical qubit count. That fallback can conflate peak scratch-inclusive width with argument width if a custom preparation does not declare its interface precisely. It can also fail if the input Circuit lacks an estimatable representation. A declaration from the actual producer is preferable to relying on that fallback.

A garbage-entangled preparation is not universally invalid for amplification: if all garbage is retained inside the amplified register and A has the correct inverse, the reflected state is the complete joint state. But the desired good projector must refer to that joint contract. An alias-sampling index marginal is not a clean chemical trial state, and a phase-gradient catalyst sitting outside the reflected all-zero convention needs special handling. This generic wrapper does not implement the shared-gradient exclusions that the unary QPE builder does.

## The shipped QPE-subspace oracle marks energies above a bound

The separate registered family is `amplitude_amplification_oracle`, whose implementation/default is `qdk_qpe_subspace`. Its [source](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/amplitude_amplification/qpe_subspace.py) has two settings: required finite `energy_lower_bound` (default NaN) and `qpe_circuit_builder=AlgorithmRef("qpe_circuit_builder","qdk_standard")`. Phase bits, unitary settings, and controlled mapper belong inside that nested builder, not at the oracle’s top level.

Despite the course’s ground-state motivation, this predicate marks decoded energies **greater than or equal to** the lower bound. There is no accompanying upper-bound setting, no default “lowest-energy” predicate, and no automatic ground-state identification. For an ordinary Pauli Hamiltonian, deliberately negating H can turn a lower-energy target of H into an upper-energy target of −H, with consistent thresholds and phase decoding. That is a model/operator transformation you must perform and track; it is not an automatic option and cannot be transferred blindly to structured SOS data.

The oracle’s run takes the Hamiltonian alone. It builds standard coherent QPE with a no-op state preparation, because the supplied register already contains the state under test. It uses the builder’s measurement-free Q# callable, not its measured standalone factory. Iterative builders are rejected: a classical sequence of majority votes and reprepared systems is not a coherent circuit that can be uncomputed. A Qiskit standard builder can pass the Python class check but does not supply the required native Q# callable in this path. Use the actual supported native composition rather than infer support from inheritance.

Supported useful combinations include a Pauli product formula with controlled Pauli mapping and an LCU walk with controlled PSP, subject to their width/phase contracts. A bare LCU block lacks the needed energy-phase law. SOSSA is not made supported by possessing a decoder: no standard controlled mapper accepts its Adj-only block. Unary QPE is likewise not a substitute for the required standard builder.

## Enumerating phase bins and respecting aliases

For m phase qubits the implementation examines all \(2^m\) bins. It calls the selected container’s `eigenvalue_from_phase` for each bin, keeps bins whose decoded energy reaches the lower bound, and coalesces consecutive accepted indices into sorted, disjoint half-open intervals `[lower, upper)`. For quantum-walk containers it canonicalizes mirrored bins so that an inclusive energy threshold treats both walk branches consistently.

This is exhaustive **classical bin enumeration**, not a constant-cost analytic threshold calculation. Its work grows exponentially with the phase-register width even if the final accepted range list is short. It does not use the actual eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian to know which accepted bins have support.

No accepted bins or every bin accepted are rejected because neither identifies a proper phase-register subspace to amplify. The bounds follow the container’s actual decoder, including time-evolution wrapping or the cosine walk law. A time-evolution energy alias chosen by the principal branch is not corrected by this enumeration. The energy bound must use the same energy convention as the decoder: ordinary molecular Pauli/LCU input omits the core scalar, whereas a decoder that includes a shift would require its total-energy convention. Do not use a total molecular bound against active-only decoded energies.

The Q# `MarkPhaseRange` routine marks integer bins through equality or lower/upper comparisons. Interior intervals use temporary comparison flags that are uncomputed. `MarkAcceptedPhase` combines interval predicates; disjointness matters because a bin flipped twice would become unmarked. The generated ranges have that property; the low-level operation is not a general automatic repair of overlapping user intervals.

The [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_amplitude_amplification.py) verify exact inclusive energy comparisons, wraparound ranges, mirrored walk bins, missing/invalid bounds, and exact-grid interior eigenstates. For example, the shipped upper-band demonstration marks bins `[0,3)` and `[14,16)` of a 16-bin walk register. That is a specific reference fixture, not a computed nitrogen filter.

## Finite-resolution tagging is not an exact spectral oracle

The intended coherent marking pattern is: allocate phase and signal ancillas, run QPE, flip a flag for accepted bins, then run QPE-adjoint. If every relevant eigenphase lies exactly on a resolved bin and both walk branches are classified consistently, the phase/workspace can return clean while the flag records good/bad membership.

Off-grid phases produce a distribution \(a_y(E)\) over bins. A measured phase filter would accept an eigencomponent with probability \(\sum_{y\in T}|a_y(E)|^2\), where T is the accepted set. That is a soft finite-resolution spectral response, not a perfect projector onto a sharply bounded energy eigenspace. Nearby energies, degeneracies, approximation errors, and wrap boundaries influence the response.

There is a stronger current implementation limit. Copying the accepted/not-accepted bit to a flag can entangle it with the finite-resolution phase distribution. QPE-adjoint then does not generally return the temporary phase register to zero. The shipped `MarkQPEPhase` allocates and releases those ancillas internally, and its own Python documentation warns that off-bin phases leave residual amplitude there. This is not a robust arbitrary off-grid oracle with an automatically quantified approximation; it can violate the clean-ancilla promise required for the construction.

Increasing m can reduce leakage but does not by itself prove exact clean release. A different robust filtering design might retain phase/workspace as part of the amplified Hilbert space or explicitly account for approximation and cleanup; that is not what this wrapper presently implements. Consequently the ideal two-dimensional amplification formula must not be promised for arbitrary nitrogen phases using this oracle merely because the circuit object can be constructed.

The successful supplied amplification fixtures deliberately use exact phase-grid energies, including nontrivial interior walk eigenvalues with both branches. They establish meaningful implemented behavior under that promise, not a general theorem for all molecular spectra. No such tests or circuits are executed here.

## A source-backed exact-grid demonstration

The following is an unexecuted version of the [repository demonstration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/amplitude_amplification.py). It is a two-qubit toy, deliberately targeting the upper state rather than claiming a nitrogen ground-state filter:

```python
import math
import numpy as np
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import AlgorithmRef, Configuration, ModelOrbitals, QubitOperator, StateVectorContainer, Wavefunction

h = QubitOperator(["ZI", "IZ"], np.array([-math.pi / 4, -math.pi / 4]))
```
