lessons.title: Executing circuits and connecting frameworks
lessons.body:
# Lesson 25 — Executing circuits and connecting frameworks

## “Run the circuit” can mean several different things

The preceding lessons constructed chemical models, trial states, and quantum circuits. We now reach an execution boundary. Generating a gate description, compiling it into QIR, simulating it on a classical computer, and submitting it to a quantum device are different operations with different prerequisites and evidence.

A successful classical simulation can validate the action of a small circuit. It does not demonstrate that a physical processor can run it reliably, that it is faster than the best classical chemistry method, or that its chemical model predicts experiment. A resource estimate is another kind of result again: a conditional calculation of cost under specified assumptions, not an executed experiment.

Our main scientific record remains neutral singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å in the selected active model. The external-framework examples below use other small molecules and models; none supplies new nitrogen results. This lesson is based entirely on source and test inspection. No imports, compilations, simulations, device jobs, credentials, or network provider operations are performed here.

## The executor contract

The [`CircuitExecutor` interface](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_executor/base.py) takes a Circuit, a shot count, and an optional QuantumErrorProfile, and returns CircuitExecutorData. The family’s default registered implementation is `qdk_sparse_state_simulator`. The other native adapter is `qdk_full_state_simulator`; the optional Qiskit Aer plugin registers `qiskit_aer_simulator`.

“Native” here means the adapter is maintained in QDK Chemistry. The actual QDK language runtime/simulator or Qiskit Aer numerical engine is an external dependency. This repository does not contain a newly written full-state simulator merely because it exposes a class with that name.

A shot executes a program’s preparation, gates, measurement, and result logic under its backend contract. The ordinary executor interface returns sampled measurement data, not a dense wavefunction. Supplying a state-preparation circuit that returns Unit is not the same as supplying a program returning the Result array expected by the native histogram adapter. Measurement wrappers, QPE builders, and Hadamard-test builders provide explicit readout programs for that reason. There is no general rule that every Circuit automatically measures all its qubits at the end.

The common abstract executor interface does not enforce every possible positivity/type constraint on `shots`; concrete paths delegate important validation to their backend or enclosing algorithm. Use a positive integer and check the returned counts rather than assume successful construction establishes a valid measurement request.

## Dense, sparse, and structured classical simulation

A generic pure state of q qubits has \(2^q\) complex amplitudes. A **state-vector simulator** stores and updates those amplitudes. In complex128 arithmetic, just the raw vector uses \(16\times2^q\) bytes. At q=30 that is 16 GiB, before indices, work arrays, compiled circuits, or parallelization. This is illustrative memory arithmetic, not a measurement of a backend in this session.

A **sparse-state simulator** stores supported basis states rather than every basis index. It can be efficient for circuits whose state remains sparse in that basis. Sparsity is not preserved by all useful gates: H on many independent qubits can turn one supported bitstring into exponentially many, and interacting evolution can quickly spread support. A sparse input CI list does not guarantee a sparse state throughout QPE or time evolution.

A **density matrix** represents mixed states, for example after averaging over unknown noise outcomes. It has \(4^q\) complex entries; a 15-qubit dense density matrix already has the same raw-entry count as a 30-qubit statevector. Noise can also be simulated through sampled trajectories rather than explicitly storing that matrix, depending on the external backend. The QDK Chemistry adapter does not prescribe all those internal numerical choices.

A **stabilizer** simulation tracks a structured description of states reachable through Clifford operations and compatible measurements/noise. Clifford gates map Pauli operators to Pauli operators under conjugation. This permits efficient classical methods for a special circuit family, not a way to cheaply execute arbitrary non-Clifford chemistry rotations. A method option named `clifford` is not permission to approximate unsupported rotations silently.

Tensor-network and matrix-product-state methods exploit limited entanglement or suitable contraction structure. Their intermediate dimensions can grow strongly with entanglement, and truncation can introduce approximation when used. They are not universally efficient alternatives to statevectors. We discuss them because the Aer adapter accepts those method names, not because this repository implements or guarantees every external method’s availability on the current machine.

## The two QDK adapters take different paths

The [native adapters](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/circuit_executor/qdk.py) both default to seed 42. Full-state execution has setting `type="cpu"`, with accepted values `cpu`, `gpu`, and `clifford`. The constructor argument is named `simulator_type`, while the registry setting is `type`. Accepted strings are configuration options, not evidence that a GPU or every required backend feature is installed.

`qdk_full_state_simulator` calls `circuit.get_qir()`, converts a supplied error profile to QDK NoiseConfig, and calls external `run_qir` with shots, noise, seed, and type. Existing QIR can be used directly; a Q# factory may first compile; QASM-only input uses the Circuit conversion path described in Lesson 17. A rendered native circuit object alone does not necessarily supply executable QIR.

`qdk_sparse_state_simulator` first checks for Q# factory data. If present, it executes the factory in its owning QDK context with the ordered classical parameter values. This direct interpreter path can support a program that the current QIR compiler cannot lower. Without a factory, it obtains QASM and calls the external OpenQASM sparse-state execution function. A QIR-only Circuit therefore does not automatically enter a native sparse-QIR path: obtaining QASM may require the optional Qiskit conversion machinery.

The presence of both QASM and a factory is consequently meaningful. Different executors can prefer different stored representations. The Circuit object does not prove those descriptions are semantically identical. Keep them produced from the same source, with controlled phases, output ordering, and target profiles validated.

A concrete current example is unary phase estimation. Its orchestration permits only `qdk_sparse_state_simulator` because the recursive higher-order Q# schedule does not lower to QIR in the other path. That is an implementation restriction, not a general theorem that unary QPE cannot be represented as a circuit. Conversely, a QIR-oriented full-state executor cannot execute that workflow merely because both are labeled QDK.

## What seeds do and do not establish

The native adapters pass the configured seed to each backend call. A seed makes pseudorandom choices reproducible under compatible software/runtime conditions. It does not eliminate quantum sampling variation as a statistical concept, prove independent trials, or make a noisy model experimentally calibrated.

Reusing the same seed for repeated builds/executions can repeat a random sequence rather than supply independent evidence. Distinct seeds are useful for reproducibility studies, but backend/version changes can still change random-number consumption and outputs. The Aer adapter supplies `seed_simulator`; its ordinary transpilation calls do not set a separate `seed_transpiler`. Do not interpret one seed field as guaranteeing every compilation and simulation choice is identical across runs.

Raw counts also depend on what the circuit returns. The [QDK executor tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit_executor_qdk.py) prepare Bell-style circuits and a deterministic X on qubit 0, checking both histogram labels and raw results. These are examples of portable action/ordering checks. They are not tests run by this writer and not measured machine performance.

## Qiskit Aer: simulator choices and fake devices

The optional [`QiskitAerSimulator`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/circuit_executor.py) first calls `Circuit.get_qiskit_circuit()`. Its defaults are `method="statevector"`, `seed=42`, `transpile_optimization_level=0`, empty `device_backend_name`, and empty pre/post-transpilation pass lists.

Accepted method strings are `automatic`, `statevector`, `density_matrix`, `stabilizer`, `extended_stabilizer`, `matrix_product_state`, `unitary`, `superop`, and `tensor_network`. These are forwarded to Aer. Extended stabilizer techniques concern non-Clifford extensions of stabilizer simulation; a unitary method represents an entire circuit matrix, while a superoperator represents a channel on density matrices. Their storage can scale even more severely than a statevector. Some methods require particular builds/devices or are incompatible with measurement/noise features. The adapter does not expose every Aer option or prove that each method fits its own counts-returning path: a method intended to save a unitary is not automatically useful with the unconditional `get_counts()` call.

With a QuantumErrorProfile, the adapter builds an Aer NoiseModel and transpiles to its basis gates. Without a profile, it still transpiles using the default basis gates from an empty Aer NoiseModel. Optional pre/post pass names must come from the repository’s transpiler module; unknown names raise. Those passes can be state-specific or preserve only an overall phase, so they must not be used blindly before a later coherent control. Transpilation changes which gates receive gate-keyed noise and can change cost/noise behavior even if noiseless unitary action is preserved.

`device_backend_name` refers **only to a fake backend**, such as `fake_manila`. The adapter constructs a `Fake...V2` class from `qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider`, builds Aer from it, and transpiles against that synthetic device description. The value must start with `fake_`; an unknown class or missing optional dependency raises. An explicit noise profile and a fake-device name are mutually exclusive.

The [plugin registration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/__init__.py) loads the IBM fake-provider module but does not register a live IBM hardware executor. The inspected executor never creates an authenticated runtime service, submits a remote quantum job, or waits in a real hardware queue. “Device backend simulation” in the tests is still classical Aer execution. A real-device integration would need a separately supported submission/authentication/result contract; none was contacted or assumed here.

After execution, Aer returns its count dictionary and a raw Aer result in `CircuitExecutorData`. It does not populate QDK-style loss bitstrings. The [Aer adapter tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_interop_qiskit_circuit_executor.py) check simple measurement circuits, noise-profile use, and fake-device validation. A passing small example is not evidence that all methods, dynamic circuits, or devices work interchangeably.

## Noise is a quantum process, not just corrupted output text

A **quantum channel** describes how a state changes when information may pass to an environment or an unobserved random process. Gate noise can alter amplitudes and coherence before measurement; it is not generally equivalent to flipping a bit in the final histogram.

The chemistry-side class is [`QuantumErrorProfile`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/noise_models.py). It stores a name, description, and a mapping from supported gate names to error-type/rate entries. The currently exposed error types are only `depolarizing_error` and `qubit_loss`. There are no profile entries here for arbitrary amplitude damping, coherent overrotation, general Kraus channels, or independently parameterized X/Y/Z error probabilities. An external simulator might support more, but this adapter does not expose that whole catalog.

**Depolarizing noise** mixes the state toward a fully mixed state on the affected gate subsystem. One common convention is

\[
\mathcal D_p(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+pI/d,
\]

where \(\rho\) is a normalized density matrix and d is subsystem dimension. Another convention describes a total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error. Those parameters differ by normalization factors. The chemistry adapters forward the supplied rate to external QDK `set_depolarizing` or Aer `depolarizing_error` without an independently derived cross-library calibration. Verify the relevant external version’s convention before comparing equal numeric rates as equal physical noise. The equation is explanatory, not a claim that this source review inspected all backend channel internals.

Qubit loss means the qubit’s measurement outcome is undefined, not simply zero or one with a higher error probability. A lost shot is tracked separately by the QDK adapter. How loss and depolarization compose in time is a simulator contract; the order of keys in the Python dictionary does not establish a universal physical channel-ordering model.

The profile constructor normalizes supported gate/error names and checks that rates are numeric. It does **not** enforce a complete finite probability interval at construction. Invalid, negative, non-finite, or otherwise unphysical rates may fail later or have backend-dependent behavior; supply valid probabilities and check external constraints instead of treating construction as certification. The default profile has no errors, not a realistic device calibration.

Gate classes include one-, two-, and three-qubit operations. Profile `basis_gates` excludes measurement/reset-like entries. Converting to QDK rewrites names such as `sdg` to `s_adj`, `tdg` to `t_adj`, `sxdg` to `sx_adj`, and `measure` to `mresetz`; unavailable gate attributes raise. For each gate it sets depolarizing noise and/or loss on the external configuration.

The [Aer noise adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/qiskit/_interop/noise_model.py) supports depolarizing errors on recognized gate arities and explicitly rejects qubit loss. It uses a uniform all-qubit error for each selected gate type, not arbitrary location-specific hardware calibration. A supported gate-name enum does not guarantee every backend accepts that gate in its noise basis. Existing [noise tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_noise_models.py) and [Aer-noise tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_interop_qiskit_noise_model.py) check these conversions and rejections.

Synthetic gate errors are not the logical failure model of an error-correcting code. They also do not by themselves describe drift, leakage, correlated faults, calibration changes, or chemistry-model error. Later QEC/resource estimation needs its own explicitly justified assumptions.

## Results, loss, ordering, and normalization

[`CircuitExecutorData`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/circuit_executor_data.py) holds `bitstring_counts`, `total_shots`, `executor`, optional `loss_bitstrings`, and an in-memory raw executor metadata object. QDK fills that raw object with per-shot results; Aer fills it with its backend result.

The QDK conversion recognizes only string forms `Zero`, `One`, and `Loss`. It reverses each returned result sequence into the standardized histogram string, placing the first returned measurement at the right. Any shot containing Loss goes into the separate dictionary, with `L` at the relevant position. Unexpected result labels raise rather than being silently treated as zero.

For example, raw `[One, Zero]` becomes `01`. A Bell circuit returning the two system measurements should yield only `00`/`11` in an ideal noiseless model. Those conventions are pinned by tests. But a returned measurement sequence need not list every allocated qubit: identity positions may be omitted by the measurement wrapper, QPE returns phase bits only, and other programs can choose their result order. Do not equate string length with peak circuit width or the underlying electron-mode count.

A dense state dump has a separate amplitude-index convention determined by its simulator and wire ordering. Histogram reversal is not a universal recipe for converting every statevector. The course’s earlier Q# dump, Pauli-label, and determinant-order distinctions still apply. The common executor output is sampled counts, not an automatically available full state dump.

Aer counts are forwarded as Aer returns them. Multiple classical registers can introduce formatting conventions such as spaces that downstream chemistry parsers may not accept as a binary integer. The adapter does not flatten every possible output schema into the native Result-array format. Use a tested measurement layout and explicit parsing conventions.

In normal QDK noisy runs, clean plus loss counts account for total shots. Clean counts alone can be smaller than `total_shots`, or empty. Normalizing only surviving shots conditions on survival and may bias an observable if loss depends on the state. The expectation estimator currently consumes clean counts only and errors on no clean counts; iterative QPE’s majority comparison can instead choose zero when neither result is present. These are consumer-specific behaviors, not a universal successful fallback.

Serialization preserves basic counts, executor name, total shots, and loss dictionaries, but does not generally serialize the arbitrary raw metadata object. Keep compiled program identity, model/basis/sector, profile, seed, versions, and rejected-shot accounting separately if the result must support scientific review. More digits in a count-derived energy cannot compensate for missing provenance.

## Profiles, readout, and ancillas must fit the backend

Mid-circuit measurements, reset, and feedback need a compatible target profile and importer. The current shared Q# context defaults to Adaptive_RIF, while the QASM-only `Circuit.get_qir` fallback requests Base. The QIR-to-Qiskit converter supports specific direct-result branch structures, not arbitrary classical control flow or loops. A program that runs directly in the sparse interpreter may fail QIR lowering or a subsequent framework conversion.

Similarly, a callable that expects a preinitialized trailing phase-gradient register cannot be executed on only its system width. Some standalone factories initialize their own gradient; their resource behavior differs from a composed shared-gradient callable. `Circuit.num_qubits` is an argument-width declaration, not all internal scratch or physical qubits. A diagram that prunes apparently classical wires does not establish a reduced executable circuit.

A serialized factory-derived Circuit commonly retains QIR but not the live Q# callable or factory. It may remain executable through one backend while no longer supporting native composition or unary interpretation. “It serialized successfully” does not mean all of its prior capabilities survived.

## OpenFermion: operator interoperability, not hardware execution

The [OpenFermion example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/interoperability/openFermion/molecular_hamiltonian_jordan_wigner.py) constructs a LiH active Hamiltonian, maps it through the optional plugin, converts the QDK Pauli operator to an OpenFermion operator, diagonalizes a small matrix, and converts it back. This is an operator/data handoff and classical reference calculation, not a circuit-execution backend.

The conversion routines preserve complex Pauli coefficients and translate explicit qubit indices into rightmost-qubit-zero dense labels. The native molecular integral convention is chemist order; the [plugin conversion](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/openfermion/conversion.py) performs the required tensor permutation and one-half scaling when constructing OpenFermion interaction tensors. The plugin maps in blocked spin order and removes the core scalar from its ordinary mapped output to follow QDK’s active-operator convention.

Third-party mapping dispatch uses `MajoranaMapping.base_encoding` by name, not a supplied custom table. Its output width can also be inferred from surviving nonidentity terms; zero/identity-only or trailing-unused-mode cases need explicit attention. Use active matrix dimension rather than an unrelated full-MO count when establishing the intended mapping size. A round-trip coefficient check does not prove correct electron sector or total-energy reconstruction.

The [sample test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_sample_workflow_openfermion.py) compares full qubit-matrix ground energies from matching mapped operators. That establishes a representation comparison for its fixture, not a general fixed-electron-sector chemistry reference. The example’s active operator ground value is not automatically the SCF total energy printed elsewhere; the omitted scalar and physical sector must be handled explicitly.

## PennyLane and exact-evolution examples need their own validation

The [PennyLane example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/interoperability/pennylane/qpe_no_trotter.py) demonstrates an external QNode workflow: construct chemistry data, form a PennyLane fermionic/Pauli observable, place phase/system wires, apply controlled `qml.evolve`, inverse QFT, and inspect `qml.probs` on `default.qubit` with `shots=None`. That final object is an analytic simulator probability array, not finite-shot experimental counts or the registered CircuitExecutorData path. PennyLane is an example dependency, not a registered chemistry executor in the inspected plugin catalog.

Its “no Trotter” intention means using exact matrix-based evolution for a small represented operator, not an efficient arbitrary large Hamiltonian oracle. Classical matrix construction and simulation still scale exponentially. More importantly, the present example should not be copied as a validated universal adapter: it stacks the pair returned by `get_one_body_integrals()` rather than explicitly selecting the expected two-dimensional spin block, includes core energy in the external fermionic constant and later adds core again, and chooses among sign/period candidates by closeness to a known CASCI reference. These are source-visible interpretation/conversion hazards. The [sample test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_sample_workflow_pennylane.py) checks process completion when dependencies are present; it does not assert a complete correct energy/sector invariant. We have not run it or changed it.

The [Qiskit no-Trotter example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/interoperability/qiskit/iqpe_no_trotter.py) similarly uses `MatrixExponential` synthesis as a small reference route rather than a general registered fast simulator. It has local feedback and energy-decoding helpers, so their sign convention must be checked against the actual synthesized exponential rather than assumed identical to the native IQPE contract. Reference-guided alias selection can hide a sign or shift discrepancy; it is not a method for discovering an unknown energy branch.

These examples illustrate useful interoperability directions, but examples, smoke tests, adapter interfaces, and scientifically validated end-to-end results are different evidence levels. Prefer small analytic operator/action checks, explicit offsets, and nonpalindromic bit-order tests before transferring an external framework’s result into the main nitrogen record.

## RDKit begins at a different boundary

The [RDKit example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/interoperability/rdkit/sample_rdkit_geometry.py) starts with a molecular graph specified by SMILES, a compact notation for chemical connectivity. It adds hydrogens, embeds three-dimensional coordinates, and applies the UFF molecular-mechanics force field. A **conformer** is one spatial arrangement consistent with molecular connectivity; obtaining one does not prove it is the global minimum or relevant experimental state.

The converter extracts atomic symbols and coordinates, multiplying Angstrom coordinates by `ANGSTROM_TO_BOHR` before constructing a QDK Structure. Charge and spin multiplicity are separately supplied to the SCF calculation. The helper does not infer all electronic-state information, basis quality, solvation, or a converged quantum-chemical geometry from the RDKit object.

UFF is a parameterized force-field approximation, not the ab-initio energy surface used by the later SCF stage. The source explicitly warns that it may not yield high-quality geometries. The [RDKit test](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_sample_workflow_rdkit.py) uses a particular approximate water geometry and SCF reference as a regression check. It does not establish general conformer accuracy, molecular stability, or chemistry outside that fixture.

PySCF and geomeTRIC, discussed earlier, occupy still other boundaries: electronic-structure methods and geometry optimization. Their optional adapters retain their method-specific limitations—for example, the PySCF SCF adapter rejects any directly supplied BasisSet object, not merely a custom basis. Interoperability is explicit conversion plus a supported contract, not automatic interchangeability of every object named molecule, basis, state, or circuit.

## Dependency and platform boundaries are part of reproducibility

The pinned [`python/pyproject.toml`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/pyproject.toml) requires Python at least 3.10 and QDK at least 1.31.0, with NumPy/SciPy and other core dependencies. Optional extras separately cover OpenFermion, Qiskit, NetworkX, chemistry plugins, and QRE. Registration depends on optional library discovery; this source review does not imply those packages are installed.

The metadata contains real platform/version exclusions: PySCF in the plugins extra excludes Windows; OpenFermion is conditioned on Python below 3.14; much of the Qiskit/PennyLane stack is excluded on Windows ARM64; Aer has an additional Python/platform wheel condition; RDKit testing also excludes Windows ARM64. Such package constraints are not scientific restrictions, but they affect whether a proposed workflow can actually be reproduced. No dependency was installed or restored during this authoring task.

Library/runtime version changes can affect compilation, noise conventions, gate sets, random streams, and reference snapshots. Preserve versions alongside results, and prefer portable physical/mathematical invariants when deciding whether a change is acceptable.

## A minimal measurement program with an explicit consumer

This unexecuted example follows the measured-QASM shape used in the executor tests:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create
from qdk_chemistry.data import Circuit, QuantumErrorProfile

program = Circuit(qasm="""
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c[0] = measure q[0];
c[1] = measure q[1];
""", num_qubits=2)
profile = QuantumErrorProfile(errors={"cx": {"depolarizing_error": 0.001}})
executor = create("circuit_executor", "qdk_full_state_simulator", type="cpu", seed=42)
# Authorized execution: result = executor.run(program, shots=1000, noise=profile)
```

The error rate and shot count are illustrative. The circuit explicitly defines readout rather than assuming all qubits are sampled automatically. Its histogram would describe this Bell experiment, not an electronic energy. A noisy histogram is evidence about the supplied synthetic channel model, not about a particular device.

For a trustworthy execution record, retain the exact circuit/representation and its origin, target profile, backend and versions, seed policy, shot request, returned clean/loss counts, measurement ordering, compiler options, noise assumptions, and full chemical or model provenance. Check what was actually executed rather than relying on a class name or an attractive diagram.

We can now interpret an execution result without confusing it with a physical quantum demonstration. The next lesson assembles the entire evidence chain: which energy was computed, which approximations and uncertainties remain, and what a scientific team can responsibly conclude before asking how much a fault-tolerant implementation would cost.

lessons.title: Interpreting the scientific output
lessons.body:
# Lesson 26 — Interpreting the scientific output

## A precise number is the beginning of a review

Suppose a colleague sends the number −108.770051792909 Hartree and says that a quantum calculation reproduced a nitrogen ground-state energy. The first task is not to admire its decimal places. It is to identify the molecule, model, state, operator, method, energy offset, measurement procedure, and reference that give the number meaning.

That number appears in the repository’s [completed tutorial record](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/ground_state_qpe_lab_notebook_completed.md). The record describes the documented QDK Chemistry 2.2.0 workflow, whose version pin is defined in [`tutorials/_versions.py`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/tutorials/_versions.py). We are reading that record at source revision `97a3ff4f`; we have not reproduced the computation in this session.

The target is neutral, intended-singlet N₂ at 1.85 Å, with a selected active-space Hamiltonian derived from the 28-spatial-orbital cc-pVDZ model. It is a fixed-nuclear-geometry electronic problem, not the equilibrium molecule’s free energy, a reaction rate, or experimental confirmation of quantum advantage. The separate notebook at 1.270025 Å is a different calculation and cannot silently supply missing evidence.

This lesson turns the entire workflow into an applied interpretation discipline. Each stage owns a different kind of statement. The final energy comparison is useful precisely when those statements remain separate.

## Reconstructing the recorded nitrogen chain

The [molecular input script](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/tutorial_describe_n2.py) fixes the bond distance, charge, and multiplicity, then compares two finite-basis Hartree–Fock calculations. The [active-space workflow tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_sample_tutorial_gs_qpe.py) record the subsequent valence and refined CASCI results.

The following are **recorded source reference values, not results executed here**:

| Stage | Reported total energy, Hartree | Meaning of the comparison |
|---|---:|---|
| HF, cc-pVDZ | −108.418633697214 | Single-determinant mean-field reference in the initial basis |
| HF, cc-pVTZ | −108.445215657498 | Sensitivity to changing the finite basis within HF |
| Valence CASCI, CAS(10e,8o), cc-pVDZ | −108.778369520882 | Correlated solution in the larger candidate active space |
| Refined CASCI, CAS(6e,6o), cc-pVDZ | −108.771051792909 | Algorithmic reference for the selected compact model |
| Documented modal IQPE reconstruction | −108.770051792909 | Result of the configured finite-bit, finite-shot tutorial protocol |

The HF basis change is about 26.582 milliHartree in magnitude. It measures sensitivity between two calculations, not the exact error of either basis relative to a complete-basis result. It also does not measure the missing correlation error of HF. Increasing basis flexibility and improving the many-electron state are different interventions.

The active-space reduction raises the recorded CASCI energy by 0.007317727973 Hartree, about 7.318 milliHartree, relative to the larger valence-space model. That is already larger than the tutorial’s later one-milliHartree algorithmic target. There is no contradiction: the later target asks whether the quantum workflow reproduces the **smaller selected Hamiltonian**, not whether that model equals the larger-space or real-molecule answer.

The candidate CAS(10e,8o) has fixed active populations (5,5) and 3,136 determinants. The refined CAS(6e,6o) has populations (3,3), 400 determinants, active full-MO indices 4–9, inactive indices 0–3, and eighteen excluded virtual orbitals. Indices are identifiers within a specified orbital representation, not universal chemical labels valid at another geometry.

The tutorial computes natural orbitals from correlated data and solves CASCI again; the recorded energy is unchanged by that representation change before reducing the active space. This is a meaningful consistency check. Merely receiving a localizer’s determinant carrier with rotated orbitals would not establish that the original correlated coefficients were preserved. The fresh correlated solve is part of the evidence chain.

The model is intended to target a singlet, but separate alpha/beta populations constrain spin projection, not generally total \(S^2\). An interpretation claiming certified spin purity needs suitable state evidence, not only `spin_multiplicity=1` at SCF or a count-derived metadata property. The reported fixed-sector reference should be described as the configured determinant-sector calculation with its stated intended physical state.

## Which object owns each constant

The term “total energy” is dangerous without a definition. In the ordinary active-space molecular route,

\[
H_{\mathrm{selected}}=E_{\mathrm{core}}I+H_{\mathrm{active}}.
\]

The scalar includes nuclear repulsion and constant frozen-inactive contributions. Interactions with inactive electrons also modify the active one-body matrix; freezing electrons is not just deleting their rows. A mapped identity Pauli coefficient is another contribution generated by operator algebra and is not automatically the same scalar.

The reference snapshot records

\[
E_{\mathrm{core}}=-99.117775726922,
\qquad E_{\mathrm{active}}=-9.653276065987,
\]

so their sum is the selected CASCI total −108.771051792909 Hartree. These component values and the recorded count of 247 retained Pauli terms are version-pinned snapshots in the [mapping tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_sample_tutorial_gs_qpe.py), not quantities assumed immutable across all software environments or representation choices. The portable check is that the mapped **same-sector** active eigenvalue plus its stored scalar agrees with the selected reference.

| Source of a number | What its value already contains | Correct bookkeeping action |
|---|---|---|
| SCF returned energy | Its solver’s molecular total-energy convention | Do not add nuclear repulsion again merely because orbitals were also returned |
| Native CAS/PMC returned total | Active solution plus the Hamiltonian’s core scalar | Compare with a matching model/sector, not a bare qubit eigenvalue |
| Ordinary mapped Pauli expectation or QPE energy | The supplied active Pauli operator, including its own identity term | Add `Hamiltonian.get_core_energy()` once for the selected molecular total |
| `Ansatz.calculate_energy()` on valid supported RDMs | Integral contraction plus stored core scalar | Do not add the same scalar again |
| SOSSA phase decoder | Shifted signal decoded with `energy_shift`, which already includes core | Do not apply the ordinary extra-core rule a second time |

An ECP changes the physical effective model: core-electron effects enter an effective potential and the explicit-electron count changes. It is not generally a single optional scalar to append to an otherwise all-electron energy. Compare consistent ECP/all-electron conventions and appropriate reference quantities; do not invent an energy for omitted core electrons and add it manually.

The lattice PPP background scalar is likewise a model charge-reference term, not automatically molecular nuclear repulsion. A field named `core_energy` can serve compatible algebraic bookkeeping while its physical origin differs by producer. Record that origin.

Orbital energies are not total energies. Summing occupied HF orbital eigenvalues double counts interaction contributions unless the appropriate energy expression is used, and correlated total energies are not obtained by summing natural occupations times arbitrary orbital energies. The returned energy and valid RDM contraction have specific contracts that must be followed.

## Validate the representation before interpreting the algorithm

The [nitrogen mapping script](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/tutorial_map_n2_to_qubits.py) validates in the 400-state (3,3) sector, not by taking the lowest eigenvalue of an unrestricted twelve-qubit Fock-space matrix. It adds the core scalar and compares with CASCI for exactly the selected orbitals. This isolates representation correctness from active-space quality.

The tensor convention matters to that check. Current molecular arrays are chemist ordered, with the mixed block alpha-pair on the left and beta-pair on the right. Flattened tensor positions, active-local indices, fermionic mode order, Pauli-string direction, and determinant phases all have explicit meanings. A permutation that changes representation must be applied to states and observables consistently. Equal qubit count and equal encoding strings do not prove equivalence.

A useful verification invariant is Hermiticity, \(H=H^\dagger\). Others include state normalization, the expected conserved-number sector, and correct small matrix action. The current classical qubit-solver wrappers can discard imaginary parts and do not generally enforce electron number; they cannot serve as universal references for arbitrary complex operators. The complex-preserving Pauli matrix utilities are useful for small explicit checks but remain exponentially costly.

Likewise, an exact round-trip through an external operator library checks representation under that round-trip’s conventions. It does not certify total-energy shifts, the physical sector, or equivalence to a real experiment. A smoke test that completes without exceptions is weaker still.

## Trial quality is not the same as algorithm success

The [trial-state script](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/tutorial_prepare_trial_state.py) ranks determinant support with deterministic near-tie handling, reoptimizes coefficients using PMC, then aligns trial and reference coefficients by determinant identity before taking a squared overlap. It does not use coefficient-list positions as though they were universal basis labels.

The recorded snapshot has one-, two-, and four-determinant fidelities about 0.48255, 0.58641, and 0.73239 relative to the selected-space CASCI state. The corresponding displayed preparation gate counts are 6, 14, and 30, all on twelve problem qubits. Those are source reference circuit statistics, not physical gate counts measured here. The leading determinant is expressed in the selected orbital gauge; its weight is not a basis-independent property of nitrogen.

Three conclusions are legitimate: this particular compact-state family improves overlap as support grows; the preparation circuits change cost; and the orbital register does not shrink just because fewer amplitudes are loaded. A fourth conclusion is not generally legitimate: that a complete fresh-state-per-bit IQPE run returns the ground energy with probability exactly 0.73239.

The current IQPE protocol reprepares the system for each bit/shot and concatenates majority decisions. Different components can influence different bits. Standard coherent QPE has a different branch-distribution interpretation. If success probability is needed for a resource calculation, specify the actual complete protocol and how success is defined rather than substituting a convenient fidelity number.

Near degeneracy, high overlap with an eigenspace can be more relevant than overlap with one arbitrarily chosen eigenvector inside it. Individual eigenvectors may rotate within a degenerate subspace without changing the physical spectrum. A state or orbital label should therefore be tracked by appropriate character, sector, and subspace, not only by sorted energy position.

## The one-milliHartree result and the coarse phase grid

The [documented IQPE chapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/tutorials/ground_state_molecular_energies_with_qpe/06_iterative_phase_estimation.rst) records twenty complete runs: `010000` appeared nineteen times and `001111` once. The modal active energy was −9.652276065987 Hartree; adding the stored core gave −108.770051792909, exactly one milliHartree above the selected reference to the displayed precision. These are **recorded development-run results**, not a distribution observed in this session.

The apparent precision conceals a crucial resolution distinction. The recorded evolution time is approximately 0.162738437655 inverse Hartree with six phase bits. Adjacent grid energies are about 0.6033 Hartree apart, not 0.001 Hartree apart. The chosen grid point is close to the known reference because the tutorial used that reference to tune the evolution time deliberately.

That is a legitimate implementation-validation exercise and an illegitimate general strategy for discovering an unknown energy. The reference was not merely compared afterward; it helped select a favorable grid. A report should state this dependence prominently rather than claim general milliHartree resolution from six bits.

The recorded 19/20 modal frequency is an empirical proportion for that configured protocol and seed set. It is not a proved future success probability, a 95% confidence guarantee, or evidence that every source of error is below one milliHartree. The rare neighboring outcome changes energy by a large grid interval. Reporting only the dominant value would hide that behavior.

A QpeResult from the core algorithms does not automatically store the complete histogram, decoder provenance, or all alias candidates. The tutorial’s surrounding record supplies additional context. For ordinary time evolution, principal-angle conversion leaves energies separated by \(2\pi/t\) ambiguous unless an appropriate prior interval is justified. For unary LCU/SOSSA protocols, the doubled-phase branch choice has its own signal-relative meaning. More decimal places in `raw_energy` do not resolve any of these ambiguities.

## Accuracy, precision, resolution, and uncertainty

**Accuracy** is agreement with the relevant target/reference quantity. **Precision** is repeatability or spread under stated conditions. **Resolution** is the spacing or distinguishability imposed by a numerical representation. **Uncertainty** summarizes what values remain plausible given the available evidence and assumptions.

An illustrative estimate with standard error 0.1 milliHartree but a model bias of 5 milliHartree is precise yet inaccurate relative to the broader target. Conversely, a fine phase grid can have poor accuracy because its evolution operator is wrong. Repeating a fixed seeded simulation and obtaining exactly the same output does not establish a narrow uncertainty from independent observations.

A confidence interval concerns the behavior of a statistical procedure under specified sampling assumptions. An empirical standard deviation describes spread among observed values; a standard error concerns uncertainty of an estimated mean. Intrinsic quantum variance describes the state’s outcome distribution for an observable. They are not interchangeable, and none automatically includes chemical-model bias.

Hartree conversion constants are supplied by the repository’s [`constants.hpp`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/constants.hpp). Approximately, one Hartree is 27.2114 eV or 627.509 kcal/mol, so one milliHartree is about 0.6275 kcal/mol. A named “chemical accuracy” target is a chosen requirement for a quantity, not a universal natural threshold guaranteeing every chemistry prediction is useful.

## A layered error budget, beginning with the physical question

The first layer is the physical Hamiltonian and nuclear description. A clamped-nuclei electronic calculation assumes fixed geometry and separates electronic from nuclear motion in the Born–Oppenheimer picture. Temperature, vibrational averaging, solvent, relativistic effects, external fields, or open-system coupling are not automatically present. An accurate solution of the chosen equation cannot repair terms that were deliberately omitted from it.

The second layer is the one-electron representation: finite AO basis, linear-dependence treatment, and any ECP. Compare basis sets while holding other assumptions fixed to assess sensitivity. A smaller basis-change difference is evidence, not proof of a complete-basis error bar; different approximations can cancel accidentally. Increasing basis size does not repair a single-determinant description of strong static correlation.

The third layer is the correlated model: active/inactive/virtual partition, determinant selection, and treatment of outside-space dynamical correlation. Low orbital entropy or occupation near zero/two is a diagnostic, not a rigorous bound on an omitted energy contribution. The nitrogen valence-to-refined energy change quantifies one specific comparison. It is not the full missing-correlation error of the refined model relative to all-electron full-basis chemistry.

MCSCF can adapt orbitals, selected CI can enlarge important determinant support, and coupled cluster or perturbation theory address other correlation regimes under their assumptions. They are not interchangeable corrections to be added without a compatible definition. Some correlated methods, including ordinary truncated coupled cluster, are nonvariational: a lower energy is not automatically a better upper bound to the exact model ground energy. The effective-Hamiltonian factory discussed earlier has no bundled concrete downfolding implementation; it cannot be invoked as an unspecified missing-error correction.

The fourth layer is numerical solution. SCF convergence, residual thresholds, iteration limits, orbital stability, CI eigensolver convergence, and nonlinear coupled-cluster convergence are not the same checks. A converged stationary solution can be unstable or the wrong state. A solver-returned object without checked convergence is not automatically accepted scientific evidence. Record the actual method/backend and relevant status rather than relying only on the final energy’s smooth-looking digits.

The fifth layer is operator approximation: integral screening, Cholesky/double-factorization truncation, Pauli screening, and changed normalization/shift representations. A tolerance on a residual matrix or coefficient is not itself an energy error bound. A representation-aware comparison can estimate a norm difference, or compare the same small model before/after approximation, but must include all changed constants and one-body corrections. Reconstructing a full four-index tensor can also defeat the memory assumptions of a supposedly compressed workflow.

## Circuit, state, and statistical error are different layers

The sixth layer is trial state and preparation. Support truncation, projected reoptimization, amplitude rounding, binary/sparse loading, and finite-precision QROM rotations can change the state in different ways. Classical fidelity to an accessible reference helps quantify one relation, but not the unknown true-molecule overlap. A coefficient-loading alias oracle with entangled garbage is not a clean trial state simply because its index probabilities match.

The seventh layer is Hamiltonian simulation and coherent control. A Trotter/Suzuki or Zassenhaus approximation differs from exact evolution; a fixed sampled qDRIFT unitary is not protected by an averaged-channel guarantee for all coherent uses. Power repetition can amplify base error. Controlled operations make previously global phases observable, so phase-dropping rewrites can become material even when a standalone state plot looks unchanged.

A finite-resolution QPE-subspace oracle can leave temporary phase ancillas dirty off the promised exact grid. In the current implementation, that is not merely another reported energy variance; it can invalidate the clean reversible-oracle premise of amplitude amplification. Likewise a requested time-dependent endpoint may fail the current unequal-final-step scale contract. A trustworthy report first establishes that the intended operation/time was realized, before estimating its error.

The eighth layer is readout and post-processing: phase-bin resolution, alias/branch selection, sample counts, grouping, majority votes, noise, and postselection. These can produce biases, discrete failures, or random fluctuations with different statistical models. Choosing the lowest observed QPE energy after many noisy runs is not an unbiased ground-energy estimator. Choosing a mode has its own meaning and must be accompanied by the complete distribution and tie rule.

The final layer, when moving beyond classical simulation, is physical implementation and logical failure under error correction. A requested logical error budget is a probability of faulty computation under a hardware/code model. It is not a bound on basis-set error or the distance between a trial expectation and a chemical ground energy. No physical quantum execution or QEC performance has been demonstrated by the records discussed here.

## Combining uncertainties only when the mathematics supports it

For independently justified deterministic energy-error bounds \(B_i\), the triangle inequality permits a conservative total bound \(\sum_i B_i\). It does not justify adding uncalibrated guesses as if they were certified. Error layers can interact, so the comparison path and scope of each bound must be stated.

For random zero-mean errors, variances add only with the appropriate covariance terms:

\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_i X_i\right)
=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).
\]

Quadrature combination of standard deviations assumes those covariance terms vanish or are otherwise modeled. Deterministic chemical biases should not be treated as independent random noise merely to produce a smaller total uncertainty.

For a difference of two estimated energies,

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat E_B-\widehat E_A)
=\sigma_B^2+\sigma_A^2-2\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat E_A,\widehat E_B).
\]

Shared approximations may cancel in an energy difference, but that cancellation must be investigated, not asserted from similar molecule names. Shared samples or common calibration can create statistical correlations as well.

Failure probabilities are a different unit. If separate bad events have bounded probabilities \(\delta_i\), a union bound gives a conservative probability at most \(\sum_i\delta_i\) that any occurs, without requiring independence. That does not turn those probabilities into Hartree uncertainties. A complete acceptance condition might specify both an energy-accuracy requirement and a probability of violating it, plus model assumptions that remain outside that statement.

When using operator-norm bounds, convert them to the relevant objective. A Hamiltonian perturbation bounded by \(\|\Delta H\|\) bounds a fixed normalized-state expectation change by that norm and can bound eigenvalue shifts under matching Hermitian finite-space assumptions. A unitary approximation bound is dimensionless; its effect on an expectation also involves the observable norm and the evolved state. Do not add such a number directly to an energy tolerance.

## Recalculating the uncertainty that grouped measurements need

For a QWC measurement group g, define each shot’s weighted score

\[
Y_g=\sum_{j\in g}h_jX_j,
\]

where \(X_j=\pm1\) is the Pauli outcome inferred from that shot. Then

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat E_g)=\frac1{n_g}
\left[\sum_jh_j^2\operatorname{Var}(X_j)
+2\sum_{j<k}h_jh_k\operatorname{Cov}(X_j,X_k)\right].
\]

The current [`qdk` expectation estimator](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/expectation_estimator/qdk.py) instead returns the diagonal plug-in sum of \(|h_j|^2(1-\widehat m_j^2)/n_g\). It omits within-group covariance and uses the plug-in n denominator rather than the unbiased n−1 correction for the mean-variance estimate. Its summary’s plus/minus square root is therefore not automatically a calibrated confidence interval.

A practical report should retain each group’s count dictionary and compute first/second moments of the score Y_g when grouped uncertainty matters. Positive covariance can increase error; negative covariance can reduce it. An eigenstate can have zero intrinsic Var(H) while separate Pauli measurements still have noisy means. These facts explain why a small `energy_variance` field is not a universal measure of state quality or algorithm correctness.

The shot request also is not necessarily the exact sampled total. The estimator allocates an equal floor share to nonidentity groups and drops the remainder. Identity-only groups are added classically. Native loss records are separate from clean counts, while the estimator uses clean counts and normalizes their sum. A survival-conditioned result can be biased if the discarded events are state-dependent. Report requested, allocated, clean, and lost counts separately when they differ.

Near a rare event, a short run can observe no failures and report zero empirical spread while substantial uncertainty remains. Approximate normal intervals can be poor in such cases. A repeated IQPE histogram with nineteen successes does not justify treating failure probability as exactly one twentieth, nor can a fixed seed set establish all future runtime environments. Statistical methodology should match the output type, rather than reusing one variance formula for expectations, modes, bit votes, and decoded phases.

## Regression references versus portable scientific checks

The [tutorial regression suite](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_sample_tutorial_gs_qpe.py) separates many portable invariants from optional exact snapshots. Examples of invariants include active-space counts, valid entropy ranges, normalized trial-state relationships, expected mapping dimensions, fixed-sector mapped/CASCI energy agreement, and consistent phase-grid decoding. Exact Pauli counts, detailed amplitudes, and circuit gate counts are guarded as version-pinned snapshots. Some small-model energy references are still checked numerically with explicit tolerances.

The snapshot mode enforces the tutorial’s public version, ignoring local build metadata. This is valuable provenance, not evidence that tests were executed here. The completed lab notebook’s statement that its required implementations passed belongs to that recorded workflow; it is not a fresh status claim from this lesson.

The repository’s [`reference_tolerances.py`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/reference_tolerances.py) distinguishes CI/SCF, plain-text, RDM, unitarity, and finite-shot comparison tolerances. Those tolerances define particular test acceptance criteria. They are not a universal total chemical error budget, and a stochastic test can occasionally fluctuate even when the underlying algorithm is unchanged.

Always distinguish absolute and relative tolerances. A comparison of the form \(|a-b|\le\mathrm{atol}+\mathrm{rtol}|b|\) can allow a surprisingly large absolute difference for a total energy near −108 Hartree. With zero absolute tolerance and relative tolerance \(10^{-5}\), the allowed difference is about 1.08 milliHartree. This is a mathematical illustration of why a seemingly small relative tolerance can be comparable to the entire teaching target. Use explicit units and justified scales for each invariant.

Global phase, determinant ordering, degenerate orbital rotations, and low-level compiler decompositions can change snapshots while preserving intended physics. Conversely, a smoke test or visually similar circuit can miss a wrong energy offset, mixed-spin permutation, lost phase, or incorrect sector. The strongest checks compare the intended mathematical action under a fully specified representation, not only a text string or process exit code.

## From an electronic energy to chemistry

Many chemical decisions depend on **energy differences**, not one absolute electronic energy. A reaction electronic energy compares products and reactants in compatible conventions. A barrier compares a transition-region configuration with a reactant minimum. A minimum is a locally stable geometry; a transition state has the appropriate unstable direction along a reaction path. One fixed stretched bond does not establish either an equilibrium structure or a reaction mechanism.

Measured equilibrium and rates often depend on free energy. **Zero-point energy** is vibrational energy remaining even at zero temperature. Thermal corrections account for thermally populated motions and states. **Entropy** quantifies the statistical multiplicity of accessible configurations. **Solvation free energy** accounts for environmental stabilization in a solvent. Pressure, concentration/standard-state conventions, conformer populations, and nuclear quantum effects can also matter.

Schematically, a chemical free-energy model combines electronic energy, zero-point and thermal contributions, entropy, and environment corrections. Those terms are not automatically appended by a fixed-geometry electronic solver or by QPE. A validated Hessian/vibrational workflow and appropriate thermodynamic treatment would be additional work, not information encoded in extra digits of the electronic result.

For an elementary transition-state-theory picture, a rate can have the form

\[
k\approx\kappa\frac{k_BT}{h}\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G^\ddagger}{k_BT}\right),
\]

where T is absolute temperature, \(k_B\) Boltzmann’s constant, h Planck’s constant, \(\Delta G^\ddagger\) the activation free energy per reacting entity, and \(\kappa\) a transmission factor correcting the idealized crossing assumption. Molar free energies require the matching molar gas constant instead of \(k_B\). This is a physical interpretation framework, not a rate calculator executed or claimed as a new built-in chemistry method here.

The [tutorial’s accuracy discussion](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/tutorials/ground_state_molecular_energies_with_qpe/01_energy_and_accuracy.rst) notes that at 298.15 K a one-milliHartree **free-energy** error can multiply an equilibrium/rate prediction by about 2.88 if other contributions are exact. It does not say an electronic QPE error automatically produces that exact experimental rate error. The exponential sensitivity explains why the target quantity and omitted contributions matter so much.

An electronic calculation can inform discovery, but it is not by itself a yield, drug efficacy, catalyst lifetime, manufacturing cost, or product value. Such conclusions require additional models and measurements. Comparing with experiment should match state, geometry/environment, temperature, observable, and uncertainty. Comparing with classical methods should use the best relevant methods and the same target/model accuracy, not an artificially weak baseline.

## An acceptance record a team can actually use

The repository’s [lab-notebook template](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/tutorials/ground_state_molecular_energies_with_qpe/lab_notebook.rst) already separates goal, model, mapping, trial state, and phase estimation. A technical report can extend it into the following acceptance record without claiming that every item has already been demonstrated:

**Scientific claim.** State the observable and reference: for this record, fixed-geometry selected-space total energy for the specified N₂ model, compared with its same-sector CASCI reference. State separately whether the goal is implementation validation, improved chemistry, or a physical quantum demonstration.

**Model identity.** Record geometry and units, charge, intended/verified spin information, basis/ECP choice, active/inactive indices and orbital representation, explicit electron populations, and any fitted or omitted interactions. Identify the larger-space and basis comparisons as sensitivity evidence, not automatically calibrated uncertainty.

**Energy ledger.** Record the object supplying each active, identity, nuclear/frozen-core, and SOS/background shift. Give the exact reconstruction expression. Confirm that the comparison uses the same total-energy convention and no constant is added twice.

**Numerical and state evidence.** Name solver/backend, convergence and stability evidence, operator/Hermiticity/sector checks, support-selection and coefficient-optimization method, reference overlap definition, normalization, and preparation representation. Distinguish intended trial fidelity from complete-protocol success.

**Quantum protocol.** Record mapping and mode order, unitary family, time/normalization/shift, powers and approximation settings, controlled-mapper assumptions, phase bits/window/branch rule, and any reference-guided parameter tuning. State which capabilities or cleanup promises were actually verified.

**Sampling and outputs.** Preserve full available histograms or per-bit records, requested/allocated/usable/lost shots, independent-run/seed policy, estimator formula including covariance handling, tie/postselection rules, and the exact fields used to calculate the reported number. Missing provenance is a limitation, not an invitation to infer it from a plot.

**Scope of acceptance.** Separate energy bias estimates, statistical uncertainty, probability of failure, and exclusions. For the completed tutorial record, the defensible statement is agreement of a configured, reference-guided classical simulation of IQPE with its compact-model CASCI reference at the one-milliHartree boundary—not experiment-level nitrogen accuracy or practical quantum advantage. This course-writing session performed no new verification run.

This record can be reviewed before any hardware-cost calculation. It makes explicit what a future implementation is being asked to reproduce, how success will be judged, and what remains outside the claim.

## The handoff to resource estimation

Four evidence levels must remain distinct: correct simulation of a specified circuit; favorable algorithmic asymptotic scaling; conditional feasibility under a fault-tolerant hardware/QEC model; and demonstrated practical advantage over the best relevant alternative. None automatically proves the next.

The logical workload must include all bits, powers, shots, independent trials, state preparations, predicate/oracle calls, reflections, scratch allocation, and classical preprocessing/post-processing—not just the largest attractive circuit diagram. A failed or insufficiently justified success assumption changes the required repetitions and therefore the resource estimate.

Lessons 27–29 will price that precisely specified workload under logical synthesis, quantum error correction, and hardware models. Those teams need target precision, total success criteria, gate/measurement structure, ancilla ownership, and repeated-use counts. Their resource estimate will answer a conditional cost question. It will not retroactively validate the active space, repair omitted chemistry, or turn a recorded simulator snapshot into a physical experiment.
