lessons.title: From ideal qubits to error-corrected machines
lessons.body:
# Lesson 28 — From ideal qubits to error-corrected machines

## A long computation changes the reliability requirement

Lesson 27 counted the complete logical workload rather than one convenient component. We now ask what it takes to execute that workload with imperfect physical operations. Twelve occupation qubits for the selected nitrogen model do not imply a twelve-qubit fault-tolerant machine. Those logical data may need many physical qubits, repeated syndrome measurements, classical decoding, routing space, and non-Clifford resource-state factories.

The chemistry sources remain pinned to `97a3ff4f`. For external models, this chapter also inspects public Microsoft QDK source at commit `95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937` and public documentation reviewed for this chapter. Those sources describe model implementations and assumptions, not a verified installed package or measured hardware. No error-correction simulation, resource estimate, or physical experiment is performed here.

Suppose N operations each have an independent fault probability p. The probability of at least one fault is \(1-(1-p)^N\), approximately Np only when Np is small. In a hypothetical million-operation experiment with p=\(10^{-6}\), that probability is about 63%. Even individually reliable operations can therefore produce an unreliable long computation.

A fault is not necessarily a wrong final answer: some faults cancel or do not affect the observable. Error correction deliberately makes many physical faults harmless. The relevant failure rate is ultimately the rate of **logical** faults that change the encoded information or computation, not simply the number of physical imperfections. The example is probability arithmetic, not a specification or measurement of any device.

## Physical and logical qubits

A **physical qubit** is a hardware degree of freedom manipulated and measured by a device. A **logical qubit** is encoded information protected across multiple physical degrees of freedom. Its basis states \(|0_L\rangle\) and \(|1_L\rangle\) are collective states of a code block, not individual hardware bits.

The no-cloning theorem forbids copying an arbitrary unknown state into independent copies. Error-correction encoding does not do that. For instance, a toy encoding can map

\[
(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle)|00\rangle
\longmapsto\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle.
\]

The output is generally entangled, not three copies of \(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\). Information is distributed into a larger correlated subspace in a reversible way. We can ask carefully chosen questions about error syndromes without learning the amplitudes \(\alpha,\beta\).

A bit-flip error acts like X. A phase-flip error acts like Z, changing relative phase rather than occupation probabilities. Y combines the two up to phase. General small errors can be analyzed through combinations of such operators, but real devices may also have leakage, loss, coherent drift, biased noise, and correlations. A code/noise model must specify what its claimed protection covers.

The **codespace** is the subspace representing valid encoded states. A **logical operator** acts nontrivially within that codespace, such as exchanging \(|0_L\rangle\) and \(|1_L\rangle\). Not every physical error produces a detectable syndrome; an unfortunate combination can mimic a logical operator.

## Measuring a syndrome without measuring the logical state

Consider the three-qubit bit-flip repetition encoding above. The parity checks \(Z_0Z_1\) and \(Z_1Z_2\) both have eigenvalue +1 for either encoded basis state, and therefore for every superposition in the codespace. Measuring these joint parities does not distinguish \(\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle\) from another logical superposition.

The pair of check outcomes is an **error syndrome**. A single X on qubit 0 gives syndrome (−1,+1); X on qubit 1 gives (−1,−1); X on qubit 2 gives (+1,−1). Under the promise of at most one bit flip and ideal checks, these outcomes identify which correction to apply. Auxiliary check qubits can collect a parity and be measured while the encoded data remain coherent.

This is not a complete quantum memory. A Z error on one data qubit changes the relative logical phase without changing those Z-parity checks. The toy code protects one error type but not arbitrary qubit errors. A quantum error-correcting code must address both bit- and phase-like errors, with a carefully compatible set of checks.

In stabilizer codes, checks are commuting Pauli operators that define the codespace by their eigenvalues. This reuses the stabilizer vocabulary from Lesson 15, but the purpose differs. Chemical tapering uses an already known conserved sector to remove redundant problem variables; QEC adds physical redundancy to protect unknown logical amplitudes. A chemical Z₂ symmetry and a hardware-code stabilizer are not interchangeable data.

Real check measurements can themselves be wrong. Repeating checks over time lets a **decoder**, a classical algorithm, infer a likely error history from changes in the syndrome. Different physical histories can give the same observed checks. Choosing a correction with the wrong logical effect produces a logical failure. A resource model that supplies a fitted logical-error rate is not automatically running a detailed decoder or simulating each noisy check circuit.

## Distance, threshold, and the assumptions behind suppression

The **code distance** d is the minimum weight of a nontrivial logical operator, where weight counts affected physical qubits, for the usual ideal code definition. A distance-d code can correct up to \(\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\) arbitrary Pauli errors under the corresponding ideal-syndrome assumptions. Faulty measurements and gates require a fault-tolerant extraction/decoding process; distance alone does not prove the complete circuit has that performance.

A **threshold** is an error-rate boundary below which increasing code size can suppress logical error under a specified noise, connectivity, extraction, and decoding model. It is not a universal material constant or a guarantee that every correlated error process is corrected. Operating above a model’s threshold cannot be repaired merely by asking the estimator for a larger d.

A common phenomenological scaling form is

\[
p_L(d)\approx A\left(\frac{p_{\mathrm{phys}}}{p_{\mathrm{th}}}\right)^{(d+1)/2}.
\]

Here A is a fitted prefactor, \(p_{\mathrm{phys}}\) a modeled physical error rate, \(p_{\mathrm{th}}\) the associated threshold, and \(p_L\) a logical-error measure for a specified operation/time unit. This is a representative model, not a universal law. Its unit—per syndrome round, per logical operation, or another exposure—must be identified before multiplying it by a workload count.

If L relevant logical exposures share this bound, the union estimate \(Lp_L\le\delta_L\) can guide a distance choice for allocated failure probability \(\delta_L\). Solving the idealized relation suggests that distance grows roughly logarithmically with required workload reliability below threshold, while patch area grows roughly quadratically in distance. This explains why modest changes in physical error or target failure probability can change resource requirements sharply. It does not justify extrapolation beyond the fit’s valid noise regime.

Biased noise means different error types have different probabilities; correlated faults can affect several qubits or times together. Leakage and loss may need additional detection/replacement mechanisms. Measurement delay, decoder latency, and fabrication/connectivity constraints affect the fault-tolerant implementation. A single scalar error rate can be useful for a model sweep and still omit important physics.

## Surface codes and repeated local checks

A surface code arranges data and check operations in a two-dimensional structure, using local parity checks to protect logical information. In a common rotated planar construction, distance d involves roughly d² data qubits plus a similar number of check ancillas. Logical information is associated with nonlocal strings across the patch; short local errors can be detected and corrected, while a spanning error chain can cause a logical fault.

The directly inspected external [`SurfaceCode` model](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/models/qec/_surface_code.py) is specifically a gate-based rotated-surface-code resource transform. It requires H, CNOT, and Z-measurement instruction data. Its default space coefficient is \(2d^2-1\), from d² data and d²−1 check qubits. Its default syndrome-cycle timing combines one one-qubit-gate layer, four two-qubit-gate layers, and measurement time, with available override/offset parameters. A modeled lattice-surgery operation takes d such cycles.

The same source uses default threshold 0.01 and crossing prefactor 0.03 in its logical-error scaling, based on cited modeling references. These are model constants, not experimental numbers discovered by QDK Chemistry. Its default distance-query domain is odd distances 3 through 25. A domain enumerates candidate model settings; it does not declare all hardware with those distances built or validated.

The physical instruction times matter differently. A very fast one-qubit gate does not eliminate slow measurement or two-qubit layers from each syndrome cycle. A cycle-time offset can represent additional modeled latency if justified; leaving it zero is an assumption, not proof that control electronics and decoding take no time.

There are other surface-code implementations and layouts. The convenience estimator’s older `surface_code` formulas are not identical to every direct `SurfaceCode` or `ThreeAux` model. The name of a code family is not a complete numerical resource specification.

## ThreeAux is a particular measurement-based surface-code model

The chemistry notebooks name `ThreeAux`, so we should explain the actual model rather than guess from its name. The external [`ThreeAux` source](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/models/qec/_three_aux.py) describes a pairwise-measurement-based surface code using three auxiliary qubits per stabilizer measurement. It requires physical X, Z, XX, and ZZ measurements, rather than the gate-based H/CNOT primitive set used above.

Its space coefficient is

\[
d^2+3(d^2-1)=4d^2-3.
\]

That is a modeled protected-operand cost, not the total application footprint. It does not include every algorithmic patch, routing region, buffer, or magic-state factory just by evaluating this expression once.

At the inspected public revision, `single_rail=False` is the default. The model uses extraction depth four for that choice and five for single rail, threshold 0.0066 or 0.0051 respectively, and prefactor 0.05. Its lattice-surgery timing value is \(t_{\mathrm{joint}}(\mathrm{depth}\,d+4)\), where \(t_{\mathrm{joint}}\) is the slower supplied XX/ZZ measurement time. Its physical error input is the maximum among the required measurement error rates.

These constants make explicit why replacing `SurfaceCode` with `ThreeAux` is not just changing a label. The required primitive operations, space, timing, and fitted suppression assumptions all change. The source’s `code_cycle_time` property also includes a distance factor in this model; do not infer a universal one-syndrome-round meaning from a property name without reading the model contract.

`ThreeAux.q(distance=[...])` asks the external estimator to enumerate such candidate code implementations. It does not perform noisy check-circuit simulations or verify the model on a device. The relevant public model cites the improved pairwise measurement-based surface-code work; those derivations and hardware realizability remain evidence inputs beyond the chemistry circuit itself.

## Floquet codes: a different check schedule and interface

A Floquet-code approach obtains protection from a repeating time-dependent pattern of checks. The logical encoding can evolve through that pattern rather than being described by one static set of simultaneously measured stabilizers. Hastings and Haah’s [Dynamically Generated Logical Qubits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02194v2) describes a construction based on two-qubit Pauli measurements; this is a distinct QEC idea, not the explicitly driven chemical Hamiltonian of Lesson 23.

The older convenience estimator exposes the model identifier `floquet_code`. Its inspected [fault-tolerance implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system/modeling/fault_tolerance.rs) accepts that built-in model with the measurement-based Majorana instruction set and rejects the gate-based pairing. Its default model formulas use threshold 0.01, prefactor 0.07, time \(3t_{\mathrm{meas}}d\), and physical-qubit expression \(4d^2+8(d-1)\), referring to planar Floquet-code modeling.

Those formulas are a coarse resource model, not a full construction or noisy-code benchmark in this course. The direct `qdk.qre.models` code catalog inspected at the same external revision does not export a corresponding `FloquetCode` class. Do not assume a convenience-interface string can be passed unchanged into the direct query-model interface or invent that constructor. Lesson 29 separates those APIs explicitly.

## A hardware architecture is a set of modeled instructions

An **instruction set architecture**, abbreviated ISA, specifies available operations and their properties: arity, time, space, error rate, and physical/logical encoding. Arity is the number of operands an operation acts on. An architecture model supplies the physical primitives; code and factory models derive protected operations from compatible inputs.

The public [`GateBased` model](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/models/qubits/_gate_based.py) takes gate and measurement times in nanoseconds, an error rate, and optionally a separate two-qubit-gate time. Its numerical defaults/required fields are external API choices, not calibrated values for the nitrogen problem. Physical qubit connectivity and detailed routing must be consistent with the operations a code model assumes, even when an abstract instruction hides that implementation.

The chemistry notebooks use `Majorana(error_rate=1e-5)`. The inspected public [`Majorana` model](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/models/qubits/_msft.py) supplies X/Z preparation and single-/two-qubit X/Z measurements plus a physical T operation. With that argument and defaults, the model assumes 1000 ns for its operations and maps the Clifford measurement/preparation rate \(10^{-5}\) to a **different physical T error rate of 0.015**. It does not assume every operation has error \(10^{-5}\).

The default error-rate options in that model are \(10^{-4},10^{-5},10^{-6}\), associated with different assumed T rates when no explicit override is supplied. They are scenario parameters from a proposed architecture model, not evidence of present device performance or a hardware delivery date. The source’s motivation mentions topological protection for some operations; the model does not demonstrate that protection experimentally or extend it automatically to non-Clifford T operations.

Also distinguish the mathematical Majorana operators used for fermion-to-qubit mapping in Lesson 14 from physical Majorana-based hardware. Using `MajoranaMapping.jordan_wigner` or a Majorana algebra engine says nothing about the physical qubit technology on which the resulting circuit must run.

## Logical operations and lattice surgery

Protected logical qubits still need to interact. **Lattice surgery** is a method of changing/combining code-patch boundaries to measure joint logical properties, then separating them again. A joint logical parity measurement can correlate patches without directly reading each logical amplitude. Appropriate sequences with ancillas implement useful logical operations.

This is not the same as executing an ideal CNOT on two unprotected physical qubits. Repeated syndrome extraction, boundary geometry, extra patches, decoding, and time are involved. A trace transform can express a many-Pauli measurement in terms of a logical lattice-surgery instruction, while the QEC model gives that instruction its modeled space/time/error.

Parallel logical operations can demand additional routing or ancillary space. A patch kept idle while waiting for a magic state still needs protection. Classical readout and decoding must keep up with the syndrome stream; delayed decisions may need buffering or conservative scheduling. A resource model can approximate these effects, but a single operation-time scalar does not automatically include every engineering latency.

The public [`Architecture` and ISA context](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/_architecture.py) record instruction properties and provenance. Compatibility requires that an available ISA actually supplies the operations required by the trace/code/factory transforms. Choosing individually attractive but mutually incompatible components should yield no valid study point, not a fictional best-of-everything machine.

## Why non-Clifford gates require another supply chain

The **Clifford group** consists of unitary operations that transform Pauli operators into Pauli operators under conjugation. Conjugating means forming U P U†, with P a Pauli operator and U the gate. H, S, and CNOT generate the usual qubit Clifford operations; their inverses and compositions remain in the group. This closure makes stabilizer tracking efficient, but Clifford operations alone do not provide arbitrary quantum computation. A T gate is a non-Clifford example.

A universal computation needs more than Clifford operations alone. One route implements a T gate by consuming a **magic state**, such as a state proportional to \(|0\rangle+e^{i\pi/4}|1\rangle\), together with Clifford operations, measurements, and corrective feedback. This procedure is called state injection. The resource state carries the non-Clifford capability.

Noisy physical preparation generally produces imperfect magic states. **Distillation** consumes several noisy states and performs a checking protocol to produce fewer higher-quality states, sometimes rejecting a batch. Output error, acceptance probability, circuit faults, and repetition must all be accounted for. It is not enough to count only the accepted output states.

A **magic-state factory** is the protected hardware/process footprint producing these resource states. It is not the algorithm-factory registry introduced in Lesson 3, nor an AI orchestration tool. A computation may need many copies running in parallel to supply T states at the rate demanded by its logical schedule.

The inspected external [`RoundBasedFactory`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/models/factories/_round_based.py) explores multi-round pipelines built from specified 15-to-1 unit models, including RM-preparation and space-efficient variants. These are quantitative protocol models, not actual distillation circuits executed by the chemistry package. Its unit error expressions include a cubic term \(35p_T^3\) plus a contribution from modeled Clifford/logical operation error, and its failure expressions include both input-state and circuit-error contributions. The cubic suppression alone is not the whole factory behavior.

The model adjusts the number of parallel units in a round to meet output-supply requirements under a default internal pipeline failure allowance of 1%, divided among its rounds. This internal distillation-rejection requirement is distinct from the application’s total allowed logical error. A batch rejected by a factory is not automatically the same event as an undetected bad magic state corrupting the algorithm.

By default, the model sums per-round space rather than assuming all physical qubits are reused across rounds; an alternative aggregation can represent reuse, but its timing/scheduling assumptions must remain consistent. Compute-code distance and factory-code distances can be chosen separately. The factory’s `code_query` must match the architecture: a gate-based default code query is not automatically compatible with a measurement-only architecture. The chemistry examples explicitly pair ThreeAux compute and factory-code queries for their Majorana scenario.

## Factory throughput can dominate the machine

Suppose a logical algorithm demands \(N_T\) resource states, and one factory produces an average usable rate r_T under its specified acceptance/error model. With F such factories, the supply rate is roughly \(Fr_T\). A simple lower-bound picture for duration is

\[
T_{\mathrm{run}}\gtrsim\max\left(T_{\mathrm{dependency}},\frac{N_T}{Fr_T}\right),
\]

where \(T_{\mathrm{dependency}}\) is the time imposed by the computation’s operation dependencies. This is an explanatory bound, not the exact QDK estimator formula. Startup, discrete batches, buffers, routing, idle protection, and time-varying demand can matter.

Increasing F can reduce supply-limited duration while increasing qubits. Slowing logical operations can reduce the required number of simultaneous factories while increasing memory time and logical-error exposure. Increasing code distance can suppress faults while increasing patch area and cycle time. These choices interact, so an optimal compute patch in isolation need not belong to an optimal whole machine.

A schematic footprint is

\[
Q_{\mathrm{physical}}\approx N_Lq_{\mathrm{patch}}(d)
+Fq_{\mathrm{factory}}+Q_{\mathrm{routing}}+Q_{\mathrm{buffer}}+\cdots.
\]

\(N_L\) is the number of simultaneous protected logical operands, not the sum of qubits over all sequential shots. The ellipsis is not free space: it identifies additional architecture-specific costs that must either be modeled or declared outside scope.

More accurate arbitrary rotations can increase T-state demand, which changes required factory throughput and footprint. Thus the chemical algorithm’s precision decision propagates through compilation into QEC/hardware design. A source-level rotation count alone cannot settle that design.

## Separate the budgets by what can go wrong

A chemical energy tolerance, a unitary approximation bound, statistical confidence, and a probability of logical failure answer different questions. “One percent error budget” does not mean an energy is within one percent of its true value, nor that a gate-noise simulation has reproduced an experimental device.

A conventional resource budget can divide allowed error among logical computation, imperfect distilled T states, and rotation synthesis. That partition is an estimator modeling convention; its components must use compatible error measures and compositional bounds. Under a union-bound interpretation, many rare error contributions are summed conservatively. A product formula such as \(1-\prod_i(1-p_i)\) carries different assumptions about independent events. The external API exposes such choices, which we inspect in Lesson 29 rather than conflating them with a confidence interval.

If a workload uses many magic states, the tolerated error per state can need to be far smaller than the desired total failure probability. If the logical data remain encoded for many cycles, idle and operation exposures both contribute. If multiple complete trials are required, the success and failure accounting must apply to the actual campaign, not one favorable bit circuit.

The resource estimator does not infer that campaign’s target-state success probability from an energy or overlap field. Fresh-state IQPE, finite-resolution amplification, postselection, and model error retain their own scientific/algorithmic limitations. A fault-tolerant machine can execute a precisely specified wrong algorithm very reliably.

## What evidence each specialist must supply

The chemistry and application side supplies the scientific model, intended state/sector, total workload, approximation tolerances, and evidence supporting the success criterion. It must distinguish active energies from core-inclusive or SOS-shifted energies and count repeated state preparations, powers, measurements, and retries correctly.

The compiler/synthesis side supplies a valid lower-level trace or logical count representation, gate-set assumptions, synthesis error allocation, dependency structure, and ancilla lifetimes. It must preserve phases needed under control and specify which adaptive or measurement-based operations it can lower.

The QEC-model side supplies the code family, distance/error scaling, supported logical operations, extraction/decoder assumptions, and factory protocol performance. A fitted threshold and prefactor need a provenance and range of validity. The hardware-model side supplies compatible primitive operations, timings, error characterization, connectivity, measurement/readout behavior, and relevant correlations or leakage assumptions.

These are functional roles, not claims about an organization’s internal team structure. The estimator integrates the models and enumerates candidate combinations; it does not create missing calibration evidence. A credible study asks for coherent parameter sets and sensitivity ranges rather than taking the best independent value from unrelated platforms or publications.

The official [resource-estimator introduction](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/intro-to-resource-estimation), inspected for this chapter, presents the same layered idea: application, architecture, error correction/factories, and an allowed error budget are distinct inputs. The public models and documents do not assert that choosing a model instantiates the corresponding physical machine.

## The proper conclusion from a modeled machine

QEC makes reliable long computations possible in principle by turning many physical operations and qubits into fewer protected logical capabilities. It also introduces substantial space, time, control, and resource-state costs. Those costs depend on the workload and on the detailed assumptions of the selected code and hardware models.

For the nitrogen course, the immediate deliverable is not a hardware date or a single qubit count. It is a reproducible mapping from the complete logical workload to compatible protected instruction models, with stated error budgets and omitted engineering effects. SurfaceCode, Floquet, and ThreeAux names identify different supported modeling paths, not interchangeable guarantees.

The next lesson turns this understanding into two concrete resource-estimation interfaces, shows how to interpret their results and Pareto frontiers, and specifies the evidence needed before reporting a conditional physical cost as a meaningful scientific engineering result.
lessons.caveats: External QEC/hardware source pinned independently to QDK 95c039f4; no installed-package inspection, execution, estimate, simulation, hardware validation, or file changes. Numeric code/factory formulas are conditional model assumptions. Direct SurfaceCode/ThreeAux differ from convenience surface_code/floquet_code; direct Floquet class not exported in inspected catalog. Majorana(error_rate=1e-5) has default modeled 1000 ns primitive time and 0.015 T error, not universal 1e-5 errors. Repetition example protects only bit flips. Threshold fits, correlations, leakage, decoder/control/routing omissions and magic-state supply/failure distinctions are qualified. No hardware timeline, commercial, or practical-advantage claim.

lessons.title: Physical resource estimation and team contracts
lessons.body:
# Lesson 29 — Physical resource estimation and team contracts

## Turn the workload into a conditional engineering statement

We now have two things that must meet: the complete logical workload from Lesson 27, and the imperfect protected instructions from Lesson 28. Resource estimation asks how many physical qubits and how much modeled execution time that combination requires at a stated reliability target. It does not determine whether the chosen active space is chemically adequate, whether the initial state has useful overlap, or whether the answer creates practical value.

Our running scientific story remains the intended-singlet nitrogen calculation at 1.85 Å. The separate `qpe_stretched_n2.ipynb` resource-estimation example uses 1.270025 Å and estimates selected iteration circuits. We will use its API pattern without confusing its geometry or component scope with the full course experiment.

This chapter follows QDK Chemistry revision `97a3ff4f` and, where the implementation is external, public QDK revision `95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937`. The examples below are unexecuted, version-bound teaching sketches, not claims about an installed environment. Chemistry declares `qdk[jupyter]>=1.31.0` and a separate `qre` extra requesting `qdk[qre,jupyter]>=1.31.0` in its [dependency manifest](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/pyproject.toml). A lower-bound dependency is not an exact reproducibility lock.

There are **two alternative interfaces**, not two required successive stages. `Circuit.estimate(...)` is a convenience route from a supported stored/live circuit to the older-style estimator parameter/result model. `Circuit.get_qre_application()` supplies an Application for the direct `qdk.qre` trace/architecture/query interface used by the notebooks. Choose the interface that matches the study and supported environment; do not feed one route’s dictionaries into the other as if their schemas were interchangeable.

## What the chemistry adapter actually selects

The [Circuit implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/circuit.py) checks available representations in a definite order:

| Available representation | `estimate` route | `get_qre_application` route |
|---|---|---|
| Live Q# factory data | Invoke the factory through its QDK context for logical counts; call those counts’ `estimate` | Construct `QSharpApplication` with the callable and positional arguments |
| QASM, without a factory | Call the external OpenQASM estimate function | Construct `OpenQASMApplication` |
| QIR only | Raise `RuntimeError` | Construct `QIRApplication` |
| Only a diagram-like Q# circuit object, or no supported input | Not a supported estimation representation by itself | Not a supported Application representation by itself |

If several representations exist, the earlier route wins. These methods do not automatically compare representations for equivalence. The factory’s parameter dictionary values are passed positionally in insertion order; merely having familiar parameter names does not repair an incorrectly constructed ordering.

The convenience method reports a discrepancy between `Circuit.num_qubits` and counted `numQubits` but does not change the declared width. It does not add qubits just because metadata declares them, nor subtract internally allocated scratch because a diagram hides it. The [Circuit tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_circuit.py) explicitly exercise a declared width of five with a two-qubit QASM count and preserve the declaration. These are read source tests, not executions performed for this course.

`get_qre_application` imports its optional external classes lazily. An unavailable `qdk.qre` import becomes a `RuntimeError` identifying the missing optional dependency. A QIR-only representation therefore has a supported route in principle, but that does not imply arbitrary QIR profiles or adaptive control flows are handled faithfully by the external importer.

## Route A: a stored-circuit convenience estimate

Assume `selected_circuit` is an existing Circuit whose exact scope has already been recorded. The following sketch illustrates the parameter structure, not a completed nitrogen estimate:

```python
params = {
    "qubitParams": {"name": "qubit_gate_ns_e3"},
    "qecScheme": {"name": "surface_code"},
    "errorBudget": 0.01,
    "estimateType": "frontier",
}
result = selected_circuit.estimate(params)
raw = result.data()
```

The input `params` accepts `None`, a dictionary, a list of parameter dictionaries, or the external `EstimatorParams` helper. A batch estimates the supplied circuit under multiple parameter choices; it does not mean execute that circuit repeatedly as a statistical experiment. In particular, a list of hardware scenarios is not a list of IQPE shots.

The helper uses snake-case Python attributes such as `qubit_params`, `qec_scheme`, `error_budget`, and `estimate_type`, while dictionaries use camel-case keys such as `qubitParams` and `errorBudget`. Its `as_dict()` performs validation and conversion. At the inspected external revision, constructing `EstimatorParams` emits a deprecation warning recommending the newer direct `qdk.qre` route. That external evolution does not remove the convenience method from the pinned chemistry adapter.

For typed batching, `EstimatorParams(num_items=...)` supports one through 1000 items. Its block inheritance is not a general recursive dictionary merge: a nonempty item-level qubit or QEC block takes precedence over the corresponding default block. Inspect the emitted per-item dictionaries rather than assuming every top-level field is inherited. `LogicalCounts.estimate` sends the generated item list to the native numerical estimator.

The stored-circuit UI tool has the same narrow purpose. [`estimate_circuit`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/tools.py) takes `project_name`, `circuit_filename`, and JSON-compatible `params`, loads the Circuit, and returns `circuit.estimate(params).data()` through its structured response wrapper. It does not build an entire application or save a new result artifact in that entry point. Its [MCP tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/ui/test_mcp_circuit_estimate.py) verify parameter forwarding and raw batch-result preservation with mocks, not physical accuracy or every real-estimator failure path.

## Choose a coherent physical and QEC model

The convenience interface exposes six built-in physical model names: `qubit_gate_us_e3`, `qubit_gate_us_e4`, `qubit_gate_ns_e3`, `qubit_gate_ns_e4`, `qubit_maj_ns_e4`, and `qubit_maj_ns_e6`. These are scenario presets, not reservations of real devices. The accepted QEC names include `surface_code` and `floquet_code`, with compatibility restrictions discussed in Lesson 28.

For example, the inspected [physical-model source](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system/modeling/physical_qubit.rs) assigns the `qubit_gate_ns_e3` preset 50 ns one- and two-qubit gates, 100 ns measurement, and the specified modeled error rates. Its microsecond-family presets have different timing and T-state-error assumptions. The older Majorana presets use 100 ns measurement assumptions; these are **not the same defaults** as the direct `Majorana` class whose default time is 1000 ns. Matching a broad hardware name across interfaces is insufficient for a fair comparison.

Custom `qubitParams` can specify `instructionSet`, operation times, operation error rates, idle error, and, for measurement-based models, separate measurement process/readout errors. A process error changes the quantum evolution; a readout error misreports a classical outcome. Accepted time strings include suffixes `s`, `ms`, `us`, `µs`, `μs`, and `ns`; the numerical result runtime uses nanoseconds. A bare timing number and an energy in Hartree are not interchangeable with such durations.

The native normalizer fills documented omissions from a selected preset or related fields. A genuinely custom gate-based model requires measurement time/error, one-qubit gate time/error, and T error in the inspected backend; missing two-qubit/T times may be derived from one-qubit gate time. The Python helper’s checks are not the entire backend contract. Supply justified values and inspect the normalized parameters rather than assuming an omitted field means zero cost or zero error.

A custom `qecScheme` can provide `errorCorrectionThreshold`, `crossingPrefactor`, `distanceCoefficientPower`, `logicalCycleTime`, `physicalQubitsPerLogicalQubit`, and `maxCodeDistance`. The [QEC model evaluator](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system/modeling/fault_tolerance.rs) evaluates formula strings with actual names such as `codeDistance`, `oneQubitGateTime`, and `twoQubitGateTime`. Some nearby explanatory comments use older snake-case names; use the implemented formula context, not a guessed spelling.

In the [threshold-distance model](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/estimates/error_correction/code_with_threshold_and_distance.rs), `distanceCoefficientPower` is a nonnegative integer b multiplying the error fit by \(d^b\): for odd distance d, the fit is \(p_L=A d^b(p/p_{\mathrm{th}})^{(d+1)/2}\). A is the crossing prefactor, p the modeled physical error, and \(p_{\mathrm{th}}\) the threshold. With b=0 this reduces to the simpler form in Lesson 28. `maxCodeDistance` limits the available distance search; it does not force every logical patch to use that distance. These are parameters of a chosen error fit, not knobs that improve hardware merely by being changed.

Formulas are supplied as a coupled model: patch geometry, timing, error suppression, and distance all refer to the same code/implementation assumptions. Syntax validation, positive evaluated resources, and threshold checks do not establish that arbitrarily assembled formulas describe a realizable machine. Do not independently choose the smallest area, shortest cycle, and best threshold from incompatible codes.

## Error budgets, synthesis, and constraints in Route A

The inspected [job-parameter backend](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system/data/job_params.rs) defaults to total error budget 0.001 and `singlePoint` estimation. With no physical/QEC override, its defaults are `qubit_gate_ns_e3` and `surface_code`. These defaults differ from the notebook’s explicit direct-model scenario and 0.01 allowance.

A scalar `errorBudget` must lie strictly between zero and one. If the logical counts contain rotations, the backend initially divides it among logical, T-state, and rotation contributions. With T demand but no rotations it uses two portions; without either it allocates the budget to logical errors. These are modeling partitions, not chemical error bars.

A manually partitioned budget allows greater control. In this inspected external revision, the **input** JSON keys are `logical`, `tStates`, and `rotations`; the Python helper is `ErrorBudgetPartition(logical=..., t_states=..., rotations=...)`. All relevant portions must be positive, irrelevant T/rotation portions may be zero, and the total must remain below one. There is a source-version trap: the chemistry skill describes `tstates`, and a single-point **output** uses `tstates`, but the inspected backend input and Python conversion use `tStates`. Do not round-trip the output blindly as input. The scalar example above avoids that spelling difference; a pinned study must verify its actual schema.

`constraints.logicalDepthFactor` is a modeled multiplier on logical depth, not an automatic geometry-aware router or decoder benchmark. `maxTFactories` caps parallel factories. `maxDuration` constrains modeled duration and `maxPhysicalQubits` constrains footprint, but those last two are mutually exclusive in this convenience interface. The typed helper rejects both together and requires positive-size constraints, with the depth factor at least one. Backend constraints also include a distillation-round limit; not every backend field is exposed by every typed helper revision.

`estimateType` is `singlePoint` or `frontier`. A frontier requests alternative feasible space/time tradeoffs, not one universally best design. The inspected [native driver](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system.rs) rejects frontier requests that also supply `maxDuration`, `maxPhysicalQubits`, or `maxTFactories`; use constrained `singlePoint` searches or generate an unconstrained frontier and filter it explicitly. If a deadline or qubit cap leaves no feasible candidate, that is a result about the chosen search/model constraints, not proof that the chemical task is impossible under every future architecture.

Distillation can use the default units or `distillationUnitSpecifications`. Inspected predefined unit names include `15-to-1 RM prep` and `15-to-1 space efficient`. A custom specification supplies a display name, input/output state counts, `failureProbabilityFormula`, `outputErrorRateFormula`, and physical/logical unit resources. At least one physical or logical specification is required by the backend. A first-round logical override needs a logical specification to override. Unit resources include `numUnitQubits` and `durationInQubitCycleTime`.

The [distillation evaluator](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system/modeling/tfactory.rs) makes `inputErrorRate`, `cliffordErrorRate`, and `readoutErrorRate` available to the formulas. A custom failure polynomial is not independently validated as a real protocol just because it parses. A predefined name and a custom typed specification are mutually exclusive; select the documented contract deliberately.

## What is calculated from logical counts

Before interpreting a physical answer, understand the layout abstraction. The external [`LogicalCounts`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/estimator/_estimator.py) carries `numQubits`, `tCount`, `rotationCount`, `rotationDepth`, `cczCount`, `ccixCount`, and `measurementCount`, with optional compute/memory fields. `rotationDepth` is the dependency depth of rotation layers, not total gate count or total circuit depth. Missing values in a manually constructed object can default to zero; missing information must not be mistaken for measured absence.

The [convenience layout implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system/data/logical_counts.rs) uses Parallel Synthesis Sequential Pauli Computation, abbreviated PSSPC. It models rotations prepared/synthesized in parallel where allowed and sequential Pauli-based logical computation. It is a resource-layout model, not a complete physical control schedule extracted from every circuit wire.

Let n be counted algorithm qubits, \(N_R\) the rotations, \(D_R\) their depth, \(N_T\) the explicit T count, \(N_C\) the sum of CCZ/CCiX counts, and \(N_M\) the measurement count. Ignoring separate memory-transfer extensions, its modeled overhead has the form

\[
Q_{\mathrm{layout}}=2n+\left\lceil\sqrt{8n}\right\rceil+1,
\qquad
N_{T,\mathrm{demand}}=N_T+4N_C+\nu N_R,
\]

\[
D_{\mathrm{layout}}=N_M+N_R+N_T+3N_C+\nu D_R.
\]

Here \(\nu\) is modeled T demand per arbitrary rotation. For \(N_R>0\) and allocated synthesis allowance \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{rot}}\), the inspected constants give

\[
\nu=\left\lceil0.53\log_2\!\left(\frac{N_R}{\epsilon_{\mathrm{rot}}}\right)+4.86\right\rceil.
\]

The constants belong to a particular synthesis/modeling construction cited by the estimator; they are not a universal exact gate-optimal decomposition for every angle. The Clifford workload is represented through this layout abstraction rather than by charging every original Clifford gate separately. That does not make protected Clifford operations free in the physical model.

This also explains why output `algorithmicLogicalQubits` can exceed input `logicalCounts.numQubits`. First there may be internal circuit scratch; then there is layout overhead; then each protected logical unit has a physical code cost. A resource count is meaningful only if its level is named.

## Read Route A results without hiding failure

`EstimatorResult.data()` returns raw dictionaries or a batch list. At the inspected revision, a one-element list is unwrapped to a single dictionary. A successful item has `status == "success"`; failed data use error code/message information and must not be interpreted as resources equal to zero.

A successful single-point item contains `logicalCounts`, `jobParams`, `physicalCounts`, `logicalQubit`, `reportData`, and relevant factory/error-budget fields. `physicalCounts.physicalQubits` is total modeled physical footprint; `physicalCounts.runtime` is duration in nanoseconds. Its breakdown includes algorithmic logical qubits/depth, final logical depth, T-state demand, number of factories/runs, and algorithm/factory physical-qubit contributions. `logicalQubit.codeDistance` is the selected compute-code parameter, not necessarily every factory’s code distance.

For a frontier, these candidate-specific fields live inside `frontierEntries`. The inspected [result producer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/resource_estimator/src/system/data/result.rs) sorts those entries by runtime. Some convenience indexing falls back to the first entry. Reading `result["physicalCounts"]` alone can therefore hide the rest of the frontier; inspect all entries and their assumptions.

The failure contract needs equal care. A failed singleton may raise `EstimatorError` rather than return a result. At this external revision that class derives from `BaseException`, so an `except Exception` clause is not a guaranteed catch for it. Batch items can preserve individual failures, but the chemistry adapter immediately accesses `result.logical_counts`, whose batch accessor uses the first item. Static inspection therefore identifies a possible `KeyError` if the first failed item lacks `logicalCounts`. Do not promise that every partial batch failure reaches the UI unchanged; preserve the actual error and rerun a permitted, isolated diagnostic only when execution is authorized.

## Route B: an Application, a trace query, and an ISA query

An **Application** describes a problem instance and how to generate resource traces. In the direct abstraction, application parameters can fix the problem, while trace parameters choose implementations of that same problem. A stored Circuit adapter generally supplies one fixed circuit trace, not an automatic family of active spaces, Trotter accuracies, or trial-state strategies.

A **trace** records operations, operands, repeated blocks, and resource-state demands in a form useful for counting/scheduling models. A **trace query** enumerates selected transformations or implementation parameters for that program. An **ISA query** enumerates available protected instructions derived from a physical architecture and QEC/factory models. These objects answer different questions: what work is requested versus how the machine can implement it.

The [`TraceQuery` implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/_trace.py) uses `*` to chain transforms in order. The [`ISAQuery` implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/_isa_enumeration.py) uses `*` for combinations of instruction sets, with later matching instruction IDs overriding earlier ones; `+` enumerates alternatives. These operators compose search descriptions. They do not multiply physical-qubit counts or repeat the application.

A `.q(...)` call creates such a query. Lists specify explored parameter domains. No-argument queries may enumerate defaults from model metadata rather than one fixed constructor default. For example, the inspected PSSPC constructor defaults to 20 T states per rotation, whereas its query domain spans 5 through 20 unless overridden. Record the actual domains in a reproducible study.

The architecture and transforms carry instruction requirements. A ThreeAux query requires measurement-based primitives; a round-based T factory needs a physical or already encoded T source plus compatible operations for its protocols. The factory’s default code query is gate-based SurfaceCode, so the Majorana notebook explicitly supplies ThreeAux for factory-code exploration too. A mathematically attractive but incompatible combination does not describe a valid ISA.

## Do not assume every Application contains the original detailed trace

The actual default matters. At the inspected external revision, [`QSharpApplication`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/application/_qsharp.py) defaults `use_trace_backend=False`. Its [interoperability helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/interop/_qsharp.py) obtains logical counts, distributes rotation counts into synthetic layers matching their count/depth, and creates repeated blocks for T-like, CCX-like, and measurement work. That trace preserves selected aggregate resource facts, not every original dependency and branch.

The external class offers `use_trace_backend=True` for direct trace generation from Q# execution, but the chemistry adapter does not pass that flag. A separately constructed external Application is a different, version-sensitive choice that needs supported-program validation. Supplying precomputed LogicalCounts cannot recover the missing detailed order; the direct-trace option rejects that combination. Also, a manually created LogicalCounts with rotations but default zero rotationDepth is not an adequate trace input: the inspected count-to-trace bridge only constructs its rotation blocks when both are nonzero.

`OpenQASMApplication` imports the supplied QASM into the QDK context and uses the count-derived trace helper in this implementation. `QIRApplication` accepts base-profile QIR text/bitcode according to its external contract. Its [QIR trace importer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/interop/_qir.py) includes a gate/measurement mapping but documents that conditional branches follow the false path, assuming zero measurement results. It skips bare RESET and several classical/runtime operations; correlated-noise instructions are unsupported.

Consequently, “QIR accepted” does not mean exact expected-cost or worst-case analysis of arbitrary adaptive algorithms. An all-zero path is not automatically the longest path. Supply an explicitly justified branch model, separate branch traces, or a supported complete workload representation when classical feedback changes cost. Noise instructions and QEC syndrome simulations are not required to count a logical trace.

## Follow the notebook’s direct-query pattern

The [nitrogen notebook](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/qpe_stretched_n2.ipynb) constructs its Application from `iqpe_iter_circuits[0]`, the largest iteration circuit. Here is an annotated, version-bound sketch using that existing object; it is intentionally still **component scope**:

```python
from qdk.qre import estimate, PSSPC, LatticeSurgery
from qdk.qre.models import Majorana, RoundBasedFactory, ThreeAux

app = iqpe_iter_circuits[0].get_qre_application()
architecture = Majorana(error_rate=1e-5)
trace_query = (
    app.q()
    * PSSPC.q(num_ts_per_rotation=[16, 17, 18, 19])
    * LatticeSurgery.q(slow_down_factor=[1.0, 2.0, 4.0])
)
isa_query = (
    ThreeAux.q(distance=[11, 13, 15, 17, 19])
    * RoundBasedFactory.q(
        code_query=ThreeAux.q(distance=[5, 7, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19]),
        use_cache=False,
    )
)
results = estimate(
    app, architecture, isa_query, trace_query,
    max_error=0.01, use_graph=False, post_process=False,
    name="Largest IQPE iteration only",
)
```

The notebook itself uses simpler default queries and `use_cache=True`. The expanded lists illustrate the sweep style actually used in the [Ising estimation notebook](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/estimation_ising_2d.ipynb), which explores rotation values 16–19 and slowdown factors 1–34, along with separate compute and factory distance domains. The shorter slowdown list above is an illustrative study choice, not a recommended optimum or a report of computed outcomes.

The direct [`estimate` function](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/_estimation.py) defaults `max_error` to 1.0, so specify a meaningful budget explicitly. When no trace query is supplied, it uses `PSSPC.q() * LatticeSurgery.q()`. Its default error composition is `ErrorComposition.UnionBound`; `ErrorComposition.Product` instead combines contributions as \(1-\prod_i(1-p_i)\). Neither choice automatically validates independence or the physical noise assumptions behind the input contributions.

## What the direct transforms do, not merely their names

The direct [PSSPC implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qre/src/trace/transforms/psspc.rs) counts Pauli measurements, rotations, T-like gates, and CCX-like gates, tracking rotation dependency depth across shared operands and Clifford interactions. It constructs the same style of layout overhead taught above, adds resource-state demand, and attaches an approximation contribution to the trace. Unsupported non-Clifford instructions raise rather than silently receiving a valid arbitrary cost.

Here the chosen integer \(\nu=\texttt{num_ts_per_rotation}\) determines a modeled per-rotation synthesis error

\[
\epsilon_{\mathrm{one\ rotation}}=2^{(4.86-\nu)/0.53}.
\]

The trace receives \(N_R\epsilon_{\mathrm{one\ rotation}}\) as a base approximation contribution. This is the cited mixed-fallback synthesis model, not an actual synthesized gate string or a chemical-energy error. Increasing \(\nu\) trades greater T demand and synthesis depth for lower modeled approximation error. It is a meaningful precision/resource knob only within that model’s assumptions.

By default `ccx_magic_states=False`, so CCX-like work contributes four T states per counted operation. Setting it true requests CCX resource states instead. A T-only RoundBasedFactory does not thereby acquire a CCX-state supply: the ISA must provide every resource type the transformed trace requires.

The direct [LatticeSurgery transform](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qre/src/trace/transforms/lattice_surgery.rs) replaces the trace with repeated logical lattice-surgery work of depth \(\lceil sD\rceil\), where D is the transformed depth and s is `slow_down_factor`. Its operation spans the transformed compute operands. It is not drawing a routed patch layout or modeling every wire movement. Slower logical progress can allow fewer simultaneous factories, but it increases protected computation time and may increase error exposure.

Compute distance and factory distances need not coincide. The optimal balance can use a large distance for a long-lived compute area and different distances in distillation rounds. The query explores these compatible options; it does not turn one hand-picked distance into an unquestionable output fact. Preserve the instruction provenance and factory details that explain each retained candidate.

## Search completeness, caching, and actual execution boundaries

`use_graph=True` is the direct estimator default. It prunes instruction choices using local space/time/error comparisons. The public source explicitly warns that this can miss globally Pareto-optimal application results: factory footprint is the number of required copies times the space per factory, and the copy count depends on runtime and discrete production opportunities. A locally attractive instruction need not produce the best whole-machine tradeoff.

`use_graph=False` enumerates the ISAs yielded by the supplied queries without that outer graph-pruning shortcut. It does not search all imaginable architectures, all code distances, or all factory protocols. Individual model/query implementations can already restrict or filter their candidates. State the generated search space and the completeness boundary rather than calling the result the globally optimal quantum computer.

The `post_process` option also needs care. At the inspected revision, its implementation samples application post-processing effects, infers per-trace resource multipliers, filters approximate candidates, and then reevaluates retained candidates. The basic sketch leaves it false. A custom post-processing function with arbitrary architecture-dependent nonlinear effects requires its own correctness review; the option is not a general proof that every adjusted frontier remains complete.

Caching is a real side effect, not part of quantum cost. The external [`RoundBasedFactory`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/models/factories/_round_based.py) defaults to disk caching. At this inspected revision its cache-path helper creates a directory before the `use_cache` condition, so **`use_cache=False` is not a guarantee of zero filesystem writes**. The Q# Application has separate optional compiled-trace caching. No calls in these sketches were executed for this read-only course preparation.

The reviewed numerical paths use local QDK compiler/interpreter and Python/Rust estimation routines, not remote quantum-job submission. They may consume substantial classical CPU/memory as traces and candidate sets grow. Telemetry hooks are present and their complete network behavior was not audited here; convenience notebook diagrams also reference an external rendering script. Local numerical estimation is therefore not the same claim as universally network-free package behavior. Neither physical execution nor a noisy QEC simulation is required merely to obtain a modeled estimate.

## Read direct results as a table of candidates

The direct return type is an [`EstimationTable`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk/blob/95c039f4b0447928aa041f5ae5ad52e7041d8937/source/qdk_package/qdk/qre/_results.py), a list-like collection of entries, not a convenience `EstimatorResult` dictionary. Each entry exposes `qubits`, `runtime`, `error`, `source`, `factories`, and additional `properties`. Runtime is an integer number of nanoseconds; `as_frame()` formats its default runtime column as a pandas duration.

`source` records how the selected ISA instructions were produced. The Ising example extracts compute distance through `entry.source[LATTICE_SURGERY].instruction[DISTANCE]` and synthesis precision through `entry.properties[NUM_TS_PER_ROTATION]`. Those are actual exported property/instruction keys, not universal string columns automatically present in every model result.

For interpretation, `add_factory_summary_column()` displays the number and type of resource-state factory copies, and `add_qubit_partition_column()` exposes modeled compute/factory/memory contributions where supplied. A display helper that substitutes zero for a missing property does not prove the architecture physically needs no such resource. Consult provenance and scope when a field is absent.

The table’s `stats` includes `num_traces`, `num_isas`, `total_jobs`, `successful_estimates`, and `pareto_results`. A search yielding no retained entries produces diagnostics about missing compatible instructions, empty query outputs, errors, or exceeding `max_error`. An empty table is **not an estimate of zero qubits and zero time**. Increasing the allowed error may expose a candidate, but that changes the scientific engineering requirement rather than fixing a numerical typo.

## Pareto frontiers make the tradeoff visible

A candidate is dominated if another feasible candidate uses no more qubits and no more time, with at least one strict improvement. The **Pareto frontier** consists of candidates not dominated in that sense. Direct estimation retains space/time-optimal entries subject to its allowed-error condition; error need not be a third optimization axis merely because it is displayed.
