| A | 200,000 | 4 hours | Smallest footprint among these choices |
| B | 400,000 | 2 hours | Uses more space to finish earlier |
| C | 300,000 | 5 hours | Dominated by A |
| D | 800,000 | 1 hour | Fastest among these choices |

A, B, and D are nondominated in this small set. A 2.5-hour deadline admits B and D, not A. A 300,000-qubit cap favors A; applying both requirements finds no feasible row here. That does not prove no configuration outside the explored set could satisfy them. In the convenience API, study such restrictions separately or inspect/filter a generated frontier because its two named hard constraints cannot be supplied together.

Unit conversion must remain explicit. A hypothetical runtime of \(7.2\times10^{12}\) ns is 7200 seconds, or two hours—not 7200 nanoseconds or two hours of laboratory wall-clock occupancy. Queueing, compilation, initialization not represented in the trace, calibration, classical preprocessing, and operational downtime can remain outside modeled quantum runtime.

Parallel shots can reduce elapsed campaign time only if their machines, factories, classical control, and initializations are supplied concurrently. Doubling throughput by duplicating the whole machine can approximately double space; sharing limited factory capacity changes that reasoning. A Pareto point for one circuit does not specify an unrestricted multi-experiment schedule.

## Compare chemistry algorithms only after matching the task

The nitrogen notebook estimates the largest Trotter IQPE iteration and the largest qubitization iteration separately under one chosen architecture/error budget. That is a useful component comparison. It is not automatically a comparison of complete algorithms that produce an energy with the same tolerance and confidence.

For fixed-base-U QPE, Lesson 27 showed why all powers sum to \(2^m-1\), while the largest power is \(2^{m-1}\). IQPE also prepares fresh states per bit and shot. An all-bit campaign includes those preparations, readouts, trial repeats, and classical aggregation. Multiplying a largest-circuit runtime by an unexplained constant is not a substitute for this ledger, especially when power mappers, reusable ancillas, or synthesis choices change component costs.

For Trotter versus LCU/qubitization/SOSSA, match molecule, geometry, orbital basis, electron/symmetry sector, target state/observable, active/core energy convention, approximation tolerance, and overall success criterion. Equal phase-bit counts do not necessarily imply equal energy resolution: evolution-time phases and block-encoding normalization/shift decoders have different energy sensitivity. The SOS shifted signal and ordinary Hamiltonian energy must be decoded and offset according to their own contracts.

Neither interface infers useful eigenstate overlap or a valid whole-run IQPE success probability. State preparation, postselection losses, and amplification oracles are work that must actually be included. Logical reliability cannot rescue a hybrid-bit IQPE outcome or an off-grid amplification construction that fails its ideal algorithmic assumptions.

The Ising notebook similarly estimates a chosen evolution circuit and explores term grouping/implementation parameters. A full time series, observable campaign, or parameter sweep repeats additional work. An entire chemical potential-energy curve includes multiple geometries, often new classical preprocessing and changed overlaps—not just the best point’s logical trace.

## Make the study record sufficient to reproduce and challenge

A transparent estimate should travel with its input record, not as a screenshot containing one impressive number. The following ledger identifies both the required evidence and the functional handoff; these roles do not assert an organization’s internal ownership structure.

| Record section | Required information and responsible contribution |
|---|---|
| Scientific contract | Chemistry/application contributors state geometry, units, basis, charge/spin/sector, active/inactive spaces, energy reference/offsets, target tolerance, classical validation, and why the model answers the question |
| Algorithm and workload | Algorithm contributors specify trial state, success evidence, evolution/block normalization, power construction, phase precision, all shots/trials, postselection/amplification, state-preparation scope, and allowed parallelism |
| Representation and compilation | Compiler contributors identify source revisions, Circuit representation selected, scratch lifetimes, count versus detailed-trace path, branch/reset limitations, rotation synthesis, and phase/control correctness |
| Physical and QEC assumptions | Hardware/QEC contributors provide compatible primitive errors/times, noise limitations, connectivity, code formulas/distance ranges, extraction/decoder/control assumptions, factories, routing, and buffers |
| Budgets and search | The study records total/partitioned reliability allowance, separate chemical/approximation/statistical targets, query domains, hard constraints, graph/post-processing choices, and cache/provenance conditions |
| Outputs and interpretation | Preserve status/errors, raw counts, units, selected and rejected feasible candidates, complete frontier, code/factory provenance, runtime/space partitions, omitted overhead, and sensitivity conclusions |

Retain exact chemistry and external QDK versions separately. Keep the normalized parameter dictionaries or explicitly enumerated query configuration alongside results. Record whether a plot represents a single largest iteration, one complete run, or a multi-geometry campaign. Distinguish a worst-case runtime bound from an expected runtime derived from an explicit probabilistic schedule.

Sensitivity analysis changes justified assumptions and reports their effect. Examples include a physically consistent range of measurement times/errors, stricter total failure allowance, finer rotation synthesis, alternative factory distances, or a larger active space with documented scientific benefit. Reoptimizing each scenario is usually more informative than assuming one factory count and code distance remain best everywhere. Such sensitivity scenarios are not statistical confidence intervals unless justified input distributions and an uncertainty-propagation method have been supplied. The result’s displayed error is a modeled algorithmic-error contribution, not an uncertainty bar on the assumed hardware performance.

If a configuration fails, preserve why: no compatible ISA, insufficient synthesis accuracy, inadequate distance range, too few factory possibilities, unsupported input, or resource constraints. Do not replace failure with a blank cell that readers interpret as free computation. A result must be qualified by the source and validity of its physical model; favorable independent parameter values from incompatible platforms should never be combined into a supposedly validated machine.

## Use resource estimates to improve the scientific design

The output closes a loop rather than ending the project. An expensive state-preparation method can justify exploring a cheaper state only if increased repetition is counted. A smaller active space can reduce resources while changing chemical predictions; its saved qubits do not erase the scientific approximation. Factorization can reduce representation/circuit cost while introducing approximation or normalization tradeoffs. Tighter phase resolution can sharply increase controlled evolution work, so precision should follow the target result rather than an arbitrary attractive bit count.

The official [resource-estimation introduction](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/intro-to-resource-estimation) and [local setup overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/install-run-resource-estimator) describe this layered external modeling workflow. The chemistry repository supplies application construction and adapters; external QDK supplies the estimator machinery, code/factory models, and physical instruction abstractions inspected here. Neither source can supply missing scientific success evidence or device validation by naming a model.

The final statement should therefore read like: under this explicit scientific model, complete algorithm, reliability/accuracy contract, and compatible hardware/QEC assumptions, these are the modeled feasible space/time tradeoffs within this search. It should not claim actual billing, commercial revenue, a hardware availability date, practical quantum advantage, or successful chemical prediction without the additional evidence those claims require.
lessons.caveats: No estimation, compilation, imports, scientific execution, installs, or filesystem changes performed. Public external source pinned independently to 95c039f4; minimum package dependency does not imply installed-version equivalence. Convenience and direct routes are alternatives with different models/defaults/results. PSSPC and code/factory formulas are model assumptions, not measured hardware or actual synthesized circuits. External convenience input tStates differs from single-result tstates and chemistry skill wording. QIR importer uses all-zero/false branches, skips bare reset, and rejects correlated noise; default QSharp/OpenQASM Application traces are count-derived. Outer graph pruning can miss Pareto candidates; disabling it only covers generated query choices, which may already be filtered. RoundBasedFactory may create a cache directory even with use_cache=False. Convenience failed-leading-batch logicalCounts access is a statically identified failure risk, not a tested runtime finding. All numerical frontier values are synthetic; notebook largest-iteration estimates remain component scope. No hardware timeline, commercial-return, billing, or practical-advantage claims.

lessons.title: Saving, identifying, and reproducing scientific data
lessons.body:
# Lesson 30 — Saving, identifying, and reproducing scientific data

## A result must survive the person and process that produced it

Imagine our nitrogen calculation has finished. We have an energy, an active-space Hamiltonian, a trial wavefunction, circuits, and a conditional resource estimate. A colleague wants to compare a better orbital-selection method next month. Another colleague wants to run the same quantum workload against a different hardware model. A third needs to understand a surprising discrepancy after a software update.

Sending them one energy or a circuit screenshot is not enough. They need scientific artifacts with conventions, identities, and a history. This workstream is where reproducibility becomes an engineering task rather than an aspiration.

**Serialization** converts an in-memory object into a representation that can be saved or transmitted. **Deserialization** reconstructs an object from that representation. A **schema** defines the fields, shapes, types, and conventions of the saved representation. **Provenance** is the record of how an artifact was produced: its inputs, choices, software, and relationship to other artifacts.

These concepts overlap, but they solve different problems. A file can deserialize perfectly while its scientific provenance is missing. A beautifully documented experiment can still be unusable if the only saved object cannot be loaded. We need both.

The [serialization guide](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/user/comprehensive/data/serialization.rst) and [common data interface](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/data_class.hpp) describe the shared mechanisms. Individual data classes determine what information is actually preserved.

## 1. Choose a format according to what must survive

QDK Chemistry uses several formats for different purposes:

| Format | Useful role | What not to assume |
|---|---|---|
| JSON | Inspectable structured text containing fields, lists, numbers, and nested records | Human-readable does not mean small, convention-free, or universally interchangeable. |
| HDF5 | Hierarchical numerical storage with groups, arrays, and attributes | The container format does not explain the scientific meaning of every array. |
| XYZ | Simple molecular geometry interchange | Charge, spin, full precision, custom isotope masses, and all model settings are not preserved by the geometry alone. |
| FCIDUMP | Exchange of electronic Hamiltonian integrals and electron-sector information | It is not a complete archive of an arbitrary QDK workflow or unrestricted Hamiltonian. |
| Cube | A spatially sampled orbital or density for visualization | A sampled picture is not the full orbital basis, wavefunction, or Hamiltonian. |

JSON is convenient when we want to inspect a small artifact in a text editor. HDF5 can store multidimensional arrays without spelling every number as text. Its groups act somewhat like folders, its datasets hold arrays, and its attributes hold associated metadata. Those are capabilities of HDF5; using it does not automatically add compression, scientific validation, or a complete experiment record.

The package uses filenames such as `nitrogen.structure.json`, `selected.orbitals.h5`, and `reference.wavefunction.h5`. The type in the middle matters: the loader checks a `name.type.extension` convention. Giving a wavefunction file a structure suffix does not convert its contents into a structure. The [Python base](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/base.py) performs these checks before opening files.

An instructional round trip looks like this:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.data import Wavefunction

reference.to_hdf5_file("reference.wavefunction.h5")
restored = Wavefunction.from_hdf5_file("reference.wavefunction.h5")
```

This is a usage example, not an operation performed during course preparation. These methods write files; a read-only inspection should not call them merely to learn what they do.

A **round trip** means saving and loading again. Success should be assessed against the relevant scientific properties: orbital identities, dimensions, coefficients, spin blocks, normalization, and energy constants. Merely obtaining an object of the right class is a weaker check.

## 2. Numerical arrays have conventions that text alone cannot convey

Suppose one program saves an array of sixteen numbers. Does it describe a four-by-four matrix, a two-by-two-by-two-by-two tensor, or sixteen unrelated coefficients? Which index changes fastest? Are the values real or complex? Which electron-spin block does the array belong to?

The [array serialization helpers](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/serialization.py) illustrate explicit answers. Real arrays are stored with both their values and shape. Complex arrays can be represented by real and imaginary parts, a shape, and a numerical dtype. **Dtype** specifies the numerical representation, such as a particular floating-point precision.

A complex amplitude is not interchangeable with its real part. Losing its imaginary component can change interference and therefore the state. Likewise, rearranging array storage without rearranging index meaning can silently change a Hamiltonian.

The molecular data model adds further structure. A restricted calculation can share alpha and beta orbital data. An unrestricted calculation may have distinct blocks. Active and inactive orbital-index sets connect an integral tensor to the relevant orbital basis. A sparse container records selected entries; a factorized container records factors from which entries can be reconstructed. Those are not equivalent file layouts, even when they represent the same operator mathematically.

One concrete historical issue makes this less abstract. Older HDF5 matrices were written from Eigen column-major storage into datasets whose dimensions were recorded as rows and columns. A generic reader exposing the raw bytes in another order would misinterpret the logical matrix. The migration helper [read_matrix](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/migrate/_io.py) deliberately reshapes and transposes that legacy layout. This is not a reason to transpose every HDF5 matrix; it is a conversion for a particular old writer contract.

The lesson is that file extensions do not encode all conventions. A compatible writer and loader do.

## 3. A scientific object and a complete experiment are different artifacts

A saved `Structure` retains structural data in its schema, but charge and target multiplicity still belong to the calculation inputs. A Hamiltonian carries its core-energy contribution, but the person comparing results must know whether a later qubit operator or energy decoder already included that contribution. A `Wavefunction` uses a particular container, whose available information may be determinant coefficients, excitation amplitudes, or selected reduced-density information.

Serialization cannot manufacture missing information. An amplitude container does not become an explicit determinant expansion simply because it has been saved and reloaded. A quantum result object that does not retain every original measurement histogram cannot reconstruct those histograms later. A live Q# callable inside a circuit is process-bound behavior, not simply a JSON number that can be restored by a generic loader. The circuit representation and metadata that survive must be inspected, as discussed in Lesson 17.

For our nitrogen story, a reproducible record should connect the structure, basis, charge and spin target, SCF settings and outcome, selected orbital space, Hamiltonian, correlated reference, chosen trial support and coefficients, qubit encoding, circuit construction, measurement or phase-decoding choices, and resource-model assumptions. The schema of one object is only one part of that record.

An **artifact graph** is a useful way to think about this: each node is a saved object or result, and each edge means that a later result used an earlier artifact. The goal is not to save every temporary variable, but to preserve the decisions and data needed to repeat, compare, and explain the computation.

## 4. Schema versions are not package versions

Every data class can carry its own serialization version. That version describes the layout of that type, not the entire package release. Two classes in the same package can have different schema versions, and a package release can leave one schema unchanged while changing another.

The shared [version validator](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/json_serialization.cpp) accepts an exact match. Otherwise it parses major, minor, and patch numbers: the major and minor components must match, while patch differences are allowed. Therefore the broad documentation phrase that only the current version is accepted should not be read as a byte-for-byte patch-version requirement.

A major or minor mismatch raises an error and directs users toward the migration utility. Silently reading an old layout as a new one would be much more dangerous than refusing to load it: the resulting arrays might have the right shape but the wrong meaning.

A **migration** transforms an old schema into the new schema through explicit, version-specific steps. It is not a new chemistry calculation and does not improve the physical accuracy of the saved model.

The supported interface is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry import migrate

migrate.convert_file(
    "old.wavefunction.json",
    "new.wavefunction.h5",
)
```

The equivalent command is `python -m qdk_chemistry.migrate OLD_FILE NEW_FILE`. Input and output formats can differ. This is again instructional syntax, not a request to modify files in the source checkout.

The [converter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/migrate/__init__.py) detects the data type from the filename and the format from the extension. It refuses to migrate in place, so the original remains available. A migration already at the current schema, a source with no registered conversion step, ambiguous type information, or unsupported data produces `MigrationError` rather than a guessed conversion.

After transforming the document, it asks the current data-class loader to reconstruct the object. This final validation prevents a migration script from declaring success merely because it created a dictionary.

## 5. What the migrations actually change

The [migration guide](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/user/migrating-data-files.rst) describes several concrete transitions:

- Orbital coefficients and energies move into symmetry-blocked storage, retaining the associated basis and index information.
- Hamiltonian integral containers move to their symmetry-blocked layouts.
- Older single-determinant, complete-active-space, and selected-CI wavefunctions move into the state-vector container family.
- Older MP2 and coupled-cluster representations move into the amplitude container.
- An `Ansatz` migrates its embedded Hamiltonian and wavefunction through their respective chains.
- `QpeResult` retains its result information while removing an obsolete evolution-time field from the old layout.

Some transformations necessarily change the storage representation without claiming new scientific knowledge. An early Cholesky container saved the full four-center integrals but not the molecular-orbital Cholesky vectors needed by the current factorized representation. The converter therefore preserves those integrals as a canonical four-center Hamiltonian. It does not fabricate missing factors. A later legacy layout that actually stored the required molecular-orbital vectors can retain a Cholesky representation.

The converter also explicitly lacks support for old `TimeEvolutionUnitary` files that did not save the scale required by the current representation. Regeneration is necessary; a guessed scale would change the interpreted operation. Complex coefficients and complex active reduced-density data are not generally handled by these migration paths and are rejected. That limitation is specific to migration, not a claim that every current data class lacks complex-number support.

The [migration examples and fixtures](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_migrate.py) show how exact old layouts are reconstructed and compared with expected new fields. They demonstrate the intended contract in source; no migrations or tests were executed for this lesson.

## 6. Content hashes identify cached work, not scientific truth

A **hash** maps a structured input to a compact identifier. If an expensive calculation is requested again with the same identified inputs, a cache can use that identifier to locate a previous result.

Native `DataClass.content_hash()` defaults to sixteen hexadecimal characters. The [native contract](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/data/data_class.hpp) explicitly treats these as cache keys within a compatible build, not stable archival identifiers across releases. Defining input data participates; lazily computed caches are excluded according to the class contract.

The [Python hashing helpers](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/_hashing.py) encode types, lengths, array shapes, dtype, and values. Arrays are made contiguous and represented with a chosen byte order. Strings can be byte-exact or explicitly normalized where the caller uses the normalized helper. It is wrong to assume that every textual spelling or mathematically equivalent representation will hash identically.

The [algorithm-run hash](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/algorithms/hashing.py) incorporates the algorithm type and implementation, sorted setting names and values, positional inputs, and sorted keyword inputs. Positional and keyword passing remain structurally distinct. Two call forms that ultimately request the same scientific operation need not receive the same identifier.

A short hash also has a finite collision probability: different inputs can in principle share it. More importantly, the hash does not automatically include every external cause of numerical change. Dependency version, compiled numerical kernels, machine characteristics, and random behavior require explicit provenance unless the particular identity mechanism includes them. A cached stochastic computation with a fixed configuration is one stored realization, not a new independent sample every time it is returned.

The practical rule is to record the explicit scientific inputs and software environment alongside hashes. Hashes help us find artifacts; they do not replace the explanation of what those artifacts mean.

## 7. A transport manifest connects metadata to numerical files

Passing a calculation between processes needs more than saving one data class. The [file serializer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/serialization.py) writes a manifest containing typed references to separate artifacts.

A **manifest** is an index: it states which values exist, how to interpret them, and which files contain larger payloads. Ordinary primitive values such as numbers, booleans, strings, and `None` can live directly in JSON. QDK data objects use HDF5 artifacts named by content identity. Supported NumPy arrays use separate `.npy` files, with loading that does not depend on Python pickle execution.

The serializer supports nested lists and tuples of supported values. Arbitrary dictionaries are not a general serializable value type in this protocol; dictionaries are used by the protocol itself. A nested `AlgorithmRef` is a specially supported record carrying algorithm identity and nested settings. Object arrays and structured NumPy dtypes are rejected on the inspected path.

These details explain why an arbitrary Python callback cannot be assumed to run remotely merely because an in-process function accepts it. A value must have a defined wire representation and a compatible reconstruction mechanism at the destination.

**Wire representation** means the format used across that boundary, even if the boundary is only a local subprocess rather than a network. The data registry associates stable type names with loaders. Plugins that define new data classes must register their loaders in both relevant environments.

The transport code writes staged artifacts before replacing the live manifest, and uses temporary files plus atomic replacement for key writes. An **atomic replacement** makes the name switch occur as one filesystem operation rather than exposing half-written JSON. Manifest paths are resolved within the designated directory and checked against traversal outside it. Those are concrete transport safeguards, not a complete authentication or trust system for arbitrary external datasets.

## 8. FCIDUMP is a useful exchange view with narrower scope

The Hamiltonian exposes an [FCIDUMP writer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/src/qdk/chemistry/data/hamiltonian.cpp). FCIDUMP is a conventional text representation used to share electronic-integral problems with many-electron solvers.

The header records quantities such as orbital count, electron count, and the alpha-minus-beta spin projection. Integral entries use one-based orbital indices, unlike the zero-based indices used throughout much of the Python API. The inspected writer uses the trivial C1 orbital-symmetry labels; it is not exporting a discovered molecular point-group classification.

This writer rejects unrestricted Hamiltonians. It obtains two-electron integrals through the container accessor, so exporting a compact factorization can trigger reconstruction of a large four-index tensor. A compact in-memory object does not guarantee compact or cheap interchange output.

FCIDUMP communicates an integral problem. It does not preserve every orbital picture, arbitrary quantum mapping table, state-preparation callable, shot histogram, or hardware-estimation parameter. The presence of an export method also should not be read as a promise that every FCIDUMP dialect can be imported into every high-level class.

Use an exchange format when connecting a compatible solver. Keep the richer native artifact and provenance when reproducibility requires more than the exchange view.

## 9. Cube data turns functions into pictures without becoming the original function

To visualize an orbital, we evaluate it at points on a three-dimensional grid. A cube file records that sampled scalar field along with grid and structural information.

The [CubeGrid and CubeGenerator API](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/include/qdk/chemistry/utils/cube_generator.hpp) defines an axis-aligned grid by origin, spacing, and point counts. Lengths are in bohr. A bounding grid pads the molecular extent by a margin. The first and last points lie on the padded box; a one-point axis has zero spacing. Invalid zero dimensions and excessive point counts are explicitly rejected.

`CubeGenerator.orbital` evaluates one orbital from its basis coefficients. `density` evaluates the supplied density matrix as a quadratic combination of basis functions. It does not automatically add spin blocks or multiply a restricted density by two. Two density matrices can have identical shape yet represent total density and half that total. Shape validation alone cannot detect the scientific distinction.

The evaluator uses the basis ordering and normalization contract; coefficients copied from another package may require permutation. With an ECP, the cube describes the explicitly represented electron contribution. Missing replaced-core density is a feature of that model, not evidence that the plotting engine lost electrons.

The Python convenience function [generate_cubefiles_from_orbitals](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/cubegen.py) offers native and optional PySCF evaluation. A subtle operational fact is that `output_folder=None` still uses temporary intermediate files before returning text, despite prose suggesting otherwise. The lower-level generator can evaluate without writing by using an empty output filename. These distinctions matter in read-only, restricted, or remote environments.

Finally, a visually smooth orbital is not a guarantee of numerical accuracy. Grid spacing, extent, selected isosurface value, and sign coloring determine what we see. **Isosurface** means a surface joining points with the same field value. It is a visualization of sampled information, not the full analytical basis representation or a literal boundary of an electron.

## 10. The handoff we want to be able to reproduce

A useful saved calculation identifies the scientific model, the intermediate data, the algorithm recipe, the actual result, and the conditions under which it was produced. We preserve original inputs before migration, use a compatible loader rather than guessing array conventions, and distinguish archival records from disposable caches.

For nitrogen, the geometry must still say 1.85 Å rather than silently becoming the separate notebook example. The active Hamiltonian and core energy must still describe the same chosen space. A restored trial state must use the same orbitals and occupation convention. A reported energy must still be traceable to its measurement or phase decoder. A resource estimate must still identify the circuit and hardware assumptions it counted.

Saving those relationships lets another team improve one stage and measure its consequences. The next lesson uses the same serialization and identity machinery to move work between processes and machines without losing the meaning of the computation.
lessons.caveats: Read-only source study at97a3ff4f; no serialization/migration/cube generation or tests executed. Major/minor schemas must match but shared validator permits patch differences. Migration is not arbitrary format conversion: current/unsupported schemas and complex legacy coefficient/RDM paths can fail. Old missing Cholesky factors migrate to four-center data; old missing unitary scale cannot be inferred. Native hashes are compatible-build cache identities, not archival identifiers. File transport supports typed lists/tuples but not arbitrary dict values/callables/object arrays. FCIDUMP writer is restricted, uses trivial C1 labels, can materialize dense ERIs. Cube helper with output_folder=None still writes temporary files; lower-level no-output evaluator is distinct.

lessons.title: Running work elsewhere and reusing results
lessons.body:
# Lesson 31 — Running work elsewhere and reusing results

## The chemistry should not depend on the computer beside your desk

Our nitrogen example is small enough to explain locally. A research campaign can be very different: many geometries, larger basis sets, expensive correlated calculations, substantial integral storage, and many quantum-circuit simulations. The person designing that workflow may not have enough memory or compute capacity on their laptop.

Moving a calculation elsewhere sounds simple: send the inputs, run the program, retrieve the results. In practice, the engineering questions are just as important as the numerical ones. Which software is installed at the destination? What if the client disconnects? Was the job submitted twice? Where are its inputs and outputs? Can we reuse an identical result rather than recompute it? Who may cancel or clean up the job?

This lesson follows the [remote execution package](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/__init__.py). Remote execution here means executing a registered QDK Chemistry algorithm through a job protocol. It does not by itself mean submitting a quantum circuit to a quantum processor. The remote algorithm may be a classical SCF calculation, a circuit-construction step, or another serializable operation.

The scientific method is chosen as before. The backend determines where and how that chosen operation is executed.

## 1. Three execution choices that must stay distinct

A direct `algorithm.run(...)` normally executes in the current process. A blocking remote call submits elsewhere and waits for the result. An asynchronous remote call returns a handle before the calculation finishes.

**Blocking** means the caller waits before continuing. **Asynchronous** means the caller can do other work while the job progresses. A **job handle** identifies and manages the submitted work; it is not the result itself.

Algorithms created through the registry accept remote and cache controls. A source-backed blocking example is:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.algorithms import create

scf = create("scf_solver", "qdk", method="hf")
energy, wavefunction = scf.run(
    structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz",
    remote="local",
)
```

The backend named `local` deliberately uses a separate process on the same computer. It exercises the transfer and job protocol without requiring an external service. It is not a faster quantum device or a cloud account.

For asynchronous work, the module-level `submit` returns a `Job`:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.remote import submit

job = submit(
    scf,
    structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz",
    remote="local",
    job_dir="job-records",
)
```

Here `job_dir` asks the SDK to persist the job record automatically. Without it, `submit` can return an in-memory job that the caller must explicitly save if it should survive the current process. These snippets explain the API; they were not run during course preparation.

The [proxy implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/proxy.py) also exposes a module-level `run` with blocking behavior. Merely writing `remote=` does not turn the normal result pair into a job object. That distinction prevents code from trying to interpret a submission identifier as an energy.

## 2. Build a portable execution request

The proxy constructs a payload containing the algorithm type and name, configured settings, positional and keyword arguments, and identifying hashes where available. It does not transmit the live C++ solver object from Python memory.

The serializer from Lesson 30 writes a manifest and separate numerical artifacts. The compute-side worker reconstructs the algorithm through the registry and reapplies its settings. A `Wavefunction` travels as supported serialized data, not as an arbitrary pointer into another process.

The compute environment therefore needs compatible QDK Chemistry code, the same required algorithm registrations, suitable data loaders, and the external dependencies used by that algorithm. A local Python object that relies on an uninstalled plugin does not become usable remotely just because it can be named in a manifest.

Nested `AlgorithmRef` settings preserve the composition of a workflow. For example, a geometry optimizer may delegate energy calculations to a configured derivative algorithm, which in turn delegates to an electronic solver. The destination must be able to reconstruct all those layers.

The [worker entry point](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/worker.py) is `python -m qdk_chemistry.remote.worker`. It loads the request, checks configured cache information, deserializes inputs when needed, creates the algorithm, applies settings, executes it, and either serializes outputs or commits them through a shared cache transport.

This is an explicit protocol, not arbitrary Python pickling. Its accepted values include the data classes, numerical arrays, primitive values, supported sequences, and nested algorithm references discussed previously. An arbitrary callback or unsupported dictionary value may not cross the boundary even when some in-process API can accept it.

## 3. A backend owns placement and transport, not the chemistry

The [RemoteBackend interface](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/backends/base.py) defines the responsibilities needed to run that protocol:

| Responsibility | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `connect` and `disconnect` | Establish and release access to the execution or storage service. |
| `upload` and `download` | Move serialized artifacts when they are not already accessible. |
| `_submit` | Launch work and return an identifier plus persistent backend state. |
| `check` | Query the current status and available diagnostics. |
| `fetch` | Retrieve and deserialize the completed output. |
| `cancel` | Request termination, when supported. |
| `cleanup_job` | Remove retained backend artifacts for a finished job, when supported. |

The asynchronous submission, status, and result-retrieval hooks are required abstract operations in the inspected base class. Cancellation and cleanup have default implementations that raise `NotImplementedError`. Some older example prose calls more of these hooks optional; the current interface is the authority.

The backend returns a persistent description of its job, such as an operation identifier or process identity and artifact locations. That state must be JSON-compatible after path normalization. The framework validates the metadata rather than silently accepting live connection objects that could not be restored.

A backend can be registered through a plugin. Registering a backend gives it a discoverable name; it does not provision a cluster, grant credentials, or install chemistry dependencies at the destination.

A custom [SSH example](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/custom_remote_backend.py) demonstrates direct execution on an SSH-accessible machine. **SSH** is a secure remote-login protocol; **SCP** transfers files through that ecosystem. This example assumes suitable remote commands and Python software. It does not implement submission to a queue scheduler such as Slurm merely because an HPC machine might use one.

A **scheduler** allocates resources among competing jobs. Integrating such a scheduler is a separate backend responsibility, not an automatic capability of the SSH transport example.

## 4. Follow the local subprocess implementation

The [local backend](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/backends/local.py) makes the mechanics especially visible.

On connection, it creates a temporary working area. For a submitted job, it creates separate input and output directories, writes the serialized request, and launches the worker with the selected Python executable. Standard output and error streams go to log files.

A **process** is a running program with its own execution state. Launching a subprocess tests that the request really can be reconstructed independently of the client object. It is useful for debugging serialization, plugin availability, and job recovery even though no network is involved.

The backend retains a process identifier and, on supported operating systems, additional process-creation identity. Process identifiers can eventually be reused, so cancellation after reconnecting must not blindly terminate whatever program currently has the old number. The local implementation checks identity before terminating a process whose original handle is no longer available.

When the original process handle exists, a successful status requires both a zero exit code and an output manifest. When reconstructing status later, the presence of the output manifest is important evidence that results are available. Missing outputs and a dead process indicate failure rather than a fabricated result.

Disconnecting the backend does not mean canceling submitted work or deleting its artifacts. It only removes the temporary connection directory if it is empty. This separation is what allows persisted jobs to remain inspectable after the original client closes its connection.

Subprocess isolation is not a claim of a hardened security sandbox. The worker still runs trusted installed code with the permissions and environment provided by the host.

## 5. A job record is a durable lifecycle record

The [Job class](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/job.py) stores the backend name and reconstructible configuration, backend-specific state, algorithm information, submission time, last-known status, input and output hashes, and whether the original output was a tuple. MCP-managed jobs can also carry workspace/project ownership information.

That last output-shape field matters. A scalar energy and a pair containing energy and wavefunction must not become indistinguishable merely because results were stored as separate items.

The main operations are `check()`, `wait()`, `fetch()`, `cancel()`, `save()`, `load()`, and `cleanup()`. A normal lifecycle proceeds from submission through running to success, failure, or cancellation. After output retrieval the local record can have status `retrieved`.

**Terminal** means that execution has reached a final state; it does not mean success. `failed` and `canceled` are terminal too. The helper named `is_successful` specifically recognizes `succeeded`, not every terminal status, so application logic should not reinterpret every completed handle as a usable result. Retrieval is its own state transition.

`wait()` polls until terminal state or the configured timeout. **Polling** means checking status periodically, rather than continuously occupying a CPU. Default backend polling and wait timeout are five seconds and 3600 seconds. A wait timeout describes how long this client waits; it does not universally impose an execution deadline on the remote service and does not automatically cancel the job. A persisted identifier lets the caller inspect the work again later.

`fetch()` obtains the result and records output information. Backend artifacts are retained by default. `fetch(cleanup=True)` requests backend cleanup after successful retrieval and persistence; `cleanup()` explicitly removes terminal-job artifacts when the backend supports it. Neither is a license to remove unrelated directories or all shared cache data.

Preserving a job JSON file alone does not preserve every output forever. Large outputs may be separate artifacts or cache entries. Reproducibility requires those payloads and their loaders to remain available too.

## 6. Cache reuse is a different optimization from remote execution

A **cache** stores a result so an equivalent identified request can avoid repeated computation. Remote execution changes where work runs. The two can be used together or independently.

A cache-backed call can look like this:

```python
energy, wavefunction = scf.run(
    structure, 0, 1, "cc-pvdz",
    cache="calculation-cache",
    remote="local",
)
```

A path resolves to a folder cache. On a complete cache hit, the result can be returned without launching the worker. On a miss, the operation runs and the result is stored.

The [FolderCache](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/cache/folder.py) separates job metadata from content-addressed artifacts. Small primitive outputs, such as an energy, can live in the job record. Numerical objects and arrays have separate files. Supported nested sequences use manifests that reference their components.

A cache entry is complete only if its output descriptors can reconstruct the expected result. A job record pointing to a missing wavefunction is not a usable hit. Some corrupted metadata and numerical-array files are treated as misses; a data-class loader can still raise a schema error. Cache behavior should not be described as a universal silent-recovery guarantee.

Writes use temporary files and replacement to avoid exposing some partially written artifacts. That does not make the whole system a distributed transaction manager or guarantee exactly-once computation under arbitrary simultaneous clients. Reuse of an already recorded in-flight job reduces duplicate submissions in the supported flow; concurrent requests and external service failures still need careful operational handling.

`force_rerun=True` bypasses cache lookup and requests a new computation. This is useful when deliberately obtaining a new stochastic realization or investigating changed external behavior. A cache hit is an old result, not another independent sample. If random seeds or external dependencies are absent from the identity, the operator must account for that limitation rather than interpret every reuse as independent evidence.

## 7. Layer local and shared caches without pretending they are the same place

A fast local cache is convenient for repeated analysis. A shared filesystem can let a compute node and several clients access the same large Hamiltonian without repeated uploads.

The [`TieredCache`](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/remote/cache/tiered.py) combines several backends in priority order:

```python
from qdk_chemistry.remote.cache import FolderCache, TieredCache

cache = TieredCache([
    FolderCache("local-cache"),
    FolderCache("shared-team-cache", is_shared=True),
])
```

The example path marked shared is illustrative. A real deployment must ensure that both the client and worker can reach the intended storage. Setting a flag does not create a network mount or grant access.

On reads, the tiered cache tries earlier tiers first. A hit in a later tier is **backfilled** into earlier tiers: copied nearer to the caller for future access. On writes, it writes through to every eligible tier. The remote view retains only the tiers declared reachable by the compute side.

This yields two different savings. A complete result can avoid computation altogether. Shared input artifacts can avoid transfer even when a new calculation is still needed. Reusing a Hamiltonian for several trial-state studies is a typical example of the second case.

The proxy can also encounter a recorded remote job still in flight. It resumes waiting on that identifier rather than immediately submitting the same identified request again. After success, it can reconstruct results directly from a shared cache or fetch them from the backend.

Job records managed through the assistant interface are additionally scoped by workspace/project ownership. That is an application-level management boundary. It is not a replacement for operating-system permissions, cloud authorization, or careful handling of shared numerical data.

## 8. The compute worker can reuse results, but cache failures are not all equivalent

The worker checks a declared remote cache before reconstructing and executing the algorithm. It can also write completed output data and a job record back to that cache.

Ordinary cache read or write failures are logged on the inspected worker path. Where normal output-file transport is available, execution and result serialization can proceed even when the optimization failed. That is appropriate when a cache is optional.

A cache-only transport is different. If the remote cache is the only supported way to return results, failing to persist the result there must be an error. The worker explicitly rejects successful completion of that transport without a retained result. Otherwise the service could report completion while the client had no recoverable output.

The [remote and serialization cases](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/test_remote.py) exercise result-shape preservation, cache bypass, staged manifests, and ownership-scoped records. These source-level scenarios help explain the intended lifecycle; no jobs or tests were run for this lesson.

## 9. The Discovery adapter is an integration, not a cloud entitlement

The repository also contains a [Microsoft Discovery backend](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/discovery/backend.py), registered when the optional Discovery SDK is available through the [plugin loader](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/discovery/__init__.py).

It requires deployment-specific information including a workspace endpoint, project, tool identifier, and node pool. A **node pool** describes the compute resources on which work may be placed. Optional configuration includes the execution image, Python path, requested CPU/GPU resources and memory, storage choices, polling, and artifact-retrieval retries.

An **image** here describes the packaged execution environment. Requesting GPUs does not make a CPU-only algorithm use them or ensure that the selected package was compiled with suitable acceleration. Compute provisioning and algorithm capability remain separate questions.

The adapter supports `auto`, `blob`, and `cache` transport modes. Blob transport uses configured Azure storage linked to the Discovery storage asset; **blob storage** stores named binary objects remotely. Cache transport requires a shared cache accessible to the compute node and a deterministic request identity. Auto mode chooses a usable configured path; it does not invent missing storage.

Authentication is delegated through [Azure credential helpers](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/plugins/discovery/_sdk.py), which support Azure CLI credentials or the configured default credential chain. The SDK reports an operation identifier that is retained for later status, cancellation, and retrieval. These mechanisms depend on an authorized external deployment. Source code availability is not evidence that a particular user has that service, quota, image, or permission.

The backend can obtain defaults from `QDK_DISCOVERY_*` environment variables, with explicit constructor values taking precedence. A persisted backend configuration needs enough information for reconnection, so operational design should avoid placing raw secrets in fields intended for ordinary job JSON. Credentials should be supplied through the supported secure authentication mechanisms.

MCP clients can override only the configuration fields the backend explicitly marks safe. For this adapter those are retry and polling/timeout controls, not arbitrary endpoints, credentials, images, or node pools. A backend subclass must make its own declaration; permission is not automatically inherited as a blanket trust decision.

## 10. Evaluate the entire operational cost

Moving a computation does not erase its cost. An illustrative wall-time model is

\[
T_{\mathrm{total}}=T_{\mathrm{serialize}}+T_{\mathrm{transfer}}+T_{\mathrm{queue}}+T_{\mathrm{compute}}+T_{\mathrm{retrieve}}+T_{\mathrm{analysis}}.
\]

Each term names time spent preparing artifacts, moving them, waiting for resources, calculating, recovering outputs, or interpreting results. This is an accounting model, not a benchmark measured here.

For a tiny SCF problem, transfer and startup may dominate. For a large integral model, memory and data movement may be the limiting factor. For a campaign of related calculations, caching shared inputs or prior results may save more than changing where the worker runs.

Remote execution therefore creates a contract between scientific workflow authors, backend/platform engineers, environment and storage operators, and users who supply authorized access. The chemistry team specifies a portable operation. The platform provides placement and lifecycle management. Serialization preserves its data meaning. Caching avoids eligible repetition. The caller remains responsible for interpreting success, preserving needed artifacts, and understanding whether the result was newly computed or reused.

The next lesson adds the human and AI-assistant interfaces that make those same operations available without writing the Python orchestration by hand.
lessons.caveats: Read-only source tracing at97a3ff4f; no imports, subprocesses, cloud/SSH operations, caches or tests executed. local is a separate local process, not hardware execution; Discovery requires optional SDK and authorized external deployment. Normal run is blocking, submit returns Job; persistence requires job_dir/save. Job.wait timeout does not universally cancel remote execution; retrieved differs from succeeded in status helper. Required backend async hooks differ from stale SSH example prose. Shared cache flag does not create connectivity; no universal distributed exactly-once guarantee or durable archival promise. Worker cache failure may be logged and bypassed for normal transport but cache-only transport must retain output. Backend parameters/job metadata are not a secret store.

lessons.title: Human and agent interfaces
lessons.body:
# Lesson 32 — Human and agent interfaces

## The same science needs more than one front door

A scientist comfortable with Python can construct objects and call algorithms directly. Another researcher may prefer repeatable shell commands. An AI assistant needs structured operations it can discover, call, and interpret. A colleague reviewing an active space may learn more from orbital pictures than from a coefficient matrix.

QDK Chemistry serves these situations through the command-line interface, the MCP server, project-based artifact management, visualization tools, and a Copilot plugin. They are not different physical theories. They are different ways to access and coordinate the scientific machinery we have already studied.

The key engineering principle is to make a tool invocation traceable to actual inputs and outputs. A friendly assistant response is not itself an SCF calculation. A rendered circuit is not proof that it executed. A file named after a molecule is not a complete description of its charge, spin, and approximation choices.

The [AI-assistant guide](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/user/agents.rst) introduces these interfaces. This lesson follows their implementations so we can distinguish convenient presentation from guarantees the code actually makes.

## 1. Python, the CLI, and MCP have related but different contracts

A **command-line interface**, or CLI, exposes operations as commands entered in a terminal. QDK Chemistry installs the executable `qc`. A command parses text arguments, calls the relevant implementation, and prints a result that a human or another program can inspect.

**MCP**, the Model Context Protocol, gives an AI client a structured way to discover and invoke tools exposed by a server. The server advertises tool names, parameter schemas, and descriptions. The client supplies structured arguments rather than inventing a Python call from scratch.

A **schema** describes expected input fields and types. A **transport** describes how requests and responses move between the client and server. Neither chooses the scientifically appropriate basis, active space, or energy accuracy on its own.

The shared [tools module](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/tools.py) contains many operations used by both CLI handlers and MCP registration. Most file-producing tools load named artifacts, create a selected algorithm, apply settings, run it, and save declared outputs. They expose an artifact workflow rather than passing arbitrary Python objects through the assistant conversation.

There is still a difference between the Python algorithm API and these tool wrappers. The wrapper catalog is finite, its accepted arguments are explicit, and not every newly registered algorithm type automatically gets an entirely new CLI command or assistant tool. Plugins can extend supported implementations behind an existing interface; exposing a new kind of task may require a wrapper as well.

## 2. Discover the actual operations before choosing settings

The tool catalog is organized around the scientific journey:

| Area | Representative operations | The handoff it supports |
|---|---|---|
| Project management | `create_project`, `list_projects`, `list_project_files` | Establish and inspect an artifact workspace. |
| Input construction | `create_structure`, model-Hamiltonian and mapping construction | Turn explicit inputs into typed scientific artifacts. |
| Classical preparation | SCF, stability, localization, active-space, correlated calculations, derivatives and geometry optimization | Produce the electronic model and useful starting states. |
| Quantum preparation | Qubit mapping, term grouping, state preparation, circuit builders | Produce a compatible encoded operator and operations. |
| Execution and analysis | Circuit execution, expectation estimation, Hadamard tests, phase estimation and dynamics | Obtain the result appropriate to the selected algorithm. |
| Data inspection | Summaries, orbital extraction, active indices, determinant/configuration inspection | Check intermediate objects rather than blindly chaining them. |
| Resource analysis | `get_circuit_stats`, `estimate_circuit` | Inspect a logical circuit and estimate costs under stated models. |
| Remote execution | Job checking, retrieval, listing and cancellation | Manage long-running work without confusing submission with completion. |
| Visualization | Molecules, orbitals, entanglement, circuits and numeric scatter plots | Present existing numerical information in an interpretable view. |

`list_algorithms` reports implementations that are actually registered. `describe_algorithm` exposes their setting schema. `get_algorithm_default_type` and `get_algorithm_default_settings` report defaults. `describe_backend` explains available remote/cache backend configuration, including what an MCP client may change.

The server deliberately exposes compact operation descriptions. Detailed usage knowledge is provided separately in the [MCP skill and reference](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/copilot-plugins/qdk-chemistry/skills/qdk-chemistry-mcp/SKILL.md). Compact descriptions reduce catalog overhead, but they do not contain every scientific caveat. A capable assistant must use both the schema and the domain guidance, and still preserve the scientific requirements stated by the user.

The [catalog checks](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/ui/test_mcp_catalog.py) enumerate the reviewed tool names and optional visualizers. Installed optional dependencies affect the live catalog, so a static tool count is less useful than discovery in the actual environment.

## 3. Bind an assistant process to the intended workspace

A plugin-launched MCP process may start in the installed plugin directory, not in the folder containing the scientist data. Resolving relative filenames against that accidental working directory would be a serious workflow mistake.

The [workspace binding mechanism](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/workspace.py) therefore binds one process to one explicit absolute workspace. It can use a single file root supplied by the MCP client or an explicit `workspace_root` argument to `bind_workspace`.

The packaged [MCP configuration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/copilot-plugins/qdk-chemistry/.mcp.json) sets `QDK_REQUIRE_WORKSPACE_BINDING=1`. Its middleware rejects workspace-dependent operations until binding succeeds, unless it can safely discover the one required client root. **Middleware** is a layer that checks a request before passing it to the actual tool.

Once bound, the process cannot be rebound to a different workspace. A different workspace needs another process. Repeating the same binding is acceptable, but rebinding for every tool call is unnecessary.

Binding establishes default `projects`, `cache`, and `jobs` storage beneath the workspace, subject to the explicit cache/job environment overrides. It does not change the global process working directory. Project-specific contexts supply the correct resolved paths for individual operations.

This matters when two requests or projects coexist: one request should not redirect another by changing a process-wide current directory. The [workspace tests](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/tests/ui/test_workspace_binding.py) express that invariant directly.

Binding is not read-only. It can create the required storage directories. Importing the UI configuration also initializes storage. Consequently, even a command intended only for inspection should not be assumed to have zero filesystem side effects merely because it does not run chemistry.

## 4. A project is a namespace for artifacts, not a physical model

The UI project directory contains files such as structures, orbitals, wavefunctions, Hamiltonians, circuits, and results. A project name groups them for tool access; it does not set a molecular charge or select a scientific method.

The [validation layer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/validation.py) requires a suitable single-component project name and verifies that resolved files stay inside the intended project. It handles both Windows and POSIX path conventions, rejects parent traversal and inappropriate absolute paths, and checks where symlinks resolve. Some tools accept nested paths explicitly, while others strip supplied directories and work with basenames.

Those policies make filename handling more predictable. They are not a complete general-purpose operating-system sandbox or cloud authorization scheme.

The type marker in a filename remains important. Helpers can insert the expected marker for an output name, but a downstream tool still needs the returned actual filename rather than an assumed spelling. A wrapper may return a file or an energy plus filename; the exact tool schema and result must be read.

For our nitrogen calculation, the structure-construction tool expects coordinates in bohr. Its `coordinates_json` input is a JSON string representing a nested array with one three-component row per atom. It checks the shape against the element list and the optional mass/charge array lengths. The [implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/tools.py) explicitly directs callers with ångström data toward `convert_coordinates`.

This differs from `Structure.from_xyz`, which interprets XYZ coordinates in ångströms. An assistant must not copy numbers between those entry points without the corresponding conversion.

## 5. Trace one tool call all the way to a saved result

The `run_scf` tool accepts a project, a structure filename, an output wavefunction filename, charge, spin multiplicity, basis name, and optional implementation/settings/execution controls.

Its flow is concrete:

1. Resolve and check the output filename.
2. Load the structure using the expected data class.
3. Create the requested `scf_solver` implementation.
4. Apply its settings, including nested references where supported.
5. Execute through the common local/cache/remote helper.
6. Save the wavefunction and return the energy with the filename.

The wrapper is not a second Hartree–Fock implementation. It coordinates the same algorithm contract we examined earlier.

Existing output handling is a separate decision. If the requested output already contains valid data and `overwrite` is false, the tool reports an `exists` status. This protects against accidentally replacing an expensive artifact.

However, an existing valid wavefunction at a filename is not proof that it came from the newly requested geometry and settings. File-existence protection and content-identity caching are different mechanisms. Before accepting an old output, inspect its provenance. Before overriding it, decide whether the original should be retained under a distinct name.

On the common execution path, `overwrite=True` is also forwarded as a force-rerun request for caching. It can therefore do more than permit replacing a file: it can cause expensive numerical work to be repeated.

## 6. Status envelopes are part of scientific correctness

The structured wrapper converts most ordinary tool results into an envelope:

| Status | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `ok` | The operation returned its normal result. |
| `error` | Validation, execution, or serialization failed; inspect the message and error type. |
| `exists` | A valid output path already exists; a replacement/reuse decision is needed. |
| `submitted` | Remote work has been recorded but is not yet complete. |

The `bind_workspace` result has its own `bound` confirmation, and visualization tools use MCP App result structures with text fallbacks. It is therefore more accurate to inspect each contract than to claim every server operation returns an identical envelope.

For remote work, the common tool helper starts the response-wait window only after a durable job handle has been recorded. If the calculation finishes within `remote_timeout`, the tool can return the normal result. Otherwise it returns submission metadata, and the caller can use `check_remote_job` and `retrieve_remote_results` later. A backend-raised timeout remains an actual error rather than being mislabeled as ordinary successful submission.

A submitted job identifier is not an energy. An `exists` response is not a newly calculated result. An exception converted into a JSON error is still a failure, even if the transport request itself succeeded.

The CLI has its own presentation formatter, so do not assume its displayed wrapper is byte-for-byte identical to the MCP result. Workflow automation should inspect documented status information rather than search for a reassuring word in a text message.

## 7. The current CLI is grouped, despite an older flat-command header

The actual [argument parser](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/cli.py) organizes commands into groups:

```text
qc run scf ...
qc data summary ...
qc config algorithms
qc project list
qc util convert-energy ...
qc workflow ...
qc describe ...
qc plugin ...
```

Some older docstrings still show flat names such as `qc run-scf`. The current `create_parser` implementation is the reliable guide for this revision.

An explicit SCF command uses `--project-name`, `--structure-filename`, `--out-wavefunction-filename`, `--charge`, `--spin-multiplicity`, and `--basis-set`, with optional implementation and JSON settings. Help text can also retain stale descriptions of defaults; the algorithm registry determines the actual default implementation.

Compound workflows support a JSON configuration file and `--set key.path=value` overrides. A **dotted path** identifies a value inside nested configuration records. Values are parsed as JSON when possible, so a numeric value, boolean, and string need not be confused. This supports configuring the child algorithms inside a larger procedure without editing Python code.

`qc --dry-run ...` previews parameters without invoking the requested calculation. A workflow dry run additionally checks known commands, required arguments, and filename references. It is not a proof of valid chemistry, available dependencies, converged algorithms, or side-effect-free module initialization.

The CLI `workflow` command runs a sequence of supported steps. References such as `$prev`, `$prev.1`, and `$step.3` connect declared output filenames from previous steps. These are workflow reference strings, not shell variables in this context. The implementation recognizes a finite set of workflow operations, not arbitrary Python expressions.

Dry-run validation can identify unresolved references or an input that must already exist. Actual execution stops on an explicit error envelope. It does not make all stages one atomic transaction: earlier results can remain after a later stage fails. The caller must also account for statuses such as `exists` and `submitted` rather than treating every non-error return as ready input to the next numerical step.

## 8. Installable skills supply guidance; the server supplies capabilities

The Copilot plugin combines two kinds of material.

**Skills** are readable domain guidance: explanations of tool contracts, method-selection considerations, remote execution, visualization, resource estimation, and coding patterns. They help an assistant choose and use tools.

The **MCP server configuration** tells the client how to launch the executable that actually performs supported operations.

A skill file does not install a scientific dependency or grant permission to a remote service. Conversely, an available server can expose a method whose safe scientific use requires more knowledge than its short description contains.

The [plugin installer](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/plugin_installer.py) integrates with Copilot plugin installation and binds the MCP command to the intended Python environment. A **virtual environment** is an isolated Python installation context used to keep package dependencies separate from unrelated projects.

For a user-scoped installation, the fetched plugin is maintained in the corresponding Copilot scope and its command is bound to the selected environment. With `--target-dir`, the installer deploys skills and relevant configuration into that workspace, including `.vscode/mcp.json` and `.github/mcp.json`, and records fetch/binding state under `.qdk_chem`.

The two configuration files use their respective expected top-level server keys. The installer merges server information instead of treating them as identical formats. Local plugin directories, marketplace specifications, and supported repository subdirectory specifications have different resolution paths.

Updates can refresh plugin files and disturb the command binding unless it is restored. The `qc plugin update` and `qc plugin rebind` paths preserve or re-establish the intended executable relationship. A stale binding to an environment that no longer exists is an operational error, not evidence that a chemistry method is unavailable in principle.

These installation operations change configuration and files. They are described here, not performed on the source repository or a reader workspace.

## 9. MCP is optional, and transport choices do not add scientific authority

The [optional integration module](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/_mcp.py) preserves shared CLI functions when the MCP dependency is absent. Installing the MCP extra enables actual server registration and the available visualization resources.

The executable `qcmcp` starts the server. The [entry point](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/mcp.py) supports standard input/output, streamable HTTP, and server-sent-events transport. Standard input/output connects directly to a client process. HTTP transports communicate through a listening endpoint; the default host is loopback, `127.0.0.1`, and the default port is 8081.

Compatibility switches can remove output-schema/UI metadata for older hosts, use sessionless HTTP, return JSON rather than event-stream framing, or relax an HTTP Accept-header requirement. They address protocol compatibility. They do not provide authentication, safe internet deployment, scientific correctness, or quantum hardware access by themselves.

Changing the server to listen beyond the local machine is an operational deployment decision. Network exposure, authorization, filesystem permissions, and secret handling need their own controls. The fact that a client speaks MCP does not make every requested action scientifically appropriate or authorized.

## 10. Visualize actual artifacts and state what the picture means

The [visualization module](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/ui/visualization.py) registers interactive MCP App resources when the required widget package is available. An **MCP App** is a view the host can render alongside a tool result. A host without that support may receive the structured/text data without displaying the interactive widget.

The available views serve different questions:

- `visualize_molecule` displays the saved nuclear geometry.
- `visualize_orbitals` evaluates selected orbital fields and displays isosurfaces with the molecule.
- `visualize_orbital_entanglement` displays the available entropy and mutual-information data using orbital labels.
- `visualize_circuit` converts a saved circuit into the widget-compatible representation.
- `visualize_scatter_plot` renders caller-supplied numerical series, with labels and optional logarithmic axes.

The molecular and orbital widgets are supplied by the broader QDK widget package. Chemistry supplies structures, basis coefficients, and grid data. The local scatter renderer builds an SVG plot from supplied numbers. It is a presentation tool, not a computation of those numbers.

Orbital visualization needs basis and coefficient information. Entanglement visualization needs the relevant reduced-density/entropy information; it does not generally run a missing correlated calculation on behalf of the viewer. Its selected-index mapping converts absolute orbital labels into the positions used by the chart, avoiding the common mistake of confusing active-space position zero with molecular orbital zero.

The circuit viewer obtains QASM and converts it through the QDK circuit representation. A `Circuit` object that lacks a supported route to that representation can fail to render. A diagram is therefore one view of an available circuit, not a universal serialization of all its executable behavior or physical cost.

Orbital views do not change the stored wavefunction, but evaluating cube data can allocate substantial memory and use temporary files through the convenience helper. More grid points can improve the picture while increasing cost; a prettier surface does not validate the basis or correlation model.

A scatter plot can help compare resource frontiers or energy curves, but it does not verify axis units, matched scientific models, or whether the supplied points came from valid calculations. The person or workflow producing the series retains that responsibility.

## 11. The assistant should preserve decisions, not hide them

An assistant can make the workflow more accessible: discover methods, construct typed inputs, call a solver, inspect a result, display orbitals, and keep track of remote jobs. The danger is collapsing this into a story that sounds successful while losing the actual choices.

A good assistant-mediated nitrogen workflow still records the geometry and units, charge and spin, basis, implementation and settings, convergence/stability evidence, selected model space, energy constants, qubit encoding, actual execution result, and any resource assumptions. It reports missing prerequisites or unsupported combinations. It does not invent an energy when a tool returns an error or label a queued job as a completed calculation.

The user-interface workstream therefore connects domain expertise, reliable software contracts, readable error/status information, and useful visual explanations. Its value is not that the scientist can forget the scientific model. Its value is that the mechanics become easier to operate while the model and evidence remain visible.

The next lesson looks underneath these interfaces at the build, dependency, testing, and release work that makes the whole package available and maintainable.
lessons.caveats: Read-only source inspection at97a3ff4f. No CLI/MCP imports/server/plugin installation, file-producing tools or visualizers executed. Actual CLI parser grouped despite flat top docstring. UI config and workspace binding create directories; dry-run prevents requested calculation but is not universal no-side-effect guarantee. Tool outputs have distinct envelope/submitted/exists semantics; bind and MCP App results differ. Existing file does not prove requested-input identity; overwrite forces rerun on shared helper. Workflow is sequential whitelist, not transactional DAG or guaranteed wait-for-submitted result. Schema/UI stripping and HTTP switches are compatibility, not authentication. Viewer relies on optional widgets and conversion/cube requirements.
