lessons.body:
# Lesson 33 — Engineering and maintaining the whole package

## An algorithm is useful only when the surrounding software works

We have followed the scientific calculation from a molecular question to quantum circuits and conditional resource estimates. We have also learned how artifacts, remote jobs, and user interfaces connect the stages. There is one large workstream left: making the package build, install, behave predictably, and remain understandable as the code evolves.

This work is sometimes treated as peripheral to the science. In reality, a wrong tensor convention at a language boundary can invalidate an energy, an unavailable binary dependency can prevent a method from being used, and an example written for the wrong release can make a correct implementation appear broken. Numerical research and software delivery are coupled.

This lesson is a tour of the engineering contracts in the repository, not a request to compile or install it. The build configurations and test sources described here were inspected read-only. No chemistry package builds, installations, or scientific tests were executed for the course.

## 1. Read the repository as a system of responsibilities

The top-level directories divide the work into recognizable responsibilities:

| Repository area | Responsibility in the product |
|---|---|
| `cpp` | Native data structures, numerical chemistry algorithms, utilities, public headers, and native tests. |
| `python` | Python packaging and bindings, quantum algorithms, plugin adapters, data/remote/UI infrastructure, and Python tests. |
| `external/macis` | Bundled many-electron numerical machinery with its own dependencies, examples, tests, and license. |
| `docs` | User concepts, API documentation, tutorials, references, example source, and figure-generation material. |
| `examples` | End-to-end notebooks, interoperability examples, input data, and shared helpers. |
| `copilot-plugins` | Installable assistant guidance and MCP server configuration. |
| `.github` | GitHub automation, ownership and issue/contribution infrastructure, and development guidance. |
| `.pipelines` | Platform-specific build/test/package scripts and the wheel-release pipeline. |
| `.devcontainer` | A reproducible development-environment recipe and setup scripts. |
| `vcpkg-overlay` and vcpkg manifests | Native dependency resolution and platform-specific dependency adjustments. |

This map is a guide to responsibility, not an assertion that each folder can be released independently or that a class appearing in a public header has a concrete algorithm behind it. Earlier lessons distinguished abstract interfaces from implemented capabilities, notably for effective-Hamiltonian downfolding.

The public C++ headers form the supported interface. Internal implementation headers beneath the source tree are a different boundary. The [C++ CMake configuration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/cpp/CMakeLists.txt) explicitly makes those internal headers available to the library itself without installing them as the public API.

## 2. Why C++, Python, and Q# all appear

C++ is used for numerical data structures and demanding classical kernels. Python makes it convenient to compose workflows, integrate community packages, analyze results, and implement orchestration. Q# expresses quantum operations and interacts with the broader QDK compiler, simulator, and resource tooling.

These are engineering roles, not a division into classical physics and quantum physics. The C++ and Python chemistry calculations solve quantum-mechanical models on ordinary computers. Q# circuit descriptions are also often compiled or simulated on ordinary computers during development.

The [Python build](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/CMakeLists.txt) creates a compiled `_core` extension using pybind11. It includes bindings for structures, bases, orbitals, configurations, wavefunctions, Hamiltonians, symmetry data, algorithm interfaces, derivatives, constants, and numerical utilities.

**pybind11** is the bridge that makes C++ classes and functions callable from Python. It manages conversions and object lifetimes; it is not itself an electronic-structure method. Errors can occur at this boundary if shapes, numerical types, ownership, or overload selection are misunderstood.

A **type stub** describes an interface to Python tools without performing the operation. The project supplies/generated stubs for compiled classes and registry-driven creation so an editor can suggest valid operations and settings. Stubs improve discoverability and catch some mistakes early, but they cannot prove that a given active space is scientifically appropriate or that a numerical algorithm will converge.

## 3. The numerical dependency stack has distinct scientific jobs

The package does not reimplement every mathematical primitive. It integrates specialized libraries:

| Dependency or subsystem | Why it exists |
|---|---|
| Eigen and BLAS/LAPACK families | Matrix operations, factorizations, and eigenvalue problems used throughout electronic structure. |
| Libint | Gaussian overlap, kinetic, attraction, and electron-repulsion integral machinery. |
| Libecpint | Effective-core-potential integral evaluation. |
| GauXC and functional kernels | Numerical integration and exchange-correlation contributions in native DFT and related basis evaluation. |
| MACIS | Configuration-interaction and selected-CI machinery used by the native many-electron adapters. |
| HDF5 and JSON libraries | Structured scientific data storage and transfer. |
| pybind11 | Language interoperability for the compiled core. |
| QDK/Q# libraries | Quantum-language compilation, standard operations, simulation and resource-estimation infrastructure. |

**BLAS**, Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms, supplies building-block vector and matrix operations. **LAPACK**, Linear Algebra Package, supplies routines such as solving systems and eigenproblems. A faster implementation can change performance without changing the mathematical task, although floating-point ordering and backend details can affect numerical reproducibility.

The build has to make these components agree on conventions such as integer widths, calling conventions, precision, and linked runtime libraries. A **calling convention** is the low-level agreement for how a compiled function receives arguments and returns results. This is why a dependency mismatch can be more serious than a missing Python import.

For native exchange-correlation evaluation, our traced source uses ExchCXX built-in functional kernels through GauXC. Broad documentation credits Libxc in the ecosystem, but that does not mean every native DFT call invokes Libxc. Likewise, the presence of GPU-capable GauXC code does not mean an arbitrary installed wheel is GPU-enabled.

The [MACIS source package](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/external/macis/README.md) includes its own broader numerical infrastructure, including sparse and iterative-solver support. Its standalone capabilities and defaults should not be confused with the narrower way QDK Chemistry configures and calls it. In the inspected C++ build, the bundled MACIS configuration disables its own Python interface, standalone examples, and MPI integration when that dependency is built through this path. Its source can contain capabilities that are not exposed by the installed QDK interface.

## 4. A build turns source and dependencies into compatible artifacts

A **compiler** translates source code into machine code. A **linker** combines compiled objects with the libraries they call. A **build system** decides what to compile, in which order, with which options, and when a changed input requires rebuilding.

QDK Chemistry uses CMake to describe the native build. CMake can generate work for a build executor such as Ninja. The C++ project requires C++20 and creates the chemistry library and its exported `qdk::chemistry` target.

Python packaging uses scikit-build-core, which connects Python package building to CMake. The [package manifest](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/pyproject.toml) declares the build dependencies, runtime dependencies, optional extras, command entry points, and packaging configuration.

The Python CMake flow first tries to find a compatible installed native chemistry library. If it does not find one, it can build the native source as a subproject. If it does use a preinstalled library, it still must include the chemistry resource files in the Python distribution. The build explicitly checks for those resources instead of shipping a binary that later cannot find its basis data.

This illustrates the difference between a compiled program and a usable package. Basis archives, configuration data, Python modules, quantum source files, and compiled components all have to arrive in compatible locations.

**FetchContent** can obtain missing build dependencies. Some dependencies are identified through pinned manifests or versions; not every configured fetch is an immutable commit. For example, the inspected linear-algebra CMake-module fetch follows its `main` branch. A reproducible engineering record should therefore include the actual resolved dependency revisions, not assume the top-level source revision alone fixes every external input.

The [vcpkg manifest](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/vcpkg.json) declares native packages such as Eigen, HDF5 C++ support, Boost components, test libraries, JSON, logging/formatting libraries, and OpenBLAS. The [vcpkg configuration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/vcpkg-configuration.json) pins a registry baseline and includes overlay ports. An **overlay port** overrides or adapts how a dependency is built; it is not a new chemistry algorithm. The included libaec and OpenBLAS overlays address dependency delivery rather than molecular modeling.

## 5. Build options are capabilities, not universal runtime promises

The native configuration exposes choices for coverage instrumentation, GPU acceleration, MPI integration, logging, resource locations, and OpenMP. Several are off by default.

**OpenMP** coordinates shared-memory work across threads within a machine. **MPI**, Message Passing Interface, coordinates work among processes, potentially on different machines. These mechanisms do not automatically parallelize every algorithm or make every combination supported.

The inspected configuration disables OpenMP on Windows and under particular Apple compiler conditions. It also checks microarchitecture consistency when using an externally installed MACIS library. **Microarchitecture** refers to CPU instruction capabilities: a binary optimized for instructions unavailable on another machine can fail there.

GPU acceleration requires the relevant build and dependencies, and it applies only to paths implemented to use it. It does not turn a classical simulator into a quantum processor. Conversely, a future quantum resource estimate does not describe the memory needed to compile C++ or run classical preprocessing.

An **application binary interface**, or ABI, is the low-level compatibility agreement between compiled components. Compiler/runtime differences, incompatible libraries, or incorrect architecture targeting can break that agreement even if all source code is individually valid.

These platform details are part of why the project publishes prebuilt distributions: most users should not have to solve the entire native dependency problem merely to try the chemistry interface.

## 6. Installation and development are different use cases

A **wheel** is a built Python distribution designed for a particular supported environment. A compatible wheel avoids compiling the package from source on the user machine. The [installation guide](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/INSTALL.md) describes published platform families, Python requirements, and native runtime prerequisites.

Optional **extras** select additional dependency groups. The minimal chemistry package is different from installing plugin, Qiskit, OpenFermion, network-graph, notebook, MCP, Discovery, documentation, testing, or resource-estimation support. `[all]` is a convenience union subject to platform/version markers, not a promise that unsupported dependencies magically become available.

Native Windows lacks the packaged PySCF dependency in this setup. Windows ARM64 has additional exclusions for dependencies without suitable wheels. The core native methods remain a different capability from those optional integrations. WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, uses the Linux environment and is often the route when a needed plugin is not available natively.

The installed package version and example source must match. A notebook from a moving development branch can refer to APIs not present in the latest published wheel. Checking out source corresponding to the actual installed release is part of reproducibility, not unnecessary ceremony.

For development, the [.devcontainer recipe](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.devcontainer/devcontainer.json) describes an environment with native/Python tooling and editor configuration. A **development container** packages an environment recipe so contributors can start from similar dependencies. It reduces setup differences; it does not make dependency downloads instantaneous or replace version records and tests.

An editable Python installation can reflect changes to Python files promptly, while changes to C++ or pybind11 code still require the relevant rebuild. Recompiling every dependency after every Python edit would waste time; skipping a necessary native rebuild would test old code instead of the change under discussion.

## 7. Compilation has its own resource-estimation problem

Native scientific C++ builds can use substantial memory per concurrent compilation job. Increasing parallel jobs because many CPU cores are available can exhaust RAM rather than make the build faster.

The repository includes [memory-aware build guidance](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.github/skills/memory-aware-build/SKILL.md). Its conservative policy budgets roughly eight gigabytes of available RAM per concurrent compile job, limits parallelism by both CPU count and memory, and falls back to one job when memory information is unavailable.

For an illustrative machine with 32 GB available and sixteen logical CPUs, that rule chooses at most four compile jobs. This is development guidance, not a universal measured peak-memory theorem for every translation unit.

The selected job count is supplied through `CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL`, including for native builds triggered indirectly by Python packaging. An out-of-memory failure calls for less parallelism and diagnosis, not increasingly aggressive job counts.

These costs belong to the software-development and classical-compute budget. They are separate from the logical and physical quantum resource estimates in Lessons 27–29.

## 8. Tests need to cover scientific contracts as well as software syntax

A **unit test** examines a focused operation. An **integration test** checks that multiple components work together. A **regression test** protects behavior that previously worked or reproduces a previously identified failure. A **reference test** compares against a trusted numerical result for a specified model.

All are useful here. We need tests that a matrix has the right dimensions, but also that its index convention and energy contraction are correct. We need serialization round trips, but also preservation of spin blocks and core constants. We need a circuit to compile, but also to prepare the intended state and apply the intended phase under the relevant ordering convention.

The C++ and Python suites cover their respective boundaries, with native GoogleTest/CTest infrastructure, Python pytest, and separate bundled-dependency tests where enabled. Optional integrations and platform-specific functionality can be skipped when dependencies are absent. A skipped capability is not a passing scientific demonstration.

Numerical assertions need meaningful tolerances. Floating-point operations can differ slightly across platforms. Stochastic quantum sampling can fluctuate. A tight golden number can be useful for a fixed reference environment but misleading if presented as a universal invariant across different solver versions.

That is why tutorial verification distinguishes portable scientific invariants from version-specific numerical snapshots. The [tutorial-compatibility workflow](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.github/workflows/tutorial-compatibility.yaml) installs the specified published tutorial package on several platforms, checks the intended dependency boundary, runs the setup/examples, and enables the full tutorial checks. It does not simply assume that testing current source proves the published tutorial environment works.

**Coverage** measures which code is exercised by tests. High coverage is useful but does not prove that assertions capture the correct physics. Conversely, an expensive physical reference test can cover few lines while protecting a crucial numerical contract. A balanced strategy combines small exact cases, property/invariant checks, representative end-to-end references, and explicit unsupported-case tests.

## 9. Automated checks reduce avoidable integration mistakes

**Continuous integration**, or CI, runs automated checks when changes are proposed or merged. It should expose defects before users encounter them.

The [build-and-test workflow](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.github/workflows/build-and-test.yaml) coordinates native dependencies, C++ builds, Python environments, numerical tests, coverage, and documentation for selected platforms. It can also test against a different QDK branch to detect changes across the chemistry/QDK boundary. Dependency caches reduce repeated compilation, but their keys and invalidation rules must follow the inputs that matter.

The [.pre-commit configuration](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.pre-commit-config.yaml) adds a different layer of checks. Formatting tools make code style consistent. Linters identify suspicious patterns and common errors. Type checking catches some incompatible uses without executing the calculation. YAML/JSON checks protect machine-readable configuration. Other checks look for accidental private keys, missing license headers, version misalignment, or missing type stubs.

These tools are complementary. A formatter cannot validate a spin convention. A type checker cannot prove a Trotter approximation meets an energy target. Secret scanning is not a complete security assessment. They reduce specific kinds of mistakes so review effort can focus more effectively on scientific and architectural correctness.

The separate [pre-commit workflow](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.github/workflows/precommit.yaml) runs the configured checks in automation. Local auto-fixing tools can modify files, so a read-only investigation should not invoke them on someone else worktree simply to inspect compliance.

## 10. Documentation is a built and versioned product

The documentation combines several sources. Public C++ comments feed Doxygen. Python docstrings and package interfaces feed Sphinx. Breathe bridges Doxygen output into the Sphinx site. Graphviz renders certain diagrams. Tutorial pages include selected portions of executable example files, so the explanation and the code can share a source.

The [documentation build guide](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/README.md) describes the sequence, including two Sphinx passes for generated stubs and references. Warnings are treated as failures by the documented build path. A broken reference or omitted API page is therefore part of the delivery surface, not only a cosmetic issue.

On Windows, the Makefile assumes tools and a shell that are not native PowerShell behavior. The documented alternative invokes the underlying tools in order. Platform-specific instructions are necessary because a correct build recipe for one shell can be invalid in another.

Figures also have provenance. Some are generated from mathematical or molecular data; others are maintained screenshots. The figure sources and maintenance instructions help contributors know which artifact to regenerate rather than hand-editing the wrong output. A diagram explaining a workflow should remain consistent with the current executable contracts, not just look plausible.

The examples directory is a separate educational and integration surface. It contains helper modules and data needed by the notebooks, so copying one notebook without its companions may fail. The [example-packaging workflow](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.github/workflows/package-examples.yaml) creates a version-associated archive for release distribution.

## 11. Release engineering turns a tested revision into something users can install

The [wheel pipeline](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/.pipelines/python-wheels.yaml) describes builds across operating systems, architectures, and Python versions. It coordinates dependency builds, wheel creation, repair/packaging steps, tests, and a separately controlled publishing path. Its publishing parameter is not enabled merely because a nightly build ran successfully.

**Wheel repair** in this context means arranging native shared-library dependencies so the wheel is suitable for its target platform. It does not mean fixing a scientific algorithm after publication. Toolchain and installation scripts encode platform-specific details that a pure-Python package might not need.

Version information comes from the repository `VERSION` file, with corresponding package and native configuration. The [Python metadata helper](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/_dev_version.py) can append `+local` to untagged source builds; a matching release tag or explicit release-build path has different behavior. This helps distinguish a development checkout from a clean published version.

Release notes, the changelog, and schema migration documentation communicate changes to users. A successful release process must consider whether saved artifacts remain loadable, whether examples still match their environment, whether optional dependencies changed support, and whether defaults alter scientific or numerical behavior.

That is a broader definition of compatibility than keeping one function name unchanged.

## 12. Logging, telemetry, support, and licensing are explicit responsibilities

**Logging** records information useful for understanding a local execution, such as progress, warnings, errors, or detailed traces. Native logging has configurable severity levels and build options. Excessively detailed logs can be expensive or noisy; missing error context makes scientific failures hard to diagnose.

**Telemetry** sends selected usage/performance information to an external collection system. The [Python telemetry implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/telemetry.py) batches metrics, and [event definitions](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/utils/telemetry_events.py) include import/use events, algorithm identity, durations, outcomes, and bucketed basis-size information.

The enabled state follows environment overrides; absent an override, development/local-version markers disable the inspected default path, while ordinary stable builds enable it. Users can disable it by setting `QSHARP_PYTHON_TELEMETRY` to `false`, `0`, `none`, or `disabled` before importing. Describing this mechanism is not a reason to send any telemetry during a read-only course investigation. The existence of metric code should also not be generalized into an unsupported promise about every external dependency policy.

The [security policy](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/SECURITY.md) directs vulnerability reports through the designated private reporting channel rather than public issues. It also warns against unpickling untrusted data and recommends the explicit JSON/HDF5 persistence interfaces. Supporting Python pickle for internal use is not permission to deserialize arbitrary files from strangers.

The [support policy](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/SUPPORT.md) points users to repository issues and discussions. That is not the same as promising a commercial support agreement or service-level guarantee. Contribution guidance includes a contributor license agreement process and a code of conduct.

The top-level project is [MIT-licensed](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/LICENSE.txt). Bundled and external dependencies have their own licenses and notices; MACIS, for example, documents its own modified BSD terms. A top-level license does not erase dependency obligations or grant trademark endorsement. Scientific publications also need appropriate citations for the numerical methods and data sources actually used.

## 13. The engineering definition of a trustworthy handoff

A scientific feature is not complete merely because an algorithm produces an attractive number on one developer machine. It needs a clear interface, correct representation conversions, documented assumptions, meaningful failure behavior, suitable numerical checks, installable dependencies, compatible serialization, usable examples, and an honest release/support story.

These responsibilities explain why this repository contains build scripts, generated bindings, test data, diagrams, plugin configuration, migration tools, and release workflows alongside electronic-structure kernels and quantum algorithms. They are the mechanisms that make the scientific work reusable by another person and another team.

The final lesson brings these responsibilities back to one complete scientific and engineering review: what we can claim about a result, what we must still measure, and how each stage affects the others.
lessons.caveats: Read-only build/configuration/test-source study at97a3ff4f, not a build or validation run of QDK Chemistry. Optional features/defaults/platform restrictions are revision-specific. Native CMake disables bundled MACIS MPI/Python/examples on inspected path; broad standalone MACIS capabilities do not imply wrapper support. Native GauXC path uses ExchCXX builtins per prior evidence. Build fetches are not all immutable revisions. Memory8GB/job is repo guidance, not universal measured peak. CI coverage does not establish scientific truth or all-platform dependency availability. Stable telemetry default versus dev/local marker and explicit override distinguished; no telemetry was intentionally sent for this course. Original MIT license does not relicense dependencies or provide trademark endorsement.

lessons.body:
# Lesson 34 — A complete scientific and engineering review

## The final deliverable is an argument supported by artifacts

Imagine presenting our work to a joint review with chemists, numerical-method developers, quantum-algorithm researchers, compiler engineers, resource-estimation specialists, and hardware/error-correction model owners.

The opening claim is not simply that we generated a circuit. It is that a specified computational workflow can answer a specified question, to a stated standard, with understood limitations and conditional costs. Every part of that claim needs evidence from a different stage.

This final lesson conducts that review. We will use the small stretched-nitrogen teaching problem to make the handoffs concrete, then explain how the conclusions change for a scientifically ambitious problem. The [repository overview](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/README.md) describes an end-to-end toolkit; our job is to understand what the ends and the connections actually mean.

No new chemistry calculation, simulation, or physical resource estimate is performed in this capstone. Recorded examples remain evidence about their stated model and revision, while the decision exercises below are illustrative.

## 1. State the scientific question before choosing the algorithm

For the teaching case, we ask for a fixed-geometry ground-state energy of neutral singlet nitrogen at 1.85 Å. We use the finite orbital representation and selected active-space model described by the [ground-state tutorial](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/tutorials/ground_state_molecular_energies_with_qpe/index.rst).

This is not a complete simulation of industrial ammonia production. It is not a free energy at a specified temperature, a chemical reaction rate, or an assertion that nitrogen needs a quantum computer. A deliberately tractable problem lets us compare transformations and algorithms against a classical reference.

A scientifically ambitious application would need a different first page: the real decision to be informed, the chemical species and environment, required comparisons, necessary accuracy, and a competitive classical baseline. Quantum computing is a candidate method, not the definition of the problem.

The first review gate is therefore a problem statement that distinguishes the physical system, the chosen mathematical model, and the quantity being calculated. An energy target without a reference and scope is incomplete.

## 2. Build an input record another team can interpret

The initial artifact is the molecular structure, with explicit elements, coordinates, and units. Charge and spin multiplicity are supplied separately. The basis defines the available one-electron functions; any effective core potential defines which electrons are explicitly represented and changes the Hamiltonian accordingly.

For our running N2 geometry, the physical all-electron count is fourteen. The named cc-pVDZ resource supplies 28 spherical atomic basis functions for the two atoms before any numerical rank reduction. A restricted reference has seven doubly occupied spatial orbitals, but that description does not assert that a correlated ground state remains a single determinant.

The separate [nitrogen notebook](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/qpe_stretched_n2.ipynb) uses 1.270025 Å. It is a useful example of additional techniques, including resource estimation, but its numerical results cannot be silently appended to the 1.85 Å tutorial record.

The input review checks more than whether a file loads. Did the XYZ ångström values become bohr correctly? Are electron count and multiplicity consistent? Are basis functions spherical or Cartesian along a supported conversion path? Are ECP effective charges separate from physical nuclear charges? Does an orbital guess still refer to the geometry and basis it claims to use?

These checks are inexpensive relative to a large calculation and prevent entire workflows from answering the wrong question.

## 3. Generate a classical starting point—and record what converged

The native `scf_solver` implementation can produce a Hartree–Fock or supported Kohn–Sham starting solution. A PySCF plugin can provide another implementation with its own capabilities and numerical semantics.

The selected approximation, basis, orbital restrictions, initial guess, and numerical convergence strategy must be recorded separately. Increasing the iteration limit does not turn Hartree–Fock into a correlated method. Choosing a larger basis does not remove the single-determinant restriction. Switching numerical backends does not guarantee identical integration grids or stopping criteria.

The output is an energy and a wavefunction carrying orbitals, not merely a number. The next teams need coefficients, orbital identities, occupations, and the associated basis.

The second review gate asks whether the calculation actually converged and whether the resulting stationary solution is appropriate. Convergence can lead to an unstable or undesired solution. Stability analysis and reoptimization can change the outcome; a transition from restricted to unrestricted orbitals must be visible in the record. Equal alpha and beta counts do not alone certify total-spin purity.

If we optimize geometry rather than hold it fixed, that is a distinct scientific task requiring derivatives and an optimizer. A small gradient does not establish whether the stationary point is a minimum or a transition-state saddle. Nor does an optimizer automatically retain the desired electronic state along a path.

## 4. Reduce the problem without hiding what was excluded

The full orbital basis can be too expensive for a complete many-electron treatment. We therefore choose a correlated representation and, often, an active space.

An active space specifies which orbitals can change occupation and how many electrons participate explicitly in that many-electron calculation. Inactive electrons are not simply erased: their influence enters effective one-electron terms and an energy constant. Empty orbitals outside the selected space cannot contribute excitations in the same way as retained orbitals.

Methods offered by the repository include valence-based and occupation-based selection, entropy-based autoCAS variants, and optional AVAS through PySCF. Each uses a different kind of evidence. Entropy selection requires suitable correlated-state information; the selector does not magically compute an otherwise intractable exact full wavefunction first.

Orbital localization and natural-orbital methods change the representation in which selection and correlation are expressed. This can improve interpretability or make an approximation more compact, but a transformation of an orbital container is not automatically a transformation of every correlated coefficient. The actual localizer output contract must be respected.

A six-electron, six-spatial-orbital space with three alpha and three beta electrons has 400 determinants in that fixed-spin-projection basis before further reductions. This makes a useful small reference problem. Choosing it is still a model decision, not proof that every chemically important effect lies inside those six orbitals.

The model-reduction review therefore needs both cost and error evidence. Which physics motivated the selected space? What happens when it is enlarged? Are we following orbital character consistently along changed geometries? Does the comparison use the same physical conditions and energy reference?

A smaller qubit count is not sufficient justification if the reduced model no longer answers the scientific question.

## 5. Solve a tractable reference and choose an affordable trial state

For a small selected space, `macis_cas` supplies a complete-active-space CI reference up to its numerical tolerances. `macis_asci` selects important determinants and can produce a useful approximation for larger spaces. Projected multi-configuration calculation optimizes coefficients in a supplied determinant set.

These are distinct tasks. Selecting the two largest coefficients and renormalizing them is not generally the same as solving again in that two-determinant subspace. The latter can improve the coefficients within the chosen support without restoring omitted configurations.

The reference wavefunction is useful for scientific interpretation and, in a small demonstration, for checking the quantum algorithm. The trial wavefunction is the state we choose to load into the quantum circuit. A compact trial can save preparation cost while reducing overlap with the target state.

For an ideal coherent energy-phase measurement, the target eigenstate weight helps determine the chance of observing its phase. That familiar statement does not automatically apply to this repository fresh-state-per-bit iterative implementation as a complete-run success law. Actual scheduling and aggregation matter.

The trial-state review asks for the preparation method, occupied-mode order, normalization, signs/phases, any truncation, and evidence for target-state overlap or success. A cheap preparation circuit with essentially no useful target overlap may make the total calculation more expensive than a larger preparation.

State-preparation methods also have different purposes. A clean molecular trial-state loader and a coefficient/index loader with entangled helper registers for block encoding are not interchangeable just because both are called state preparation.

## 6. Construct and compress the Hamiltonian carefully

The molecular Hamiltonian must agree with the chosen orbital space and electron model. Its integral convention, spin blocks, storage form, and constant-energy contribution travel with it.

Canonical four-center storage, Cholesky factors, double-factorized representations, and sparse model containers have different access and reconstruction costs. Thresholded factorization changes the represented numerical operator; it is not merely a different file format. A threshold on an integral residual does not automatically certify an energy error of the same magnitude.

The third review gate checks numerical equivalence where equivalence is intended, and quantified approximation where terms or factors have been discarded. A consumer that reconstructs a full tensor can remove the memory advantage of compact storage. A specialized algorithm may need exactly the factorization or positivity assumptions that its interface expects.

Do not fill an absent implementation with a conceptual promise. At this source revision, effective-Hamiltonian downfolding has interface infrastructure but no concrete registered implementation in the inspected factory. Its theory can explain an important research direction, but the course should not present that direction as a shipped end-to-end routine.

Likewise, MCSCF is accessed through the supported PySCF integration rather than a universally available native orbital optimizer. Native MP2 amplitudes and optional CCSD results have container and downstream-access limitations. Choosing a method includes choosing a compatible consumer of its output.

## 7. Translate the model into a compatible quantum workload

Fermion-to-qubit mapping translates creation/annihilation algebra into qubit operators. Jordan–Wigner, Bravyi–Kitaev, parity-related representations, and custom mappings differ in what the qubits and operator strings mean.

The initial state, Hamiltonian, observables, register ordering, and any symmetry reduction must use compatible conventions. Equal width does not prove compatibility. Renaming the encoding field does not perform the required state transformation. Permuting wires does not generally implement every fermionic remapping.

Symmetry can reduce storage or the quantum register, but those are different operations. The specialized tapering path in this revision should not be advertised as a general automatic point-group or Clifford-symmetry compiler. Fixing electron parities also does not uniquely fix exact electron number.

The quantum-model review checks the sector, transformation, phase conventions, and any auxiliary codespace. A lowest eigenvalue in the wrong sector is still the wrong scientific answer.

The [quickstart](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/docs/source/_static/examples/python/quickstart.py) illustrates a concrete handoff from selected orbitals and a sparse trial state to qubit mapping and sampled expectation. It is one branch through the library, not a substitute for inspecting compatibility in every alternative route.

## 8. Choose the algorithm according to the quantity and precision required

The major quantum routes answer related but different questions:

| Route | What it aims to obtain | Main cost and interpretation concerns |
|---|---|---|
| Pauli expectation sampling | Mean value of an observable in the prepared state | Group compatibility, shot allocation, covariance, state-preparation repetitions, and sampling uncertainty. |
| Standard phase estimation | Eigenphase information from a coherent phase-register circuit | Controlled evolution, phase-register size, state overlap, finite resolution, aliases and decoding. |
| Iterative phase estimation | Phase bits through repeated controlled-operation circuits and feedback | Longest powers, per-bit state preparation, majority aggregation, and implementation-specific success semantics. |
| Unary/SOSSA route | Phase information through its specialized block/walk construction | Correct normalization/shift, required operation capabilities, simulator restrictions and specialized decoding. |
| Hadamard tests | Real or imaginary parts of a controlled-unitary overlap | Controlled phase conventions, repeated measurements, available adjoints and register layout. |
| Time-dependent simulation | Observable responses under a specified driven Hamiltonian | Time discretization, supported drive model, accumulated circuit prefixes and fresh measurements. |

Hamiltonian time evolution can be constructed with product formulas, randomized approaches, or block-encoding/walk techniques. Trotter error, randomized-channel guarantees, coherent fixed-circuit error, and finite factorization error are not the same kind of statement. Comparing algorithms requires matching the scientific model, target accuracy, success criterion, and full workload scope.

A qubitized walk avoids a particular Trotter approximation for its ideal represented operator, but it does not eliminate imperfect input models, state preparation, factorization thresholds, rotation synthesis, or measurement limitations.

Amplitude amplification can improve an ideal good-subspace probability using repeated reflections. It does not supply a free exact ground-state oracle. The actual marking circuit, phase resolution, uncomputation, and repeated preparation costs must be included. Off-grid cleanup limitations matter to whether the ideal two-dimensional amplification picture applies at all.

## 9. Keep an energy and error ledger

A final energy should be accompanied by a ledger explaining how it was reconstructed:

| Artifact or stage | Quantity to track |
|---|---|
| Fixed nuclei | Nuclear or effective core–core repulsion under the selected model. |
| Active-space construction | Constant core/inactive contribution and active electronic terms. |
| Ordinary molecular Pauli mapping | Mapped operator energy, with the molecular core contribution generally retained separately on this route. |
| SOS representation | Its own normalization and energy-shift convention, which can already include the molecular core contribution. |
| Trial-state expectation | Energy of the prepared state, not automatically an exact ground-state eigenvalue. |
| Phase decoding | Phase sign, time/scale, periodic branch, and shift used to turn phase information into energy. |
| Reported total | The intended model quantity with every required constant included exactly once. |

The table is a review aid, not an instruction to add the core energy indiscriminately. The ordinary Pauli and SOS paths have different conventions. A total-energy decoder followed by a second core-energy addition gives a wrong but potentially plausible answer.

We also distinguish four words that are often used too loosely. **Accuracy** is closeness to a specified reference. **Precision** concerns the spread of repeated results. **Resolution** describes distinguishable numerical intervals. **Uncertainty** expresses what values remain plausible under the available evidence and assumptions.

A result printed to twelve decimal places need not be accurate to twelve decimals. A stable but incomplete active-space model can be highly repeatable and scientifically biased. A fine phase grid does not remove finite sampling or a wrong phase branch.

The error ledger should include physical-model choices, basis/ECP approximation, active-space and correlation omissions, numerical convergence and factorization, state-preparation effects, Hamiltonian simulation/synthesis, phase resolution, statistical sampling, and hardware failure assumptions. Deterministic error bounds, variances, and probabilities cannot be added indiscriminately because their units and meanings differ.

The current expectation-estimator variance field omits within-group covariance. It is not automatically a certified uncertainty interval. The iterative QPE output does not preserve every histogram and decoder choice. These limits motivate preserving additional records where an application needs defensible statistical conclusions.

## 10. Count the complete calculation before estimating a machine

A resource estimate is conditional on the workload supplied. Estimating one largest QPE iteration can be useful for comparing components, but it is not the total cost of every bit, shot, repetition, and geometry in a campaign.

The nitrogen resource notebook explicitly selects a largest iteration circuit. The review must identify what is excluded before anyone interprets its table as the price of answering the chemistry question.

Logical accounting tracks problem qubits, helper registers, peak live allocation, gate types, dependencies/depth, measurements, classical feedback, and repeated state preparation. Sequential peak widths should not simply be added together, while operation counts and repetitions often must be accumulated. A reused phase-gradient register is not free unless its preparation and ownership are accounted for in the chosen boundary.

The broader QDK estimation tools combine that application with physical-operation and error-correction assumptions. The [Circuit adapter](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/python/src/qdk_chemistry/data/circuit.py) exposes two alternative routes: `estimate()` delegates to QDK counting/estimation facilities, while `get_qre_application()` supplies an application for direct `qdk.qre` studies.

Neither method manufactures a trustworthy overlap estimate, determines the scientific validity of the active space, or infers all omitted workflow repetitions. Those are application inputs.

## 11. Make the partner-team contracts explicit

Functional responsibilities help prevent a problem from disappearing between teams. They are not a claim about any particular corporate organizational chart.

| Functional workstream | Supplies | Needs from the rest of the workflow |
|---|---|---|
| Application and chemistry | Scientific objective, model, tolerances, meaningful comparisons and interpretation | A real customer/scientific decision and suitable reference evidence. |
| Classical numerical methods | Orbitals, integrals, correlated approximations, derivatives and reduced models | Accurate structures, conventions, compute/memory budgets and required outputs. |
| Quantum algorithms | Compatible state loading, operator constructions, measurement/phase procedures and success assumptions | A precise model, usable trial state and error budget. |
| Compiler and execution | Supported quantum-program representations, gate transformations, simulation/execution semantics | Valid circuits, correct control/phase behavior and declared target capability. |
| Error-correction specialists | Code and logical-operation models, distance/error assumptions, factory constructions | Logical workload and required reliability. |
| Hardware-model specialists | Physical operation times, errors, connectivity and supported instruction assumptions | A stated architecture and evidence for parameter values. |
| Resource estimation | Consistent enumeration and comparison of physical space/time alternatives | Compatible application, hardware, QEC, synthesis and failure-budget inputs. |
| Platform and reliability | Packaging, jobs, storage, provenance, interfaces and diagnostics | Supported dependencies, typed contracts and deployment/permission requirements. |

The resource-estimation and error-correction teams are not merely the last box after chemistry. Their results can send us back to improve state preparation, active-space choices, factorization, or precision allocation. Conversely, making a circuit cheaper is not useful if it violates the chemistry accuracy requirement.

A Pareto frontier describes tradeoffs among feasible candidates under the modeled assumptions. It is not a list of devices known to exist, a delivery date, a bill, or evidence of scientific advantage.

## 12. Operational delivery is another evidence layer

The workflow must retain artifacts and versions, handle optional dependencies, and distinguish newly computed results from cached ones. Remote submission must yield a durable identifier, meaningful status, and retrievable output. A finished process with missing output is not a complete handoff.

The user interfaces from Lesson 32 can lower the effort needed to operate this process, but they must not hide units, settings, existing-output decisions, or submitted-job status. Visualizing orbitals and entanglement can improve understanding; a visualization cannot validate information absent from the underlying wavefunction.

Build and release checks from Lesson 33 ensure that another environment can install and use the package. Published wheels, supported plugins, source-main behavior, and documentation versions are different compatibility boundaries. A source capability unavailable in a particular wheel/platform should be reported as unavailable, not worked around by inventing output.

The final operational record should make it possible to rerun or diagnose the study without relying on a scientist memory of a notebook session. That includes scientific configuration, code and dependency versions, hashes and saved payloads, random seeds where relevant, convergence/status information, and the parameters used to produce visual or resource reports.

## 13. The alternative examples are part of the system, not distractions

A complete understanding of the repository also includes paths that do not begin with our nitrogen geometry:

- The para-benzyne quickstart illustrates sparse-state preparation and sampled energy comparison.
- Lattice models such as Hubbard, PPP, Ising, and Heisenberg can enter at a model-Hamiltonian stage, bypassing molecular basis/integral preprocessing under different physical assumptions.
- The extended-Hubbard notebook connects a molecularly motivated problem to a reduced model; it does not establish that every reduced model is quantitatively ab initio.
- Driven-evolution examples study time-dependent observable behavior rather than a single static ground-state energy.
- Qiskit, OpenFermion, PennyLane, and RDKit interoperability examples illustrate representation or workflow boundaries, not interchangeable capabilities without conversion checks.
- C++ and Python language examples show different user-facing routes through the native library and bindings.
- Remote/backend and assistant examples explain operation and artifact management, rather than a new electronic-structure approximation.

The [examples overview](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry/blob/97a3ff4f/examples/README.md) identifies their dependencies and companion files. Their results belong to their own models, geometries, versions, and execution conditions.

## 15. Conduct the final go/no-go review

A useful review separates different kinds of readiness instead of giving the entire project one undifferentiated green light.

**Scientific readiness:** the question matters, the model and comparison are appropriate, and remaining approximation errors are acceptable for the intended decision.

**Algorithmic readiness:** the encodings, state preparation, operator constructions, measurements and decoding are consistent, and success/accuracy assumptions are justified for the actual implementation.

**Engineering readiness:** artifacts can be reconstructed, errors are surfaced, supported environments are known, and the workflow can be repeated and maintained.

**Resource readiness:** the complete workload is counted and compatible physical/QEC models yield a credible feasibility range with sensitivity analysis.

**Practical advantage:** a fair comparison shows a benefit over the relevant classical alternatives at the required quality and full cost. None of the preceding readiness checks alone establishes this strongest claim.

For a teaching benchmark, successfully reproducing the matching classical selected-space result is already valuable. It exercises the entire translation and makes errors visible. For a proposed useful quantum application, that is a beginning rather than the final argument.

If resources are too large, we can investigate better representations or algorithms, but must preserve scientific validity. If model error dominates, a smaller quantum-circuit approximation error may be irrelevant. If trial-state success is poorly understood, a precise per-circuit resource count may still leave the full workload unknown. If an interface exists without an implementation, the honest outcome is a development need, not a fabricated calculation.

The team work is therefore a feedback loop: choose a meaningful question, build and validate a model, prepare and execute a compatible computation, interpret the evidence, estimate its complete cost, and revise the limiting stage. The repository gives us interoperable tools for that loop. Engineering judgment consists of knowing what each tool actually contributes—and what responsibility remains outside it.
